requirements.text: | 640×350 | 16 | the EGA floor: guaranteed-safe **default**; ties to the [MicroANSI](3.3-microansi-fonts.md) "640x350 EGA" font record |

requirements.heading: Resolution tiers as shipped
requirements.text: | 1024×768 | 16 / 256 | the ceiling actually exposed |

requirements.heading: Resolution tiers as shipped
requirements.text:
- **Ceiling: 1024×768 at 256 colors.** The 2.0 and 2.30 manuals contain no 15/16/24-bit mode anywhere - no "32,768", "65,536", or "16 million color" text exists in either manual - and every entry in the readable 2.0 video-mode database is 16 or 256 colors at ≤ 1024×768 (RIPTERM.DOC mode dialog; `RIPTERM.VID`). Direct-RGB mode therefore **always** resolved to closest-match palette colors on the shipping DOS clients; no shipped configuration rendered true RGB.
- **1280×1024 was prepared but never exposed:** the [MicroANSI container](3.3-microansi-fonts.md#resolution-directory-60-byte-records) carries a complete 1280×1024 terminal-font set, the [widget images](3.5-ui-resources.md#img-widget-images---format-decoded) include a 1280×1024 tier, and the 2.30 `RIPTERM.EXE` contains mode-identifier strings up to `VESA1280x1024X`/`Y`/`YY` - but no shipped video-mode database entry reaches past 1024×768 and no manual mentions the resolution as selectable. _(Whether some undocumented path could activate it is unverified.)_
- Driver plumbing (immaterial to reimplementation, noted for provenance): the mode list was data-driven from a per-video-card database, `RIPTERM.VID` - plain text in 2.0 (`TOTAL=117` entries like `DEV=0x1A22 DESC="VESA Super VGA" HRES=800 VRES=600 COLORS=256 STATUS=-1`), a binary compile in 2.30 covering "over 237 different kinds of video cards" (2.30 RIPTERM.DOC) - with generic VESA Super VGA and 8514/A fallbacks. None of this affects the tier table above.

requirements.heading: Implementation notes for emulators
requirements.text:
- A faithful "2.x terminal" is a palettized 256-color surface at one of the four shipped canvas sizes, defaulting to 640×350×16 EGA; 16-color modes use the desktop-palette semantics, 256-color modes the full drawing palette with the default table.
- Direct-RGB commands must still render in palettized environments via closest-match against the active palette (spec, [Palette Mapping and Direct RGB Mode](../ripscrip/2.0-color-modes-and-palettes.md#palette-mapping-and-direct-rgb-mode)); the default 224-entry cube is designed so the match is a constant-time index computation (`INDEX = 32 + BLUE + GREEN*4 + RED*32`) rather than a search.
- The 16↔256-color duality is why the default palette's first 16 entries exactly match the ANSI text palette: text windows and graphics share one palette, and [CP437 text](3.3-microansi-fonts.md) renders with the same 16 base colors in either depth.
- Color 0 is the screen background everywhere; changing it repaints the whole screen (spec).
- Canvas-size and aspect-ratio policy for modern renderers lives in [version/implementation.md](../../implementation.md), not here.

It also preserves the withdrawal of an earlier claim that RIPtel pie/chord primitives leaked because they flood-filled an assembled boundary. The [2.0](../ripscrip/2.3-shapes-and-fills.md#rip_fill) and [3.0](../../3.0/ripscrip/2.3-shapes-and-fills.md#rip_fill) language entries point here for the separate legacy RIP_FILL discussion.

requirements.heading: §BUG.6 - withdrawn pie/chord flood-leak attribution
requirements.text: An earlier edition adopted RIPlib's `§BUG.6` as proof that original TeleGrafix pie/chord handlers drew an arc plus separate radial lines and then flood-filled the boundary. The original RIPtel driver contradicts that construction: I/i helpers call **GDI Pie**, _ calls **GDI Chord**, and skewed filled curves pass complete contours to **Polygon**. Native traces execute the handlers and capture those calls with borders enabled and disabled; see the [primary-source derivation](../../3.0/research/issue-14-arc-sweeps.md).
requirements.reason: Historical renderer evidence. The current RIP_FILL command entry defines the RIPv3 wire behavior.

requirements.heading: §BUG.6 - withdrawn pie/chord flood-leak attribution
requirements.text: Consequently this record no longer attributes a manual boundary-gap flood leak to those original paths or generalizes it backward to 2.x. This correction does not claim every historical rasterizer free of defects. The actual recovered whole-turn and radial-closure quirks are in the [3.0 angle reference](../../3.0/ripscrip/2.2-curves.md#angle-ordering-and-sweeps), independently of exact pixel coverage.
requirements.reason: Historical renderer evidence. The current RIP_FILL command entry defines the RIPv3 wire behavior.

requirements.heading: RIPlib's patterned flood attribution
requirements.text: RIPlib `§DEAD.7` attributes a solid border-color flood to the original DLL. The verified PC Micro RIPtel 3.1 route dispatches to a bare return. RIPlib's later crosswalk identifies that same inactive route. Its own two-pass fill remains a separate legacy implementation. [Original and RIPlib evidence](../../3.0/research/issue-279-rip-fill-framing.md).
requirements.reason: Historical comparison, cross-reference or descriptive material accompanying the RIP_FILL clarification.

requirements.heading: The seed-stack drop
requirements.text: Documented in full at [1.54](../../1.54/techspecs/2.1-pattern-fill-rasterization.md#fill-styles-and-patterns), with corpus figures and source citations in the [2.0 errata](../ripscrip/errata.md#rip_fill-declared-removed-but-still-implemented): the underlying BGI flood fill queues its seeds on a fixed-capacity stack (492 entries as RIPterm builds it) and **silently drops** seeds once it fills, so a complex region can come back partly unfilled. Artists did not avoid the command despite this - 3,787 `!|F` uses across 78 of the 118 scripts in the RIPtermJS 1.5x corpus.
requirements.reason: Historical renderer evidence. The current RIP_FILL command entry defines the RIPv3 wire behavior.

requirements.heading: Guidance
requirements.text:
- Implement region membership and pattern application independently for a portable legacy flood fill; growable work storage avoids silently dropping seeds. Period reproduction may deliberately retain a specific client's limitations when explicitly identified.
- Use the command-specific [3.0 angle contract](../../3.0/ripscrip/2.2-curves.md#angle-ordering-and-sweeps) for pie/chord empty, full and wrapped cases. Their topology is established by original consumers; the withdrawn manual-flood explanation is not a reason to change their wire semantics.
requirements.reason: Historical renderer evidence. The current RIP_FILL command entry defines the RIPv3 wire behavior.

requirements.heading: Drawing Composition
requirements.text: This page states the RIPscrip 2.x drawing contract inherited by 3.0. It separates geometry, source-color selection and the operation on the destination. The [3.0 drawing delta](../../3.0/techspecs/2.3-drawing-composition.md) applies these rules to POINT and reconstructed skewed contours. RIPscrip 1.54 has a narrower command/mode matrix and is unchanged.

requirements.text: NOT ignores S. In an indexed 16-color example M=0x0F; in a 256-color example M=0xFF. Palette lookup follows the logical indexed-color operation; do not substitute an operation on unrelated host RGBA bytes. RGB drawing applies the same Boolean operations to the resolved color bits; this contract specifies no alpha blending.

requirements.heading: Operations and operands
requirements.text: `RIP_WRITE_MODE` governs PIXEL, standalone line/curve/polygon outlines, region fills and graphics text where their attributes say Write Mode. It is an output rule, independent of the backend API. A color-replacement-only pixel/rectangle/glyph call cannot implement XOR, OR, AND or NOT without additional composition.

requirements.heading: Operations and operands
requirements.text: **Different NOT operation:** bitmap PUT/LOAD commands have their own mode field. Their mode 04 complements the **source image** (`S XOR M`); drawing W04 complements the **destination** (`D XOR M`). For S=0x3C and D=0xA5 with M=0xFF, those are 0xC3 and 0x5A respectively. Global W is not an extra operation to apply after a command's explicit bitmap mode.

requirements.heading: Source selection and gaps
requirements.text: A standalone stroke uses Draw Color on its line-pattern on bits. A transparent line gap contributes nothing; an opaque line gap uses Back Color as S. These gap policies are the documented LINE_STYLE off_draw values 0 and 1. Internal client state bits are not additional protocol parameters. A primitive explicitly limited to solid outlines uses Draw Color throughout its stroke, so the line-gap policy has no effect there.
requirements.reason: Indexed fill, stroke and border fixtures check source selection, contour membership and the order of writes. Mixed-color composition is exercised through the shared surface.

requirements.heading: Source selection and gaps
requirements.text: Region filling uses Fill Color on one bits of the fill pattern and Back Color on zero bits. A zero fill-pattern bit is a background-colored contribution, **not** a transparent line gap. Fill pattern 00 therefore fills with Back Color. Polygon holes, determined by the fill rule, are genuinely outside the fill region and receive no fill contribution.
requirements.reason: Indexed fill, stroke and border fixtures check source selection, contour membership and the order of writes. Mixed-color composition is exercised through the shared surface.

requirements.heading: Filled objects and border order
requirements.text: The protocol defines two **logical** phases: fill the region using current W; then, if N enables the border, stroke the outline using **COPY**. The border uses Draw Color and current line thickness. Polygon-related borders also use the current line pattern; the documented circle/ellipse/pie/rectangle/rounded-rectangle borders are solid. The backend may combine calls only when its result is equivalent to these phases.
requirements.reason: Indexed fill, stroke and border fixtures check source selection, contour membership and the order of writes. Mixed-color composition is exercised through the shared surface.

requirements.heading: Filled objects and border order
requirements.text: A border contribution copies its selected Draw/Back Color over the already-filled destination. It does not apply W again to that pixel. N does not alter the stored W or line/fill style. N0 suppresses the outline, including closing edges and any radial contour segments; it does not change the fill rule or fill operands. BAR is explicitly borderless and is unaffected by N.
requirements.reason: Indexed fill, stroke and border fixtures check source selection, contour membership and the order of writes. Mixed-color composition is exercised through the shared surface.

requirements.heading: Repeated visits and polygon fill
requirements.text: Separate drawing contributions operate sequentially on the latest destination. Two genuine visits by the same standalone XOR stroke restore D; two NOT visits restore D; OR and AND are idempotent for a repeated identical S. Replacing all visits by a single coverage union changes XOR/NOT and is incorrect. Shared endpoints/joins are not automatically two visits merely because two adjacent segment records mention the same vertex; exact join/edge pixel coverage is outside this abstract contract.
requirements.reason: Screen drawing composes against the visible destination. Connected samples cover affine fill and outline, retraced strokes, solid and patterned borders, and the full-pie seam. Native vectors cover the remaining write modes and offscreen drawing.

requirements.heading: Repeated visits and polygon fill
requirements.text: A polygon's repeated traversal instead participates in its specified fill rule. For even-odd filling, two complete coverings produce a hole, three produce an interior. Evaluate that region first and apply its fill operation once; do not emit one fill operation per winding. Its optional border is still COPY, so repeated identical border visits are idempotent. Distinct fill commands, unlike windings within one polygon, are separate sequential operations.
requirements.reason: Indexed fill, stroke and border fixtures check source selection, contour membership and the order of writes. Mixed-color composition is exercised through the shared surface.

requirements.text: | RIPscrip v1.x icon files | `.ICN` | `.MSK` | `.HOT` |

requirements.heading: The extension mapping
requirements.text: | RIPscrip v2.x icon files | `.BMP` | `.BMM` | `.BMH` |

requirements.heading: The extension mapping
requirements.text: The specification records the same rename: "Changed all icon references to the new icon, hot icon, and icon mask extensions (.ICN is now .BMP, .HIC is now .BMH, and .MSK is now .BMM)" (spec revision note v2.A2, [Introduction](../ripscrip/1.0-introduction.md)). Note the manual's `.HOT` vs the published 1.54 specification's `.HIC` for the 1.54 hot-icon extension - see the [icons asset README](../../2.0/assets/icons/README.md#the-2x-icon-taxonomy) for discussion.

requirements.heading: The extension mapping
requirements.text: All three 2.x extensions denote the **same underlying file format**: a Windows 3.x BMP. The extension encodes the file's _role_ (icon, mask, pressed-state), exactly as `.ICN`/`.MSK`/`.HIC` did in 1.54. The client's file dialogs filter on `*.bmp *.bmm *.bmh` (string in `RIPTERM.EXE`, `~/src/rip-tools/artifacts/ripterm-2.30/extracted/`).

requirements.heading: The extension mapping
requirements.text: Icon files of every kind live in the `ICONS\` sub-directory of the RIPterm directory, alongside host-supplied `.JPG` images, `.WAV` sounds, and `.RIP` scripts (RIPTERM.DOC §2.1.4 - see the [connection directory model](4.0-connection-directory-model-delta.md)). On the wire they are referenced by [RIP_BUTTON](../ripscrip/4.3-buttons.md#rip_button) (icon buttons), [RIP_LOAD_ICON / RIP_WRITE_ICON](../ripscrip/9.0-command-reference.md), the `$<FILE.BMP$` [local bitmap playback](../ripscrip/5.3-local-playback.md) prefix, and transferred via [RIP_ENTER_BLOCK_MODE](../ripscrip/5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md) - either as file type 2, "designated for Icon Files only (.BMP, .BMH and .BMM)" (spec v2.A2), or through the batch DYNAMIC modes (file types 4 and 5), whose per-extension routing tables place `BMP`/`BMH`/`BMM` "in proper directory" alongside `RIP`, `JPG` and `GIF`.

requirements.heading: `.BMP` - the icon format as shipped
requirements.text: The specification's Icon/DIB File Format appendix (ALPHA 4 draft §6.1.1 "DIB FILE HEADER", `../text/RIPScrip-2.0-alpha-4.txt` lines 18916-18990; concept-level summary at [content file roles](../ripscrip/6.1-content-file-roles.md)) defines the icon as a Device-Independent Bitmap and walks the `BitmapInfoHeader`, color table, and pixel-block layouts; that page is accurate for everything from the info header onward and is not repeated here. Two corrections/clarifications against the shipped files:

requirements.heading: `.BMP` - the icon format as shipped
requirements.text:
- **Shipped icons are full BMP files, not bare DIBs.** The spec text says the info header is "at the beginning of the file (at offset 0)", but every icon distributed with RIPterm 2.0 and 2.30 begins with the standard 14-byte `BITMAPFILEHEADER` (`BM` magic, u32 file size, u32 reserved, u32 pixel-data offset), with the 40-byte `BITMAPINFOHEADER` at offset 14. Evidence: all 207 preserved 2.x-generation icons ([assets](../../2.0/assets/icons/README.md)) start `42 4D` and carry a valid file header.
- **`biCompression` erratum:** the spec's struct comment reads "1=no compression" while its own body text (correctly) mandates 0 = uncompressed. Every shipped icon has `biCompression = 0`.
requirements.reason: Wire bitmap loads recognize the BMP container and translate the inherited mask extension on lookup.

requirements.heading: `.BMP` - the icon format as shipped
requirements.text: Supported pixel depths are 1/4/8/24 bits per pixel, uncompressed only, bottom-up rows padded to 4-byte boundaries, BGR color order - per the spec appendix. RIPtel 3.1 additionally accepts ordinary 16/32-bit BI_RGB loads; its color-key path has separate depth limitations ([3.0 delta](../../3.0/techspecs/3.0-bitmap-mask-delta.md)). The 2.30 distribution contains 4-bit, 8-bit, and 24-bit icons (e.g. the 36×36 8-bit `RWBTN*` set and the 18×18 24-bit `RWICON10/11` pairs - [inventory](../../2.0/assets/icons/README.md#ripterm-220230-additions-112-files)).

requirements.heading: Observed writer conventions
requirements.text: The icons authored by TeleGrafix's own tooling share a fixed header-field pattern, verified programmatically across all 95 files of the 2.0-era icon set (`~/src/rip-tools/RIPTerm2.0/extracted/ICONS/`, carried unchanged into 2.30):

requirements.heading: Observed writer conventions
requirements.text:
- `biSizeImage = 0`, `biClrUsed = 0`, `biClrImportant = 0`
- `biXPelsPerMeter = biWidth` and `biYPelsPerMeter = biHeight` - the writer takes the spec's own suggestion that these fields "could easily be set to zero, or the width and height of the image" literally
requirements.reason: Observations about period assets and terminology. The v3 bitmap header, explicit masks and hot-image commands have their own requirements.

requirements.heading: Observed writer conventions
requirements.text: Worked example - `BUTTON.BMP` (322 bytes, 22×17, 4-bit; `version/2.0/assets/icons/BUTTON.BMP`):

requirements.heading: Observed writer conventions
requirements.text:
```text
offset  bytes                    field
0x00    42 4D                    "BM" magic
0x02    42 01 00 00              file size = 0x142 = 322
0x06    00 00 00 00              reserved
0x0A    76 00 00 00              pixel data offset = 0x76 (14 + 40 header + 16×4 palette)
0x0E    28 00 00 00              biSize = 40
0x12    16 00 00 00              biWidth = 22
0x16    11 00 00 00              biHeight = 17
0x1A    01 00                    biPlanes = 1
0x1C    04 00                    biBitCount = 4
0x1E    00 00 00 00              biCompression = 0 (uncompressed)
0x22    00 00 00 00              biSizeImage = 0
0x26    16 00 00 00 11 00 00 00  biXPelsPerMeter = 22, biYPelsPerMeter = 17 (= width, height)
0x2E    00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00  biClrUsed = 0, biClrImportant = 0
0x36    AA 00 00 00 …            16 RgbQuad palette entries (B,G,R,reserved)
0x76    …                        pixel rows, bottom-up, 2 px/byte, rows padded to 4 bytes
```

requirements.heading: `.BMH` - hot bitmaps
requirements.text: A `.BMH` is a **plain Windows BMP** whose extension marks it as the _pressed/highlighted_ state of a same-named `.BMP`. There is no format difference whatsoever. Byte evidence from the shipped pairs (`~/src/rip-tools/RIPTerm2.0/extracted/ICONS/`, also preserved in [assets](../../2.0/assets/icons/README.md#ui-controls-8-bmp--3-bmh)):

requirements.heading: `.BMH` - hot bitmaps
requirements.text:
- `BUTTON.BMP` / `BUTTON.BMH` - identical size (322 B), identical headers and palette; `cmp -l` reports 141 differing bytes, the first at file offset 118, which is exactly the pixel-data offset (0x76) - every difference is in the pixel raster.
- `RADIO.BMP`/`.BMH` (206 B, 27 pixel bytes differ) and `RADIOBUT.BMP`/`.BMH` (322 B, 26 pixel bytes differ) show the same pattern.

requirements.heading: `.BMH` - hot bitmaps
requirements.text: Semantics (spec, [RIP_BUTTON](../ripscrip/4.3-buttons.md#rip_button) flag 4096 "Make icon button use hot icons", v2.A3): when an icon button with the hot-icon flag is depressed, the client displays the same-named `.BMH` image in COPY mode; if no `.BMH` exists, the normal `.BMP` is displayed inverted (NOT mode); if neither file exists, the RIP_BUTTON command is ignored. The 2.30 distribution ships 22 `.BMH` files (the three 2.0-era UI controls plus 17 `RWBTN*V` and 2 `RWICON*` hot states); RIPscrip 3.0 (RIPtel) uses the identical convention unchanged - see the [3.x file-formats page](../../3.0/ripscrip/6.1-content-file-roles.md#bmh---button-highlight-variants).

requirements.heading: `.BMM` - icon masks
requirements.text: `.BMM` is the 2.x rename of the 1.54 `.MSK` icon mask (see the [1.54 icon format](../../1.54/techspecs/3.0-icon-format.md)). Documented evidence of the extension:
requirements.reason: Wire bitmap loads recognize the BMP container and translate the inherited mask extension on lookup.

requirements.heading: `.BMM` - icon masks
requirements.text:
- The RIPTERM.DOC glossary: "Icon files may end in .BMP, .BMM (mask files), or .BMH (hot icons - used with buttons)".
- The RIP_ENTER_BLOCK_MODE extension table: "BMM ... Place mask icon in proper directory" (spec v2.A2, [Level 3-9 commands](../ripscrip/5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md)).
- `RIPTERM.EXE` contains the filter strings `*.BMM`/`*.bmm` and the extension string `.BMM` (both the 2.0 and 2.30 binaries), and the 1.54-to-2.x icon converter renames `.MSK` → `.BMM` (RIPTERM.DOC §2.1.5 conversion table).
requirements.reason: Observations about period assets and terminology. The v3 bitmap header, explicit masks and hot-image commands have their own requirements.

requirements.heading: `.BMM` - icon masks
requirements.text: No `.BMM` sample has been recovered from the known RIPterm 2.0/2.30 or RIPtel 3.1 installs. Its raster behavior in the **2.x clients** remains unverified; neither a 1-bit-only rule nor a nonzero-index transparency rule is established for them.

requirements.heading: `.BMM` - icon masks
requirements.text: For the pinned **RIPtel 3.1 / RIPscrip driver 3.0.7** contract, the [bitmap-mask delta](../../3.0/techspecs/3.0-bitmap-mask-delta.md) now derives behavior from the original executable: BMM is an explicitly loaded BMP with ordinary put modes, with no automatic same-name mask load. It gives accepted profiled depths, palette-sensitive AND/OR stamping, independent dimensions/missing-file behavior, the separate flag-8 color-key algorithm and a distinguishing four-pixel oracle. This later-client evidence does not retroactively prove the 2.x behavior.

requirements.heading: Conversion from 1.54 icons
requirements.text: The 2.x client retains read support for 1.54 icons by conversion, not native rendering: at start-up it scans `ICONS\` and offers "Convert icon ... to 2.0 BMP format?" (disable with the `-I` command-line switch), and it converts on the fly when a script references a legacy icon. The original file is **deleted** after conversion, the extension is rewritten per the table above, and the file date/time is preserved so host icon-update queries ([RIP_FILE_QUERY](../ripscrip/5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_file_query)) still match (RIPTERM.DOC §2.1.5). This paragraph records the **2.x client documentation**, not a verified cross-generation filesystem guarantee. The later RIPtel 3.1 export `RIP_ConvertIconToBmp` uses a fixed EGA palette and attempts source deletion, but its timestamp path queries the already-closed source descriptor and uses uninitialized fields. Its always-BMP output naming and actual post-transfer invocation also differ from the inherited description; see the [3.0 conversion contract](../../3.0/ripscrip/6.1-content-file-roles.md#legacy-icn-icons-ripscrip-154) and [exact RGB table](../../3.0/techspecs/3.0-bitmap-mask-delta.md#legacy-icon-conversion-palette).

requirements.heading: Conversion from 1.54 icons
requirements.text: Adjacent, but not an icon format: the `ICONS\` directory of the definitive distribution also carries `.JPG` photographic images (baseline JFIF, displayed via [RIP_IMAGE](../ripscrip/4.1-jpeg-images.md#rip_image) and the `$(file.JPG$` playback prefix) - see the [asset inventory](../../2.0/assets/icons/README.md#jpeg-images-7-jpg---the-first-shipped-jpeg-content) and the [JPEG page](3.1-jpeg-images.md).

requirements.heading: JPEG Images (.JPG)
requirements.text: RIPscrip 2.x introduced photographic image display: host-supplied JPEG files rendered into a scalable image area of the viewport.
requirements.reason: Wire image style and JPEG draw commands use the selected port and image area. Connected fixtures inspect the final decoded image.

requirements.heading: Wire surface (brief)
requirements.text:
- [RIP_IMAGE](../ripscrip/4.1-jpeg-images.md#rip_image) - `!|1p <res:4> <filename>` (v2.A0): display a JPEG from the terminal's `ICONS\` directory in the current image area.
- [RIP_IMAGE_STYLE](../ripscrip/4.1-jpeg-images.md#rip_image_style) - `!|1i <x0> <y0> <x1> <y1> <flags:4> <res:12>` (v2.A0): define the image area and display flags for subsequent images (details under Rendering below).
- `$(FILE.JPG$` - the local image playback host-command prefix, the JPEG analogue of `$>file.rip$` ([Local File Playback](../ripscrip/5.3-local-playback.md)).
- Delivery: [RIP_ENTER_BLOCK_MODE](../ripscrip/5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md) transfers `.JPG` files into `ICONS\` (routing details in the [connection directory model](4.0-connection-directory-model-delta.md)); [RIP_FILE_QUERY](../ripscrip/5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_file_query) checks existence/size/date; RIP_FILE_DELETE (v2.A4) removes "unneeded JPEG or WAVE files".
requirements.reason: Wire image style and JPEG draw commands use the selected port and image area. Connected fixtures inspect the final decoded image.

requirements.heading: The format as shipped
requirements.text: For an implementation, baseline sequential 8-bit YCbCr decoding covers all known original content. The 320×200 authoring size is the classic quarter-VGA photo size of the era; images are scaled to the image area at display time (below), so the stored size is not a constraint of the format.
requirements.reason: Literal 1p connects baseline JPEG MEDIA loading to the explicitly bound DEVICE image style and palette, with void nonfatal parser recovery and independent three-canvas expectations. Active JPEGs ignore flag 8. Macro expansion, image-style wire/default ownership, delivery/deletion and ambiguous non-COPY clear/margin cases are separately pending/blocked; this is not active application or hardware-palette coverage.

requirements.heading: Decoder envelope (what the client could and could not decode)
requirements.text: RIPterm's decoder is derived from the Independent JPEG Group's libjpeg - its characteristic error strings are embedded in `RIPTERM.EXE` (2.30 build; the same JPEG engine ships from 2.0). Those strings define the supported envelope, and they matter to implementers because any historical content had to fit inside it:
requirements.reason: Historical shipped-content evidence, table scaffolding, format provenance or reference introduction; executable decoder envelope and rendering requirements are tracked in their own source blocks.

requirements.heading: Decoder envelope (what the client could and could not decode)
requirements.text:
- `Unsupported JPEG data precision` - 8-bit samples only; 12-bit JPEG is rejected.
- `Empty JPEG image (DNL not supported)` - the image height must be in the SOF frame header, not a deferred DNL marker.
- `CCIR601 upsampling not implemented yet` / `Fractional upsampling not implemented yet` - component sampling factors limited to the common power-of-two ratios (1×1, 2×1, 2×2 chroma subsampling).
- `Bogus JPEG colorspace` / `Unsupported color conversion request` - YCbCr/grayscale JFIF-style color only.
- Whether the shipped build decodes **progressive** JPEG is unverified - no error string settles it and no progressive file appears in any distribution; all shipped content is baseline. Implementations targeting historical fidelity can treat baseline as the interchange profile.
requirements.reason: SyncTERM additionally accepts complete progressive grayscale and YCbCr JPEGs. Native tests verify the decoded RGB values and reject truncated scans.

requirements.heading: Decoder envelope (what the client could and could not decode)
requirements.text: The client's file-open dialog filters "JPEG images / BMP images / All files" with `.JPG` (strings in `RIPTERM.EXE`) - **no GIF support shipped**, even though RIP_IMAGE_STYLE flag 8 anticipates GIF palettes (below).
requirements.reason: Historical shipped-content evidence, table scaffolding, format provenance or reference introduction; executable decoder envelope and rendering requirements are tracked in their own source blocks.

requirements.heading: Rendering to the canvas
requirements.text: From [RIP_IMAGE_STYLE](../ripscrip/4.1-jpeg-images.md#rip_image_style) (v2.A0-A4):
requirements.reason: Historical shipped-content evidence, table scaffolding, format provenance or reference introduction; executable decoder envelope and rendering requirements are tracked in their own source blocks.

requirements.heading: Rendering to the canvas
requirements.text:
- **Image area** - `<x0> <y0> <x1> <y1>` in the current viewport; coordinates beyond the viewport are clamped. All-zero coordinates disable image viewing entirely. With no RIP_IMAGE_STYLE processed, the image area defaults to the full viewport, and it resets to full viewport on [RIP_RESET_WINDOWS](../ripscrip/1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_reset_windows)/[RIP_HEADER](../ripscrip/1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#rip_header).
- **Scaling** - the image is scaled to fit the image area (v2.A1). Flag `1` preserves aspect ratio, letterboxing the unused margins in black - without it the image stretches to the area.
- **Flags** - `2` delete the image file after display (for block-mode/UU-encoded delivery); `4` skip clearing the image area to the background color first; `8` commit the image's palette to the hardware color lookup table - "typically only of use … with GIF files. This flag is ignored with JPEGs" (v2.A4).
- **Color reduction** - the spec does not define how a decoded 24-bit image maps onto a 16- or 256-color video mode; that quantization/dithering is necessarily the terminal's own (RIP_IMAGE lists Write Mode, Viewport, Port, and Base Math as the attributes used). A modern true-color canvas can simply render the decoded RGB; a mode-faithful renderer must quantize to the active palette (see [Canvas Tiers, Palette & RGB](2.0-canvas-palette-rgb.md)).
requirements.reason: The inherited all-zero disable rule is superseded by the v3 zero-area and viewport fallback rules in chapter 4.1.

requirements.heading: Rendering to the canvas
requirements.text: `RIPTERM.DOC`'s glossary frames JPEG for its users simply as "a compressed graphic file format" with lossy compression (2.30 manual, glossary entries "JPEG", "lossy"). The RIPterm Pro Test Drive 2.11 changelog notes JPEG decoding was made ~20% faster - an implementation note only; the format envelope did not change (see [history.md](../../history.md)).

requirements.heading: FastFont Outline Fonts (.FF1 / .RFF)
requirements.text:
- **`.FF1`** - Atech's native FastFont container, as shipped in RIPterm Professional 2.0 (January 1995) and carried byte-identical (md5-verified) into the 2.20 distribution.
- **`.RFF`** ("RIPscrip FastFont") - a **reformat, not a rename**, introduced with the definitive **RIPterm 2.30** (files dated April 1997): the fixed header is reorganized and the style table expanded, while the glyph payload is carried over byte-for-byte. `RIPTERM.EXE` correspondingly changes its font-browser filter from `%s*.ff1` to `%s*.rff` (binary strings, 2.0 vs 2.30). RIPtel 3.1 ships these exact five `.RFF` files byte-identical and adds three families - see the [3.x delta](../../3.0/techspecs/3.2-fastfont-additions.md).

requirements.text: The size delta is exactly the added style records: 9 × 46 bytes for four families, 8 × 46 for Default (its `.FF1` already carried two records - see below). For every family, the file content is **byte-identical from the end of the FF1 style table to end-of-file**, modulo one rewritten absolute offset: `FF1[gso+4 ..] == RFF[0x206 ..]` where `gso` is the FF1 glyph-section offset (0x64, or 0x92 for Default) - verified as an exact common suffix of 62,207 / 31,078 / 41,553 / 56,008 / 43,083 bytes respectively.

requirements.heading: Style records (46 bytes each)
requirements.text:
- Each `.FF1` carries only its **base face**: one record (e.g. handle 0x03E5, flags 0x00, scale 100, "Dixon"). `DEFAULT.FF1` uniquely carries two: "DEFAULT" and "DEFAULT EX" (flags 0x08, scale **140**).
- Each `.RFF` carries **ten records**: base + `Th`/`Cn`/`Wd`/`Ex` + Hollow versions of all five (`Ho`, `HT` 0x11, `HC` 0x12, `HW` 0x14, `HE` 0x18) - the exact family-suffix names scripts pass in `RIP_EXTENDED_FONT_STYLE` (e.g. `!|y…marin` in [SHADOW.RIP](../../2.0/assets/icons/README.md#shadowrip)). The converter synthesized the missing styles at standard scales but **carried over** existing records: DEFAULT.RFF's "DEFAULT Ex" keeps the FF1's 140% scale while every other family's Ex is 150% - direct provenance evidence that the `.RFF` files were machine-converted from these exact `.FF1` files.
requirements.reason: Earlier asset inventory and reverse-engineering example. The v3 assets, style names and kerning-table format have separate entries.

requirements.heading: Glyph section
requirements.text: At the glyph-section offset (`u16@0x22` in FF1; 0x202 = end of the 10-record style table in RFF) begins a block that opens `u16 = 1`, then a **u16 absolute file offset** pointing 16 bytes ahead (FF1 DIXON: `01 00 74 00` at 0x64 → 0x74; RFF DIXON: `01 00 12 02` at 0x202 → 0x212) - this is the only byte that differs between the FF1 and RFF payloads, because it is absolute and the section moved. The pointed-to address is the **glyph base** (`base` below; FF1 0x74, DEFAULT.FF1 0xA2, RFF 0x212): every offset inside the glyph section is relative to it.

requirements.heading: Glyph section
requirements.text: The outline encoding below was decoded 2026-08-08 by direct byte analysis of the shipped files (no prior public documentation of the FastFont glyph encoding was found in a same-day web search - the format's only other known holder is PageTech, the Atech spin-off that inherited AllType/FastFont). Verification: a strict parser (record framing, opcode set, hint-block accounting, bbox containment of all on-curve points) passes **2,905 of 2,912 glyph records** across all thirteen shipped files - five FF1, five RFF, three RIPtel-only RFF - with zero unexplained bytes, all 3,157 contours of the five 2.x-generation families closing exactly onto their start point; the 7 failures are [shipped corruption in SYMBOL's tail](#symbol-tail-corruption-shipped-defect), byte-identical in both generations. Scanline renderings of decoded glyphs (DIXON A/B/g/O, MARIN S/8, COBB R, BRUSH e) reproduce the expected letterforms, including two-contour counters and correct descenders.

requirements.heading: Global bounding box and header copies
requirements.text: All four global bbox coordinates are **signed little-endian 16-bit font-unit values**, with the same y-down convention as the glyph bboxes: negative Y lies above the baseline, positive Y below it. The fields are coordinate extrema. In particular, metrics +0x1A is horizontal xmax and +0x1C is vertical ymax; neither is an independent ascender or advance-width metric. The separately stored maximum-advance metric at +0x24 and per-glyph advances at +0x4C remain distinct.

requirements.text: All coordinates are s16 absolute values in font units (1000/em), **y-down**: negative y is above the baseline, so a descender reaches positive y (DIXON `g` bbox ymax = +210). The record is self-describing - total length = 14 + `pathLen` + `tailLen`:

requirements.heading: Glyph record
requirements.text:
```text
u16  tag       = 1  (constant, all 2905 valid records)
s16  xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax     ; glyph bbox, y-down
u16  pathLen                    ; byte length of the opcode stream
u16  tailLen                    ; byte length of end marker + hint block
byte[pathLen]  opcode stream:
     00 x y                     ; moveto - starts a new contour
     01 x y                     ; lineto
     02 x1 y1 x2 y2 x3 y3       ; curveto - cubic Bezier, two control points
                                ;   plus endpoint
byte[tailLen]  (absent when tailLen = 0):
     02 00                      ; end marker
     u16 nXhints
     u16 nYhints
     (nX+nY) x { s16 edge1, s16 edge2, s16 width }   ; grid-fitting hints
```

requirements.heading: Glyph record
requirements.text:
- Contours are implicitly closed; in every shipped glyph the last point of a contour coincides with its moveto point.
- The end-marker byte is also `02` - a parser must frame the opcode stream by `pathLen`, not by scanning for a terminator.
- The curves are cubic (PostScript-style), consistent with the fonts' Type 1 heritage via Atech's AllType converter; DEFAULT - the TeleGrafix-rebuilt face - is almost pure polylines (3,476 linetos vs 17 curvetos) while the Atech faces are curve-heavy (COBB: 3,015 curvetos).
- Hint records bracket stems for grid-fitting (X hints: left/right x of a vertical stem; Y hints: horizontal features; `width` ≈ `edge2 - edge1`, off by one in some records). They are not needed for plain rasterization.
- The blank glyph (space) is a bare 14-byte header: tag 1, bbox all zero, `pathLen` = `tailLen` = 0.

requirements.heading: Glyph record
requirements.text: **RIPtel 3.1 consumer clarification:** raw glyph coordinates and style records alone do not specify the raster policy or a Unicode encoding. The [RIPtel rendering contract](../../3.0/techspecs/3.2-fastfont-additions.md#riptel-31-rendering-contract) establishes nonzero interior winding, size/DPI-dependent hollow stamps, per-glyph masked COPY and direct unsigned-byte table indexing, including SYMBOL. Its recovered consumer treats metrics bytes +0x12/+0x13 (the 0x0204 constant above) as bold/hollow strength coefficients 4/2. Those client-specific results are not assumed for earlier RIPterm releases. _Evidence: [primary derivation](../../3.0/research/issue-22-fastfont-rendering.md)._

requirements.heading: SYMBOL tail corruption (shipped defect)
requirements.text: SYMBOL's glyph data physically outruns its file in both generations (byte-identical, so an original Atech build defect, not a conversion artifact): the records for chars 248 and 249 extend **past the header's trailer offset** (0xA810 falls mid-record inside char 248's data - there is no valid kerning table in SYMBOL; the u16 at its trailer offset is 0x0201, not the tag 1 every real trailer record carries); char 247/250's shared record is truncated mid-path by the `B7 BC BA AB BE` separator and copyright text; chars 251-255 point at or beyond end-of-file. Renderers must bounds-check glyph records against the file and treat out-of-range or truncated records as blank.

requirements.heading: `ATF.CFG` - the engine's font catalog cache
requirements.text:
```text
0x00  u16  0x218E                      ; differs per generation (RIPtel: 0x2654);
                                       ; meaning unverified - not a constant magic,
                                       ; not a simple byte-sum checksum
0x02  u16  fileCount   = 5
0x04  u16  totalStyles = 6
0x06  u32  0
0x0A  fileCount × 78-byte entries:
        char[14]  filename, NUL-padded ("COBB.FF1", "DEFAULT.FF1", …)
        u16       index of this font's first record in the style list (0,1,3,4,5)
        u32       0
        byte[54]  verbatim copy of the font's 0x00-0x35 header
        byte[4]   zero padding
0x18C (= fileSize - 48 × totalStyles = 0x0A + 78 × fileCount - 4):
      totalStyles × { u16 fileIndex, 46-byte style record }, ending exactly at EOF
        fileIndex = 0-based index of the owning file entry (0,1,1,2,3,4)
        style record = the 46-byte format above, carrying the engine handle from
        the source font; name padding carries uninitialized/cache data
        (ascending u32 sequences, leaked filename fragments)
```

requirements.heading: MicroANSI Terminal Fonts (RIPTERM.FNT / .MAF)
requirements.text: The "RIPterm v2.0 MicroANSI Font File" container holds the fixed-cell bitmap fonts that render the 2.x text side - the ASCII/ANSI terminal emulation and RIPscrip [text windows](../ripscrip/2.0-color-modes-and-palettes.md) - in every graphics resolution the client supports, one complete 256-glyph **CP437** set (the code page of DOS-era BBS terminals and hosts; character codes 0x00-0xFF) per resolution.

requirements.heading: MicroANSI Terminal Fonts (RIPTERM.FNT / .MAF)
requirements.text: It ships as `RIPTERM.FNT` in the RIPterm program directory (263,585 bytes; RIPterm 2.0, 1995-02-01) and as **`RIPTERM.MAF`** in the definitive 2.30 distribution - the same 263,585-byte container, revised only in glyph artwork (see [the MAF revision](#the-maf-revision)) - and the same container format continues unchanged into RIPscrip 3.0 as `RIPscrip.maf`, see the [3.x delta](../../3.0/techspecs/3.3-microansi-maf-delta.md). It shares only a filename with the 1.54-era 18,596-byte `RIPTERM.FNT`, a different format ([1.54 bitmap fonts](../../1.54/techspecs/3.2-bitmap-fonts.md)).

requirements.heading: MicroANSI Terminal Fonts (RIPTERM.FNT / .MAF)
requirements.text: All integers little-endian. All offsets verified programmatically against all three recovered copies (`~/src/rip-tools/RIPTerm2.0/extracted/RIPTERM.FNT`, `~/src/rip-tools/RIPTerm2.22/RIPTERM.MAF`, `~/src/rip-tools/artifacts/ripterm-2.30/extracted/RIPTERM.MAF`).

requirements.heading: Container layout
requirements.text:
```text
0x00  byte[0x28]  magic: 04 20 "RIPterm v2.0 MicroANSI Font File " 04 0A 0D 00 1A
                  (\x04 SP … SP \x04 \n \r \0 \x1A - TeleGrafix's standard container
                  magic convention, used across the client's own container files)
0x28  u16         resolutionCount        ; = 5
0x2A  u32         directoryOffset        ; = 0x26917 - NOT necessarily 0x3C!
0x2E  byte[14]    zero
0x3C  …           data (see caveat below)
```

requirements.heading: Container layout
requirements.text: **Caveat - stale directory snapshots:** the file carries **four** copies of the directory, of which only the last is valid. The writer emitted a directory snapshot before the font data and again after most resolution blocks, each one record longer and with the not-yet-final records' width/height fields wrong: 3 records at 0x3C (a zero-offset "640x350 EGA" record, then two records with live offsets but partly wrong dimensions), 3 records at 0xAC3A (after the 640×480 fonts), 4 at 0x16431 (after 800×600), and the canonical **5 at 0x26917** (after the 1024×768 fonts) - the only copy with all five `width`/`height` fields correct, and the one `directoryOffset` points to. Parsers must follow the u32 at 0x2A and ignore everything else that parses like a directory. (In RIPtel's `RIPscrip.maf` the u32 happens to be 0x3C, which is why earlier analysis missed this field's significance; the [3.x container](../../3.0/techspecs/3.3-microansi-maf-delta.md) writes a single directory and no snapshots.)

requirements.heading: Resolution directory (60-byte records)
requirements.text: At `directoryOffset`, `resolutionCount` consecutive records:

requirements.heading: Resolution directory (60-byte records)
requirements.text:
```c
struct MafResolution {              /* 60 bytes */
    uint16_t width, height;         /* screen resolution */
    uint32_t fontOffset[5];         /* absolute offsets of 5 font subrecords */
    char     name[36];              /* NUL-terminated, zero-padded */
};
```

requirements.heading: Resolution directory (60-byte records)
requirements.text: (Note: the [RIPtel triage](../../3.0/research/riptel-binary-formats.md) described these as 64-byte records with `name[40]`; the correct stride, verified by the directory ending exactly at the first following font subrecord in both this container and `RIPscrip.maf`, is **60** bytes with `name[36]`.)

requirements.text: The shipped directory:

requirements.heading: Resolution directory (60-byte records)
requirements.text: | Record | Resolution | Name | Font offsets (order: 80×43, 91×43, 80×25, 91×25, 40×25 cells) |

requirements.heading: Resolution directory (60-byte records)
requirements.text: The five fonts per resolution correspond to the five selectable System Fonts of the text mode - 80×25 (default), 80×43, 40×25, 91×43, 91×25 (RIPTERM.DOC §4.4 "System Font Setup", Ctrl-Alt-F): "Any subsequent text/ANSI displayed on the screen will appear in the chosen system font unless the host explicitly tells RIPterm to use another font for the text window."

requirements.heading: Resolution directory (60-byte records)
requirements.text: The cell sizes are exactly the five text modes at each resolution: e.g. at 640×350, 8×14 → 80×25, 8×8 → 80×43 (350⁄8 = 43), 7×14 → 91×25 (640⁄7 = 91), 7×8 → 91×43, 16×14 → 40×25. The internal font names state the cell and, from 800×600 up, the mode ("`10x13 (80x43)`", "`80x43 font`", …). Note the fifth record: the container carries a complete **1280×1024** font set even though no shipped video-mode database entry reaches past 1024×768 - see [Canvas Tiers, Palette & RGB](2.0-canvas-palette-rgb.md#resolution-tiers-as-shipped).

requirements.heading: Font subrecords
requirements.text:
```c
struct MafFont {                    /* 50-byte header + glyphs */
    uint16_t cellWidth, cellHeight; /* pixels */
    char     name[30];              /* NUL-terminated ("8x14", "10x13 (80x43)", …) */
    uint16_t lastChar;              /* 0x00FF in all 25 fonts */
    uint16_t bytesPerGlyph;         /* = ceil(cellWidth/8) * cellHeight */
    uint8_t  reserved[12];          /* observed zero */
    uint8_t  glyphs[255][bytesPerGlyph];  /* characters 0x01-0xFF; 0x00 not stored */
};
```

requirements.heading: Font subrecords
requirements.text: Glyph bitmaps are row-major, one row = `ceil(cellWidth/8)` bytes, MSB = leftmost pixel, characters **0x01-0xFF** of CP437 in order - character 0x00 has no stored bitmap and renders blank, so char c lives at `fontOffset + 50 + (c - 1) × bytesPerGlyph`. Verification: every font ends at exactly `offset + 50 + 255 × bytesPerGlyph`, which is the next font's offset (or a directory snapshot, or end-of-file - see the caveat above), across all 25 fonts in all three recovered copies; and the classic CP437 glyphs render directly - char 0x01 of the 8×8 font at 0xF0 + 50 = 0x122 is `7E 81 A5 81 BD 99 81 7E`, the smiley face. The file ends exactly where the last font's char 0xFF ends (0x3660F + 50 + 255 × 160 = 0x405A1) - there is **no truncation**.

requirements.heading: Font subrecords
requirements.text: (Framing note, corrected 2026-08-08: this section previously described a 42-byte header with 256 glyphs and a "truncation quirk" losing most of the final char 0xFF. That reading only fits fonts whose `bytesPerGlyph` is 8 - for the 8-byte-per-glyph fonts the two framings give byte-identical glyph positions, which is how it survived spot-checks. The 50/255 framing was established by locating full-block char 0xDB and the char 0x01 smiley in fonts of several cell sizes across this container, `RIPTERM.FNT`, and RIPtel's `RIPscrip.maf`; the [3.x page](../../3.0/techspecs/3.3-microansi-maf-delta.md) documents the same verification against the successor file.)

requirements.heading: The MAF revision
requirements.text: `RIPTERM.MAF` differs from `RIPTERM.FNT` in exactly 6,885 bytes (FNT md5 `a0f64c…`, MAF md5 `47c240…`; the `.MAF` byte-identical across the 2.20.01 and 2.30 trees), **all inside glyph bitmaps** - the magic, directory, and every subrecord header are byte-identical. The client binaries name their respective file (`RIPTERM.FNT` string in the 2.0 `RIPTERM.EXE`; `RIPTERM.MAF` in 2.30's), and both log "Shutting down MicroANSI font system". The revision redrew extended-CP437 artwork (accented letters 0x7F-0xA7, box/block drawing 0xB0-0xDA, a few Greek/symbol cells 0xE0-0xEE) in the fonts of the three lower resolutions, and touched nothing at 1024×768 or 1280×1024:

requirements.heading: Audio (.WAV)
requirements.text: Digitized audio is a RIPscrip 2.x headline feature: background `.WAV` playback while graphics commands continue streaming from the host.
requirements.reason: Historical/file-format introduction, preserved distribution provenance or illustrative shipped-file description. Exact independent PCM fixtures exercise the adapter; this does not claim the historical RIPTERM.WAV payload was tested.

requirements.heading: The WAVE (PCM) interchange format
requirements.text: The [Audio Formats section](../ripscrip/4.5-audio-files.md#audio-sound--music-formats) (spec v2.A4) fixes the interchange format: **Microsoft WAVE containing uncompressed PCM**. Clients on non-WAVE-native platforms must translate - including translating file sizes reported back to the host so [RIP_FILE_QUERY](../ripscrip/5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_file_query) update checks still match. No narrower profile (rate, depth, channels) is documented anywhere, so a conforming player should accept the general PCM WAV family; RIPterm's own output path handles 8- or 16-bit, mono or stereo (RIPTERM.DOC §4.3).
requirements.reason: The wire and local playback paths resolve a WAV asset and use the session audio service. Native WAV and replacement tests cover playback while the RIP interpreter proceeds.

requirements.heading: The WAVE (PCM) interchange format
requirements.text: A WAVE/PCM file is a RIFF container:
requirements.reason: Historical/file-format introduction, preserved distribution provenance or illustrative shipped-file description. Exact independent PCM fixtures exercise the adapter; this does not claim the historical RIPTERM.WAV payload was tested.

requirements.heading: The WAVE (PCM) interchange format
requirements.text:
```text
0x00  "RIFF"  u32 riffSize  "WAVE"        ; riffSize = file size - 8
      "fmt "  u32 fmtSize (= 16 for PCM)  ; format chunk
        u16 wFormatTag        ; 1 = PCM (the only tag the spec's "WAVE (PCM)" admits)
        u16 nChannels         ; 1 = mono, 2 = stereo
        u32 nSamplesPerSec    ; sample rate in Hz
        u32 nAvgBytesPerSec   ; rate × block align
        u16 nBlockAlign       ; channels × bytesPerSample
        u16 wBitsPerSample    ; 8 (unsigned samples) or 16 (signed, little-endian)
      "data"  u32 dataSize    ; dataSize bytes of raw samples follow
```
requirements.reason: RIP-specific read-only RIFF/PCM validation walks word-aligned chunks and checks declared bounds, format, rate/alignment and whole frames before shared libsndfile decoding. Independent 8/16/24/32-bit fixtures, odd chunks/data padding and all truncated prefixes are covered without opening a physical device.

requirements.heading: The WAVE (PCM) interchange format
requirements.text: Chunks are word-aligned and other chunk types may appear between `fmt ` and `data`; a robust parser walks chunks rather than assuming fixed offsets (the one shipped file happens to be the minimal fixed layout below).

requirements.heading: Worked example - `RIPTERM.WAV`
requirements.text:
```text
0x00  "RIFF" 12 25 01 00 "WAVE"      ; RIFF size 0x12512 = 75,026
0x0C  "fmt " 10 00 00 00             ; fmt chunk, 16 bytes
0x14  01 00                          ; wFormatTag = 1 (PCM)
0x16  01 00                          ; nChannels = 1 (mono)
0x18  77 2B 00 00                    ; nSamplesPerSec = 0x2B77 = 11,127 Hz
0x1C  77 2B 00 00                    ; nAvgBytesPerSec = 11,127
0x20  01 00                          ; nBlockAlign = 1
0x22  08 00                          ; wBitsPerSample = 8
0x24  "data" EE 24 01 00             ; 74,990 sample bytes (~6.7 s), unsigned 8-bit
```

requirements.heading: Worked example - `RIPTERM.WAV`
requirements.text: The odd 11,127 Hz rate (nominal 11.025 kHz hardware clocking) is characteristic of period sampling tools. This is the client's own sound effect, not BBS content - but it is a useful conformance fixture: 8-bit mono PCM at ~11 kHz is exactly what a 2.x-era host would have assumed any terminal could play.

requirements.heading: Playback semantics
requirements.text:
- [RIP_PLAY_AUDIO](../ripscrip/4.5-audio-files.md#rip_play_audio) - `!|1w <res:4> <filename>` (added v2.A3). Starts **background** playback of a local `.WAV` (graphics continue streaming); the file must live with the bitmapped icons in `ICONS\` (RIPTERM.DOC §2.1.4 routes "Sound Files - .WAV" there; there was never a dedicated audio directory - see the [connection directory model](4.0-connection-directory-model-delta.md)). A missing file is silently ignored; a new command **replaces** any sound already playing; the literal filename `$OFF$` stops playback. The 4-character `<res>` field is reserved ("0000").
- `$)FILE.WAV$` - the local audio playback host-command prefix ([Local File Playback](../ripscrip/5.3-local-playback.md)), the audio analogue of `$>file.rip$`, introduced because "you cannot be certain solely from a filename or a file extension if the file is truly a sound file" (v2.A4 revision notes).
- **Reset** - `$RESET(SOUND)$` ([terminal reset options](../ripscrip/5.1-text-variables.md#reset)) aborts any playing digitized sound immediately.
- **Delivery/management** - [RIP_ENTER_BLOCK_MODE](../ripscrip/5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md) transfers `.WAV` files via the generic file type - `WAV` has no row in the DYNAMIC-mode extension tables, so audio falls to the catch-all and is placed in the proper directory unprocessed (see [block-mode routing](4.0-connection-directory-model-delta.md#block-mode-routing---the-extension-table)); RIP_FILE_QUERY checks existence/size/date so hosts can push updates; RIP_FILE_DELETE (v2.A4) removes "unneeded JPEG or WAVE files".
- **Capability negotiation** - the `$IFS$` [text variable](../ripscrip/9.1-text-variable-reference.md) exposes an `_AUDIO` category whose sole listed member is `WAV`.
- **No sequenced music** - the spec's preamble promises "both digitized and sequenced music", but no sequenced-music (MIDI) format, command, or file ever appears in the specification or any recovered 2.x-generation distribution. The 1.54-era `$MUSIC$`/`$SOUND()$` tone variables remain in the language as the legacy PC-speaker path, distinct from digitized audio.
requirements.reason: The wire and local playback paths resolve a WAV asset and use the session audio service. Native WAV and replacement tests cover playback while the RIP interpreter proceeds.

requirements.heading: Client implementation notes (passing reference)
requirements.text: RIPterm implements WAV playback exactly along those lines - "A new feature in RIPterm is the support for digitized sound, in the form of .WAV files" (RIPTERM.DOC §2.1.3, identical framing in the 2.0 and 2.30 manuals) - via HMI's "Sound Operating System" DOS drivers (`HMIDRV.386`/`HMIDET.386` in the program directory), with sound-card selection and output options in Audio Setup (§4.3) and a `-A` command-line switch to disable audio entirely (§2.3). None of that affects the interchange format above. Notably, **no shipped demo script exercises the audio commands** - a scan of every `.RIP` file in the recovered 2.0 and 2.30 `ICONS\` directories finds no `!|1w` command and no `$)…$` prefix - so `RIPTERM.WAV` is the only WAV in any 2.x-generation distribution.
requirements.reason: Historical/file-format introduction, preserved distribution provenance or illustrative shipped-file description. Exact independent PCM fixtures exercise the adapter; this does not claim the historical RIPTERM.WAV payload was tested.

requirements.heading: UI Resources (.FNT / .IMG)
requirements.text: RIPterm draws its own user interface - dialogs, menus, check-boxes, radio buttons - with a private set of per-resolution assets: four proportional UI fonts (`0640X350.FNT`, `0640X480.FNT`, `0800X600.FNT`, `1024X768.FNT`) and twenty-six planar widget images (`*.IMG`). These are client resources, not wire formats, but they are direct evidence of the 2.x engine's resolution-scaled UI and their formats are documented nowhere else. The RIPterm 2.0 install ships them as loose files in `FONTS\`; in the definitive 2.30 distribution the loose files are gone from `FONTS\` while `RIPTERM.EXE` still carries every one of the filenames as strings - the assets evidently moved into the client's own resource packaging, a detail of the original software that doesn't affect the formats documented here _(cf. the [resource-container research notes](../../3.0/research/riptel-resource-containers.md))_. The loose files are preserved byte-exact in [`version/2.0/assets/fonts/`](../../2.0/assets/fonts/README.md).
requirements.reason: Private RIPterm menu, dialog and widget assets are client artwork. Protocol fonts and images are reviewed in their own chapters.

requirements.heading: `.IMG` widget images - format (decoded)
requirements.text: Small 16-color images for the check-box and radio-button controls, pre-scaled for each display resolution (640×350, 640×480, 800×600, 1024×768, 1280×1024 - the numeric infix is the vertical resolution, `1024` meaning the 1280×1024 set) plus one TeleGrafix glyph. Layout, verified against all 26 files (the size formula `12 + 4 × height × bytesPerPlaneRow` matches every file exactly):
requirements.reason: Private RIPterm menu, dialog and widget assets are client artwork. Protocol fonts and images are reviewed in their own chapters.

requirements.heading: `.IMG` widget images - format (decoded)
requirements.text:
```c
struct ImgWidget {                   /* 12-byte header */
    uint16_t width;                  /* logical image width in pixels */
    uint16_t height;                 /* rows */
    uint16_t bitShift;               /* pre-shift of the raster, in pixels (see below) */
    uint16_t bytesPerPlaneRow;       /* row stride of one plane, in bytes */
    uint16_t always1;                /* observed 1 in all files; meaning unverified */
    uint16_t always4;                /* observed 4 in all files; plane count (unverified) */
    /* followed by 4 × height × bytesPerPlaneRow bytes of pixel data */
};
```
requirements.reason: Private RIPterm menu, dialog and widget assets are client artwork. Protocol fonts and images are reviewed in their own chapters.

requirements.heading: `.IMG` widget images - format (decoded)
requirements.text: Pixel data is **plane-sequential**: all `height` rows of plane 0, then plane 1, plane 2, plane 3. Bit _p_ of a pixel's 4-bit color index comes from plane _p_ (EGA order: blue, green, red, intensity), MSB = leftmost pixel. The raster is stored **pre-shifted right by `bitShift` pixels** - the EGA-era optimization of baking the destination bit alignment into the image so it can be latched to the screen without run-time shifting. The logical image occupies pixel columns `[bitShift, bitShift + width)` of each `bytesPerPlaneRow × 8`-pixel row; columns outside that window are junk (background fill on the left, uninitialized buffer garbage on the right - several files leak fragments of other shifted copies).
requirements.reason: Private RIPterm menu, dialog and widget assets are client artwork. Protocol fonts and images are reviewed in their own chapters.

```text
0x02  u8    nameLen                 ; Pascal-style length prefix (9, 10, 11, 11)
0x03  char[nameLen] name           ; "sys08 8x8", "SYS16 8x13", "SYS 24 9x13"
…     byte[…]                      ; fixed-size name/style buffer, padded with
                                    ; uninitialized memory (leaked "…ormal" fragments
                                    ; of the string "Normal" appear in 0640X350.FNT)
0x32  char[10] "METAFONTP\0"        ; container tag
0x3C  u32   fileSize                ; equals the file's own byte length in all four
                                    ; files (0x0C8B, 0x0E8B, 0x1045, 0x15C5)
```

requirements.heading: Per-resolution system `.FNT` fonts (partially decoded)
requirements.text: Beyond the header the structure is **only partially decoded** and is documented here as observed: at ~0x52 a field group reading `20 FF 08 00 08 00 …` is consistent with firstChar = 0x20, lastChar = 0xFF and an 8×8 cell for `sys08` _(interpretation unverified)_; from 0x11C runs an ascending u16 table of 45 entries with a constant stride of 8 (0x240, 0x248, 0x250, … 0x3A0), consistent with per-glyph data offsets for an 8-byte 8×8 glyph; and the file tail contains what appear to be per-character width bytes for the proportional metrics. The internal pointer tables contain values that overlap the table region itself, so the exact base of the glyph-data pointers has not been established; a full decode needs the loader code in `RIPTERM.EXE` disassembled. Implementers do not need this format - it renders no host-visible content - but any future decode should live on this page.

requirements.heading: RIPscrip 2.00 - Technical Specifications
requirements.text: Original byte-level documentation of the binary file formats and implementation details of the RIPscrip 2.x product family - RIPterm Professional 2.0 through the final **RIPterm 2.30** release, which is treated throughout as the definitive reference. These are original techspecs, not spec conversions: every reverse-engineered claim cites the ALPHA 4 specification section, a recovered document, or an artifact path with observed bytes, and details that could not be verified are marked as such. Note that none of the open-source RIP reference implementations (SyncTERM `ripper.c`, icy_tools, RIPtermJS, PabloDraw) parses the 2.x binary containers documented here - they implement the 1.54 wire language - so these pages are currently the only implementer documentation for these formats.

requirements.heading: 1.0 Introduction
requirements.text: _Reconstructed edition - every claim carries an evidence tag; see [Contents](README.md) for the legend._

requirements.heading: 1.0 Introduction
requirements.text: The RIPscrip 3.x generation - the completed, shipping form of the 2.0 redesign: its inherited design goals, the 3.0 identity evidence, the revision history and its differences from 1.54 and from the last published specification draft, the state of modern implementations, and the evidence model this reference rests on.

requirements.heading: What RIPscrip 3.x Is
requirements.text: _Evidence: WP; 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: What RIPscrip 3.x Is
requirements.text: RIPscrip ("Remote Imaging Protocol script") is TeleGrafix Communications' text-based graphical scripting language for online services. It encodes vector graphics, bitmapped images, mouse-driven user interfaces, fonts, audio, and terminal text into a stream of 7-bit printable ASCII that can be transmitted over any connection capable of carrying text, and intermixed freely with ordinary TTY and ANSI/VT-102 output. The language is object-oriented rather than raster-oriented: a scene is a sequence of compact drawing commands, not a bitmap.

requirements.heading: What RIPscrip 3.x Is
requirements.text: RIPscrip 3.x is the third generation of the language - the completed form of the 2.0 design that TeleGrafix circulated as the ALPHA specification drafts of 1993-1994, shipped in RIPterm 2.0 and RIPtel 3.1, and described publicly in the December 1996 [RIPscrip 3.0 Technical White Paper](../text/RIPScrip-3.x-technical-whitepaper.txt). It adds to the 1.54 baseline: [drawing ports](../../glossary.md) and offscreen bitmaps, [world coordinates](../../glossary.md) and resolution independence, 256-color and direct-RGB color, data tables with protection, a save/restore backup system, outline fonts, JPEG images, WAV audio, a flowed-text column system, and a greatly expanded text-variable/host-command language.

requirements.heading: Design Goals Inherited from the Original Language
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: Design Goals Inherited from the Original Language
requirements.text: The founding rationale of the language, in TeleGrafix's own words from the 2.00 specification, applies unchanged to 3.x. As system operators of many bulletin board systems, they had wished for some form of Graphical User Interface for their boards, found every existing solution inadequate in one way or another - incomplete, difficult to implement, too complex, or lacking in graphics development tools - and so decided to write their own graphical script language.

requirements.heading: Design Goals Inherited from the Original Language
requirements.text: RIPscrip is a text based script language for displaying online graphics. The script language conforms to 7-bit ASCII, avoiding the use of Extended ASCII characters. This allows transmission over X.25 networks and other carriers that do not support full 8-bit binary transfers easily. RIPscrip allows RIPscrip graphical statements to be mixed with printable ASCII text and [de facto standard] ANSI/VT-100 directives. RIPscrip can dynamically determine what is graphics and what is text and display them appropriately in separate windows (a graphics window and a [text window](../../glossary.md)). And if you must have your own proprietary commands, RIPscrip has room for that too.

requirements.heading: Design Goals Inherited from the Original Language
requirements.text: The language's efficiency stems from its compactness and developmental planning. It is entirely Object Oriented instead of Raster Oriented for efficient transmission of data and powerful editing capabilities. Earlier graphical script languages (Avatar and Skypix among others) used special command characters; traditional script languages use English words ("BOX 0,0 100,50") - incredibly bulky when pictures are comprised of hundreds or thousands of individual graphical operations. The main strategy was therefore to make the language as efficient as possible without going completely binary, allowing immediate installation onto any ASCII text-based host system. The unreadability of the language was justified by the limited bandwidth of the era's modems - the language must be compact.

requirements.heading: Design Goals Inherited from the Original Language
requirements.text: The RIPscrip language is made publicly available and is freely licensed by TeleGrafix Communications, Inc. - the language can be used in the creation of other products, but it is not public domain; TeleGrafix maintains the copyright. RIPscrip, RIPaint, RIPdraw, and RIPterm are trademarks of TeleGrafix Communications, Inc., and products that use RIPscrip were required to state so with the trademark statement. _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: Evidence Basis for This Edition
requirements.text: Unlike the [1.54](../../1.54/ripscrip/README.md) and [2.0](../../2.0/ripscrip/README.md) references, this edition is **not** a conversion of an official document. TeleGrafix's own product list advertised a "RIPscrip 3.0 protocol specification," and the white paper promises a "RIPscrip 3.0 Language Reference," but no such document has ever been located. This edition therefore reconstructs the 3.x language from five converging sources:

requirements.heading: Evidence Basis for This Edition
requirements.text:
1. **The RIPscrip 2.00 ALPHA 4 specification** (December 1994) - the last published TeleGrafix language reference, and the documented baseline that 3.x completes. Where 3.x evidence shows a behavior unchanged from 2.00a4, this edition adapts the [2.0 reference's](../../2.0/ripscrip/README.md) text.
2. **The RIPscrip 3.0 Technical White Paper** (December 1996) - architecture and feature prose, [preserved in full](../text/RIPScrip-3.x-technical-whitepaper.txt) as the verbatim source document.
3. **RIPSCRIP.HLP recovered strings** - the complete error-message and command-name string table of the RIPSCRIP.DLL 3.0.7 parser, extracted from the RIPtel 3.1 install. It fixes the 3.0 command inventory (~90 `RIP_*` names) and many hard limits. See the [help extraction report](../../3.0/research/riptel-help-extraction.md).
4. **The 116-script RIPtel demo corpus** - TeleGrafix's own demo scenes (22,921 parsed commands, self-documented with 305 prose comments), the primary source for on-the-wire opcodes and syntax. See the [script census](../../3.0/research/riptel-script-census.md).
5. **SyncTERM's implementation** - `ripper.c` in the Synchronet source tree, the only open-source implementation that answers the version query as RIP 3.0. Cited by line number throughout.

requirements.heading: Evidence Basis for This Edition
requirements.text: Every section in this edition carries an _Evidence:_ line naming which of these sources supports it (`2.00a4`, `WP`, `HLP`, `corpus`, `SyncTERM`); editorial inferences are marked _(hypothesis)_. The full legend is in the [Contents](README.md). Material inherited from the published 2.x specification additionally keeps the spec's own revision markers - `_Added in RIPscrip v2.A1._` lines and `_(v2.A3)_` margin notes - exactly as the 2.0 reference preserves them, so a reader can always tell which ALPHA draft introduced a given behavior.

requirements.heading: The 3.0 Identity
requirements.text: _Evidence: HLP; corpus; SyncTERM (ripper.c:7619)._

requirements.heading: The 3.0 Identity
requirements.text: "RIPscrip 3.0" is a renaming, not a redesign. The evidence from RIPtel 3.1 (October 1997) is unambiguous:

requirements.heading: The 3.0 Identity
requirements.text:
- RIPtel 3.1 ships **driver version 3.0.7** of RIPSCRIP.DLL, per its readme.
- The engine's internal file headers self-identify as **"RIPterm v2.0"** - the resource file, the MicroANSI font file, and the help resources all carry `RIPterm v2.0` signatures.
- The original driver’s autosense and RIPVER producers return **`RIPSCRIP030001`**, 14 bytes; the RIPTEL.HLP FAQ prints only the incomplete `RIPSCRIP03000` quote. See the [exact reply/reference profile](9.2-versions.md) and [primary derivation](../research/issue-7-framing-identification.md) (DLL; HLP).

requirements.heading: The 3.0 Identity
requirements.text: In other words, RIPscrip 3.0 **is** the completed RIPscrip 2.x engine: the 2.00 ALPHA feature set, finished, debugged, and shipped under a new major version number. This is why the 2.00a4 specification remains the structural backbone of this edition.

requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; WP; HLP._

requirements.text: | 1.54 | 1993 | Last published 1.x specification; the universal interoperability baseline. See the [v1.54 reference](../../1.54/ripscrip/README.md). |

requirements.heading: Revision History
requirements.text: | 2.00 A0-A4 | 1993-Dec 1994 | The five ALPHA drafts of the 2.0 specification, introducing ports, tables, world coordinates, UltraNums, and the rest of the modern architecture. Per-revision change logs are preserved in the [2.0 Introduction](../../2.0/ripscrip/1.0-introduction.md). |

requirements.heading: Revision History
requirements.text: | 2.0 / 2.1 / 2.2 | 1995-1997 | The undocumented "RIPscrip-2" product era: the engine as shipped in RIPterm Professional 2.0 (Jan 1995), 2.20.00 (Nov 19, 1995), 2.20.01 (Nov 28, 1995), and 2.30 (Oct 27, 1997), with **no specification published after ALPHA 4** (no product labeled "2.1" has surfaced). The shipping engine moved past the draft from day one - RIPterm Pro 2.0 already used the 26-character RIP_EXTENDED_FONT_STYLE argument block (SHADOW.RIP) rather than ALPHA 4's 13-character form, and v2.20.01 added the icon-transparency flag (`<flags2>` bit 128) to RIP_BUTTON_STYLE, absent from the ALPHA 4 table. Features often credited to "3.x" were already shipping in the January 1995 2.0 release - background **.WAV audio playback** (specified since ALPHA 3; HMI sound drivers), JPEG image display, SVGA/256-color modes, BMP icons, and Atech `.FF1` outline fonts (see the [RIPterm 2.30 font assets](../../2.0/assets/fonts/README.md)). See [4.5 Audio Files](4.5-audio-files.md). |

requirements.heading: Revision History
requirements.text: | 3.0 | 1995-1996 | The 2.x design finalized and renamed. Publicly described by the Dec 1996 white paper; no language reference published. |

requirements.heading: Revision History
requirements.text: | 3.0.7 | Oct 1997 | Driver shipped with RIPtel 3.1 "Visual Telnet" - the concrete engine this edition documents. |

requirements.heading: Revision History
requirements.text: One notable change between the 2.00a4 draft and the shipping 3.0: **GIF support was dropped.** The 2.A4 draft added GIF alongside JPEG for compressed images, but the white paper explains it had to be removed "due to outrageous licensing conditions for the compression algorithm LZW," leaving JPEG as the sole compressed image format (with PNG named as the intended successor). See [the white paper on image formats](../text/RIPScrip-3.x-technical-whitepaper.txt).

requirements.heading: The 2.0 ALPHA Drafts and the Shipping Engine
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: The 2.0 ALPHA Drafts and the Shipping Engine
requirements.text: The 2.00 ALPHA 4 draft ("RIPscrip Graphics Protocol Language, Technical Reference" - Version 2.00, Revision ALPHA 4, December 13th 1994) is the last published specification of any kind, and its ALPHA lineage matters for reading this reference: the drafts were an ongoing culmination revised as A0 through A4, each sub-revision flagged in the document's margin (`_(v2.A3)_`-style markers, preserved throughout this reference on inherited material). The A0 draft defined the resolution-independent coordinate system, 24-bit color encoding, the 36-slot text-window/viewport/style tables, and base-math variation; A1 added the header command, save/restore protection, extended fonts, and UU-encoded data blocks; A2 added command grouping and borderless fills; A3 added drawing ports, WAV audio, and file deletion; A4 reworked text variables, data tables, and the extended text window. The complete per-revision change logs - creator-relevant history for understanding why commands look the way they do - are carried in full in the [2.0 Introduction](../../2.0/ripscrip/1.0-introduction.md). The shipping 2.30-generation clients already diverged from the draft in documented places (auto-sense reply, the Base Math opcode, the extended-font layout - see the [2.0 reference's spec-status note](../../2.0/ripscrip/1.0-introduction.md)); the 3.0 engine this edition documents inherits those shipping resolutions, not the draft positions.

requirements.heading: Differences from 2.00 ALPHA 4
requirements.text: _Evidence: corpus; HLP; WP._

requirements.heading: Differences from 2.00 ALPHA 4
requirements.text: Relative to the last published specification draft, the shipping 3.0 engine differs as listed below. Note that these differences accumulated **across the 2.0-2.2 product releases as well as the 3.0 renaming** - with no specifications published after ALPHA 4, the exact release where each feature landed is mostly unrecorded; where evidence exists (e.g. WAV audio and the reworked extended-font-style block shipping in RIPterm Pro 2.0), the relevant section says so.

requirements.heading: Differences from 2.00 ALPHA 4
requirements.text:
- **Adds new drawing primitives** never documented in any spec: skewed ovals (`&`, `-`, `]`, `[`, `+`), the filled oval chord (`_`), markers (`;`), poly-polygons with even-odd fill (`<`), and bounded text (`"`). All are named or demonstrated in TeleGrafix's own NEWCMDS.RIP and companion demos - see [the script census](../../3.0/research/riptel-script-census.md) and the [2.2 Curves](2.2-curves.md) and [2.3 Shapes & Fills](2.3-shapes-and-fills.md) pages.
- **Resolves the 2.00a4 opcode collision**: RIP_SET_BASE_MATH is level-0 `J` on the wire, leaving `b` to RIP_EXTENDED_TEXT_WINDOW. See [1.2 Math & Coordinates](1.2-math-and-coordinates.md).
- **Adds the flowed-text column system** - `1e` column regions, linked multi-column layouts, overflow paging, and RIP_SelectArticle - the "powerful column system" advertised for newspaper-style presentation. See [3.1 Column Text System](3.1-column-text-system.md).
- **Adds a conditional/macro layer**: `<<IF …>> <<ELSE>> <<ENDIF>>` inline conditionals, `<<NAME>>` macro expansion, the `$&VAR$` dereference form, and `ID=n:` mouse-field identities. See [5.2 Templates & Conditionals](5.2-templates-and-conditionals.md).
- **Adds web integration**: `$GOTOURL(var)$` launches a URL held in a text variable - 1997-era web/BBS convergence.
- **Formalizes scene header segments** - a per-scene header mechanism carrying data-table flags and entries, coordinate size, direct-RGB bit count, general flags, and a revision code. See [1.1 Protocol & Command Hierarchy](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#scene-header-segments).

requirements.heading: Differences from 1.54
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP; corpus._

requirements.heading: Differences from 1.54
requirements.text: Everything the 2.00 ALPHAs introduced applies: ports, tables, backup areas, world coordinates, 256/direct-RGB color, base-math variation, and the expanded command levels - the fundamentals chapters of this edition cover each. For interoperating with 1.54-era content, 3.x provides the **`$COMPAT$`** text variable, which sets the environment to RIPscrip 1.54 settings - the classic 640×350 EGA coordinate space and defaults. TeleGrafix's own demo scenes issue `$COMPAT$` before playing 1.54-style artwork (21 uses in the corpus), making it the standard bridge between the two coordinate worlds. The driver also retains 1.54 `.ICN` icon handling, converting old icons to BMP on the fly ("Can't convert RIP 1.54 Icon %s to 2.0 BMP format!").

requirements.heading: Differences from 1.54
requirements.text: Two backward-compatibility subtleties inherited from the 2.0 redesign are worth restating for authors converting 1.54 material: XOR (and the other raster write modes) now apply to **all** primitives including curves and filled areas, where 1.54 limited XOR to simple line primitives _(v2.A1)_; and the resolution-independent fill model means filled rectangles inset one pixel from their right and bottom coordinate lines, which can open one-pixel gaps in 1.54 artwork replayed under a non-1.54 environment - see [1.2 Math & Coordinates](1.2-math-and-coordinates.md#the-mathematics-of-graphics-and-coordinates) for the full rules _(v2.A1)_. Filled objects' borders, always drawn in 1.54, can be turned off from 2.0 onward (they default on for compatibility) _(v2.A3)_. _Evidence: 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: Implementation Status
requirements.text: The practical takeaway: **1.54 is the interoperable floor**, SyncTERM is the only living implementation of anything beyond it, and the original RIPSCRIP.DLL 3.0.7 driver (via RIPtel under emulation) remains the reference behavior for the full language. See [1.1 Protocol & Command Hierarchy](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#ansi-sequences-auto-sensing) for version identification details.
