requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; corpus; SyncTERM (ripper.c:18516-18608)._

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: RIPscrip is organized into 10 levels of graphical commands (low Level-0 to high Level-9). Level-0 commands are the building blocks of RIPscrip. The basic graphics primitives of the system are all Level-0, including the commands Line, Rectangle, Circle, Color, Font, etc. Each level of RIPscrip gets progressively higher-level in concept. For example, Level-1 commands use Mouse Regions, Icons, and Formatted Text Regions.

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: The basic syntax rules are as follows:

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 1. A RIPscrip command line starts at the beginning of a line of text. A RIPscrip command line moved to the middle of a line of text is treated as literal text. This prevents people inserting mischievous things in teleconference messages, or similar pranks. The only exceptions to this rule is stated below under item 6, "continuation of long lines", and item 12 "alternate RIPscrip starting sequences".
requirements.reason: The stream collectors handle introducers, quoted bytes, continuations, command-specific numeric boundaries and comments. Split-input and connected drawing fixtures exercise dispatch and recovery.

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 2. A RIPscrip command line begins with an exclamation mark `!` (ASCII code 33 decimal).
requirements.reason: The stream collectors handle introducers, quoted bytes, continuations, command-specific numeric boundaries and comments. Split-input and connected drawing fixtures exercise dispatch and recovery.

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 3. Every RIPscrip command is preceded by the universal RIPscrip delimiter, vertical-bar `|` (ASCII code 124 decimal).
requirements.reason: The stream collectors handle introducers, quoted bytes, continuations, command-specific numeric boundaries and comments. Split-input and connected drawing fixtures exercise dispatch and recovery.

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 4. Individual RIPscrip commands may be combined on the same line providing they are separated by the vertical bar delimiter. There are some exceptions to this ([RIP_ENTER_BLOCK_MODE](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_enter_block_mode), and a few others). See individual command descriptions for exceptions. _(v2.A1)_
requirements.reason: The stream collectors handle introducers, quoted bytes, continuations, command-specific numeric boundaries and comments. Split-input and connected drawing fixtures exercise dispatch and recovery.

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 5. RIPscrip commands or command lines may be split across multiple lines with a backslash `\` (ASCII code 92 decimal) just before each split. This helps RIPscrip commands conform to right margins and escape word wrapping.
requirements.reason: The stream collectors handle introducers, quoted bytes, continuations, command-specific numeric boundaries and comments. Split-input and connected drawing fixtures exercise dispatch and recovery.

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: An example:

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 6. RIPscrip must allow for normal text to be intermixed with RIPscrip commands. If unrecognized text appears after a RIPscrip command, on the same line, the text is ignored (the command is not ignored). A line that does not begin with `!|` is considered raw text and is routed to the TTY text window (see "8" below).
requirements.reason: The stream collectors handle introducers, quoted bytes, continuations, command-specific numeric boundaries and comments. Split-input and connected drawing fixtures exercise dispatch and recovery.

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 7. RIPscrip makes provisions for multiple Graphical Windows and multiple Text Windows. A Graphical Window is where all RIPscrip graphics appear. A Text Window is where raw text appears. Raw Text includes ANSI color and cursor movement codes (a subset of VT-100 terminal emulation), and possibly other terminal emulations like VT-100, VT-102, VT-220, etc.

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 8. The vertical bar (`|`) of a RIPscrip command can be followed by a level number. If the 1st character after (`|`) is a numeric digit (1-9), then that's the RIPscrip Command Level. If the very 1st character is NOT a digit 1-9, then it is the command type character and the command is a Level-0 command. If the 1st character is a digit 1-9, and the second character is also a digit, then that defines a sub-level of a RIPscrip level. For example:

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text:
```text
         !|L     RIPscrip Level-0 Command "L"
        !|1L     RIPscrip Level-1 Command "L"
       !|15L     RIPscrip Level-1, sub-level 5 Command "L"
   ```

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: Each of the above examples are unique commands not to be confused with each other. You may continue the sub-levels up to a maximum level of 9 (e.g., `!|123456789<cmd>`").

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 9. Every RIPscrip command includes a command type character. In Level-0 commands, this character immediately follows the vertical bar. At all other levels, it follows the level digits. The command type character may be any of the following characters:

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text:
```text
   ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ
   abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz
   @#$&*()[]{}<>:;'",.?-_=+!
   ```

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 10. Following the command type character are 0 or more parameters. If the command requires a text-string, it is always the LAST parameter. Numeric parameters DO NOT have any delimiters (commas, dashes, spaces, etc.). A variable width numeric parameter may be used as the last parameter. This allows for maximum efficiency.

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: If a RIPscrip command does not have a string parameter, but does have numeric parameters, the last parameter may be shortened to get a bit more efficiency out of it. If the last parameter is more than one digit long and the left-most digits are zeros, they may be omitted. At least one digit must remain though after all of the shortening is done (eg, "0001" can be shortened to "1" but "0000" cannot be shortened to "", it can only be shortened to "0"). _(v2.A3)_
requirements.reason: Numeric-only handlers permit a short last transmitted field at the delimiter. The block-mode string prefix consumes all five fields before the filename.

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: For example, the [RIP_COLOR](2.0-color-modes-and-palettes.md#rip_color) command, used to set the current drawing color, requires one parameter - a color number. If we were going to set color 1 (usually dark blue), then the command would appear formally as follows: _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: Under this shortening clause, you could omit the "0" and make the command appear like this: _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: This allows you to shave one byte off of the command. If you were trying to set color number zero (normally black), then you could still shorten the parameter, but you still have to leave at least one digit there (0), so the command would appear like this: _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: There is an additional optimization that can be used for commands that have no string parameter, and have a reserved parameter as the LAST parameter for that command. In this case, the reserved parameter may be omitted completely, and the value should be assumed to be zero (`0'). Please take note that the previous paragraphs still apply! You can omit the reserved parameter AND shorten the last transmitted parameter so as to squeeze out as many unnecessary characters from the command as possible. _(v2.A2)_

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: Numbers are normally represented in base-36 (unless altered by a RIPscrip command). This compacts numbers down to roughly 3/5 of their decimal form. This numbering system, technically called "Hexa-Tri-Decimal" or "MegaNums" is unlike Hexadecimal which uses 0-9 and A-F. MegaNums take advantage of the entire alphabet, using characters 0-9 and A-Z. _(v2.A0)_

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: See [1.2 Math & Coordinates](1.2-math-and-coordinates.md) about Base Math variations. _(v2.A0)_

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 11. An exclamation mark (`!`) or vertical bar (`|`) character can appear in a RIPscrip text parameter by preceding it with a backslash (`\`). This is known as "quoting" a special character. A literal backslash is represented with a double-backslash (`\\`). Also, in some situations you need to quote specific characters so that they are not misinterpretted. For example, in a button host string, the characters `[`, `]`, `(`, and `$` are used as special host command characters and will need to be quoted (eg, `\[`, `\]`, `\(` and `\$` respectively). See rule #14 below for more details on quoting these special sequences. _(v2.A3)_
requirements.reason: The stream collectors handle introducers, quoted bytes, continuations, command-specific numeric boundaries and comments. Split-input and connected drawing fixtures exercise dispatch and recovery.

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 12. A RIPscrip sequence CAN begin in a column other than column #0, if the exclamation mark prefix is replaced with a Ctrl-A (Start Of Header [SOH] - ASCII character 1) character, or Ctrl-B (STX - ASCII character 2) character. Since 99.9% of all BBS' do not allow users to enter most control characters, users will be unable to begin RIPscrip sequences in the middle of a command line. Only the host should be able to do this. This prevents people from cluttering teleconference, or other areas of a host with spurious RIPscrip sequences.
requirements.reason: The stream collectors handle introducers, quoted bytes, continuations, command-specific numeric boundaries and comments. Split-input and connected drawing fixtures exercise dispatch and recovery.

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: Let's take an example, where we have a piece of raw text and then a RIPscrip command immediately following the text before the carriage return (in this example `<STX>` stands for the STX character): _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text:
```text
    This is raw text<STX>|c01|@1010hello world
    ```

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: In the above example, the text "This is raw text" would be sent to the active text window, then the RIPscrip sequences would be processed - set the color to blue (01), then print the text "hello world" on the screen at (10,10) in meganums or (36,36) in decimal. _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 13. If the last couple of bytes on a RIPscrip text line are backslashes, special care must be taken to make sure that they are not interpreted as a line-continuation. If a literal backslash is desired as the last position on the line, it must be specified as a double-backslash (eg, `\\`). If a line-continuation is used then there would have to be three backslashes used on the line as in the following example: _(v1.54)_
requirements.reason: The stream collectors handle introducers, quoted bytes, continuations, command-specific numeric boundaries and comments. Split-input and connected drawing fixtures exercise dispatch and recovery.

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text:
```text
    !|@2233this is a text line with a literal \\\
    used in the message
    ```
requirements.reason: The stream collectors handle introducers, quoted bytes, continuations, command-specific numeric boundaries and comments. Split-input and connected drawing fixtures exercise dispatch and recovery.

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: This would text output at (22,33) [meganum] the message: _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text:
```text
    this is a text line with a literal \used in the message
    ```

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 14. Some character sequences in text parameter strings can be misinterpreted as RIPscrip command sequences (eg, `$`, `<>`, `((`, `))`, `[`, `]`, `[]`, etc). To avoid syntax confusion these sequences can be "escaped" to indicate that they are actually literal sequences, not to be confused with a RIPscrip command sequence identifier. For example, the sequence: _(v2.A1)_

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text:
```text
    $Name$
    ```

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: would normally be interpreted as a RIPscrip text variable that requires the user's response. If however, you wanted this sequence to be interpretted as literal text, you should perform the following escape sequences:

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text:
```text
    \$Name\$
    ```

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: This makes it so a RIPscrip terminal doesn't misinterpret the dollar signs as text variable delimiters.

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 15. Extraneous information. If too much data is encountered for a particular RIPscrip command, or too little information is found (aside from a short last parameter) then the command is considered "hopelessly corrupted" and discarded. The RIPscrip parser should synchronize to the next vertical bar delimiter to begin the next command. _(v2.A1)_
requirements.reason: Historical v2.A1 surplus rule. The 3.0 numeric collection and dispatch section specifies delimiter wait for completed fixed numeric commands and command-specific collection for counted data. The stream resumes at the next delimiter after malformed input.

requirements.heading: Command Syntax - Parser-Exact Behavior
requirements.text: _Evidence: DLL; [primary traces, artifact identity, native buffer/RIP/ANSI probes and controlled-service limits](../research/issue-7-framing-identification.md)._

requirements.heading: Command Syntax - Parser-Exact Behavior
requirements.text: These sections describe the original RIPtel 3.1 driver’s input pipeline. The original outer buffer consumer tries RIP framing first when RIP emulation is enabled; unconsumed/fallback bytes then enter the text path, where ordinary ANSI parsing remains available. Column-flow interception and disabled text/ANSI paths can consume text separately; the following ANSI examples assume the normal ANSI-enabled text path.

requirements.heading: Introducers
requirements.text: In idle RIP framing, SOH (0x01) or STX (0x02) can introduce a sequence between raw-text bytes. `!` (0x21) is accepted when the preceding byte is CR, LF or form feed and ANSI is idle, or when the client’s beginning-of-line callback returns true. Every introducer must then be followed by `|`; otherwise both the failed introducer and the following byte go through the raw-text fallback. A stray exclamation therefore remains ordinary text.

requirements.heading: Introducers
requirements.text: The client predicate is explicit: RIPtel supplies client-maintained line state. SyncTERM’s separate display-cursor-column rule is not established as this driver’s universal rule. SOH/STX acceptance is an idle-framing rule, not a promise to interrupt an already buffered RIP argument or reset pending ANSI. The [priority examples](#esc-priority-and-resumption) distinguish these states.

requirements.heading: Levels and Sublevels
requirements.text: The original parser accepts **up to nine consecutive digits `1`..`9`** after the initial/chaining pipe. All those digits form the level key; the next non-level digit/byte is the opcode. A **third digit is another level digit**, unlike SyncTERM’s two-digit parser. `0` is never a level digit at any position: `!|0X` attempts level-zero opcode `0`, not a level-zero form of command X. A tenth level digit discards the current command.
requirements.reason: The opcode collector accepts up to nine digits from 1 through 9. A tenth discards the command and 0 always occupies the opcode position.

requirements.heading: Levels and Sublevels
requirements.text: The complete shipped dispatch table defines commands at level zero and single-digit keys 1, 2, 3 and 9 only. Recognizing a deeper key syntactically does not define commands for it: `!|123L…` is an unknown level-123 command, not opcode `3` under level 12. Unknown commands scan to a pipe or line ending. Opcode bytes need not be printable; ESC is the actual opcode in level-1 query, level-2 directory-switch and level-9 block-mode commands.
requirements.reason: The stream descriptor table matches the shipped single-digit levels and their ESC opcode entries. Unknown opcodes and levels skip to a pipe or terminating line ending.

requirements.heading: Levels and Sublevels
requirements.text: **Shipped stale-prefix defect:** after a multilevel prefix, its second byte can remain in the parser’s reused key buffer. Level-zero lookup checks that stale byte and can skip all level-zero records even after a pipe or new line. Checked input `!|123L00000000|c01` plus CRLF dispatches neither command. A subsequent `!|1K|c01` plus CRLF dispatches both: the one-digit prefix clears the stale second byte. A full parser reset also clears it. Implementations that clear unused key bytes correct this defect; do not mistake the defect for a two-digit depth limit or reinterpret a third digit as an opcode.
requirements.reason: SyncTERM resets its level prefix at every command boundary. Split-input tests verify a following level-zero command after both unknown multilevel keys and excessive prefixes.

requirements.heading: Parameters
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4 rules 9-10._

requirements.heading: Parameters
requirements.text: Zero or more parameters follow the command character, with no delimiters between numeric fields. Numeric parameters are fixed-width [MegaNums or UltraNums](1.2-math-and-coordinates.md) per the current base math. A text parameter, if present, is always last. For a command without a text parameter, drop leading zeros from its last transmitted numeric field to shorten it (`!|c01` → `!|c1`). Keep at least one digit in that field. A trailing _reserved_ field may be omitted when the command's receive rules allow it. Omission supplies `0`. The [delimiter](#numeric-collection-and-dispatch) finalizes a short field or an allowed omission. A [period at the start of a numeric field](#period-as-a-zero-field) supplies zero in one byte.
requirements.reason: Command descriptors distinguish short final numbers, optional reserved suffixes and mandatory string prefixes. The wire transfer reads each prefix field at its actual encoded length.

requirements.heading: Chaining, Continuation, and Line Endings
requirements.text: _Evidence: DLL, original byte parser; [checked streams](../research/issue-7-framing-identification.md#distinguishing-streams-and-stages)._

requirements.heading: Chaining, Continuation, and Line Endings
requirements.text: An unquoted pipe dispatches/finishes the buffered command and starts the next command on the same line. **CR, LF and form feed terminate commands**; LF is not unconditionally swallowed inside a command. CRLF is accepted as a physical line ending. Thus `!|Tleft` LF `right` CRLF draws `left`, then routes `right` CRLF as raw text; it does not concatenate the two words.
requirements.reason: The shared live and scene framer dispatches at an unquoted pipe, CR, LF or form feed. Native all-splits cases and exact connected replies/cells distinguish command and raw line endings.

requirements.heading: Chaining, Continuation, and Line Endings
requirements.text: A backslash at a physical line ending continues the current parsing state across CR/LF/form-feed bytes. In a string, `abc\` CRLF `def` becomes `abcdef`. A literal trailing backslash is doubled; two backslashes preserve the literal and allow the line to terminate, while a third continues it. These rules apply to the framing state, before macro/host interpretation.
requirements.reason: The shared framer removes one continuation backslash and skips CR, LF and form-feed runs before resuming. Native even and odd trailing backslash cases, allocation recovery, and live mixed delimiter continuations verify the boundary.

requirements.heading: Escaping in Text Parameters
requirements.text: _Evidence: DLL, text escape branch RVA `0x3aa63–0x3aae2`; [framing capture and original-host-stage checks](../research/issue-7-framing-identification.md#distinguishing-streams-and-stages)._
requirements.reason: Original-driver address and reproduction provenance for the following framing rule.

requirements.heading: Escaping in Text Parameters
requirements.text: Framing does **not** globally remove every backslash. Within a RIP string, quoting SOH, STX or `|` removes the backslash and inserts that byte as data. Other quoted bytes retain both the backslash and the following byte in the string passed to the command consumer. In particular, `\$`, `\[`, `\]`, `\(`, `\!` and `\\` survive framing; continuation at a line ending is the separate rule above.
requirements.reason: All-splits native transcript checks SOH, STX, pipe, other quotes and adjacent command boundaries. Connected raw replies and the 4096-byte working prefix verify wire quote removal before host parsing.

requirements.heading: Escaping in Text Parameters
requirements.text: The subsequent consumer interprets its own text/macro/host syntax. In the ordinary dollar-code scanner, enabled backslash processing removes one quote and skips interpretation of the following character. Host response processing makes [two ordinary passes](5.2-templates-and-conditionals.md#shipped-processing-order), deferring backslash removal in the first and applying it in the second. The preprocessor and command-block parsers have their own scans, so quoting is stage-specific.
requirements.reason: Framing consumes the three wire quotes and passes all others to their consumers. Native command-byte checks and connected host replies verify that ordinary expansion still owns its quotes.

requirements.heading: Escaping in Text Parameters
requirements.text: Checked host text `\$SHIFT\$` transmits literal `$SHIFT$` and never queries SHIFT. Quoting only the opening dollar, `\$SHIFT$`, is insufficient in this two-pass path: the first pass evaluates SHIFT and the second removes the remaining quote; with Shift down the output is `1`. Preserve the quotes through framing and quote both dollar delimiters for the literal-variable example. SyncTERM’s global `\X` collapse before command consumption is a distinct implementation behavior.
requirements.reason: Live CP437 and UTF-8 queries transmit literal SHIFT with both dollars quoted and expand the variable when only its opening dollar is quoted.

requirements.heading: ESC Priority and Resumption
requirements.text: _Evidence: DLL, original buffer consumer `0x57a2`, RIP parser `0x39e90`, ANSI parser `0x37b7c`, autosense `0x355d9`; [native derivation](../research/issue-7-framing-identification.md)._
requirements.reason: Historical provenance, field definitions or table context for the separately tested autosense behavior.

requirements.heading: ESC Priority and Resumption
requirements.text: ESC does not globally preempt all unfinished input. RIP framing runs before ordinary ANSI handling while enabled. In a pending RIP text argument, ESC is data; in numeric fields it can corrupt the command; in the opcode position it can be a valid level-1/2/9 opcode. Only bytes routed to the text path are candidates for ANSI interpretation.
requirements.reason: The stream collectors handle introducers, quoted bytes, continuations, command-specific numeric boundaries and comments. Split-input and connected drawing fixtures exercise dispatch and recovery.

requirements.heading: ESC Priority and Resumption
requirements.text: ANSI recognizes a new ESC sequence while idle. ESC received during its pending ESC/CSI sequence is handled by that state rather than universally restarting at ESC; the checked unsupported ESC final clears the pending sequence, leaving subsequent `[`/`!` as ordinary text. CAN (0x18) and SUB (0x1a) explicitly cancel a pending ANSI sequence. Starting RIP with SOH while ANSI is pending does not itself clear ANSI state.
requirements.reason: Connected TCP cases and a native stream fixture verify ANSI/RIP ownership, nested ESC cancellation, resumable framing and intact local-scene caller input.
requirements.scope: Starting a RIP command via SOH preserves the pending terminal-parser state. ESC, CAN and SUB follow SyncTERM's ordinary ANSI rules.

requirements.heading: ESC Priority and Resumption
requirements.text: Disabling RIP skips RIP framing but leaves the normal ANSI path available. `ESC[2!` can therefore re-enable RIP, including for the next byte in the same buffer. Enable changes the emulation flag; it does **not** reset parser state or reinterpret bytes received while disabled. If an API/menu action disables RIP during a buffered string, re-enabling resumes that string with the disabled interval omitted. Send a new command at a valid framing boundary (for example CRLF then `!|`, or idle SOH followed by `|`); enable is not an implicit scene reset.
requirements.reason: Connected TCP cases and a native stream fixture verify ANSI/RIP ownership, nested ESC cancellation, resumable framing and intact local-scene caller input.

requirements.heading: Raw Text and Error Handling
requirements.text: A line with no accepted introducer is raw text, routed to the current text path (or consumed by active [column flow](3.1-column-text-system.md)). A malformed numeric field discards the command. The parser resumes at the next pipe or line ending. Recovery after multilevel prefixes remains subject to the [stale-prefix defect](#levels-and-sublevels).
requirements.reason: Raw ANSI and active column text retain their existing routing. Malformed ordinary numeric fields and HEADER or Bézier typed records recover at the next pipe or terminating line ending. Level prefixes clear at each boundary.

requirements.heading: Numeric collection and dispatch
requirements.text: While collecting an ordinary numeric field, apply the command's documented radix and its [receive alphabet](1.2-math-and-coordinates.md#working-with-meganums-and-ultranums-by-hand). A lowercase letter therefore discards an unfinished MegaNum command, and a dash discards an unfinished command in either radix. Framing bytes follow their framing rules. A [leading period](#period-as-a-zero-field) completes the field with value zero. After a numeric prefix switches into text collection, use the command's text grammar for the remaining bytes. Lowercase letters and dashes can occur in filename text.
requirements.reason: The stream validates ordinary numeric fields with the descriptor and active ENV radix. Lowercase digits are valid in UltraNum. A completed numeric prefix enables text quoting and preserves literal filename characters.

requirements.heading: Numeric collection and dispatch
requirements.text: For an ordinary fixed-field numeric command such as `L` or `f`, consuming the declared fields ends numeric collection. The parser keeps those values pending across receive chunks and ignores surplus bytes, including further numeric digits, until the command delimiter. A pipe dispatches the pending command and starts the next command on the same line. A terminating CR, LF or form feed dispatches it and closes the line. The handler runs once when the delimiter arrives. The earlier ALPHA 4 draft calls for rejecting surplus bytes. The 3.0 behavior here follows the original fixed-field collector. [Source trace and staged captures](../research/issue-237-fixed-numeric-dispatch.md).
requirements.reason: All 72 positive-count fixed numeric descriptors discard unused bytes in the framer after the fields complete. The original collector and native split-input tests cover the transition to delimiter wait. The connected fixture exercises changing coordinate widths and RGB fields.

requirements.heading: Numeric collection and dispatch
requirements.text: An opcode with zero numeric arguments and no text argument enters the same delimiter wait as soon as the opcode is recognized. For example, bodies `#extra`, `(extra`, `)extra`, `*extra`, `eextra` and `>extra` each dispatch once with zero arguments at the following CR. The [comment opcode](#rip_comment) has a text argument, so `!extra` instead passes `extra` to its text consumer. [Descriptor and state derivation](../research/issue-270-coordinate-and-fixed-field-edges.md#zero-argument-commands).
requirements.reason: All eleven no-field, no-text descriptors discard their suffix and dispatch at any pipe or terminating CR, LF or FF. Original collector captures and packet-split tests include quoted pipes and continuation limits. Comment text takes its own no-expansion path.

requirements.heading: Numeric collection and dispatch
requirements.text: While still collecting a field, a delimiter can finalize a nonempty shortened final number under the [parameter rules](#parameters). A space within unfinished numeric fields instead discards the command. An ordinary counted polygon (`P`) is a variable-argument command. Its count defines the number of vertices, while numeric collection continues to the delimiter under the existing [polygon limits](2.3-shapes-and-fills.md#polygon-counts-and-wire-limits). A space after the listed vertices can therefore discard that polygon.
requirements.reason: A delimiter can finalize a short numeric field. Counted P remains in the numeric collector until the delimiter, so a space even after the declared vertices discards the command and the next pipe remains active.

requirements.heading: Period as a zero field
requirements.text: When the ordinary numeric collector expects the first byte of a field, a period (`.`, byte `0x2e`) supplies the entire field with value zero. This applies in both bases and to any current field width. Advance by one argument using one input byte. If another field follows, its first byte comes immediately after the period and uses that next field's own width and radix. If this completes a fixed numeric-only command, retain the decoded arguments until the delimiter.
requirements.reason: The stream and command readers consume a period at field start as one whole zero argument, including successive fields before a transfer filename.

requirements.heading: Period as a zero field
requirements.text: A period after any digits in an unfinished field is malformed input and discards the command. At that point a delimiter could end a permitted short final field. A period after all fixed numeric-only fields are complete belongs to the ignored surplus. [Original collector trace and supplied captures](../research/issue-240-period-zero-field.md).
requirements.reason: A leading period completes an ordinary numeric field. The stream discards a period within a number as malformed and ignores one in surplus beyond fixed fields.

requirements.heading: Description of RIPscrip Command Levels
requirements.text: As previously described, RIPscrip is composed of ten different levels of commands. The distribution of commands over different levels is done in a rather organized fashion based on command type. Each level of command in general, is progressively higher level in concept. For example, level 0 commands are the most basic building blocks of RIPscrip (eg, graphical primitives, protocol setup, etc). Level one commands are simple user interface objects. Level 2 commands are higher level still in that they deal with context swapping issues. At the highest level, level-9, we deal with binary transfer modes like file transfer protocols, etc. A more formal definition of the currently used levels are:

requirements.heading: ANSI Sequences (Auto-Sensing)
requirements.text: Queries 0/3 while disabled produce no reply. The callback uses only the first ANSI parameter (later parameters are ignored); other selectors produce no reply. The ordinary ANSI decimal accumulator wraps to 16 bits, so `65536` reaches selector 0. Private-prefixed `ESC[?0!` does not invoke this callback. As described [above](#esc-priority-and-resumption), these sequences require the ANSI path; their printed bytes inside an unfinished RIP text argument do not become controls.

requirements.heading: ANSI Sequences (Auto-Sensing)
requirements.text: The phrase format is **`RIPSCRIPxxyyvs`**: two decimal major digits, two minor digits, one vendor code and one vendor subversion. The vendor allocation is 0 generic/unspecified, 1 RIPterm/TeleGrafix, 2 Qmodem Pro. Thus RIPtel’s `030001` means language 03.00, vendor 0, subversion 1; the last two digits are not a two-digit language revision. Product version RIPtel 3.1 and driver build 3.0.7 are separate identities.

This is an interoperability choice permitted by this reconstruction, not a claim to be TeleGrafix. The [complete byte/reply reference](9.2-versions.md#generic-implementation-profile) gives exact bytes and separates this profile from historical replies.

requirements.heading: Scene Header Segments
requirements.text: The shipped [`RIP_HEADER`](#rip_header) is one `h` command with a base block of eight digits in its full-width spelling, followed by concatenated typed segments. The base fields are revision, global flags and segment count; each segment has a type digit and its own fixed fields. A pipe or line ending terminates the complete header. All header numbers use base 64. See the [complete field/flag tables and checked examples](#rip_header); the Alpha 4 flag list is not the shipped 3.0.7 layout. Audio is a stop-playback segment with no table slot.
requirements.reason: The full-width scene header, shortened wire forms and typed segments are verified in RIP3 collections and connected sessions.

requirements.text: _Evidence: corpus._

requirements.heading: Wire-Format Observations from the Corpus
requirements.text: The 116 TeleGrafix-authored RIPtel demo scripts are the best available picture of real 3.x on the wire:

requirements.heading: Wire-Format Observations from the Corpus
requirements.text:
- **SOH marks scene start.** 111 of 116 files begin their _first_ command line with SOH + `|`, then use `!|` for every subsequent line - SOH apparently flags start-of-scene to the 3.0 stream parser, while `!|` remains the 1.54-compatible introducer. (Three files invert the pattern, nearly all-SOH.)
- **The standard prologue** opens 90+ files: `J10|n2000|M08|fZKQO` - base math 36, 2-digit coordinates, 8-bit palette color mode, 1280×960 world frame (see [1.2 Math & Coordinates](1.2-math-and-coordinates.md)).
- **Trailing text after fixed-length arguments is tolerated** and used as inline commentary - the driver stops reading once the fixed fields are consumed: `!|fZKQO                 Set world coordinats to 1280x960`. Chained `!|command|! comment` forms (the `!` comment opcode) are ubiquitous.
- **Harmless corpus typos.** A missing `!` introducer (`|1<ESC>0000$COMPAT$`, CURVES.RIP) and bare `!|` lines pass through the shipping driver without visible failure. For a separator such as `!|----`, the first dash selects [RIP_FILLED_SKEWED_OVAL](2.2-curves.md#rip_filled_skewed_oval). The next dash is invalid in its first numeric field, so the collector discards the command without drawing.
- **Line endings are CRLF**, with `\` continuation across physical lines for long vertex lists (POLYPOLY.RIP). See [6.0 Writing 3.x .RIP Files](6.0-writing-rip-files.md) for authoring conventions.

requirements.text: _Evidence: editorial; format follows 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: The chapters of this reference detail the reconstructed RIPscrip 3.x command set (the consolidated index is [9.0 Command Reference](9.0-command-reference.md)). Each command has these aspects:

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **SYMBOL** - the symbolic constant that is referenced in RIPscrip documents. This is the universal name for the command. _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **FUNCTION** - A short description of the command.

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **LEVEL** - The Command Level. Sub-levels (if any) are represented with decimal points (eg, 1.3.5 for Level-1, Sub-level 3, Sub-Sub-level 5). This is for discussion purposes only. The decimal points are never part of the actual command.

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **COMMAND** - The character identifying the command

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **ARGUMENTS** - The arguments or parameters for the command. Commands that do not require any parameters after the command type character are shown here as "\<none\>". Each parameter is shown in the order it appears in the command, and is represented by a name. If a parameter is numeric, it is followed by a width specifier indicating how many meganum or ultranum digits the parameter consists of (e.g., ":2" means a 2-digit number, or a value between 0 and 1295 for meganums, or 0 and 4095 for ultranums). If a parameter does not have a width specifier, it is by default a text parameter, and should be the last parameter of the command.

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: If a command is variable length (see [POLYGON](2.3-shapes-and-fills.md#rip_polygon)), then it will appear with an ellipe (...), meaning that the command repeats the specific parameters a variable number of times. _(v2.A2)_

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: If the parameter is a variable-width coordinate that can be set by the [RIP_SET_COORDINATE_SIZE](1.2-math-and-coordinates.md#rip_set_coordinate_size), or via the [RIP_HEADER](#rip_header) commands, then the parameter will be followed by a coordinate specifier (e.g., ":XY" means that the parameter is a variable-width coordinate). _(v2.A2, revised v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: A `:CM` color field uses the [active color mode's width and radix](2.0-color-modes-and-palettes.md#color-mode-wire-format). Other color fields use the rules in their command entries.
requirements.reason: Notation or setup for the numeric command examples.

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **FORMAT** - This represents the format of the command, with the starting `!|`, the level digits, the command type character, and the parameter list, with the parameter names in angle brackets. (These parameters are spaced apart, but these spaces never appear in the physical commands.)

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **EXAMPLE** - An actual example of the RIPscrip command. In this reconstructed edition, examples are drawn from the RIPtel corpus wherever one exists.

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **DRAW COLOR** - If YES, then this command uses or affects the current Drawing Color.

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **BACK COLOR** - If YES, then this command uses (or affects) the current background pen drawing color. _(v2.A1)_

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **LINE STYLE** - If YES, then this command uses or affects the current Line Style Pattern.

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **FILL COLOR** - If YES, then this command uses or affects the current Fill Color.

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **FILL PATRN** - If YES, then this command uses or affects the current Fill Pattern.

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **WRITE MODE** - If YES, then this command will take advantage of the current Write Mode (eg, COPY, or XOR).

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **FONT STYLE** - If YES, then this command uses or affects the current Font Style/size/orientation. _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **VIEWPORT** - If YES, then this command adheres to the graphical viewport (draws inside it). Any RIPscrip command that adheres to the graphical viewport will be drawn (when received) only if the viewport is activated. If the viewport is deactivated, then the command is parsed, but completely ignored. _(v1.54, revised v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **USES PORT** - If YES, then this command adheres to, is affected by, or modifies the definition of a [port](7.0-drawing-ports.md). _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **BASE MATH** - Indicates which base math this command responds to. The possible settings are N/A (does not apply), Meganums (uses meganums ONLY), Ultranums (uses Ultranums ONLY), and Current (uses current base math setting as set by either RIP_HEADER or [RIP_SET_BASE_MATH](1.2-math-and-coordinates.md#rip_set_base_math)). _(v2.A2)_

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: In addition - because this is a reconstructed edition - every command entry carries an **_Evidence:_** line naming the sources for that command: `2.00a4`, `HLP` (the RIP_* name in the 3.0.7 inventory), `corpus` (with file names), and/or `SyncTERM` (with ripper.c line cites). Commands attested only by a single source, and argument layouts inferred rather than documented, are flagged in the entry.

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: All fields, including every segment, use **base 64 regardless of current base math**. Spaces shown in the grammar are explanatory and are not sent. `revision` accepts 0 or 1, `flags` accepts 0..31, and the declared segment count accepts 0..10. The accepted revision tags are the inherited 00/01 tags, not a client version number or a new `03` tag; the driver remembers the tag for the scene.

requirements.text: The full-width byte grammar is shown below. The [numeric shorthand rules](#numeric-shorthand-and-segment-selectors) also apply.

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text:
```text
!|h RR FFFF NN S1 S2 … SNN terminator
RR:2, FFFF:4, NN:2                 all base 64
terminator = command pipe, CR, LF, or form-feed

requirements.reason: RIP3 session validates a complete base-64 header before applying staged flags and ordered typed segments. Native split, validation and setup-failure vectors and connected keyboard/mouse, table, backup, reset, snapshot and screen observations cover this source unit. requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: Segments are concatenated **without pipes, commas, spaces or nested introducers**. A pipe ends the entire header and starts the next command. The segment count is not a byte-level terminator: the parser consumes typed segments until a command/line terminator, then validates the declared count and decoded argument length. Ordinary backslash line continuation works inside fields and between segments. Do not append unmarked prose after the final segment.
requirements.reason: The typed collector reaches the command delimiter across receive splits and backslash continuation. Count validation happens after collection.

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: The driver validates the entire decoded header before performing global resets or segment actions. A bad revision, flag value, slot or segment count suppresses its application. Runtime failures in an individual operation do not roll back earlier operations. Segments run in wire order; repeats are permitted. A shipped validation exception is that a declared count of zero ignores parsed extra segments; those extras are not applied. Well-formed headers still send exactly the declared segments.
requirements.reason: RIP3 session validates a complete base-64 header before applying staged flags and ordered typed segments. Native split, validation and setup-failure vectors and connected keyboard/mouse, table, backup, reset, snapshot and screen observations cover this source unit. Refresh, distinct physical port target and remaining reset or clipping effects are tracked separately.

requirements.heading: Numeric shorthand and segment selectors
requirements.text: The three base fields and all ordinary segment fields use the common numeric collector. A period as the first numeric byte completes the whole field with value zero. A period after a digit discards the header. A pipe, CR, LF or form feed can finish the last field of the active base or segment record if that field has at least one digit, even when fewer digits were sent than its stated width. The delimiter then ends the entire header. An empty final field or an incomplete earlier field prevents header dispatch. In the full-width spelling, digits continue filling the current field to its stated width before the next field or selector begins.
requirements.reason: Leading periods supply zero. A delimiter accepts a nonempty short final number; an incomplete header does not apply its operations.

requirements.heading: Numeric shorthand and segment selectors
requirements.text: The original 3.0.7 collector also accepts `<` within an ordinary numeric field. It completes that field immediately with the buffered value, or with zero if the field is empty. It can therefore finish an earlier field while collection continues. Use full-width fields, a leading period, or final-field shortening for the documented wire forms. At a segment selector boundary `<` discards the header. [Original driver evidence](../research/issue-281-header-numeric-shorthand.md#numeric-collection-and-selector-boundaries).
requirements.reason: The stream pads a field completed by < to its descriptor width, treating an empty field as zero. A selector-position < discards the header.

requirements.heading: Numeric shorthand and segment selectors
requirements.text: Each segment starts with a literal ASCII digit `0` through `9`. The same byte selects the segment layout and supplies its first argument. A period or a bare DEL (0x7F) where the type digit is expected discards the header. Within an ordinary numeric field DEL is ignored. Backslash continuation is consumed both within ordinary numeric fields and at selector boundaries. In either position, a pipe ends or discards the current header as appropriate and starts the next command, including after a backslash. [Original driver evidence](../research/issue-281-header-numeric-shorthand.md).
requirements.reason: The stream distinguishes literal selectors from numeric fields and preserves pipe recovery after continuation. Native receive splits cover DEL in both positions.

requirements.heading: Scene Input Gates
requirements.text: In the portable profile, a successfully validated HEADER releases both previous scene gates at its unlock stage. With global flag 4 it then sets both gates, selects pointer 6 (wait), and requests a return to arrow when the mouse gate is released. Apply subsequent header options and segments in their normal order. The mouse gate suppresses pointer-event delivery. The keyboard gate suppresses keyboard activation and ordinary forwarding. The [RESET input actions](5.1-text-variables.md#reset) release just their respective gate.
requirements.reason: Validated HEADER and NO_MORE order, independent device gates and pending arrow rules are exercised through the live session. The optional idle timeout is currently unconfigured.

requirements.heading: Scene Input Gates
requirements.text: NO_MORE, including a configured scene-end timeout, releases both remaining gates. A new validated HEADER performs the same gate release before any relock. If the mouse gate is still set and the return to arrow is pending, select pointer 0 on release. A cleared mouse gate leaves the pointer selected at scene end. The full release also clears the pending return. A pointer appearance change alone leaves both input gates in place. A successful [MCURSOR variable](5.1-text-variables.md#mcursor), a shared SOFT or HARD pointer reset, or an ENV selection that changes the pointer cancels the pending scene return. Wire `RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR` leaves it pending. [Original lock and pointer-release helper](../research/issue-286-reset-input-lock.md).

requirements.heading: Port Zero Initialization
requirements.text: Type-2 **bit 1** deletes unprotected nonzero definitions, selects logical PORT 0, and then initializes the existing PORT 0. **Bit 8** deletes other unprotected nonzero definitions while preserving the current definition and its original protection, then initializes **PORT 0 only if the logical current index is nonzero at that stage**. Bit 8 does not select 0 or initialize the current nonzero port. Its condition is logical selection, not the cached physical rendering target. The segment's supplied slot is not a selector without bit 2.

requirements.heading: Port Zero Initialization
requirements.text: This is an intermediate field initializer, not a full SOFT/drawing reset and not HEADER's later active-gated bounds-only or black-fill leaf. It does not apply SOFT's old-current image-style exception, default unrelated tables, reset TW/ANSI state, clear the outline metric snapshot or the [ESC 7/ESC 8 snapshot](1.4-terminal-ansi-view.md#snapshot-initialization-and-lifetime), or delete a backup. In a surviving nonzero current/protected port, cursor/image/query/pair/viewport state is retained. Definitions actually deleted by bit 1/8 lose their owned state normally; their previously drawn screen pixels remain. Backups, other table selections/configuration, global WORLD and floating queries retain their state unless another requested header operation changes them.

requirements.heading: Port Zero Initialization
requirements.text: The stage order still matters: bit 1 runs before bit 2 selection, which runs before bit 8. With bits 1 and 8 and no intervening nonzero selection, bit 1 initializes 0 and bit 8 subsequently skips initialization because logical current is now 0. A bit-2 selection of a nonzero port before bit 8 can make its condition true. Later activation/bounds/fill/query bits act on the resulting state under their own contracts; they are not implicit initializer effects. Skipping bit 8's initializer leaves every PORT-0 field intact, including its narrow V, image state, cursor and remembered pair.
requirements.reason: The connected initializer changes four PORT 0 fields at the documented stages. Native and live fixtures establish retained activation, queries, raster, selection and backup/pair lifetime.

requirements.heading: Port Bounds Reset and Black Fill
requirements.text: Let **B** be the target port's full stored rectangle, in its backing surface's DEVICE coordinates, **V** its stored viewport, and **S** its physical storage extent. For a screen port, B addresses the shared screen canvas at its stored position; for a bitmap port, B addresses its own bitmap (normally `[0,width) × [0,height)`). Let **C** be the full RIP screen canvas, `[0,0,screen_width,screen_height)`. All rectangles use half-open DEVICE coordinates.

requirements.heading: Port Bounds Reset and Black Fill
requirements.text: **Fill rectangle and color:** use the full B, even when V is much narrower or differently positioned. The viewport's active flag is the **eligibility gate**; V is not the geometric clip for this particular clear. Limit writes to B and the target's actual backing extent; never write outside available storage. The full fill is opaque RGB black, independent of current PAL index 0, STYLE drawing/background colors, W/fill pattern, ANSI background, image-style flags and graphics color-mode precision. It is not an XOR/pattern fill, a stored `PAL[0]` token or permission to rewrite a protected palette to manufacture black. Use the same [fixed black color model as the outer clear](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#physical-screen-clear-and-palette-ordering); index-0 palette changes do not reinterpret these clear pixels as index 0. Bitmap storage must supply the same logical black result when subsequently copied under normal COPY/color rules.
requirements.reason: Connected current/all port fill uses clipped fixed RGB black, with native and live tests of repeated damage, retained viewport, definition state and copied bitmap pixels.

requirements.heading: Port Bounds Reset and Black Fill
requirements.text: This is distinct from the [type-3 TW erase](#text-window-geometry-erase-and-caret-profile), which uses the adopted contract for index 0 of the current graphics palette and homes TW cursors. A type-2 port black fill homes **no graphics/text cursor** and changes no stored cursor request.

requirements.heading: Port Bounds Reset and Black Fill
requirements.text:
- **Screen target:** clear only its full B intersect the physical screen. Screen ports share pixels, so overlapping graphics/TWs can be overwritten even when their definitions are protected; their records are unchanged.
- **Bitmap target:** clear only its own B intersect its bitmap storage. It does not clear/select screen port 0 or copy the bitmap to the screen. Later explicit copies/drawing use the updated bitmap normally.
- **All form:** visit existing active ports 0..35; inactive/undefined entries are skipped and protection does not shield content. The screen result is the union of eligible screen rectangles, plus each eligible bitmap's own clear. Active full-screen port 0 can therefore clear the entire screen; inactive 0 is not silently activated.
requirements.reason: Connected current/all port fill uses clipped fixed RGB black, with native and live tests of repeated damage, retained viewport, definition state and copied bitmap pixels.

requirements.heading: Port Bounds Reset and Black Fill
requirements.text: **Temporary clipping scope — explicit portable completion:** the original screen branch selects a full-port DC region and fills with BLACK_BRUSH; the bitmap branch requests the full rectangle on its own DC without selecting that region in this leaf. Inherited native DC clipping/palette realization is not a portable extra state contract. Apply the black clear over B intersect S uniformly to both kinds; neither a previously narrow bitmap-DC clip nor an OS presentation region defines another protocol mask.
requirements.reason: Connected current/all port fill uses clipped fixed RGB black, with native and live tests of repeated damage, retained viewport, definition state and copied bitmap pixels.

requirements.heading: Port Bounds Reset and Black Fill
requirements.text: After this operation, there is **no separately observable clipping state** beyond the existing port/viewport records. V was not enlarged: subsequent protocol operations still use their own target's V and physical bounds under their usual rules. An implementation may cache host regions, but must scope/refresh them so that an old shared-DC region cannot change later commands' required clipping. Do not serialize a second clip selector, create a damage/scene buffer, or treat the last screen region in the all-port loop as a persistent protocol setting. This is a deliberate portable completion, not a claim to reproduce all historical inherited-DC coverage.
requirements.reason: Connected current/all port fill uses clipped fixed RGB black, with native and live tests of repeated damage, retained viewport, definition state and copied bitmap pixels.

requirements.heading: Port Bounds Reset and Black Fill
requirements.text: **Other state:** the fill retains logical current port, definition/bounds/V, activation/protection, resident/floating queries, graphic/text cursor coordinates, stored image-style rectangle/flags, STYLE/ENV/PAL state and independent backups. It is ordinary erasure, so the [remembered copy pair](7.0-drawing-ports.md#remembered-copy-pairs) is retained and no transfer pair is published. Geometry reset changes only V; its existing DEVICE-relative pair offsets survive as for another viewport edit. Stored image style is not reset as by SOFT; ordinary viewport-fallback interpretation follows an applied new V. Other header bits/global prelude/segments still have their separately specified effects, including any explicit selection, activation, deletion or query reset.

requirements.heading: Port Bounds Reset and Black Fill
requirements.text: Flags `0100` = 4096. On a defined unprotected port with narrow V but **inactive** viewport, it leaves V and inactivity unchanged. On an active unprotected target it sets V=C without painting; on an active protected target it skips the geometry change. The current-fill example still clears that protected active target. `!|h01000001201G00` adds activation bit 1024 to 4096 (total 5120), so an otherwise eligible inactive current port is activated first and then receives C. Flag 2048 (`!|h01000001200W00`) applies the same canvas rectangle to each eligible port, including both targets of the MVP example. Both geometry flags preserve the image style and remembered copy pair. [MVP example](5.1-text-variables.md#mvp).

requirements.heading: Text-window Geometry, Erase and Caret Profile
requirements.text: The geometry helper used by **1024/2048**, and by the existing slot-zero geometry actions of **1/4**, is a maximization that retains its font and window kind, not live `RESET(TW,0)`'s fresh-record initializer. Geometry applies only to an already **defined, active, unprotected** target. It does not create or activate a missing/inactive window; a protected target is skipped entirely, including the geometry operation's cursor home. Eligibility is tested at the operation's stage, after any earlier selection/activation action; it is not frozen at header entry.

Fill with **index 0 of the graphics palette current at this operation**, independently of the current/target ANSI background brush, STYLE background, W/fill pattern and graphics PORT selection/activation/viewport clip. The target is a screen text window even when an offscreen graphics port is selected. This is indexed erase, not a fixed RGB-black clear. The native iterator shares the ANSI-brush paint path recorded for e/ETW; that implementation source is not substituted for the documented portable color rule.

requirements.heading: Character-set descriptor defect
requirements.text: Type 9 advertises only `type:1 charset:2`. Its consumer stores 0 (USASCII) or 1 (KANJI) in the [shared SDCS metadata](5.1-text-variables.md#sdcs). However, validation and application advance **three decoded arguments**, while the byte parser supplies only two. A standalone type-9 segment therefore fails validation. A following segment can instead be read at the wrong offset: constructed `!|h01000002900200060` parses as type 9 followed by a port segment, but validates/applies as charset 0 followed by a mouse segment with flags 0; it performs no port switch. Other malformed combinations can read outside the intended argument structure. There is no independently usable, consistently framed character-set segment in this driver; do not invent a third reserved wire field. This discrepancy is preserved as a shipped defect, not an alternative grammar for well-formed scenes.

requirements.heading: RIP_NO_MORE
requirements.text: This command indicates that RIPscrip commands are complete. This allows the terminal program to activate Mouse Regions, or respond to queued up Mouse Clicks without disturbing the natural flow of the script transmission.

requirements.heading: RIP_NO_MORE
requirements.text: For noise-immunity, the Host should transmit three or more RIP_NO_MORE command consecutively to make sure the message gets to the terminal. The terminal should also time-out if no data is received for a while, and assume RIP_NO_MORE.

requirements.heading: RIP_NO_MORE
requirements.text: The actual duration of the "time-out" is entirely up to the implementor of their terminal program. A good recommended setting would be at least an entire second or more after the receipt of the last RIPscrip command. Raw ASCII/ANSI text does not contribute to the time-out in any way. Only an actual RIPscrip command could cause the time-out counter to be reset (thus starting the time-out countdown all over again). Timing-out is not a pre-requisite to supporting RIPscrip. It is a highly desirable feature to do this, but it is not required. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: RIP_NO_MORE
requirements.text: This command also releases both [scene input gates](#scene-input-gates) previously set with RIP_HEADER. This is useful to prevent the user from clicking on buttons before the scene is completely drawn. See the RIP_HEADER command for more details on this mode of operation. _(v2.A1)_

requirements.heading: RIP_COMMENT
requirements.text: A comment may be embedded inside a RIPscrip file. A comment is one line or longer in length. A comment is a special case of a RIPscrip command letter. In this case, it is the command letter "!". If a "!" is encountered right after a "!|", a "SOH |" or an "STX |" sequence, then the remainder of the command line is a comment. Comments may be line-continued with backslashes just like regular RIPscrip commands can. Some examples of comments might be:

!|c0F|!this is a very long, continued\
comment line.  Line-continued comments\
adhere to standard RIPscrip line continuation rules
```

requirements.heading: RIP_COMMENT
requirements.text: The RIP_COMMENT is treated exactly like any other RIPscrip command for the purposes of parsing RIPscrip commands, EXCEPT that the string is explicitly ignored for [text variables](5.1-text-variables.md). Any use of `|` will be interpreted as the beginning of the next command, and `\` will interpreted as a line continuation. No other characters need be escaped out.

requirements.heading: RIP_GROUP_BEGIN
requirements.text: This command has one special usage, that is to group blocks of commands together into logical groupings. This has no functional use to a terminal program, but to a paint program, it can be used to perform block moves of commands from one area in a scene to another. In order to accomodate this, a standardized method of doing group definitions is being created.

The connected CP437 and UTF-8 tests also execute a numeric command between markers on the same line.

requirements.heading: Numerical Parameters - Formats and Base-Math Variations
requirements.text: Throughout the RIPscrip specification, numeric parameters are used extensively to indicate where to draw things, how to draw things and various other pieces of information. For compactness, we do not use numbers that are normal decimal numbers (base-10). By default, RIPscrip uses base-36 numbers (Hexa-Tri-Decimal or more fondly, MegaNums) which use the digits 0-9 followed by A-Z. This was the original numbering system used in the 1.xx specification.

Working with MegaNums and UltraNums by hand
requirements.text: Both systems are plain positional numerals in RIPscrip's own digit alphabets - **not** the RFC 4648 "Base32"/"Base64" encodings, which share nothing with these beyond the number 64.
requirements.reason: Representation terminology or worked-example table header; behavior is covered by the adjacent digit/value requirements.

requirements.heading: Working with MegaNums and UltraNums by hand
requirements.text:
- **MegaNum digit alphabet (base 36):** `0`-`9` (values 0-9), then `A`-`Z` (values 10-35). Lowercase letters are invalid in a MegaNum field.
- **UltraNum digit alphabet (base 64):** `0`-`9` (values 0-9), `A`-`Z` (values 10-35), `a`-`z` (values 36-61), `#` (value 62), `&` (value 63). Case is significant - `A` is 10 but `a` is 36.
requirements.reason: The wire decoder rejects dashes in both radices and lowercase in MegaNum. UltraNum preserves its lowercase digits. Fixed complete numeric bodies ignore surplus and validate before dispatch. Filename collection preserves case.

requirements.heading: Working with MegaNums and UltraNums by hand
requirements.text: Both receive alphabets exclude the dash (`-`). Use `0` for a zero digit. The [ordinary numeric collector](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#numeric-collection-and-dispatch) describes invalid bytes, the separate period shorthand and how these rules interact with command delimiters. [Original driver derivation](../research/issue-250-meganum-receive-alphabet.md).
requirements.reason: The wire decoder rejects dashes in both radices and lowercase in MegaNum. UltraNum preserves its lowercase digits. Fixed complete numeric bodies ignore surplus and validate before dispatch. Filename collection preserves case.

requirements.heading: Working with MegaNums and UltraNums by hand
requirements.text: **Calculating multi-character values:** most-significant digit first, each position worth a power of the base - value = d₀·bⁿ⁻¹ + d₁·bⁿ⁻² + … + dₙ₋₁ (b = 36 or 64). To _decode_: MegaNum `1M` is 1×36 + 22 = 58; MegaNum `HR` is 17×36 + 27 = 639; UltraNum `R9a` is 27×64² + 9×64 + 36 = 111,204. To _encode_ a decimal value, take `value ÷ b^k mod b` for each position, highest power first: decimal 250 as a 2-digit MegaNum is 250 ÷ 36 = 6 remainder 34 → `6Y`; the same 250 as a 2-digit UltraNum is 250 ÷ 64 = 3 remainder 58 → `3w`; decimal 360 (a full circle in degrees) is `A0` in MegaNums.
requirements.reason: Number conversion uses positional base 36/64 arithmetic. J decodes in base 36, sets the current environment and falls back to MegaNums for an invalid setting. Environment and connected wire tests cover changes of width and radix.

requirements.heading: Working with MegaNums and UltraNums by hand
requirements.text: **Fixed widths and zero padding:** the full width of a `:2` field is two digits in the current base, zero-padded on the left (decimal 10 is `0A` as a 2-digit MegaNum, `0A` as a 2-digit UltraNum too). Numeric parameters have no delimiters between them - the fixed widths are what let the parser slice them apart, so a missing pad digit shifts every following parameter. A [period at the start of a field](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#period-as-a-zero-field) supplies a complete zero in one byte. `:XY` coordinate parameters are 2 digits by default, adjustable via [RIP_SET_COORDINATE_SIZE](#rip_set_coordinate_size); `:CM` color parameters use [two current-base digits in Color Map mode or four UltraNum digits in Direct RGB mode](2.0-color-modes-and-palettes.md#color-mode-wire-format). Per-command field widths are collected in [9.0 Command Reference](9.0-command-reference.md).
requirements.reason: Number conversion uses positional base 36/64 arithmetic. J decodes in base 36, sets the current environment and falls back to MegaNums for an invalid setting. Environment and connected wire tests cover changes of width and radix.

requirements.heading: Working with MegaNums and UltraNums by hand
requirements.text: **Last-parameter rules:** a variable-width numeric parameter may be used only as the last parameter of a command, and syntax rule 10 allows the last numeric parameter to be shortened by dropping leading zeros (`!|c01` → `!|c1`); a trailing reserved parameter can be omitted when its command permits it ([framing and parameter rules](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#parameters)). A text string is likewise always last and never number-encoded.
requirements.reason: The final numeric and omitted reserved cases follow each command descriptor. Numeric fields before transfer filenames retain their required boundaries.

requirements.heading: Working with MegaNums and UltraNums by hand
requirements.text: **Base Math switching:** the global setting starts at base 36, is changed with [RIP_SET_BASE_MATH](#rip_set_base_math) or the [RIP_HEADER](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#rip_header) flags, and resets to base 36 on any [RIP_RESET_WINDOWS](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_reset_windows). Commands documented as exceptions ignore it - direct-RGB color values and drawing-palette RGB parameters are always UltraNums, and RIP_SET_BASE_MATH's own parameter is always a MegaNum.

requirements.heading: Working with MegaNums and UltraNums by hand
requirements.text: Parser-side edge cases (early termination behavior, out-of-alphabet bytes, and the like) are implementer material - see the [MegaNum encoding techspec](../../1.54/techspecs/1.1-meganum-encoding.md) and the [2.0 stream conventions delta](../../2.0/techspecs/1.0-stream-conventions-delta.md).

requirements.heading: Choosing MegaNums vs UltraNums
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; corpus; SyncTERM (ripper.c:9107-9131)._

requirements.heading: Choosing MegaNums vs UltraNums
requirements.text: Which base a command's parameters use is a **global mode**, not a per-command choice: after `!|J10` every base-math-governed field in every subsequent command reads as base-36; after `!|J1S`, base-64. Individual commands differ only in whether they _obey_ the mode - each command entry in this reference carries a base-math line, which is one of:

requirements.heading: Choosing MegaNums vs UltraNums
requirements.text:
- **current setting** - the common case: coordinates, dimensions, radii, vertex counts, and most numeric fields.
- **MegaNums only** - commands that must parse before the mode is knowable or that reset it: [RIP_SET_BASE_MATH](#rip_set_base_math) itself (its `10`/`1S` argument is always base-36), and anything that follows a [RIP_RESET_WINDOWS](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_reset_windows) (a reset silently returns the mode to base 36 - re-send `J` immediately if the scene needs otherwise).
- **UltraNums only** - direct-RGB color values and drawing-palette RGB parameters (see [2.0 Color Modes & Palettes](2.0-color-modes-and-palettes.md)).
- **not numeric** - text parameters (always last in a command) ignore base math entirely.

requirements.heading: Worked encodings
requirements.text: A field's value is `first_digit × base + second_digit` (and so on for wider fields). Digit values: `0`-`9` = 0-9, `A`-`Z` = 10-35, then (UltraNums only) `a`-`z` = 36-61, `#` = 62, `&` = 63.
