requirements.heading: Interoperability caution
requirements.text: _Evidence: corpus; SyncTERM._

requirements.heading: Interoperability caution
requirements.text: **No UltraNum usage has been observed in the wild.** All 116 TeleGrafix demo scripts run `J10` MegaNums, and SyncTERM cannot parse UltraNums at all - its number reader (`parse_mega`, ripper.c:9107-9131) treats `a`-`z` as _case-insensitive base-36 digits_, so a base-64 scene would silently mis-decode rather than fail. MegaNums are the only wire-proven encoding; treat UltraNums as documented-but-unexercised.

requirements.heading: World Coordinate Systems
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A0._

requirements.heading: World Coordinate Systems
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; WP §4.1; corpus._

requirements.heading: World Coordinate Systems
requirements.text: Starting with the v2.0 specification of RIPscrip - carried unchanged into 3.x - the language is resolution independent through a "world coordinate system": you can alter the base coordinate system used to address the video's physical device coordinate system. Each coordinate system is called a "Coordinate Frame". There are two distinct levels of coordinate systems, from the lowest (least abstract) to the highest level (the drawing board):

requirements.heading: World Coordinate Systems
requirements.text: 1. **DEVICE COORDINATE FRAME** - the resolution of the actual display device. This is not determined as part of the RIPscrip language itself, it is actually determined by the terminal - based upon whatever type of video hardware is present (and what mode the user has chosen).

requirements.heading: World Coordinate Systems
requirements.text: 2. **[WORLD COORDINATE FRAME](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_set_world_frame)** - This is the master coordinate system. This is the global set of coordinates, set by [RIP_SET_WORLD_FRAME](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_set_world_frame) (wire opcode `f`). Ideally, it should be higher in dimensions than the Device Frame so that you do not lose resolution when "mapping" X/Y coordinates from the world coordinate system to the device coordinate system. If the dimensions of the World Frame are the same as the Device Frame then the mapping operation between World and Device Frames are identical and can be skipped entirely since an X/Y coordinate in the World Frame directly corresponds to a pixel location in the Device Frame.

requirements.heading: World Coordinate Systems
requirements.text: The white paper advertises a maximum **32,767 × 32,767** world frame, but that is **not the recovered RIPtel 3.1 setter limit**. The original [RIP_SET_WORLD_FRAME](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_set_world_frame) handler accepts **0..65535** in each dimension, including zero and 32768..65535, and stores/activates those unsigned word values. The [WORLD variable](5.1-text-variables.md#world) normally stores the same range and has an additional asymmetric oversized-value defect. Do not infer a signed-16-bit world-dimension validation gate from the white paper or confuse stored dimensions with the signedness of individual drawing coordinates. _Evidence: [original wire/macro handlers and native boundary matrix](../research/issue-23-environment-query-names.md#native-callback-activation-and-wire-checkpoint)._ Since versions of the RIPscrip specification prior to v2.0 were based on a 640x350 resolution without any World Frame, the World Frame defaults to 640 across and 350 high for backward compatibility; the `$COMPAT$` text variable restores that whole 1.54 environment (see [1.0 Introduction](1.0-introduction.md#differences-from-154)).

requirements.heading: World Coordinate Systems
requirements.text: A real 3.x example, from the RIPtel demo prologue:

requirements.heading: World Coordinate Systems
requirements.text:
```text
!|fZKQO                 Set world coordinats to 1280x960
```

requirements.heading: World Coordinate Systems
requirements.text: (comment and spelling TeleGrafix's own, ONLINE.RIP): `ZK` = 35×36+20 = **1280**, `QO` = 26×36+24 = **960**. The demos thus run in a 1280×960 world regardless of the user's actual screen mode. Alternate frames observed in the corpus: `HSDC` = 640×480, `HR9S` = 639×352, `HRDC` = 639×480. _Evidence: corpus._

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A0._

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4 (the treatment carries into 3.x unchanged)._

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Mathematics, unlike graphics, is abstract in nature. Graphics on the other hand, is very discrete in nature. A pixel in graphics is the smallest displayable element on a graphics screen (Picture Element). The corresponding concept in mathematics is a single point. A pixel has a discrete size and shape in graphics whereas in mathematics, a point is infinitely small and occupies no physical space in the cartesian coordinate system in which it exists.

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: In graphics we use the concept of coordinates and points to specify where a pixel is located. If graphics were like mathematics where a pixel was infinitely small, a graphics monitor wouldn't show anything other than black because a pixel would be infinitely small surrounded by blackness. But this is not the case. Graphics hardware has to have pixels defined as discrete areas of the screen - addressable areas of the screen that can be set to a particular color. This is how we see things on the screen, as individual pixels of data used together to represent some kind of image.

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Just like the point in mathematics, a line is infinitely thin, but has length. A line is composed of an infinite number of points between the beginning and ending locations of the line.

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Relating these two distinctly different concepts to each other though doesn't always lend itself to a simple situation to understand. On the surface, a pixel's coordinate location appears to be the same thing as it is in mathematics. But, when you get into deeper issues of graphics theory this isn't truly the case because of the difference in sizes of a point compared to a pixel. In math, points don't have to be on even integer boundaries - they can be fractional. A point can be at (2.53,1.295), whereas in graphics, a pixel cannot be at a fractional location - there's no such thing as a part of a pixel!

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: A graphics screen is designed so that every pixel location on the screen has a unique location specified (in human terms) as an X/Y coordinate pair. This is called the Cartesian Coordinate System. It is by far one of the easiest ways of representing a coordinate in a two-dimensional world like a monitor. If you zoom in closely on a monitor and look at the layout of pixels and their relationships to coordinates, you might see something like this:

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: If you look at the previous diagram, you can see that there is a grid of pixels that is 24 pixels wide (the X direction) and 10 pixels high (the Y direction). Each of the squares is a black pixel. The pixels contain a "#" are considered white pixels. There are four pixels that are ON in this diagram, at locations (11,2), (12,2), (11,3) and (12,3). This is how graphics hardware addresses graphics pixels, by specifying an X/Y coordinate location for a pixel to turn it on or off (or more generally, to set it to a particular color).

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: If you look closely at the locations of the coordinates in the previous diagram, the X/Y coordinates address the physical pixel cells themselves. Each pixel cell is separated by infinitely thin lines - the pixel cells' borders so to speak. Now, each pixel is physically adjacent to the ones next to it and there are no gaps between them. This is the way graphics hardware works.

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Now that we've described the way graphics hardware addresses pixel locations, let's look at why it's not really the best way of describing graphics mathematically. For the hardware, this is the best way of handling things, but mathematically, it's not.

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: The world of graphics hardware has many different facets. One graphics display device can often times display graphics at different resolutions. A typical video card on the IBM-PC can display graphics at 320x200, 640x350, 640x400, 640x480, 800x600, 1024x768 and even as high as 1280x1024 and higher. That's quite a bit of difference in pixel grids (like the one shown earlier). Not only can the number of pixels change horizontally and vertically, but when the resolutions get higher, the pixels get smaller and harder to see. When graphics hardware can achieve a resolution of infinity by infinity, then we will have achieved perfect sight (like what we see around us). But obviously, this will probably never happen in our lifetimes (or our great granchildren's for that matter).

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: What would happen if you had a line drawn on a graphics screen from coordinates (0,0) to (639,349) at 640x350 resolution? You would have a nice little line on the screen that stretches from the upper-left corner to the lower-right corner. Now, if you drew the same line at 800x600 resolution? Your line would no longer go all the way to the bottom of the screen or to the far right of the screen. It would stop about 2/3'rds of the way down and over.

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: The problems start to come up with mathematics and graphical representations when we try to make something look the same at one resolution as it does in another (resolution independence). Sure you can translate a coordinate in one resolution to some other coordinate in a different resolution. All you need to know are the dimensions of each resolution and a bit of algebra. But pixels aren't the same thickness! The line described previously could still be drawn properly to the lower-right of the screen, but it would appear a lot thinner. You could try drawing two lines offset by one pixel location and you would come "close" to the original thickness of the line at 640x350 resolution, but it wouldn't be a perfect match. A perfect match is a rare thing when dealing with different resolutions.

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Now, on to the real issue at hand here: translation of coordinates. We won't worry about the size of pixels, but will concentrate on getting the locations of points correct at different resolutions. Let's say you have a screen at 640x350 resolution with two filled rectangles drawn on it. The first rectangle is drawn from (2,1) to (4,3) and the second one is drawn from (5,1) to (7,3) like this:

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Now, you notice that both rectangles are right next to each other. There are no gaps between them. Now, if you tried to draw these same two rectangles on a graphics screen that was 1280x700 pixels in size, and tried to make it appear in the exact same location and size on the monitor, you would have to translate the corners of the rectangles to the new resolution and re-plot the rectangles. Now, 640x2 is 1280 and 350x2 is 700 so our new resolution is exactly twice as large in both the X and Y directions (this is RARELY the case!). So, in order to translate our original coordinates to this resolution we simply multiply the numbers by 2. Pretty simple. Our previous rectangles in their old untranslated state and the newly translated ones would be:

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: |             | Untranslated  | Translated      |

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Now, let's plot these two rectangles on our new graphics screen at the newly translated coordinates:

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: What happened? We now have a black line in between the two rectangles. That's definitely not what we wanted to happen. Why did this happen? It's partly because of the nature of graphics hardware in the way they address pixels, and partly the way we humans think of pixels mathematically from a programming standpoint. What we need is a better mathematical representation of pixels and graphics coordinates so that when we translate coordinates these things don't happen.

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: As we mentioned earlier, the lines on the above diagram represent the borders around each pixel. Each of these lines, like their mathematical counterparts, are infinitely thin. The only thing in the above diagram that has any size (or area) physically are the pixels themselves. Since the boundary lines around the pixels are defining the area that the pixel will occupy, it makes sense that we should think of those lines as the actual coordinates. If we think of the areas in between the pixels as the actual coordinates, we can think of pixels as the areas in between coordinates that are filled in with color. So, if we said to draw a filled in rectangle like we did earlier, we would actually be saying "fill in this rectangle's interior". Just like coloring books as a child, you have to stay inside the lines (or at least we're supposed to). Think about pixels as spots between the lines that get filled in with color just like a coloring book - the only difference is, a pixel cannot go outside the lines (don't you wish you were a pixel when you were younger?).

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Using this new way of thinking of graphics is not very difficult, it just seems a bit odd -especially if you've been working with graphics for awhile. To draw the previous two rectangles properly the coordinates for them would have to be changed somewhat - like this:

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: **(old method)**

requirements.text: |             | Untranslated  | Translated      |

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: **(new method)**

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: |             | UNTRANSLATED  | TRANSLATED      |

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Notice that the untranslated rectangles' coordinates are almost the same. In fact, the upper-left coordinates haven't changed at all. The only coordinates that have changed are the lower-right coordinates, and only by one pixel location. Now, if we draw these two rectangles using our new mathematical model for graphics, we would get the following (in both resolution examples:

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: If you look closely at the two graphs above you may notice a subtle difference in the numbering of the coordinates. The numbers are all there, but instead of labeling the cells themselves with coordinates, we have labeled the lines in between as the coordinates. When we say to draw a rectangle from (2,1) to (5,4) we are saying to draw a filled in area "between" coordinate lines 2 and 5 in the X direction and 1 and 4 in the Y direction. If you look closely at the upper left diagram, you will notice that is exactly what we have done. Now look closely at the upper right diagram. There are no gaps between the rectangles now. Also if you look at the translated coordinates, the right edge of the first rectangle is at X coordinate 10, and the left edge of the second rectangle is also at X coordinate 10. But they don't overlap each other. That's the part about this new way of thinking about things that gives people the hardest time.

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: So far so good. Let's look at another example - one which draws the same two rectangles but this time, let's not fill them in. The diagram below shows the two at both example resolutions:

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Not what you thought would happen, was it? This example illustrates a key point in our mathematical model of graphics: that there is a difference between filled objects and outlined objects. Filled objects fill everything inside an enclosed area whereas an outline (one or more lines) uses pixels to approximate an infinitely thin line. When lines and points are plotted on the video device, they are "rounded up" to the next highest pixel location. So, a point at (4,2) would not be on the intersecting lines at (4,2), it would be a pixel activated between 4 and 5 on the X axis and 2 and 3 on the Y axis. Look at the upper right diagram to convince yourself this is the case. Filled-in areas on the other hand, do not round up to the next highest pixel locations. They always fill in an area in-between the boundary lines. This means that in a filled-in rectangle, the right and bottom edges are "off by one" so to speak.

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: To better illustrate these two different situations, we will draw a filled-in rectangle and a non-filled rectangle both using the same dimensions at the same resolution, then we will superimpose them on top of each other to better show the differences;

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Notice that the two rectangles are not the exact same size. Both the left and top edges are at the exact same locations, but in the case of the unfilled rectangle, the right and bottom edges are one pixel over and down. This shows that lines and points are rounded up to the next highest pixel location (the first pixel after the coordinate), but filled areas fill between the boundary lines. This seemingly odd way of doing things becomes extremely important when you deal with one image at different resolutions - as you saw with the case of translating two filled-in rectangles earlier from one resolution to another.

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: In a very real sense, you could easily think about coordinates and graphics in two different ways. The way to think about them depends on the type of graphics operation being performed. If you are dealing with a fill operation of some kind, then you think about the drawing surface with coordinate lines "in between" the physical pixel cells. If you are dealing with a line drawing situation (or drawing points, circles, etc), then you can think of coordinates directly addressing the pixel cells themselves (just like when we began this conversation at the beginning of this section). When dealing with line drawing operations, there is no difference in mathematical models - there's only a difference when you get into filling areas in. Whichever method of thinking of things works best for you, use.

requirements.text: Other filled objects work the same way as do filled rectangles. For example, consider an unfilled polygon with the following vertices: _(v2.A4)_

requirements.text: With this polygon we would have a polygon that looks like the left diagram below. The right diagram is what it would look like if it were filled and had a border drawn at the same time (the different shaded blocks indicates which is border, fill-color, or both): _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Taking a second example. Let's consider an unfilled oval centered at (7,3) with a horizontal radius of 8 and a vertical radius of 4. The unfilled oval is depicted in the left diagram below. The diagram on the right is the same oval with the border drawn and also filled in. Notice how the border is drawn in relation to the filled-in interior and how it adheres to resolution independence. _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: If you look closely at the right diagram, you will notice that the oval isn't "balanced". This is because in this situation, the oval is centered about a particular point, but the filled oval is partially offset on an odd-boundary - the filled interior is 8 pixels to the left of the center point (inclusive), and 7 pixels to the right of the center point (inclusive). This is due to the resolution independent nature of filled regions. If you need to draw a perfectly smooth filled oval, draw one with a solid fill and with borders enabled, both with the same drawing and fill color. _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: **Practical summary:** for fills, think "coordinates between pixels"; for lines, points, and curves, think "coordinates address pixels" - the models only diverge for filled interiors. Filled polygons and curved regions follow the same fill-between-lines rule, with their borders (optional since 2.0, see [2.3 Shapes & Fills](2.3-shapes-and-fills.md)) rounding up like lines. _Evidence: 2.00a4 (the treatment carries into 3.x unchanged)._

requirements.text: This command sets the Base Math used extensively throughout the RIPscrip language. By default, the RIPscrip language uses Base-36 math for all of its numeric parameters. A two digit Base-64 number can hold a number from 0-4095 which is considerably larger.

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_COORDINATE_SIZE
requirements.text: This command sets the full digit width for subsequent fields marked `:XY`. The default XY width is two digits. Fields with literal widths retain those widths, including the four two-digit corners in [RIP_TEXT_WINDOW](1.4-terminal-ansi-view.md#rip_text_window). This command allows you to alter this size. In 1.x versions of RIPscrip, the maximum size of a parameter was in the X direction and the maximum value was 639. This could safely be represented in two meganum digits. In 2.0 of RIPscrip and beyond, we introduce a world coordinate system into the specification which allows you to use a much higher resolution for your drawing environment. This facilitates resolution independence. To provide for future expandability when ultra-high resolution devices might exist, the possibility of an X or Y coordinate exceeding 4095 might occur. Since this is the largest value that can be accomodated in a 2-byte UltraNum, we offer an option that provides for extensibility.
requirements.reason: Native and connected vectors verify active Base Math and XY width, omitted or encoded reserves, malformed recovery and reset to width two.

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_COORDINATE_SIZE
requirements.text: Using this parameter to expand the byte size beyond 2 will make a RIPscrip file bigger. This is because every X/Y coordinate will be expanded in size by a certain number of bytes, and since these are the fundamental values in any graphical environment, it will result in larger RIPscrip files. In practice, this command should be used with caution. When situations permit, do not use this command, or use it with a byte size of 2 (the default). This will keep files from ever getting larger than they would be by default.

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_COORDINATE_SIZE
requirements.text: Values 2–5 set both the active XY width and the saved width of the current environment. Value 0 sets both to 2. A nonzero value outside 2–5 leaves both widths as they were without a width error. With graphics processing disabled, the command leaves the width alone. Otherwise, a protected current environment rejects the change and reports its protection error before evaluating the width. [Original handler and setter](../research/issue-270-coordinate-and-fixed-field-edges.md).
requirements.reason: Wire width 0 selects 2, invalid nonzero sizes preserve the active width, and current ENV protection rejects the change. The optional reserve is checked in active Base Math and discarded.

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_COORDINATE_SIZE
requirements.text: Both fields use active Base Math. The three-digit reserve is optional at the delimiter. It can also be supplied as fewer valid digits or as one [leading period](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#period-as-a-zero-field). Every accepted spelling supplies reserve zero. For example, `!|n3`, `!|n3A`, `!|n3.` and `!|n3001suffix` followed by CR all set XY width 3 in an unprotected current environment. In the last case the three digits complete the reserve, so the suffix is ignored. `!|n0` and `!|n.` request width 2. `!|n` lacks a width, and `!|n30.` has a period inside the reserve. Both are discarded. [Staged cases](../research/issue-270-coordinate-and-fixed-field-edges.md#staged-captures).

requirements.heading: The Port Model at a Glance
requirements.text: A drawing port is an area where graphics can be drawn. At any moment there is exactly one **current drawing port** - the port that receives graphical drawing operations. Ports come in two types:
requirements.reason: WORLD/device ratios, port selection, projection and clipping run through the live drawing and viewport paths. The geometry fixture checks both directions of the conversion.

requirements.heading: The Port Model at a Glance
requirements.text:
1. **Screen (visual) drawing ports** - rectangular regions of the user's actual screen. Drawing to a screen port appears immediately. Screen ports divide the display into separate drawing areas that can be switched between at will.
2. **Offscreen bitmap drawing ports** (also called **clipboard ports**) - drawing surfaces that are not part of the visible screen. Graphics drawn to an offscreen port are invisible until copied to a screen port. Offscreen ports are used to compose scenes out of sight and reveal them whole, to cache bitmaps loaded from disk, to save screen regions under dialog boxes, and to drive transition animation.
requirements.reason: WORLD/device ratios, port selection, projection and clipping run through the live drawing and viewport paths. The geometry fixture checks both directions of the conversion.

requirements.heading: The Port Model at a Glance
requirements.text: The 3.0 driver additionally distinguishes **snapshot ports** - offscreen ports created by capturing screen contents - in its error strings ("No mouse/button fields on offscreen drawing ports"). _Evidence: HLP._
requirements.reason: Original-driver names for offscreen storage. Capture and mouse eligibility are defined under the corresponding RIP commands.

requirements.heading: The Port Model at a Glance
requirements.text: Ports live in a 36-slot [data table](7.1-data-tables.md), entries numbered 0-35. **Port 0 is always the screen** - it is the full size of the display, exists at all times, and cannot be created, deleted, or redefined (confirmed verbatim by the 3.0.7 driver's error strings "Can't delete graphics port #0" and "Can't create drawing port #0"); ports 1-35 are user-definable ("The given port number is invalid (1-35 only)"). Mouse fields, clickable buttons, text windows, and resident query expressions are screen-only and may not be placed on an offscreen port. _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._
requirements.reason: WORLD/device ratios, port selection, projection and clipping run through the live drawing and viewport paths. The geometry fixture checks both directions of the conversion.

requirements.heading: The Port Model at a Glance
requirements.text: Each port has its own coordinate origin - (0,0) is the upper-left corner of the port - and its own remembered drawing state, and every port has an associated **viewport**: a clipping rectangle inside the port that defines its drawing limits and shifts the drawing origin to its own upper-left corner. Anything drawn beyond the viewport's edge is truncated (clipped). By default a port's viewport is the full size of the port. So a point at (50,50) inside a viewport that starts at (40,40) inside a port that starts at (25,25) on the screen lands at screen position (25+40+50, 25+40+50) = (115,115). _Evidence: 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_WORLD_FRAME
requirements.reason: Reconciled with adopted PR #56 range/target contract. ENV stores unsigned word WORLD dimensions 0..65535 independently of device size. Wire f rejects either oversized dimension; WORLD rejects only when both exceed 65535 and otherwise stores each low word. WORLDH/W two-argument CUR errors while any other target edits current; query targets retain normal validation. Native literal 0/1/32767/32768/65535/65536/65537 matrices cover both wire radices, current/noncurrent storage, both axes, defined/undefined/invalid target text and recovery. Positive 65535 frames project with wide arithmetic; zero records remain observable while projection requests reject before division. Real CP437/UTF-8 sessions on five rasters verify maximum-frame pixel placement, zero-state queries and nonfatal drawing rejection, asymmetric overflow, axis defects and drawing after restoration. No existing-art corpus replay or unsafe native zero-frame behavior is claimed.

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_WORLD_FRAME
requirements.text: This command sets the dimensions of the World Coordinate Frame. This Frame is the Global Coordinate Space of the RIPscrip drawing screen. It is not the exact size of the Device Frame - that is a lower level coordinate system. With this frame, you can "map" your scenes into something, say a 1024x1024 grid and let the terminal worry about mapping it into whatever device coordinates it is using (eg, 640x350, 800x600, etc). Any coordinates used for setting viewports or other such things will be specified in World Frame Coordinates. Actual drawing primitives will use the current Drawing Frame's coordinates - another level of coordinate mapping. This allows you to do things like draw full screen images inside a tinier window, leaving additional drawing space on the screen for other images.

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_WORLD_FRAME
requirements.text: This command is the single biggest semantic change of the 2.0/3.x era: it redefines the logical coordinate space away from 1.54's fixed 640×350, making every subsequent coordinate frame-relative. It closes the standard corpus prologue in over 100 files as `!|fZKQO` - `ZK`/`QO` decode to **1280×960**, the square-pixel MegaNum world frame recommended by the [2.00a4 RIP_HEADER discussion](../../2.0/ripscrip/1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#rip_header) and supported by the shipped [environment header segment](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#rip_header). Alternate observed frames: `HSDC` = 640×480, `HR9S` = 639×352, `HRDC` = 639×480 (BLUEFADE.FN works at 640×350 and TELPORT.FN's comments then "reset our environment back to 1280x960 world coordinates"). ONLINE.RIP demonstrates the driver's argument-parsing tolerance with an inline trailing comment: `!|fZKQO                 Set world coordinats to 1280x960` _(sic)_. _Evidence: corpus._

requirements.heading: Precision of translation
requirements.text: If the World Coordinates are larger than the Device Coordinates, then when you translate World Coordinates to Device Coordinates, there will be pixel-perfect translation. This means that translation will be unambiguous - they will convert to pixel coordinates without there being any discrepency. For example, if your Device Coordinates are 640x350 and your World Coordinates are 1280x700, then a Point in World Coordinate space at (0,0) and (1,0) will both translate to the Device Coordinates (0,0) and (0,0) respectively. This is because the World Coordinate space is twice as large as the Device Coordinate space. If on the other hand the Device Coordinates were 1280x700 and the World Coordinate space were 640x350, then the World Points (0,0) and (1,0) would translate to (0,0) and (2,0) respectively. Notice that in the World Coordinates, the pixels were adjacent. But in the Device Coordinates, they are separated by a one pixel gap.
requirements.reason: WORLD/device ratios, port selection, projection and clipping run through the live drawing and viewport paths. The geometry fixture checks both directions of the conversion.

requirements.heading: Precision of translation
requirements.text: In summary, World Coordinates should always be equal to or greather than the size of the Device Coordinate Frame, otherwise disparity will exist in the translations. Since coordinate translation will almost ALWAYS be from World -> Device coordinates, everything will be fine if the World Frame has a larger resolution than the Device Frame. The same holds true for the inverse equations to translate from Device to World coordinates. If the World Coordinate Frame is larger than the Device Coordinate Frame, then any point that is translated from Device -> World Coordinates (a Mouse X/Y location for example), might not translate over precisely - skipping over pixel spaces in the World Frame - this is simply because of the precision of translation and cannot be overcome mathematically since a Mouse Pointer's location is pixel based - it doesn't have any finer locations than on pixel boundary locations (there's no such thing as a fractional pixel location in graphics hardware - only mathematically).

requirements.heading: RIP_VIEWPORT
requirements.text: This command defines the (X,Y) pixel boundaries of the RIPscrip graphics window, which will contain all RIPscrip graphics output. ASCII/ANSI text will be displayed in the current TTY window defined by the [RIP_TEXT_WINDOW](1.4-terminal-ansi-view.md#rip_text_window) command. (x0,y0) defines the upper-left corner of the graphics viewport, and (x1,y1) defines the lower-right corner (inclusive). The viewport may be deactivated by setting all parameters to zero (0). This suppresses graphical operations such as IMAGE display; it is not a universal gate on configuration commands. In RIPtel 3.1, wire [IMAGE_STYLE](4.1-jpeg-images.md#rip_image_style) still replaces the stored image rectangle/flags while inactive, and reactivation preserves that new setting. Its IMGSTYLE macro counterpart has a separate inactive-target rejection. _Evidence: [original setter/activation/display sequence](../research/issue-21-image-style.md#integration-review-inactive-viewport-wire-setter)._

requirements.heading: RIP_VIEWPORT
requirements.text: The viewport belongs to the current [drawing port](7.0-drawing-ports.md), but the shipped RIPtel 3.1 producer differs from the draft's port-relative/clamped description. It converts both supplied corners directly from world to device coordinates, normalizes their order, adds one to right/bottom for the inclusive endpoint, and stores the result as the port's viewport in its drawing context. It **does not add the screen port's origin or intersect the rectangle with port bounds**. A screen port's initial viewport is copied from its screen bounds; a later viewport definition replaces it with these directly converted values. Drawing is then clipped by that stored rectangle and by the underlying drawing surface. _Evidence: original handler 0x20f87 / helper 0x33cc6 and [producer/placement probe](../research/issue-11-pixel-pen-units.md#viewport-producer-and-screen-port-origin)._

requirements.heading: RIP_VIEWPORT
requirements.text: Coordinates that specify the boundary of the Graphics Viewport are specified in World Coordinates. The interior area of the Viewport is then considered the Drawing Frame. The Drawing Coordinate frame are set to the same size/dimension as the World Coordinate Frame area that the viewport inhabits. For example, if you define a viewport from (100,100) to (299,299) in World Coordinates, then your Drawing Frame will be a drawing area with a resolution of 200x200 logical drawing pixels. In other words, when you set a viewport, you immediately have a 1:1 mapping of logical drawing pixels to World Coordinate Pixels. If you wish to change the X/Y Drawing Frame resolution to some other value, use the RIP_SET_DRAWING_FRAME command after setting the viewport. If you draw anything before executing this command, then the privimitives will be drawing things in the current Drawing Frame's coordinates (a sub-set of the World Coordinates). The Drawing Frame's coordinates do not take on another mapping until you actually set them with a RIP_SET_DRAWING_FRAME command. _(v2.A0)_

requirements.heading: Viewport Projection Range
requirements.text: For a viewport definition, compute the mathematical WORLD-to-DEVICE projection of each corner using the active axis extents. For a decoded nonnegative coordinate `n`, the result is `floor(n × DEVICE / WORLD)`. Use sufficient precision for the product and final addition. Normalize the projected corners, then add one to each inclusive far coordinate to form the half-open DEVICE rectangle.
requirements.reason: Connected DEVICE queries and drawing check projection, both exclusive edge limits, rejection with an active or inactive view, and recovery on the same stream.

requirements.heading: Viewport Projection Range
requirements.text: The portable `v` contract requires each of the four **final stored boundaries**, including the exclusive right and bottom, to fit the signed 32-bit DEVICE range −2,147,483,648 through 2,147,483,647. If any boundary is outside that range, reject the complete definition. The previous stored viewport and its active state remain in effect for drawings, queries and transfers. Consume the command normally and continue the stream. A range-valid rectangle is stored exactly as projected, even where it is outside the port or physical surface. Its consumers still apply their ordinary clipping. [Projection and storage derivation](../research/issue-313-viewport-projection-range.md) · [Physical storage and sample coverage](7.0-drawing-ports.md#physical-storage-and-sample-coverage).

requirements.heading: Viewport Projection Range
requirements.text: The range check includes the final increment. An inclusive projected endpoint of 2,147,483,646 can produce an exclusive boundary of 2,147,483,647. An inclusive endpoint of 2,147,483,647 exceeds the stored range when incremented. A new rectangle also requires positive WORLD extents on both axes. The all-zero deactivation form uses its usual deactivation rule.
requirements.reason: Connected DEVICE queries and drawing check projection, both exclusive edge limits, rejection with an active or inactive view, and recovery on the same stream.

requirements.heading: Viewport Projection Range
requirements.text: For example, start with active PORT 0 viewport `[10,10,20,20)` on a 640 × 480 device. Set WORLD to 1 × 480 while retaining this stored viewport. With UltraNum and XY width 5, receive `!|v00000000000G00000001`, which requests corners (0,0) through (4,194,304,1). The mathematical right coordinate is 2,684,354,560 inclusive and 2,684,354,561 exclusive. Reject the definition. After restoring WORLD to 640 × 480, the portable result of `$PORTX1(0,VIEW,DEVICE)$` is decimal `20`. A drawing sample at final DEVICE position (0,0) still lies outside the old clip. [PORTX1](5.1-text-variables.md#portx1).

requirements.heading: Physical Screen Clear and Palette Ordering
requirements.text: The outer clear targets the entire physical screen canvas, independently of the previously selected screen/offscreen port, viewport origin/clip, viewport activation, STYLE background, write mode or fill pattern. The source passes literal raw color `0x00000000` to a solid **RGB-black** brush and fills the physical screen rectangle **before** resetting/uploading the palette table. It does not pass a palette-index token or resolve STYLE's background. There is therefore no selected palette supplying the clear color, and PAL selection is not switched to 0 as a side effect.

requirements.heading: Physical Screen Clear and Palette Ordering
requirements.text: **Explicit portable display rule:** after `*`, cleared screen pixels represent RGB black `(0,0,0)`, including when the retained protected current palette has a nonblack entry 0. Do not recolor that clear from the retained palette's entry 0 or a later palette upload. This defines the visible canvas result without requiring obsolete Windows palette realization/dithering behavior. A strictly indexed backend must supply the black clear consistently with this rule; the command does not rewrite a protected palette to manufacture a black entry. Subsequent palette-index drawing continues to use the retained current PAL and may therefore draw a nonblack index 0. This clear differs from [wire `e`/`$ETW$`/extended-window flag 16](1.4-terminal-ansi-view.md#text-window-erase-sources), whose adopted protocol source is palette index 0.

requirements.heading: Text, Graphics, Environment and Input State
requirements.text: Before discarding/selecting TW slots, the outer path performs an ANSI reset on the **old current TW**, including a protected one. That changes its ANSI colors to 7/0, clears rendition and insert mode, homes its live cursor if active, zeros its saved cursor, restores full-height scrolling margins and the default tab map. This is an allowed terminal-state operation on a protected definition, not deletion/redefinition. Its other per-window modes and charset fields are not blanket-cleared by that preliminary ANSI reset. Protected noncurrent TW records do not receive this preliminary effect. TW 0 then receives the ordinary-definition defaults described above. Its tab map is the result of the preliminary reset if it was old-current; otherwise ordinary redefinition retains TW 0's existing map.
requirements.reason: Native and connected SOFT vectors verify the old-current window's reset ordering and supported state.
requirements.scope: SOFT resets supported rendition, cursors, vertical margins and tabs in the old current window. Ordinary insert mode is outside the acceptance condition.

requirements.heading: HEADER Versus Live HARD
requirements.text: HEADER validates the whole command before application; when both global HARD bit 1 and SOFT bit 2 are set, HARD takes precedence. After the shared HARD operation, HEADER records its supplied revision, releases any prior scene input lock, optionally locks input again with global bit 4, then performs other requested global operations and segments in their established order. Thus revision-1 `!|h01000100` ends with marker **1**, default tables and unlocked input. A later segment may deliberately change the just-reset state. The segment-free header itself does not execute an HCL reply.
requirements.reason: Native responses keep the input lock and clear the immediate revision marker. HEADER sets the explicit revision then applies its lock and segment stages.

requirements.heading: HEADER Versus Live HARD
requirements.text: Immediate `$RESET(HARD)$` performs the shared operation with marker **0**, preserves the connection’s current scene input restrictions and uses the shared reset stages. It returns no inserted text; later literal text, variable providers and template lookups in the current response continue under the usual preprocessing/two-pass/block rules. Because template slots were cleared, a **later** lookup cannot fetch their old bytes; bytes already copied into an owned working program before HARD remain part of that program. A later explicit ordinary definition may create a new slot normally. If HARD removes the field owning the current committed action, retain that action's captured source/FIELDID until return; subsequent associated writes/redraws still require the original live owner and cannot attach to a replacement.
requirements.reason: Native responses keep the input lock and clear the immediate revision marker. HEADER sets the explicit revision then applies its lock and segment stages. The portable mouse and keyboard gates now release independently, with shared SOFT/HARD retaining their current state.

requirements.heading: HEADER Versus Live HARD
requirements.text: Pending ANSI syntax belongs to the connection parser, not the old TW record or saved ESC snapshot. With the fresh active TW 0 current, subsequent routed raw bytes complete that retained syntax against TW 0's new state. For example, pending `ESC [ 31` followed after HARD by `mZ` applies red ANSI foreground and draws Z in the new window; it does not display the pending prefix as text or restore the old window. Normal intervening routed control/newline bytes still have their ordinary effects. HARD is not an inbound-stream discard or a TCP/session restart.
requirements.reason: The fresh-window path preserves incomplete connection syntax and resets per-window state. Both live encodings complete the partial CSI and preserve the connection.

requirements.heading: Independent HARD Vectors

requirements.heading: Viewports and Text Windows - Overlapping Issues
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: Viewports and Text Windows - Overlapping Issues
requirements.text: Since there are multiple text windows and [ports](7.0-drawing-ports.md) (with their viewports) allowed in the RIPscrip specification, some elaboration needs to be made on what happens if any overlap each other. Very simple, they do what they have always done - draw text, or draw graphics. For example, if a viewport overlaps a text window and you draw some graphics (say a circle) over the top of some text in a text window, and the text window subsequently scrolls, all or part of the circle could scroll with it! Now, of course, from the viewport's standpoint, the graphics are no longer what you originally sent to the viewport, but that doesn't matter - you don't preserve any of the commands you used to create the graphics - you simply draw the graphics and that's it. So with this in mind, even if multiple viewports overlap each other it doesn't matter because the final result is what's on the screen - doing things in one viewport might do some overlapping graphics in another viewport but that is alright.

requirements.heading: Viewports and Text Windows - Overlapping Issues
requirements.text: If a text window overlaps another text window, the same thing happens. To a RIPscrip terminal, text is simply just a piece of graphical information that is being placed on the screen in a formatted fashion. If two text windows overlap and text is placed on an area that overlap the other window, then you will be drawing graphics (essentially) on top of another text window. The same thing as the circle example above would happen if that text window scrolled.

requirements.heading: Viewports and Text Windows - Overlapping Issues
requirements.text: No compositing occurs anywhere in this model - RIPscrip preserves no record of _what_ drew a pixel; the final screen state is the only truth. Mouse regions are the one place ordering matters: overlapping regions are scanned most-recent-first on a click (see [4.2 Mouse Fields & Pointer](4.2-mouse-fields-and-pointer.md)). _Evidence: 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: Text Windows and Terminal Emulation
requirements.text: A text window is a screen region where raw (non-RIPscrip) text is routed, with ANSI and VT-102 emulation: colors, cursor movement, scrolling margins, wrap/chop. Up to 36 text windows are defined in the text window [data table](7.1-data-tables.md); the default is full-screen 80×25. A deactivated current window silently discards incoming text - the demos lean on `$DTW$` (deactivate text window) constantly to keep stray host text off their graphics.

requirements.heading: ANSI Mode 2 Keyboard Gating
requirements.text: On the ordinary ANSI-enabled receive path, `CSI 2 h` (hex `1B 5B 32 68`) sets Keyboard Action Mode in the selected TW and disables its keyboard actions. `CSI 2 l` (hex `1B 5B 32 6C`) clears it. The normal 3.0 profile accepts a single mode number in ordinary CSI h and l. A compound list such as `CSI 2;4 h` or `CSI 4;2 l` is consumed without a mode change. Send separate sequences. A DEC private sequence beginning `CSI ?` does not address this mode. [Original mode callbacks and ECMA-48 scope](../research/issue-289-ansi-keyboard-action-mode.md).
requirements.reason: ANSI Keyboard Action Mode and ordinary key routing are terminal behavior. RIP scene gates and authored field activation have independent requirements.

requirements.heading: ANSI Mode 2 Keyboard Gating
requirements.text: The mode is part of the selected TW's live ANSI state, initially clear in a fresh definition. An inactive TW retains its bit. Its ordinary receive path discards the bytes of a mode control while inactive, so reactivate it before sending CSI 2 l. The outgoing key gate tests the selected TW's stored mode even if that window is inactive. If both keyboard gates are clear, the inactive window still permits ordinary keyboard forwarding and RIP keyboard actions. Its display continues to discard local echo input. [TW definition and activation](#ordinary-definition-state-boundary).

requirements.heading: ANSI Mode 2 Keyboard Gating
requirements.text: Blocked key events are discarded. Changing mode 2 by itself preserves the existing field focus and pointer capture and generates no input. The scene gate has its own focus lifecycle. Client-local controls can consume their keys before terminal delivery, for example to operate menus, scrollback and local dialog editors. A shortcut that submits terminal data or activates a RIP field follows the same gate as the corresponding ordinary action. Received host data, automatic protocol replies and pointer-based actions keep their own routing. [RIP keyboard activation](4.3-buttons.md#keyboard-activation) · [Tab navigation and focus](4.2-mouse-fields-and-pointer.md#tab-navigation).

requirements.heading: ANSI Mode 2 Keyboard Gating
requirements.text: `RESET(KEYBOARD)` clears only the scene keyboard gate. NO_MORE clears the scene gates. Each leaves the selected TW's stored mode as it was. The TW mode follows the existing definition, reset, selection, copy and snapshot rules for per-window modes. Selecting a different TW changes which record supplies the bit. [RESET](5.1-text-variables.md#reset) · [Selection](#selection-first-use-and-partial-ansi-input) · [ESC snapshot payload](#snapshot-payload-and-other-save-operations).
requirements.reason: The connected two-window sequence verifies independent scene release, selected TW state, copy, fresh definitions and ESC snapshots.
requirements.scope: Only RESET(KEYBOARD) and NO_MORE releasing their RIP-owned scene gates. They do not need an ANSI mode 2 implementation.

requirements.heading: ANSI Mode 2 Keyboard Gating
requirements.text: For a two-window example, start with defined active TW 0 and 5, both with mode 2 clear. Select TW 5 and send `CSI 2 h`. Then send a valid HEADER with flag 4 and no table reset or selection. Select TW 0 and try a key. The scene keyboard gate blocks it even though TW 0 is clear. After `RESET(KEYBOARD)`, an ordinary key is eligible in TW 0. Select TW 5 and try a key again. Its stored mode blocks the key, including after NO_MORE. Send `CSI 2 l` in TW 5 and the next ordinary key is eligible. TW 0 stayed clear throughout. No earlier blocked event is replayed.

requirements.heading: ANSI Mode 4 Insert and Replace
requirements.text: `CSI 4 h` (hex `1B 5B 34 68`) enables insert mode in the selected active TW. `CSI 4 l` (hex `1B 5B 34 6C`) selects replace mode. These are ordinary ANSI controls with exactly one parameter, as for mode 2. DEC-private forms such as `CSI ?4 h` and compound lists such as `CSI 2;4 h` leave mode 4 unchanged. The inactive TW receive path discards these controls and retains the stored mode. Neither control draws or moves the cursor. [Mode and write-path derivation](../research/issue-298-ansi-insert-mode.md).
requirements.reason: Ordinary ANSI editing is outside RIPscrip acceptance.

requirements.heading: ANSI Mode 4 Insert and Replace
requirements.text: **Portable rendering.** For each graphic character routed to ordinary ANSI display, first determine its destination using the TW's usual wrap or chop rule. In replace mode, write the character at that position. In insert mode, shift the visible contents of that row from the destination cell through the TW's last character column one cell to the right, discarding the contents that pass that column, then write the character in the opened cell using current rendition. Advance the cursor as for an ordinary character write. A displayed space is a character for this purpose. The shift preserves already rendered content, including its colors and any graphics in the moved span. The horizontal bound is the TW's own last character column even with scroll margins, a different graphics viewport or a protected TW definition. The shift itself stays within one row.
requirements.reason: Ordinary ANSI editing is outside RIPscrip acceptance.

requirements.heading: ANSI Mode 4 Insert and Replace
requirements.text: A character written in the last column replaces that cell in either mode because the shifted cell has nowhere to go. With wrap enabled, the next graphic character after a deferred wrap inserts in the new destination row after normal wrapping and any scroll. The deferred wrap itself causes no row shift. With chop enabled, a character that would be truncated causes no shift or draw. [Text window placement](#text-window-placement).
requirements.reason: Ordinary ANSI editing is outside RIPscrip acceptance.

requirements.heading: ANSI Mode 4 Insert and Replace
requirements.text: `CSI @` (Insert Character) edits the row directly in either mode. It shifts the same span by the requested number of cells and fills the vacated cells with the current ANSI erase background. With no count it inserts one cell. An explicit count of zero edits nothing. A count reaching or exceeding the remaining width erases from the cursor through the last column. The cursor stays in place. If it is logically past the right edge awaiting wrap or chop, there is no insertion and the pending position is preserved. ANSI erase controls such as `CSI J` and `CSI K` erase in place without shifting. The ordinary 3.0 profile consumes unsupported `CSI Ps b` (REP) without drawing. If a separate ANSI extension implements REP by displaying repeated characters, each displayed repeat takes the same path as a literal printable character.
requirements.reason: Ordinary ANSI editing is outside RIPscrip acceptance.

requirements.heading: ANSI Mode 4 Insert and Replace

The outer SOFT reset clears insert mode in its old current TW. requirements.heading: ANSI Mode 12 and Local Echo
requirements.text: On the ordinary ANSI receive path, `CSI 12 h` (hex `1B 5B 31 32 68`) selects full duplex and turns local echo off. `CSI 12 l` (hex `1B 5B 31 32 6C`) selects half duplex and turns local echo on. Use one ordinary decimal mode parameter. A private sequence such as `CSI ?12 h`, a mode list such as `CSI 4;12 l`, or input discarded by an inactive TW leaves local echo as it was. These controls affect local display of outgoing terminal input. The underlying transport continues to handle sending and receiving. [Send/Receive Mode and original callbacks](../research/issue-302-ansi-local-echo.md).
requirements.reason: Ordinary ANSI local echo and Telnet negotiation are outside RIPscrip acceptance.

requirements.heading: ANSI Mode 12 and Local Echo
requirements.text: **Scope and transport.** Local echo is live connection state shared by the TWs. TW selection, definition, activation, ANSI `ESC c`, `ESC 7/8`, table backups, RIP RESET (including SOFT and HARD), HEADER resets and NO_MORE preserve the setting on the same connection. An inactive TW can suppress display while the setting is on. Reconnecting initializes a new live value. The portable defaults are full duplex for a raw connection and half duplex for Telnet before negotiation of peer ECHO. An explicit connection profile may supply the starting value. [TW snapshots and backup](#snapshot-payload-and-other-save-operations).
requirements.reason: Ordinary ANSI local echo and Telnet negotiation are outside RIPscrip acceptance.

requirements.heading: ANSI Mode 12 and Local Echo
requirements.text: On Telnet, when the peer's ECHO option changes to enabled through successful negotiation, turn local echo off. When the peer's ECHO changes to disabled, turn it on. Apply completed peer ECHO changes and received ANSI mode 12 updates in stream order. Each updates the live value immediately. Duplicate or rejected option exchanges leave the value as it was. An ANSI mode update sends no Telnet option command. Peer data returned as an echo is ordinary host receive data. [Telnet ECHO option](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc857.html) · [Portable precedence derivation](../research/issue-302-ansi-local-echo.md#portable-connection-and-input-rules).
requirements.reason: Ordinary ANSI local echo and Telnet negotiation are outside RIPscrip acceptance.

requirements.heading: ANSI Mode 12 and Local Echo
requirements.text: **Keyboard delivery.** Apply mode 2 and the RIP scene keyboard gate before ordinary terminal key delivery. A consumed event, for example a RIP hotkey or focused control action, follows the consumer's own behavior. For a delivered key in full duplex, transmit normally with no local echo. In half duplex, apply the following local display action before submitting the outgoing bytes to the transport. [Keyboard gating](#ansi-mode-2-keyboard-gating).

requirements.heading: ANSI Mode 12 and Local Echo
requirements.text: A user paste routed to terminal input follows the input gates. Treat it as a batch. In half duplex, echo its admitted display bytes once, in order, without applying the per-key Enter or Backspace translations. Submit the paste bytes to the normal transport path. Generated send data such as a button action or protocol reply uses its own output path. Mode 12 alone adds no local echo to a generated send or local playback.

requirements.heading: ANSI Mode 12 and Local Echo
requirements.text: For a raw connection with active TWs 0 and 5 and both keyboard gates clear, receive `CSI 12 l` in TW 0 and type `A`. Display and send `41`. Select TW 5 and press ordinary Enter. Display `0D 0A` there and submit `0D` for sending. Receive `CSI 12 h` in TW 5, select TW 0, and type `B`. Send `42` with no local display. On Telnet, an accepted peer WILL ECHO disables local echo. A subsequent `CSI 12 l` enables it, and a duplicate WILL ECHO leaves it on. Receiving `CSI 12 h` turns it off again. An accepted peer WONT ECHO then turns it on.

requirements.heading: ANSI Backspace and Key Transmission
requirements.text: [`BSMODE`](5.1-text-variables.md#bsmode) controls display erasure when the ANSI text window receives a byte `08`. [`BSXMIT`](5.1-text-variables.md#bsxmit) controls the byte posted by the ordinary Backspace key path. Each is independent of the other.
requirements.reason: Introduces the two RIP variables. Their explicit arguments, replies and integration with existing terminal settings are reviewed under their entries.

requirements.heading: ANSI Backspace and Key Transmission
requirements.text: In a live ANSI text window, received `08` at column greater than zero moves the cursor one column left on the same row. In DEST mode it paints an ASCII space in the new cell using the text window's current ANSI foreground and background and the space glyph from the current ANSI face. In NONDEST mode it preserves the cell. At column zero the screen and cursor stay put. A focused application or operating-system edit control handles its own Backspace editing, while a RIP hotkey that consumes the event follows its own action. These paths are outside ordinary terminal Backspace transmission.
requirements.scope: Verify the supported erasure setting selected by an explicit BSMODE call. Ordinary Backspace and default behavior remain the ANSI engine's rules.

requirements.heading: ANSI Backspace and Key Transmission
requirements.text: For a Backspace event that passes the [keyboard gates](#ansi-mode-2-keyboard-gating) and reaches the ordinary keyboard path, the client sends the selected byte when connected. With half-duplex local echo, it displays the original `08` in both transmit modes and with either Ctrl state. The same display erasure rule applies to that echo. In full duplex the keystroke itself has no local display effect. A byte later sent back by the host is processed as received text. A literal control byte generated by a host expression, button action or send macro is delivered by that output path as constructed.

requirements.heading: ANSI Backspace and Key Transmission
requirements.text: RIPtel 3.1 owns both settings in the front end. Its unconfigured defaults are DEST and BS. Loading a saved dial-entry profile can replace either setting with the profile's value. RIP resets and connection changes that leave the current profile in force preserve both. Setters update the live client settings, and a separate client configuration-save path can persist them. Local RIP playback can run the same setters and available ANSI text playback uses the same display policy. An offline client has no connection on which to send the keyboard byte. A driver embedded without the client hooks starts with DEST and BS in the driver instance.
requirements.reason: Historical RIPtel key translation, local echo and front-end defaults. The explicit BSXMIT and BSMODE contracts are reviewed under those variables.

requirements.heading: ANSI Backspace and Key Transmission
requirements.text: For a cell vector, use ordinary ANSI mode with a visible window. Send hex `1b 5b 48 41 42 1b 5b 33 37 3b 34 34 6d 08` to home the cursor, print `AB`, set SGR 37 and 44 and apply a literal BS. In either mode the cursor moves to the second cell. DEST paints a space with white foreground and blue background. NONDEST retains `B` with its previous appearance. Move to column zero and send another `08` to check the screen boundary. For a wire vector use a connected terminal with no key binding that consumes Backspace. Set DEL, then press Backspace and Ctrl+Backspace in separate steps. The host receives `7f` then `08`. A generated host response containing literal `08` still sends `08`. Repeat with BS. In full duplex both ordinary Backspace events send `08`. In half duplex they send `08` and `7f` respectively and both echo `08`. For the Ctrl case supply an ordinary Backspace character event with Ctrl held so the fixture exercises the RIP key branch directly. Query each mode via normal [RIP_QUERY response framing](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_query).
requirements.scope: Verify the supported erasure setting selected by an explicit BSMODE call. Ordinary Backspace and default behavior remain the ANSI engine's rules.

requirements.heading: Designation, Invocation and Emulation Mode
requirements.text: With ANSI parsing enabled, both ANSI and VT-102 modes accept `ESC ( A`, `ESC ( B`, `ESC ( 0` to designate G0 as UK, US or special graphics, and `ESC ) A`, `ESC ) B`, `ESC ) 0` to designate G1. These controls change the selected designation without emitting a glyph or moving the cursor. Unknown designation final bytes have no designation effect. Initial G0 and G1 are both US, and initial invocation is G0.
requirements.reason: ANSI and VT-102 byte, designation and glyph behavior is terminal emulation.

requirements.heading: Designation, Invocation and Emulation Mode
requirements.text: The ANSI-versus-VT-102 choice is global client state, separate from each TW's designations. In ANSI mode the designation state is still recorded, but display bytes use the CP437 bank without UK/special translation. In VT-102 mode the invoked set's mapping below applies. Changing the emulation choice does not reset the designations or invocation; returning to VT-102 exposes the retained set again.
requirements.reason: ANSI and VT-102 byte, designation and glyph behavior is terminal emulation.

requirements.heading: Designation, Invocation and Emulation Mode
requirements.text: For this recovered RIPtel byte profile, **SI (`0x0f`) and SO (`0x0e`) do not change invocation**. In VT-102 mode they are consumed without a glyph or cursor advance. In ANSI mode they display CP437 bank glyphs `0x0f` (☼) and `0x0e` (♫), respectively, without changing invocation. The original VT-102 router calls an invocation helper that is a one-byte return; no effective SI/SO set switch is recovered. A normal stream starting at the initial state therefore keeps G0 invoked even after SO; designating G1 does not make it visible. Implementors must not silently substitute modern DEC SI/SO semantics for these rules. A separate extension providing working G1 invocation must identify that additional behavior.
requirements.reason: ANSI and VT-102 byte, designation and glyph behavior is terminal emulation.

requirements.heading: Byte-to-Glyph Mapping
requirements.text: **Explicit portable glyph-stage completion:** recognize ANSI syntax and incoming controls from the original input bytes, then translate only bytes selected for display. Draw a translated bank identity directly: for example, special-set `d` displays bank `0x1b` (←), rather than opening a new escape sequence. Do not translate ANSI designation/CSI payload into drawing glyphs or reinterpret mapped C0-bank values as incoming controls. The original table and its chosen identities are source facts; this clean syntax/glyph boundary is an interoperability choice, not a claim that all native translated-control paths produce these results. UTF-8 remains outside this profile.

requirements.heading: ANSI ESC 7 and ESC 8 Snapshot
requirements.text: **Completed 3.0 profile:** ANSI `ESC 7` (bytes `1B 37`) saves one interpreter-owned TW snapshot; `ESC 8` (`1B 38`) restores it into the **currently selected TW**, without selecting another slot. They are available on the ordinary ANSI-enabled text path and do not require a VT-102 emulation option. Existing RIP/column-flow routing and inactive-window input discard still apply. This is separate from per-window `CSI s/u` and whole-TW backups.
requirements.reason: The ordinary ANSI ESC 7/8 snapshot is terminal behavior. RIP text-window backup commands have independent requirements.

requirements.heading: ANSI ESC 7 and ESC 8 Snapshot
requirements.text: The accepted [#104 evidence](../research/issue-104-terminal-character-sets.md#reset-definition-and-saved-state) establishes a complete native record copy and the live-cursor overwrite of its initial saved-coordinate bytes. The logical payload, safe ownership, protection/target rules, empty/lifetime and failure boundaries below are **explicit portable completion**; [derivation and independent vectors](../research/issue-150-ansi-esc-snapshot.md). A historical `0xf1`-byte record is not a wire/file format or permission to copy pointers, reserved bytes or undocumented fields. This profile does not change RIPscrip 1.54 or require new VT-102/flowed-text commands.
requirements.reason: The ordinary ANSI ESC 7/8 snapshot is terminal behavior. RIP text-window backup commands have independent requirements.

requirements.heading: Snapshot Payload and Other Save Operations
requirements.text: The interpreter owns **one optional value S**, initially absent, across TW selection. A successful ESC 7 reads the current **defined, active** window, including a protected source, and atomically replaces S with an independently owned logical copy. It leaves the source record, its CSI-saved coordinates, current index and displayed pixels unchanged. An ineligible source leaves S unchanged. Saving again replaces the one value; this is not a per-window slot or stack.

requirements.heading: Restore Target, Resources and Failure
requirements.text: ESC 8 with **no S**, or an **undefined, inactive or protected current target**, performs no restore, creation or selection and retains S. It does not fall back to TW 0, the original source slot, CSI u or a default record. Inactive text may already be discarded before forming an ANSI sequence; neither route bypasses that gate. Graphics PORT activation/protection is not this TW eligibility check.

requirements.heading: Restore Target, Resources and Failure
requirements.text: For an eligible target, restore into its existing numeric slot. The saved source index is not payload or a binding to that original object. Source deletion, redefinition, live reset or a whole-TW restore therefore does not invalidate the owned snapshot. Destination 0 always remains defined/unprotected even if the source was a protected nonzero window. A nonzero destination receives saved protection; that can make a subsequent ESC 8 a protected-target no-op until separately unprotected. Normal successful capture has active state; restoring hidden cursor visibility does not disable the window's raw text path.

requirements.heading: Restore Target, Resources and Failure
requirements.text: Resolve saved logical font/metric requirements and any supported binding identifiers against current resources. Missing/incompatible resources are a recoverable failure; do not copy an old handle, silently substitute a font, refit geometry, auto-create a flowed object, or select an article/column. A reused identifier refers to the compatible currently live resource under its ordinary identifier rules, not the original native object's address. Copy/retain owned query text and all other payload values before publication.

requirements.heading: Restore Target, Resources and Failure
requirements.text: **Failure/publication boundary:** failed ESC 7 retains the old S, including absence. ESC 8 prepares the entire logical target/resource replacement before commit; failure retains the target definition, fixed query, selection and S without a partial record swap. A successful restore replaces the target logical state as one operation and leaves S unchanged for reuse. This explicitly chosen ESC boundary does not change COPY or whole-family restore recovery rules. No query, macro/provider, flow operation or host command executes as part of saving/restoring state.

requirements.heading: MicroANSI Fonts (`.maf`)
requirements.text: Terminal text is rendered from **MicroANSI** bitmap fonts shipped as `RIPscrip.maf` - header `RIPterm v2.0 MicroANSI Font File`. The format is inherited directly from RIPterm Professional 2.0, whose `RIPTERM.FNT` (preserved in the [2.x font assets](../../2.0/assets/fonts/README.md)) carries the identical header; RIPterm 2.0 additionally ran EGA 640×350 as a native video mode. RIPtel still supports 640×350 - as the default world view, for 1.54 compatibility - but treats it like any other world resolution, scaled to the display, so it needs no 350-line MicroANSI table of its own. The file carries per-resolution tables for **three display resolutions** - 640×480, 800×600, and 1024×768 - each with about five font-size subtables, so text windows keep proportion as the device resolution changes. (Text-mode geometries offered by RIPtel: 80×43, 91×43, 80×25, 91×25, 40×25.) Byte-level format details are in the [MicroANSI `.maf` techspec](../techspecs/3.3-microansi-maf-delta.md). Graphical text uses the separate font systems: BGI stroked `.CHR` vector fonts and the `.RFF` outline fonts of RIP_EXTENDED_FONT_STYLE, covered in [3.0 Text Output & Fonts](3.0-text-output-and-fonts.md).

requirements.heading: RIP_TEXT_WINDOW
requirements.text: This command specifies the dimensions of the virtual TTY window that will display all ASCII/ANSI (non-RIPscrip) data coming across the connection. (x0,y0) defines the upper-left corner of the window in text-based character-cell coordinates. (x1,y1) defines the lower-right corner of the window (inclusive). There may be two simultaneous windows on the screen, one for TTY text, and one for the display of RIPscrip graphics (a viewport), and they may overlap.
requirements.reason: The connected window fixtures exercise retained and reinitialized attributes, partial-input continuity, window-local cursor placement and erase bounds. The applicable RIP effect is the change made by the window command.

All bytes that don't conform to the RIPscrip syntax are treated as ANSI/ASCII and displayed in the TTY window (if defined). User keystrokes that are echoed by the BBS would also appear in the text window by this scheme.

requirements.heading: Font sizes
requirements.text: The font sizes in the preceding table vary depending on the resolution that the terminal software is running under. The actual cell sizes of each font are calculated based on the number of rows and columns required. For example, at a resolution of 800x600, the cell sizes are calculated by dividing the horizontal resolution by the number of columns (800/80) which yields a cell width of 10. By doing the same thing for the same height we get 600/43 which equals 13.95348837. You obviously cannot have a fractional cell size so we round down. This gives us a cell height of 13. This gives a vertical region of 559 scan lines of text information yielding 41 extra scan lines that don't get used. This method can be used to determine the cell sizes for any arbitrary resolution. _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: Text window placement
requirements.text: Now that we know what the font cell sizes are, or more acurately, how to calculate them, we need to establish a standardized way to determine screen placement for text characters. RIPscrip 1.54 was based on 640x350 resolution and text placement was very straightforward. Now that we have the upper-left corner of the text window, calculating an arbitrary row/column in the text window is simple based on the cell size. _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: Text window placement
requirements.text: Under resolutions other than 640x350, we need to take very special care to make the text characters appear as close to the 640x350 counterparts as possible. In order to calculate the text window's orientation as closely as possible in other resolutions, calculate the upper-left corner of the text window at 640x350 coordinates and scale those coordinates up to the actual resolution used on the terminal. This will insure that the text window is located as closely to the 640x350 counterpart as possible. As previously described, the font cell sizes can leave some "slop space" due to fractional columns/rows. This means that you cannot be pixel-for-pixel accurate with text window placement at varying resolutions. In this matter, the RIP_TEXT_WINDOW command is not truly resolution independent (see [RIP_EXTENDED_TEXT_WINDOW](#rip_extended_text_window) for a truly resolution independent way of creating text windows).

requirements.heading: RIP_EXTENDED_TEXT_WINDOW
requirements.text: This version of a text window works by establishing a bounding rectangle that is to contain the actual text window display region. requirements.heading: Extended Bounds and Validation
requirements.text: The four coordinates are absolute WORLD coordinates relative to the screen. Convert both endpoints independently to device coordinates with the current WORLD/device scale, rounding down, then order each endpoint pair. Do not add the current graphics PORT or viewport origin, use its clipping rectangle, or add one to the far edges. The result is `[left,right) × [top,bottom)`. A rectangle with zero device width or height after conversion is rejected; a positive WORLD extent can collapse to zero during conversion. The stored bounding rectangle is not clipped to the screen before fitting. Actual drawing is limited to addressable screen pixels, independently of graphics PORT/viewport clipping.

requirements.heading: Fitting the Text Window
requirements.text: **Cell metrics:** use the device cell width and height of each selected terminal font, consistently for fitting, display placement and cell queries. With a loaded MicroANSI table, these are its stored raster dimensions, not a fresh division by the nominal 80/91/40 columns and 43/25 rows. RIPtel initially computes nominal-grid floor metrics as a fallback, then replaces them with successfully loaded MAF metrics. At 1024×768 the supplied fonts are 12×17, 11×17, 12×30, 11×30 and 20×24 for fonts 0–4. In particular, font 4 is 20×24, not 25×30. See the [MAF metric table](../techspecs/3.3-microansi-maf-delta.md#the-new-resolution-set). The ordinary `w` nominal-grid/640×350 reference-origin description above does not define extended `b` fitting metrics.

requirements.heading: Fitting the Text Window
requirements.text: 1. The font number is checked. If a narrower or shorter font is available in the RIPscrip text window system, it will be chosen, then everything will be recalculated to see if the width and/or height can now be fit inside the bounding rectangle. If it can, then this new font will be used to accomodate the request. This evaluation process is incremental in nature. If the width and/or height is too large, then the next smaller font is checked, so on and so forth.
