requirements.heading: Fitting the Text Window
requirements.text: If a new font must be chosen, then you evaluate whether you need to shrink the font in the width, height or in both directions. Consult the preceding table to determine which font number to check next. If the entry specifies "n/a", then you cannot shrink the font any further and must move on to step number 2 (see below).
requirements.reason: Connected default/current ordinary and extended window behavior with independent geometry/state/pixel expectations; full nonzero TW table/protection/query lifecycle remains separately pending.

requirements.heading: Fitting the Text Window
requirements.text: 2. If the current candidate has `n/a` for its overflow direction and you still cannot obtain the desired height and width of your text window, you have no alternative then to reduce the width and/or height to make it fit inside the bounding rectangle. This is a last resort situation, but must be done if the text window is to fit inside the bounding rectangle. If the width is too wide, then one column will be trimmed off of the text window and then its new pixel width would be evaluated. If it still doesn't fit, you keep removing more columns, one-by-one, until you either get a window that fits, or you hit zero columns. If your bounding rectangle is so small that you can't have even a one column wide or one line tall text window then the text window is made exactly one line tall, or one column wide to accomodate the situation and the bounding box is adjusted accordingly to fit exactly the outer dimensions of the newly defined text window (albeit an incorrect one).
requirements.reason: Connected default/current ordinary and extended window behavior with independent geometry/state/pixel expectations; full nonzero TW table/protection/query lifecycle remains separately pending.

requirements.heading: Fitting the Text Window
requirements.text: For the final chosen font with positive metrics `(cw,ch)` and bounding size `(BW,BH)`, the dimension-reduction step is exactly `columns = max(1, min(requested_columns, floor(BW/cw)))` and `rows = max(1, min(requested_rows, floor(BH/ch)))`. Do not reduce counts while another transition is available: every candidate is tested against the original requested counts.
requirements.reason: Connected default/current ordinary and extended window behavior with independent geometry/state/pixel expectations; full nonzero TW table/protection/query lifecycle remains separately pending.

requirements.heading: Fitting the Text Window
requirements.text: **Explicit undersized-box completion:** when even one cell cannot fit on an axis, keep that axis's near edge and extend its far edge to exactly one cell beyond it. Leave the other bounding axis unchanged unless it also needs extension. The draft requires a one-cell minimum and adjusted bounding box, but does not establish this anchoring; this is the portable rule, not a claim about all original error/recovery paths. After adjustment, center the display rectangle: `display_left = left + floor((BW - columns*cw)/2)` and `display_top = top + floor((BH - rows*ch)/2)`, with exclusive far edges one full display width/height later. An odd leftover pixel stays on the right/bottom. Flag 16 clears this final adjusted bounding rectangle, including its margins, clipped only to the physical screen.

requirements.heading: Fitting the Text Window
requirements.text: Every accepted `b`, including one identical to the previous definition, homes both live and saved cursor to window-relative `(0,0)`, resets rendition and per-window terminal modes, sets full-height scrolling margins, and sets ANSI colors to normal light gray on black (7/0). Wrap/chop is then selected by flag 1. Existing cursor visibility is retained unless flag 2 hides it; absence of flag 2 does not turn a previously hidden cursor on. The explicit tab-stop map and character-set selectors are reset, unlike changed ordinary `w`, which retains them. Incomplete ANSI parser state and global client emulation options are retained, as distinguished in the [ordinary state boundary](#ordinary-definition-state-boundary). This is a window-state reinitialization, not an ANSI parser reset. Without flag 16, definition preserves screen pixels; newly included areas are not implicitly filled. Flag 16 is applied before the final cursor display and before flag 4 deactivates the window; flag 32 protects the completed definition.
requirements.reason: Identical ordinary definitions retain the current keyboard lock and origin, and apply the requested wrap. Changed ordinary definitions, repeated extended definitions and live slot-zero reset reset the supported per-window modes. Connected input verifies when the host receives a physical key.
requirements.scope: RIP redefinition of the existing native window state, including margins, character set, tabs, cursor requests, parser ownership and supported modes.

requirements.heading: Fitting the Text Window
requirements.text: For example, using the supplied 1024×768 MAF metrics, a 40×25 automatic request in device box `[10,1010) × [20,620)` selects font 4 immediately: display size 800×600, display box `[110,910) × [20,620)`, bounding box unchanged. A 40×25 request in `[0,800) × [0,500)` overflows height with font 4 and follows 4→0, yielding 480×425 centered at `(160,37)`. A 1×1-cell request in the nonempty device box `[20,21) × [30,31)` follows the both-axis path 4→0, then expands the box to `[20,32) × [30,47)` for one 12×17 cell. These are source-derived calculations with the stated completion rule, not native pixel captures.

requirements.heading: Flags
requirements.text: It should be noted that there are some fundamental differences in nature from the extended text window command and the older normal text window command. This one is obviously more powerful and has the benefit of being resolution independent. When working with [text variables](5.1-text-variables.md) to query the status or configuration of text windows, some text variables cannot query particular pieces of information about extended text windows (eg, `$TWX0$`, `$TWY0$`, `$TWX1$` and `$TWY1$`). The types of information that cannot be obtained are the text cell coordinates of the upper-left and lower-right corners of the extended text window - there aren't any - they're specified in graphical coordinates, not in text coordinates like with the RIP_TEXT_WINDOW command. The `$ISEXTWIN$` variable reports whether a given window is an extended one. See the [shared geometry-query table and ordinary/extended examples](5.1-text-variables.md#text-window-geometry-query-grammar): omitted TYPE requests legacy ordinary cell corners, while explicit TEXT/BOUND requests graphical edges. Only TWW/TWH(TEXT) accept the matching COLS/ROWS domain.

requirements.heading: Selection, First Use and Partial ANSI Input
requirements.text: **The first-use rules differ.** Wire `2T` copies the current TW definition into an undefined nonzero destination, as its protocol entry states. `$CUR(TW,n)$` instead gives an undefined destination a fresh full-screen ordinary window using the user's default font, as CUR's own table states. Do not read CUR as an automatic first-use clone. The original driver's common low-level selector uses the latter default-window fallback even for wire `2T`; that implementation limit does not replace the explicit wire protocol's copy rule. Existing destinations use their own retained state in both forms.
requirements.reason: Wire first use clones the current window independently, including direct colors, cursor requests, margins and explicit tabs. CUR first use applies fresh defaults. Table selection preserves independent graphics selections and the connection-owned escape snapshot.

requirements.heading: Selection, First Use and Partial ANSI Input
requirements.text: **Explicit portable first-use completion:** for wire `2T`, copy the source's complete per-window logical definition/ANSI state listed below, then mark the new destination defined and **unprotected**. This specifies the otherwise incomplete meaning of “definition copied”; it is not a claim that the native fallback cloned those fields. For CUR first use, use the stated fresh defaults. A protected source can supply the copied definition. Selection alone retains the protection of an already defined destination. The copied values are independent, not shared mutable aliases. These successful-selection rules do not add transactional guarantees for resource-allocation failures.
requirements.reason: The wire selector retains used windows and clones the defined source state for a fresh destination. The new slot starts unprotected; destination flags run afterward. The CUR provider retains its independent fresh-default policy.

requirements.heading: Selection, First Use and Partial ANSI Input
requirements.text: An unfinished ANSI ESC/CSI/designation or **supported** ANSI string sequence belongs to the connection's terminal parser. Selection neither discards it nor stores/copies it in either window. With an active destination, subsequent raw bytes continue that same sequence and any resulting terminal operation addresses the newly current TW. This ownership rule does not require support for otherwise undocumented OSC/DCS/string sequences; if provided by an implementation, their partial input follows the same boundary. Selecting an inactive window retains the parser; the separately adopted deactivated-window input-discard rules still apply.

requirements.heading: Selection, First Use and Partial ANSI Input
requirements.text: Selection preserves displayed screen pixels. It does not clear, scroll, relocate, redraw or restore text/graphics, and first use copies no logical cells, bitmap contents or scrollback/history. Only the visible cursor overlay changes: remove it from the departing window and present the target's requested cursor if that target is active and visible. A cell-backed implementation must not repaint a window merely because it becomes current. Other family selections and the source's logical TW state are unchanged by successful selection.
requirements.reason: Connected wire first use clones represented per-window state from protected or unprotected sources into an unprotected independent target; CUR first use creates active full-screen MicroANSI defaults with empty explicit tabs. Existing selection retains target state. Native tests use literal CSI saved coordinates, colors/margins and split CSI/OSC at every boundary after destroying the source. TCP bitmap tests verify protection, activation, defaults, pixels and nonfatal allocation failure in CP437/UTF-8. Charset designation, interpreter-owned ESC7/8 snapshot and resident queries remain separate pending requirements. Client default is font 0 with wrap; entry raster/grid remain independent.

requirements.reason: Wire e, > and host ETW are connected for the current/default entry TTY and ordinary positioned window. Whole erase uses current graphics PAL index0 and homes only the live cursor; wire > resolves STYLE background through ENV precision/current PAL and retains the live cursor. The same clipped absolute DEVICE rectangle is COPY-filled into the shared RIP index plane independently of PORT, viewport, protection, fill pattern and W; repeated same-index paint records damage to overwrite later ANSI ink. Selectors/arguments prevalidate before effects; undefined nonzero slots and deactivated TTY ignore valid operations. Malformed references and renderer failures recover nonfatally. With the same width, `!|g0102` supplies `(36, 2)` in Base Math 36 and `(64, 2)` in Base Math 64 because the first three digits are `010`. requirements.heading: RIP_GOTOXY
requirements.text: This command sets the position of the text cursor in the TTY Text window, if it is active. If inactive (if the dimensions are 0,0,0,0), then this command is ignored. With ANSI origin mode off, the comparable ANSI cursor-address sequence is `ESC[row+1;column+1H`: its row precedes column and both are 1-based, whereas RIPscrip `g` supplies zero-based X then Y.
requirements.reason: Wire g/H are callable in connected sessions on the entry grid and positioned default window. g reads a two-digit X and a one- or two-digit Y in the active base; H is argumentless. RIP3-owner native placement clamps against full-window bounds independently of ANSI origin/vertical/horizontal margins, commits Unicode and clears pending wrap without fabricated input. It retains ANSI modes, margins and saved cursor; following ANSI CUP remains margin-relative. Deactivated default TW ignores movement; malformed commands/renderer failures stay within the existing nonfatal RIP3 boundary. Native independent cell expectations cover both encodings, endpoint clamps, pending wrap, outside-margin text, confined scrolling, EL bounds and cursor restoration. CP437/UTF-8 TCP captures cover full entry and positioned windows on five actual rasters.

requirements.heading: RIP_GOTOXY
requirements.text: Coordinates are absolute within the full text window: X is column and Y is row, both zero-based. Clamp to `0..columns-1` and `0..rows-1`; ANSI origin mode and scrolling margins neither offset nor restrict this RIPscrip operation. It does not scroll or change margins, saved cursor or origin mode. `$TWGOTO$` follows the same positioning rule for a chosen window, with its own optional-argument syntax. TW definition protection does not prohibit cursor movement, and graphics PORT/viewport state is irrelevant. See [the macro entry](5.1-text-variables.md#twgoto).

An undefined/deactivated TW is a no-op; definition protection and graphics PORT/viewport state do not block movement.

Erase operations replace covered pixels, independently of graphics write mode, fill pattern, PORT bounds and viewport clip; they can visibly overwrite overlapping graphics/windows. End-of-line erase covers display cells only, leaving bounding margins intact. [The macro entries](5.1-text-variables.md#etw) retain their all-arguments syntax validation before effects.

requirements.heading: Overlapping Windows and Viewports
requirements.text: Multiple text windows and viewports may overlap freely, and no compositing occurs - everything is just pixels on the screen. Draw a circle across a text window and then scroll the window, and part of the circle scrolls with it; text written where two windows overlap is simply graphics on top of the other window. RIPscrip preserves no record of _what_ drew a pixel; the final screen state is the only truth. The full inherited discussion is in [1.3 World View & Virtual Canvas](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#viewports-and-text-windows---overlapping-issues); mouse regions are the one place ordering matters - overlapping regions are scanned most-recent-first on a click.

requirements.heading: Color Palettes and Hardware - Color Translation
requirements.text: With versions of RIPscrip prior to v2.0, the color palette was limited to 16 colors maximum out of a total of 64 colors in the Master Color Palette. This was due to the hardware origins of the language in its initial releases. With the popularity of higher color video sub-systems, RIPscrip needed to grow to accomodate these advancing trends. In addition, it needed to be open-ended enough to accomodate yet unknown hardware environments that might provide for even higher color resolution.

requirements.heading: Color Palettes and Hardware - Color Translation
requirements.text: The 1.xx RIPscrip specification provided for 16 colors out of a palette of 64 colors. This 64 color palette corresponded to 2-bits of Red, Green and Blue information each, giving you four levels of color saturation in each of the three categories. Unlike typical RGB implementations the color palette entry numbers are not sequentially ordered based on the R, G and B components. The bit-layouts of the color values as follows:

requirements.heading: Color Palettes and Hardware - Color Translation
requirements.text: Under RIPscrip 2.0 and later, we deal with the concept of a 256-entry color lookup table (otherwise known as the drawing palette). This palette of RGB colors is used to cross-reference a particular color number to some arbitrary RGB color combination much like the earlier 1.xx palette counterparts, but with some more important differences. The RGB palette commands carry full component bytes. A color value is a raw binary number without any frills or complications. If the bit value were 00100100 then the actual color saturation level would be 36, not encoded in a strange bit swapped fashion as in the older color palette commands. It is prophesized that the older color palette commands will not be used much (if at all) in the newer 2.0 environments due to their complexity - about the only way that the older commands will be used is via software packages that only output colors in the older syntax.

requirements.heading: Color Palettes and Hardware - Color Translation
requirements.text: No matter what hardware configuration your actual RIPscrip software is running under, there is some low-level inherent bit-precision for each RGB color component (whether it be 2 bits each, 4, 6, 8 or more bits per color component). With this in mind, the actual "set palette" commands need to internally convert any RGB color values to the "native" values of the target operating system's graphics environment. The actual discussion of this goes beyond the scope of this document, however the actual conversion should be rather trivial.

requirements.text: This same algorithm should work relatively well for any color component mapping operation from any bit precision to another where the source bit precision is less than the target's precision. Some "fractional" component operations may need to be performed to compensate for non-integral divisions, but this shouldn't pose any problems in a real-world scenario. In fact, this same algorithm can equally be used by the 2.0 extended "set palette" commands to map the RGB color component values to the actual "bit precision" of the target graphics environment's video hardware.

requirements.heading: The Drawing Palette
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._

requirements.heading: The Drawing Palette
requirements.text: Now that we've discussed how to translate an RGB color from one environment to another, now let's discuss the larger picture as far as RIPscrip is concerned: The Drawing Palette.

requirements.heading: The Drawing Palette
requirements.text: The Drawing Palette in RIPscrip is a table of 256 entries, where each entry is a set of RGB color component values. This table is a mechansim to "map" color codes (from 0-255) to arbitrary RGB color values.

requirements.heading: The Drawing Palette
requirements.text: It may be distinctly possible that the RIPscrip software is running in an environment that allows for an actual "color palette". If this is the case then this color lookup table will match the color palette of the video hardware entry-for-entry. Color 5 in the lookup table would correspond with color 5 in the video system's hardware color palette. This works for environments where the color palette is "completely redefinable". What this means is that the RIPscrip software can completely control the entire video hardware color palette.

requirements.heading: The Drawing Palette
requirements.text: It is also very possible that the RIPscrip software could be running on a video system that cannot support 256 simultaneous colors, and only has a color palette of smaller size (typically 16 colors). In this case, the lowest 16 colors (the desktop palette) would typically map one-for-one with the actual hardware color palette, although the programmer might opt to choose a more intelligent approach of color selection based on color distribution. This rather complex issue goes beyond the scope of this discussion and it is recommended that for simplicity, the lowest 16 colors of the drawing palette be mapped to the target palette.. This again, assumes that the RIPscrip software has complete control over the video color palette system and can change any or all of the entries at its discretion.

requirements.heading: The Drawing Palette
requirements.text: There are two other important situations that can occur:

requirements.heading: The Drawing Palette
requirements.text:
1. The video hardware doesn't have a color palette (eg, its a 24-bit color system and doesn't have an actual palette), or
2. The operating system is running in an environment with only a certain number of colors (eg, 256, 16, etc), but you cannot redefine any or them, or you can only redefine some of them (eg, Microsoft Windows under many configurations, etc).

requirements.heading: The Drawing Palette
requirements.text: Situation #1 is the easiest to work with. You don't have an actual color palette to modify, so any color values (from 0-255) simply lookup the RGB data in the color lookup table and use that raw color component data to set the color of the current drawing operation. In this manner, the lookup table is "pretending" to be a hardware video palette. This is a situation where having the lookup table is very important. It isn't extremely important when you have a one-to-one mapping of lookup colors to actual hardware color palette colors because the lookup table does the exact same thing as the hardware color palette. But, in modes where you have no palette, this information becomes vital. In practice, this local lookup table aids in color translation of image files (JPEG, GIF, BMP, etc), and also aids in color translation in other situations.

requirements.heading: The Drawing Palette
requirements.text: Situation #2, where you don't have complete control over the target video palette is much more complicated. For example, under Microsoft Windows, you typically cannot redefine the colors black or white. This gives you only a sub-set of the actual palette to work with. Also, other applications in the environment may have "locked" several entries in the color palette for their own exclusive use. This can reduce your target color palette even further. How you handle which colors in the lookup table to "activate" (if any), and in what order you activate them is entirely up the discretion of the programmer(s) of the RIPscrip package dealing with this kind of environment. The topic of algorithms for this situation goes completely beyond the scope of this RIPscrip specification. Suffice it to say that the programmer would have to determine some way of mapping the lookup table to a suitable set of colors in the actual destination color environment. If he uses strange methods of dithering (like Windows does), or other mechanisms to achieve the desired color to the user, so be it.

requirements.heading: Palette Mapping and Direct RGB Mode
requirements.text: Under RIPscrip 2.0 and later, you have two methods of specifying color values. You have already seen how colors can be specified by a color index number into the color lookup table (from 0-255). What RGB color that actually maps to is based on the contents of that entry in the actual color lookup table. This is called "Palette mapping mode". In palette mapping mode, most locations in RIPscrip commands that allow for color values take a color number (from 0-255) which references some RGB value in the color lookup table.
requirements.reason: The palette and drawing commands resolve active inks, apply the selected write mode, and compose against screen or bitmap destinations. Native truth-table tests and connected palette, mixed-color and blink-plane checks exercise the result.

requirements.heading: Palette Mapping and Direct RGB Mode
requirements.text: We also allow for another mode in RIPscrip, called "Direct RGB Encoding". This mode allows you to specify actual "raw RGB" values instead of color lookup table indices. When a direct RGB value is found, it is decoded (ie, breaking up the red, green and blue components) and is used for the actual color. What happens at this particular moment depends on the environment that the RIPscrip software is running under.
requirements.reason: The palette and drawing commands resolve active inks, apply the selected write mode, and compose against screen or bitmap destinations. Native truth-table tests and connected palette, mixed-color and blink-plane checks exercise the result.

requirements.heading: Palette Mapping and Direct RGB Mode
requirements.text: If the software is running in an environment with a color palette, where the hardware video palette is set to some combination of the colors used in the color lookup table, then the RGB encoded data is matched to the "closest" color in the actual target hardware video palette and that color number is actually used. Under many situations, this color value will be the same one as used in the actual color lookup table (for situations where the software is running on a 256-color palette environment with complete control over the hardware palette). Under modes that are more limited, but where a hardware palette is still being used, the same algorithm can still be applied - but there won't be a one-to-one mapping of color lookup table values to the hardware palette. This is unavoidable and in the case of direct RGB encoding, irrelevant.
requirements.reason: The palette and drawing commands resolve active inks, apply the selected write mode, and compose against screen or bitmap destinations. Native truth-table tests and connected palette, mixed-color and blink-plane checks exercise the result.

requirements.heading: Palette Mapping and Direct RGB Mode
requirements.text: If the software is running in an environment like 24-bit mode, then life couldn't be simpler. Simply take the color value and use its RGB components (possibly with some color component remapping), and and activate that color in the environment.

requirements.heading: Palette Mapping and Direct RGB Mode
requirements.text: Direct RGB encoding mode, unlike palette mapping mode, allows you to specify the bit-precision of RGB color codes used subsequently in RIPscrip code (where direct RGB colors are permitted - not all RIPscrip commands permit direct RGB encoded color codes). This allows you to have color values with the same flexibility as "set color palette" commands, where you can specify arbitrary precisions of RGB data to potentially accomodate high-end color systems like 24-bit, 16-bit, 15-bit, etc).
requirements.reason: The palette and drawing commands resolve active inks, apply the selected write mode, and compose against screen or bitmap destinations. Native truth-table tests and connected palette, mixed-color and blink-plane checks exercise the result.

requirements.heading: Palette Mapping and Direct RGB Mode
requirements.text: By default, RIPscrip operates in palette mapping mode, Whenever a reset operation occurs (any type of reset), palette mapping mode is once again re-enabled. In order to go to RGB encoding mode, you must explicitly specify a [RIP_SET_COLOR_MODE](#rip_set_color_mode) command, or a `$COLORMODE()$` text variable to activate direct RGB encoding mode. When you specify direct RGB encoding mode, you indicate how many bits of precisions to allow for each red, green and blue component. This value is used for all three components. For example, if you specify 8 bits of precision for each component, then combined they will amount to 24 bits of RGB data (eg, 24-bit mode). This is unlike some unusual environments on the IBM-PC where 16-bit modes (5 red, 6 green and 5 blue bits) are allowed on some VGA environments.
requirements.reason: The palette and drawing commands resolve active inks, apply the selected write mode, and compose against screen or bitmap destinations. Native truth-table tests and connected palette, mixed-color and blink-plane checks exercise the result.

requirements.heading: Palette Mapping and Direct RGB Mode
requirements.text: **The shipped reality.** The 2.00a4 design allowed arbitrary per-component precision; the recovered **wire RIP_SET_COLOR_MODE handler** accepts RGB mode only with **8 bits per channel** (24-bit values). The distinct **[COLORMODE variable](5.1-text-variables.md#colormode) accepts and reports 1..8 bits** through the shared active setter. An eight-only statement about the entire driver would incorrectly describe that macro path ([original range matrix](../research/issue-23-environment-query-names.md#native-callback-activation-and-wire-checkpoint)). The RIPtel demo prologue sets `M08` - palette-mode operation declared with 8-bit components - in 90 of 116 scripts. On palette hardware a direct-RGB color is matched to the closest available palette color; on 24-bit hardware it is used exactly. Palette-less (24-bit) environments treat the drawing palette purely as a lookup table for index-mode colors.

requirements.text: The exact determination of this color palette was very carefully chosen. The lowest 16 colors, which happen to default to the basic colors of ANSI color codes (universally used throughout the computer world seemingly), are a good sub-set of colors for basic 16 color operations. The next 16 colors are defined as a dedicated gray-scale color palete (only of use in 256 color modes), and gives a very good breakdown of the gray-scale monotone color palette. The remaining 224 entries are broken down mathematically (as you've seen above) with 7 levels of red, 8 levels of green and 4 levels of blue. This seemingly odd configuration of color distrubution was very scientifcally chosen. _(v2.A4)_
requirements.reason: Reference scaffolding, historical evidence or rationale; normative palette values, mapping and write behavior are tracked separately.

requirements.heading: Default RGB Values of Color Lookup Table
requirements.text: Extensive experimental research has determined that the human eye is more susceptible to particular "hues" of light than others. Specifcally, the human eye is most susceptible to subtle changes in the shade of green than any other color. Next comes red, then finally blue at the very lowest end of the perceptivity scale. If you recall, red is at the lower end of the light spectrum (eg, near infrared), and blue is at the upper end of the spectrum (near ultra-violet). Green is in the middle. This tells us that our eye is most responsive to light in the middle-to-lower bands of the color spectrum. After scientific analysis, our eye was determined to be responsive to the following levels of each color band (comparitively based on an 8 level scale, 1 being lowest): _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: Default RGB Values of Color Lookup Table
requirements.text: Taking this information into account, we constructed a default palette which reflected the best distribution of color that the human eye can perceive. By no means is it perfectly suited for all environments, but it is a "best case" situation for most images and environments. As you can undoubtedly guess, a photograph with a lot of blues and violets would be significantly degraded in quality in this color environment, but many typical images where a broad range of colors is used works very well, and when dithering is used, the situation improves even more. _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: Color mode wire format
requirements.text: The ordinary [final-field shortening rule](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#parameters) applies in both modes. Remove leading zeros and keep at least one digit when a delimiter follows the shortened field. The delimiter finalizes that number in the field's own radix. For example, `!|c4` and `!|c0004` both supply value 4 in RGB mode when terminated by CR. Bytes following a full field use the ordinary [fixed-field collection and dispatch rules](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#numeric-collection-and-dispatch).

requirements.heading: Color mode wire format
requirements.text: For RGB input, pack the components with blue in the lowest N bits, green in the next N and red in the highest N, where N is the selected component precision. For example, the six-bit components `011011 001001 100100` pack to decimal 111,204. The full UltraNum field is `0R9a`. For a final field, `R9a` followed by a delimiter encodes the same value.

These examples show the arguments received by the handlers, where color values are interpreted and validated.

requirements.heading: RIP_BACK_COLOR
requirements.text: This command alters the setting of the background pen drawing color. This color is used for fill operations for the background pixels of the fill as well as some erase functions. The color of the foreground pixels of the fill pattern are specified with a [RIP_FILL_STYLE](2.3-shapes-and-fills.md#rip_fill_style) and [RIP_FILL_PATTERN](2.3-shapes-and-fills.md#rip_fill_pattern) command. requirements.heading: RIP_BACK_COLOR
requirements.text: The background color can also affect the way line patterns/styles appear on the screen. Normally a line pattern is a sequence of on and off pixels where the on pixels are drawn in the normal RIPscrip foreground drawing color as set by the [RIP_COLOR](#rip_color) command. The other pixels (the off pixels) are normally not drawn at all (ie, transparent). When you use the [RIP_LINE_STYLE](2.1-lines.md#rip_line_style) command, you can specify that these off pixels are to be drawn in the current background color (set with this command). See the RIP_LINE_STYLE for exact syntax on using this mode.

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_PALETTE
requirements.text: The collector requires sixteen color fields in active Base Math. Each takes two digits at full width. A [leading period](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#period-as-a-zero-field) supplies one value zero. The delimiter can finalize a nonempty shortened last field. A malformed wire field discards the command before any palette change.

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_PALETTE
requirements.text: With an unprotected current palette, process the sixteen decoded master colors in order from entry 0 through 15. Each value 0–63 writes the corresponding stored RGB. On the first value above 63, report a range error and stop. Keep the entries already stored, leave the failing entry and remaining entries as they were, and issue no palette publication for the failed command. A protected palette rejects before any store or publication. After sixteen valid values, publish the low sixteen entries using the [master-color mapping](#master-color-storage-and-publication).
requirements.reason: Live RIPv3 master-color edits implement the adopted PR #276 collection, storage and publication rules.

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_PALETTE
requirements.text: For example, fifteen `04` fields followed by `1S` in Base Math 36 store red component 42 in entries 0–14. The last value decodes to 64, so entry 15 and the published mapping retain their prior values. [PALENTRY](5.1-text-variables.md#palentry) reads the updated stored prefix immediately. A subsequent selection or full palette republication publishes it. If the last field is `0?` instead, the parser discards the command and all entries retain their prior values. [Original store and publication order](../research/issue-275-master-palette-publication.md).

requirements.heading: Master-color storage and publication
requirements.text: With graphics processing disabled, both commands leave the palette alone. The portable profile publishes all 256 logical entries when a palette is selected or fully republished. A successful `Q` or `a` publishes only the entries it writes. A failed `Q` leaves the stored prefix available to PALENTRY, copy and backup operations while the previous published colors stay in use. Indexed pixels use the published colors. Pixels stored as RGB keep their own colors. Palette writes retain the current slot's selection, definition and protection.

requirements.heading: Master-color storage and publication
requirements.text: Historically, `Q` requests a batch update of entries 0–15 after the final store. `a` requests a single GDI update below index 236. The logical write still reaches entry 236 through 255. This physical GDI cutoff does not limit portable indexed publication. [Original conversion, stores and host requests](../research/issue-275-master-palette-publication.md).

requirements.text: This command updates consecutive entries in the current 256-entry Drawing Palette from RGB inputs.

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_DRAWING_PALETTE
requirements.text: `<num>` is the number of decoded color fields. After count, start and precision, collect repeated four-digit color fields until the command delimiter. The delimiter can finalize a nonempty shortened last color. A [leading period](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#period-as-a-zero-field) completes one field with value zero, including a color field. A period inside a field discards the command. Collection continues even after reaching the declared count. An invalid byte such as a space before the delimiter discards the command. At dispatch, the handler requires the decoded color count to equal `<num>` before writing any entries.
requirements.reason: D and d use UltraNum and require precision eight. Period supplies one zero field and a nonempty final color can be short. D validates exactly the decoded count before publication; d accepts surplus after its fixed color.

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_DRAWING_PALETTE

requirements.heading: Stored Color and Palette Publication
requirements.text: For an accepted write with 8-bit RGB input, `D` and `d` store the same six-bit components in the current writable palette. For each input component `c`, retain `q = floor(c / 4)`. This is the persistent value used by [PALENTRY](5.1-text-variables.md#palentry), palette selection, copy and backups. Neither write changes the slot's definition or protection status. The precision of an RGB drawing mode is a separate setting.
requirements.reason: D and d publish the same stored six-bit colors, preserving their mapping through palette selection, copy and restore. Connected fixtures verify indexed pixels and exact PALENTRY results.

requirements.heading: Stored Color and Palette Publication
requirements.text: **Portable indexed renderer rule.** Publish the new palette mapping when the write completes. For each stored component, publish `255` when `q = 63` and `4q` otherwise. Apply that same mapping after either write, after selecting a defined palette, and whenever a palette is republished from its stored entries. Reapplying a palette preserves its stored six-bit values and reproduces their published colors. Indexed pixels that use the current drawing palette retain their indices and resolve to the newly published mapping. Pixels stored as RGB retain their own color.
requirements.reason: D and d publish the same stored six-bit colors, preserving their mapping through palette selection, copy and restore. Connected fixtures verify indexed pixels and exact PALENTRY results.

requirements.heading: Stored Color and Palette Publication
requirements.text: **Range.** For decoded `D` fields, require `0 ≤ start ≤ 255` and `0 ≤ num ≤ 256 − start`, with exactly `num` color values. Validate the entire update before modifying or publishing entries. An out-of-range update rejects as a whole, with zero RGB or publication changes. A valid zero count is a no-op. Entry 255 is a regular logical entry even on clients with fewer physical color slots. This is the portable remaining-range rule.
requirements.reason: D validates consecutive entries and the complete payload before applying an update. Connected and native coverage includes entry 255, out-of-range rejection and zero-count no-op. Whole-update validation enforces exact decoded count and the remaining range. Tests include 256 one-byte zero colors, zero count, and malformed updates that leave the palette unchanged.

requirements.heading: Stored Color and Palette Publication
requirements.text: **Historical Windows publication.** RIPtel 3.1's native `d` handler can request a single GDI entry update with the full submitted RGB when that index is backed by an available logical slot below 236. `D` rebuilds its GDI requests from the stored six-bit colors. It substitutes black when all stored components are at most 3. The normal selection upload also expands the stored components, but its near-black check uses the expanded bytes, so only stored black meets that threshold. Those are display requests specific to the Windows backend. A portable renderer uses the same published color for `D` and `d`, including near-black values. [Original calls and portable policy](../research/issue-174-palette-publication.md)

requirements.text: This command physically switches the currently active drawing color palette. When this happens, any graphics currently on-screen will immediately change colors based on the new palette (providing the terminal is running in a hardware mode that allows for color palettes). If the terminal is running in a mode that doesn't allow for color palettes (ie, 24-bit mode, etc), then only the internal color lookup table is changed for subsequent color palette mapping mode operations.

It ignores surplus after the fields. Source protect and unprotect execute before selection; destination protect and unprotect execute afterward. Protect zero is diagnosed without skipping later actions. Connected indexed pixels resolve the selected palette after the switch.

requirements.heading: RIP_WRITE_MODE
requirements.text: **Protocol composition:** X and j apply the selected operation to every covered pixel on screen and offscreen ports. Standalone outlines and region fills use current W; an optional **filled-object border uses COPY**, as specified by [RIP_SET_BORDER](2.3-shapes-and-fills.md#rip_set_border). The [PolyMarker pen](2.1-lines.md#marker-fill-and-stroke) is selected by marker flags and uses current W. A fill-pattern zero bit supplies Back Color, while a transparent line gap supplies no contribution. Contributions are ordered, and a genuine second stroke visit applies the operation again. See the [shared equations, pass/gap matrix and independent pixel vectors](../../2.0/techspecs/2.3-drawing-composition.md), plus [3.0 primitive roles](../techspecs/2.3-drawing-composition.md).

requirements.heading: Scope and color effects
requirements.text: _Editor's note: RIPscrip 1.54 offered only COPY (`00`) and XOR (`01`), and its per-command attribute matrix already applied them to lines, rectangles, polygons, filled polygons, poly-lines, beziers and graphics text - but marked circles, ovals, arcs, oval-arcs, pie slices, bars, pixels and flood fills `Uses Write Mode: NO`. The 2.x draft adds OR, AND and NOT and turns the matrix on for every level-0 drawing primitive, and 3.x carries that forward. (Per-command `Uses Write Mode:` lines in `RIPScrip-1.54.txt` and `RIPScrip-2.0-alpha-4.txt`; see [Canvas, Clipping & Write Modes](../../1.54/techspecs/2.0-canvas-clipping-write-modes.md#write-modes-rip_write_mode).)_

requirements.heading: Scope and color effects
requirements.text: The effects of OR, AND, XOR and NOT can cause distinctly different resultant colors in 16 color modes as compared to 256 color modes. For example, if you have a color of 7 (0111 binary) in a 16 color mode, and you NOT that color, you get 8 (1000 binary). Under a standard 16 color palette, color 7 is light gray and color 8 is dark gray. Under a 256 color palette though, color 7 (00000111 binary) will convert to 248 (11111000 binary). This color is definitely not dark gray - it is by default, an RGB of (63,54,0) which is a shade of brownish yellow. _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: RIP_PIXEL
requirements.text: **Shipped origin defect:** X computes a viewport-offset rectangle for invalidation but passes the **unoffset** converted dx/dy to the actual SetPixel call. The selected drawing context is the master screen for an onscreen port, or that port's own bitmap for an offscreen port. Clipping still uses the current viewport rectangle in that context. Consequently a viewport whose stored device origin is (65,65) clips away X(2,2)'s attempt at (1,1). It does not move that attempt to (66,66). A newly initialized screen subport likewise does not make X add its origin. _Evidence: [original drawing/DC/clip path](../research/issue-11-pixel-pen-units.md#original-drawing-path-derivation)._

requirements.text: **Write operation:** apply current W (COPY/XOR/OR/AND/destination-NOT) to each covered pixel, on screen and offscreen ports. The [independent nonblack-destination matrix](../../2.0/techspecs/2.3-drawing-composition.md#independent-pixel-vectors) defines their required results; an old client's SetPixel/FillRect boundary is not a protocol exception.

These are observable differences, replacing the earlier hypothesis that only j performs world conversion.

requirements.heading: RIP_POINT
requirements.text: The origin is already expressed in the drawing context's coordinates: do **not** add the screen port's origin again. A new screen subport's default viewport begins at its screen origin; a new offscreen port begins at bitmap (0,0). The shipped [RIP_VIEWPORT](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_viewport) producer has its own origin defect: it stores the directly converted viewport coordinates without adding the screen port's origin. For example, on a port beginning at screen (25,25), viewport input world (80,80)..(118,118) under 2:1 reduction stores device `[40,40,60,60)`, and j(2,2) plots (41,41), **not** (66,66). _Evidence: [original viewport producer and probe](../research/issue-11-pixel-pen-units.md#viewport-producer-and-screen-port-origin)._

requirements.heading: RIP_POLYLINE
requirements.text: This command will draw a multi-faceted line. It is identical in nature to the [RIP_POLYGON](2.3-shapes-and-fills.md#rip_polygon) command, except that the last point is NOT connected to the first point. Generally speaking, a Poly-Line is not an "enclosed area". The segments of the Poly-Line are drawn using the current drawing color, line pattern, thickness and Drawing Write Mode.

requirements.heading: RIP_POLYLINE
requirements.text: The `<npoints>` parameter indicates how many (x,y) coordinate pairs (vertices) follow. An open Poly-Line with N vertices has **N-1 segments**, joining consecutive pairs without a closing segment. _Editorial correction: the inherited sentence incorrectly equated the vertex and segment counts; its own five-segment/six-vertex example below establishes the distinction ([derivation](../research/issue-11-pixel-pen-units.md))._ The original two-digit count reaches **1295 vertices in MegaNum or 4095 in UltraNum**, independently of coordinate width. See [polygon counts and wire limits](2.3-shapes-and-fills.md#polygon-counts-and-wire-limits) for the exact maximum prefixes and the historical 4096 advertisement: its stale extra scratch conversion does not add an input vertex or a closing segment. The N2_TITLE.RIP example above is a 14-vertex (`0E`) newspaper rule.

requirements.heading: Thickness units and stored width
requirements.text: After the applicable conversion and minimum clamp, the original stores **only the low eight bits** of the width and passes that byte to CreatePen. This is truncation, not saturation: unscaled 256 stores/passes 0, 257 gives 1, and 4095 gives 255. Width 0 at the GDI boundary is a cosmetic one-device-pixel pen; POINT instead uses the stored byte in its square rule above, so zero also gives a 1×1 point. A modern implementation that supports larger widths without this truncation is repairing a historical limitation. _Evidence: original store 0x1ce35 and CreatePen call 0x1ce83; [native checks](../research/issue-11-pixel-pen-units.md#exact-widthflag-handling); Microsoft's [CreatePen contract](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/wingdi/nf-wingdi-createpen) defines its zero-width behavior._

requirements.text: **Format:** `!|; <x> <y> <marker> <width> <height> <rotation> <flags>`

requirements.heading: RIP_MARKER
requirements.text: The DLL names this command `RIP_PolyMarker()`. Four fields use the current XY width, and the three scalar fields have width two in the current Base Math. At XY width 2 the payload has 14 digits. Marker indices are **0–35**, rotation is **0–359** whole degrees, and valid flags are **0–3**. Reject an out-of-range scalar before drawing. Width and height are the full world-space extents. The [marker demos](../research/riptel-script-census.md#0---rip_marker-hypothesized-name) exercise the command 361 times. [Original source and verification](../research/issue-212-polymarker.md)
requirements.reason: The connected PolyMarker vectors exercise final flag shortening for all four modes and preserve the established scalar ranges.

requirements.heading: Marker Contour Projection
requirements.text:
1. Convert the center and the full dimensions separately from WORLD to device coordinates. Apply X scaling to X and width, and Y scaling to Y and height. Truncate each nonnegative ratio to an integer. Add the current viewport's device origin to the center once. Replace either projected dimension of zero with one.
2. For marker **0**, use the [shared Q14 ellipse sampler](../techspecs/2.1-arc-consumer-contract.md#reproducible-q14-numeric-profile), with each device radius the integer half of its projected full dimension. Sample parameters 0 through 360 inclusive with the requested rotation. A projected dimension of one gives a radius of zero along that axis.
3. For markers **1–35**, obtain the normalized vertices for the marker index from the [complete contour data](../techspecs/data/polymarker-contours.json). Iterate in the supplied order and close the path from its last vertex to its first. Use the same separate [Q14 sine and cosine tables](../techspecs/data/skewed-ellipse-q14.json) as the ellipse sampler.

requirements.heading: Marker Contour Projection
requirements.text: For a normalized vertex `(px,py)`, let `Q = 16384`, `r = (360 - rotation) mod 360` and `floorQ(z) = floor(z/Q)`, including negative values. Let `(cx,cy)` be the translated device center and `(dw,dh)` the projected full dimensions. For the 35 table contours use:

requirements.heading: Marker Contour Projection
requirements.text:
```text
sx = floor(dw * Q / 100)
sy = floor(dh * Q / 100)
u  = floorQ(px * sx)
v  = floorQ(py * sy)
x  = cx + floorQ(u * C[r] - v * S[r])
y  = cy + floorQ(u * S[r] + v * C[r])
```

requirements.heading: Marker Contour Projection
requirements.text: Keep the two scale truncations, both signed shifts and the rotation dot products in that order. Positive authored rotation turns counterclockwise in screen space. With unit WORLD scale, viewport origin (0,0), center (100,100) and size 100×60, marker 14 starts at **(100,70)** for rotation 0 and **(70,100)** for rotation 90. The two base-36 commands with flags 1 are `!|;2S2S0E2S1O0001` and `!|;2S2S0E2S1O2I01`. At rotation 0 its fourth vertex is **(109,129)**, showing the staged truncation on the positive Y extent. With scale X=1/2, Y=1 and viewport origin (5,7), the same center and extents yield device center (55,107), size 50×60 and rotated tip **(25,107)**.

requirements.text: The flags determine both contributions independently of [N](2.3-shapes-and-fills.md#rip_set_border). The fill uses the even-odd interior and current Fill/Back Color pattern. requirements.heading: Angle ordering and sweeps
requirements.text: For A/V/I/i/_, the driver compares computed integer ray endpoints before issuing an arc operation. Equal endpoints give a zero-length line for A/V, a **center-to-edge radial contour for I/i**, and no drawing for _. The protocol draws that radial outline only with N1, using the filled-border COPY rule; N0 supplies no outline contribution. Original-client call observations do not create an N0 exception. Thus a zero-length angular interval is not a uniform empty command across the family. The [exact ray rule and API boundary](../techspecs/2.1-arc-consumer-contract.md#axis-aligned-endpoint-rays) also explain radius-dependent quantization and the distinction between equal integer endpoints and equal projected rays.
requirements.reason: The curve command path projects the radii, computes the integer rays and dispatches ellipses, sectors and chords. Independent native vectors cover equality, wrap, aspect ratio and closure.

requirements.heading: The Skewed-Oval Family - 3.x Census Discoveries
requirements.text: The six commands below exist in no published specification - not 1.54, not 2.00a4. They were recovered from the RIPtel demo corpus, where NEWCMDS.RIP demonstrates each new primitive over a coordinate grid with TeleGrafix's own naming comments ("Show RIP*SKEWED_OVAL", "Show a RIP_SKEWED_OVAL_PIE_SLICE", …), making the canonical names verbatim TeleGrafix. They add what the 1.54/2.0 [RIP_OVAL](#rip_oval) family cannot do: ellipses whose axes are **rotated to an arbitrary angle**. Original dispatch and point-generation instructions now establish the widths and degree units; see the [angle derivation](../research/issue-14-arc-sweeps.md). The filled members honor [RIP_SET_BORDER](2.3-shapes-and-fills.md#rip_set_border) like the documented filled primitives - NEWCMDS.RIP demos each "With a border" and "Without a border". None of these commands appear in the RIPSCRIP.HLP name inventory or in SyncTERM. The filled members of the family stay on this page with their outline siblings, as the 3.x record groups them.

requirements.text: An XY pair is X followed by Y, each of current XY width. All fields use current Base Math. The fill digit for pie and chord selects stroke when zero and fill when nonzero. The full parameter totals are `6 × XY`, `10 × XY` and `10 × XY + 1` digits as applicable.
requirements.reason: Each coordinate uses XY or the one-byte zero field. Unfilled affine arcs and both whole ovals allow a short final Y. Pie and chord require the final one-digit fill value. Complete commands ignore surplus.

requirements.heading: Affine Ellipse Commands
requirements.text: `C` is the center and `A` and `B` are the endpoints of the two conjugate radii. They may be nonperpendicular. `S` and `E` are points determining the directions of the start and end rays from C, including points within the ellipse. The [affine contour algorithm](../techspecs/2.1-arc-consumer-contract.md#affine-ellipse-contours) specifies WORLD projection, axis ordering, the 72 integer samples, endpoint selection, missed rays and degeneracy.

requirements.heading: Affine Ellipse Commands
requirements.text: An outline uses current line style, thickness, Draw/Back Color and W. A closed filled result uses the even-odd interior with current Fill/Back Color, pattern and W. N enables an optional patterned border using COPY. Its opaque and transparent line gaps have the [same policy as other polygon-related borders](../techspecs/2.3-drawing-composition.md#affine-ellipse-composition). An open result takes the standalone stroke route. A one-point result supplies no drawable segment. Draw on the selected port with ordinary viewport clipping.

requirements.heading: Affine Ellipse Commands
requirements.text: At unit WORLD scale, Base Math 36 and XY width 2, `!|,2S2S462S2S1O462S2S1O` has C=(100,100), A=(150,100), B=(100,60), S=A and E=B. It draws an open 19-vertex quarter arc from (150,100) to (100,60). Change the opcode to colon and append `1` to fill the corresponding closed pie. requirements.heading: RIP_BEZIER
requirements.text: `cnt` has a full width of **two digits in the current base**, independently of XY width. Its range is 0–1295 in base 36 and 0–4095 in base 64. The [last-field shortening rule](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#numeric-collection-and-dispatch) permits one digit at a delimiter. The [period shortcut](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#period-as-a-zero-field) applies to the numeric fields, including coordinates. **Use at least 2.** RIPtel forwards 0/1 to Polyline without a command-level rejection; these counts cannot draw a curve. For N>=2, it submits **N points and N-1 connecting edges**, not N straight segments or N+1 points. It generates the start, samples at **t=i/N for i=1..N-2**, then the endpoint at t=1. Thus N=2 is a straight endpoint-to-endpoint line, and the normal `(N-1)/N` sample is missing. The example's `14` means **40 points** in base 36.

requirements.heading: RIP_BEZIER

These are exact original consumer semantics; captured drawing calls do not establish Windows pixel rasterization or historical XOR join defects.

requirements.heading: Counts, limits and rejection
requirements.text: `count` is the requested point count **per curve**, using the same sampling as [`Z`](#rip_bezier). Let C be the number of curve records and L the number of point records, so `num=C+L`. The complete decoded input occupies **2+7*C+3*L numeric values**, including both headers and every type. This must fit the original parser's **8193-value** collection capacity; each header is also bounded by its two-digit encoding. For example, no more than 1170 all-curve records fit, while base-64 permits 2730 all-point records. This input limit is separate from the generated limit below.

Independent literal numeric grids, overflow vectors and 8193-input/4094-generated budgets plus original complete z/t vectors are tested. requirements.heading: Counts, limits and rejection
requirements.text:
```text
N = count
if C*N + L + 1 > 4095:
    N = floor((4094 - L) / C)
if N == 0:
    reject whole primitive
submitted_points = C*N + L
```

requirements.heading: Counts, limits and rejection
requirements.text: Thus **4094 is the maximum actual submitted point count**, not 4096, and reduction applies uniformly to every curve. For example, two curves and one point requested at 2047 use N=2046 and submit 4093 points. Each curve's N-point output includes its next record's start when N>=2; that following record also supplies its own start, so join duplicates are retained. N=1 contributes only the curve start to the submitted array. The generator's extra scratch endpoint for N=1 is not an additional drawn point.

requirements.heading: Counts, limits and rejection
requirements.text: Invalid types, incomplete records or disagreement with `num` reject the whole primitive; they do not draw a prefix or silently omit a bad terminal record. Most common-consumer failures are silent, while `num=0` reports “Too few segments”. Oversized numeric input is truncated by the byte parser and rejected when its resulting vector fails validation. See the [consumer contract](../techspecs/2.2-bezier-consumer-contract.md) for the exact numerical and capacity boundaries.

No terminal point is required to repeat the first point, and t adds no closing edge.

requirements.reason: Reconciled K against adopted #33 / PR #63. STYLE retains original line type 0..4 separately from its resolved/custom mask, validated and preserved by copy/selection/protection/backups. Flags exactly 1 partition opaque pen/brush coverage into one operation per pixel; flags 0/2/3 fill first then apply a transparent-gap pen, preserving sequential ROP on overlaps. Degenerate/no-border, normalized/wide/clipped geometry, context fill phase, RGB/NOT unused ink and allocation/recovery paths are covered. With N1 it then draws a **solid COPY border** using Draw Color and current line thickness; N0 suppresses that border. (x0,y0) and (x1,y1) are opposing corners. requirements.heading: RIP_FILLED_RECTANGLE
requirements.text: The earlier [RIPtel K pen/ROP observations](../research/issue-33-filled-rectangle-borders.md) describe a particular client's behavior. They do not override the protocol's explicit filled-border COPY/solid rule. A dotted or custom line style therefore does not make K's border dotted/custom, and W01 does not make that border XOR. Only the interior uses W01. Backend calls may be combined only if equivalent to fill followed by COPY border; they do not define another protocol pass policy.

requirements.heading: RIP_ROUNDED_RECT
requirements.reason: U/u use current-base XY fields at widths 2..5, including a shortened final radius. They ignore surplus after all five full-width fields. Opposing corners normalize and project in wide integer arithmetic; radius uses X only, then the corner semiaxes fit device spans independently. U always uses its logical pen; u uses the bound N state and context-phased brush. Both use current ROP, fixed type-4 DASHDOTDOT and wide solid pens. Opaque flags combine disjoint brush/pen coverage; other flags fill then stroke. All curve/side allocations precede painting. Independent circular-distance/perimeter and Boolean-operation oracles cover all canvases, screen/offscreen ports, both bases/widths/scales, styles/flags/modes, state preservation, literal U/u examples, oversize/zero/degenerate shapes, low-WORD Y sign/zero cases, wide endpoints, unused inks and nonfatal recovery.

requirements.heading: Rounded-Rectangle Geometry
requirements.text: On a **640×350 world / 640×480 canvas**, radius 20 becomes **20 device pixels on both axes**, giving a 40×40 corner ellipse. World corners `(20,35)` and `(100,105)` become `(20,48)` and `(100,144)` with zero viewport origin; the request is `(20,48,101,145,40,40)`. Thus Y placement scales by 480/350 while the corner's ordinary radius stays 20. On a 1280×960 world / 640×480 canvas, radius 20 instead becomes 10 device pixels and the corner ellipse is 20×20. These are device-coordinate circles before any oversize fitting; the inherited unrestricted claim of truly circular corners is too broad.

requirements.heading: Rounded-Rectangle Geometry
requirements.text: **Oversize fitting:** the RIP driver neither rejects nor pre-clamps an oversized radius; it forwards the corner ellipse to GDI. In the ordinary compatible device-coordinate geometry, GDI fits the ellipse's absolute diameters **independently** to the available X/Y spans: `dx=min(abs(ellipse_width),R-L)`, `dy=min(abs(ellipse_height),B-T)`. Semiaxes are dx/2 and dy/2. This happens after coordinate/radius conversion and compatible-mode far-edge adjustment; it is not a common circular-radius clamp to half the smaller dimension. For example, an 8×6 span and r=5 fits to an 8×6 ellipse, rather than a circle of radius 3. Fine curved-edge rounding remains a canvas raster decision. _Evidence: original unchanged requests, Microsoft's [RoundRect diameter contract](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/wingdi/nf-wingdi-roundrect), and separately identified [GDI conformance vectors](../research/issue-38-rounded-rectangle-geometry.md#gdi-boundary-reconciliation)._

requirements.text: **Shipped high-radius defect:** the actual request is `ellipse_width=2r` using the full converted DWORD, but `ellipse_height=2×(int16_t)(r & 65535)`. Thus r=32768 produces height -65536, r=65535 height -2, and r=65536 height 0. GDI's ellipse handling uses the magnitude for negative dimensions and treats a zero dimension as square-corner geometry; this is not a second radius unit. Modern geometry code should distinguish the normal X-world radius rule from this original truncation/sign defect. Extreme DWORD multiplication/doubling overflow is also original fixed-width arithmetic, not an additional advertised coordinate range. _Evidence: original U/u argument preparation, exhaustive WORD-radius native captures and the separately sourced [GDI boundary](../research/issue-38-rounded-rectangle-geometry.md#gdi-boundary-reconciliation)._

requirements.text: The exact maximum-command prefixes are `!|J10|lZZ` and `!|J1S|l&&`, respectively, followed by 1295 or 4095 XY coordinate pairs. Replace `l` with `P` or `p` for the closed or filled commands. J's own parameter always uses MegaNum. For example, keeping default XY=2, the UltraNum command supplies 8191 numeric values (one count plus 8190 coordinates). Do not transmit a separate closing vertex unless it is intentionally part of the N supplied vertices; Polygon closes the last-to-first edge automatically, while Polyline stays open.

requirements.heading: Polygon counts and wire limits
requirements.text: The historical readme/HLP advertisement of **4096 vertices** does not establish a reachable wire count. Two digits have no representation for 4096 and the original parser has no special count encoding. The original handlers actually convert **N+1** pairs from scratch storage while passing **N** to Polygon/Polyline; at the maximum UltraNum count, that is 4096 scratch conversions and 4095 drawn vertices, even for an open polyline. The extra pair comes from stale argument slots, not an implicit closing point supplied by the host. A new implementation should read exactly N pairs and validate the complete count/length relationship before drawing.

requirements.text: RIPtel does **not** enforce a three-vertex minimum for P or turn a one-vertex shape into POINT. The one-vertex GDI failure is ignored by the driver; no additional RIP error is reported. Microsoft’s [Polygon](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/wingdi/nf-wingdi-polygon) and [Polyline](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/wingdi/nf-wingdi-polyline) contracts require at least two points, and neither changes the GDI current position. A two-vertex closed outline uses the ordinary selected pen/write operation; this does not promise a renderer-independent pixel mask or override line style, thickness or write mode.

Filled p shares the zero/one-count guards; two vertices enclose no fill area, with any outline still controlled by its ordinary border state. _Evidence: original parser/handlers,0..3 counts at every supported width/radix with state snapshots and [223,367 native checks](../research/issue-13-polygon-counts.md#post-pr-small-count-results), reconciled with the GDI contracts above. requirements.heading: RIP_POLY_POLYGON
requirements.text: A multi-contour polygon: an initial contour count and first vertex count, followed by coordinate pairs and later contour counts/pairs using the exact [width and aggregate rules below](#multi-contour-widths-and-aggregate-limits). Contours are filled by the even-odd rule - POLYPOLY.RIP places a colored circle behind the figure "so you can see the transparency aspect" through the holes - and the border is switched via [RIP_SET_BORDER](#rip_set_border) ("With borders:" / "Without borders:"). The example above encodes 3 contours (a 4-vertex outer box and two triangular holes). Vertex lists may be split across physical lines with the standard `\` continuation. This is a genuinely new object type: 2.00a4 has nothing comparable, and the single-contour [RIP_FILLED_POLYGON](#rip_filled_polygon) even-odd overlap behavior is only an accident of its fill rule.
requirements.reason: A live truecolor scene distinguishes retraced outlines, XOR fill, an even-odd hole and patterned COPY borders. The skewed and typed-path matrices cover closed contours and transparent gaps.

requirements.heading: Multi-contour widths and aggregate limits
requirements.text: These maxima are `min(base²-1, floor(8192/5))`: each minimal contour costs one count and four coordinates, in addition to the initial C. Increasing C can reduce the remaining vertex allowance. With XY=2, the maximum **aggregate** V is 4094 in MegaNum (counts 1295,1295,1295,209) or 4095 in UltraNum (counts 4093,2, or one contour of 4095). With XY>=3, MegaNum also reaches 4095, using first-contour count 2 and later-contour count 4093. All three multi-contour vertex-boundary constructions use 8193 numbers and are verified through the original parser and PolyPolygon consumer. There is no separate 4096-vertex allowance for every contour.

Historical transcription errors are corrected: preset 04 row five is **0E = 14 = MegaNum 0E = UltraNum 0E**; preset 05 row one is **F0 = 240 = MegaNum 6O = UltraNum 3m**; every FF/255 row is **MegaNum 73 / UltraNum 3&**; preset 0B rows three and seven are **22 = 34 = MegaNum 0Y = UltraNum 0Y**. The [numeric alphabet](1.2-math-and-coordinates.md#numerical-parameters---formats-and-base-math-variations) assigns digit 63 to `&`; `@` is not an UltraNum digit. The preserved original specifications under `text/` retain their historical errors.

requirements.heading: Fill-pattern origin and scaling
requirements.text: **Reconstructed from RIPtel 3.1:** predefined and custom patterns tile from **(0,0) of the drawing device context**, with an **eight-device-pixel period** in each direction. Onscreen ports share the master screen drawing context; each offscreen bitmap has its own bitmap-local origin. This is the graphics drawing surface's origin, independent of where the application window sits on the desktop. Changing the port, viewport, clipping rectangle or primitive does not restart the tile within that context. World scaling converts shape coordinates to device coordinates but does not resize the 8×8 mask.

requirements.heading: Fill-pattern origin and scaling
requirements.text: For a covered device-context pixel `(x,y)`, use `M[y mod 8] & (0x80 >> (x mod 8))`, with modulo residues 0–7. A nonzero result selects the fill color; zero selects the pen background color, subject to the current write mode. Evaluate this after world conversion and geometry placement, using the final context coordinates. [RIP_VIEWPORT's original placement behavior](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_viewport) determines those coordinates; do not separately add a screen port's origin a second time. Adjacent primitives sample the same tile continuously.

requirements.heading: Fill-pattern origin and scaling
requirements.text: For example, let a screen port start at `(2,1)` and its stored viewport start at device-context `(5,3)`, with world and device sizes both 640×480. Set custom rows `80 00 00 00 00 00 00 00` (MegaNum command `!|s3K0000000000000001`, fill-color index 1). Draw filled objects over neighboring world-coordinate ranges `x=0..8` and `x=8..16`, both spanning `y=0..8`. Their placement starts at context X=5 and X=13. Interior samples `(8,8)` and `(16,8)` both select foreground, while `(9,8)` and `(10,9)` select background. Restarting at the viewport would instead put a set bit at `(5,3)`; restarting at the port would put one at `(10,9)`. The native probe captures the original placement and unchanged brush; these sample colors follow from the context-origin rule, independently of exact shape-edge rasterization.

The [derivation](../research/issue-12-fill-masks.md#consumers-and-exact-phase-derivation) combines those original calls with Microsoft's [default brush-origin contract](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/gdi/brush-origin). requirements.heading: RIP_SET_BORDER
requirements.text: **Protocol rule:** fill the region using current W, then draw an enabled border using **COPY** and current line thickness. Polygon-related borders honor the current line pattern; other documented filled-object borders are solid. Patterned borders use Draw Color on bits, Back Color on opaque gaps, and no contribution on transparent gaps. N0 suppresses every optional outline portion, including radial/closing segments, while retaining the fill phase. N does not reset stored W. This is the explicit ALPHA 4 rule; historical K/u native selections do not supersede it. See the [full pass matrix and independent vectors](../../2.0/techspecs/2.3-drawing-composition.md) and [3.0 family classification](../techspecs/2.3-drawing-composition.md).
requirements.reason: Screen drawing composes against the visible destination. Connected samples cover affine fill and outline, retraced strokes, solid and patterned borders, and the full-pie seam. Native vectors cover the remaining write modes and offscreen drawing.

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_BORDER
requirements.text: **Value domain and normalization:** decode `borders:2` using current base math, then store disabled for zero and enabled for **every nonzero value**. This is a Boolean normalization, not a 0/1 range check or a test of bit 0. The ordinary two-digit domains are 0–1295 in MegaNum and 0–4095 in UltraNum. `!|N02` and MegaNum `!|NZZ` therefore enable borders just like `!|N01`; under UltraNum the protocol value in `!|N&&` is 4095 and also enables them. Standard [final-numeric-field shortening](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#ripscrip-protocol---syntax-and-general-structure) permits `!|N0`, `!|N1` and `!|N2`; at least one digit must remain. The field is not reserved and cannot be omitted.

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_BORDER
requirements.text: The setting belongs to the current graphical STYLE. When that style is protected, N reports the protected-data error and leaves its border setting unchanged; it does not update another style or alter the stored write mode. Repeating N with a different nonzero value stores the same enabled state.

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_BORDER

requirements.heading: RIP_FILL
requirements.text: RIPtel 3.1 recognizes `F` as soon as its opcode arrives. The original descriptor has zero arguments and no text field. The collector enters the [fixed-command delimiter wait](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#numeric-collection-and-dispatch), discarding surplus instead of decoding coordinates or border color. It dispatches once at a pipe or terminating CR, LF or form feed. The original handler returns immediately, leaving graphics and protocol state alone. Base Math and coordinate width are irrelevant.

requirements.heading: RIP_FILL
requirements.text: `!|F|c01` and `!|F1E180F|c01` followed by CR dispatch the same no-op and color command. In the surplus state, an ESC byte is discarded without reaching ANSI. A pipe immediately after a backslash still dispatches because this state does not collect quoted text. The usual physical line continuation rules apply to line endings. A partial `!|F` remains pending until a delimiter. [Original descriptor, delimiter paths and captures](../research/issue-279-rip-fill-framing.md).

requirements.heading: RIP_MOVE
requirements.reason: PORT now owns a context-absolute wide integer cursor. MOVE converts current WORLD coordinates and adds the stored viewport origin without needing text/style/ink bindings. Classic TEXT advances X by the signed low WORD of the whole rationally scaled/truncated metric, independently of orientation/justification; Y is retained. Nonzero classic TEXT_XY draws at its converted anchor but stores raw input X/Y plus origin/metric for every orientation. Empty TEXT is silent; empty TEXT_XY diagnoses unchanged; inactive calls preserve state. Independent all-canvas coherent captures, the published 800x600/1280x960 example, all ten magnifications, both encodings and failure/recovery checks cover these rules. Classic font-zero TEXT_XY now uses the owned cached outline width with raw anchors in every direction/justification. Ordinary outline text and complete scene reset remain separately pending.

requirements.heading: RIP_TEXT
requirements.text: This command displays text at the current graphics cursor of the selected port. The [classic font-zero rendering rules](#classic-font-zero-in-text-and-text_xy) apply to both this command and TEXT_XY. For RIPtel 3.1, every accepted nonempty TEXT call advances stored X by the signed low-word width returned by the selected font's metric routine and leaves Y unchanged. **There is no orientation or justification gate.** The inherited horizontal/left-only rule does not describe this driver. Classic text uses the classic width routine; outline text uses the cached outline width routine. The update is not conditional on pixels being produced. _Evidence: [original handler and native cursor matrix](../research/issue-24-drawing-state-ownership.md#text-cursor-stores)._
requirements.reason: Native DEFAULT EX layout vectors and connected text cover current CLASSIC style, canvas spacing, WORLD DPI, anchor, shadow, startup/reset/restore and independent cursor and TEXT_METRIC policies.

requirements.heading: RIP_TEXT
requirements.text: **Completed 3.0 protocol policy:** the [outline advance and cache contract](../techspecs/2.4-outline-advance-and-cache.md) defines the ordinary scalar, per-byte rounding/spacing, unsigned cached measurement and snapshot lifecycle. Its explicit choices fill documentary gaps; they do not require native sign extension, byte-index loops or intermediate WORD overflow. The signed low-word cursor handoff and the following cursor-store branches remain adopted.

requirements.heading: RIP_TEXT
requirements.text: The cursor belongs to the [port](7.0-drawing-ports.md#the-port-table), independently of the selected graphics style. MOVE stores a world-to-device converted point plus viewport origin. The [TEXT_XY compatibility rules](#rip_text_xy) include a different classic path; stored coordinates must not be assumed to remain in world units. Empty TEXT and a disabled viewport leave the cursor unchanged. A RIP_ERASE_VIEWPORT does not reset it; drawing reset initializes the current cursor.

requirements.heading: RIP_TEXT
requirements.text: **Historical FastFont glyph-copy behavior:** in RIPtel 3.1, extended outline-font glyph bitmaps use fixed masked replacement rather than the current vector Write Mode. requirements.heading: Portable Point Size and Spacing
requirements.text:
1. Prepare the metrics at `Q,P`. If the original size is zero, the metric extents are nonpositive or the face/metrics are unavailable, reject the fit.
2. Let `B_w,B_h` be the device box extents and `M_w,M_h` the measured starting extents. Choose the trial size `floor(Q × min(B_w/M_w, B_h/M_h))`, capped at 4,095. A trial of zero rejects. At the original spacing, remeasure at each point size as needed. Step down by one until both extents are positive and fit, or reject when no positive size remains. Then step up by one as long as both extents are positive, fit and the size stays in range. Use the last fitting size. This permits enlargement as well as reduction.
3. At that size, if the measured width is strictly smaller than the box width, try increasing the spacing by five percentage points at a time, up to 4,095. Stop at the first trial that reaches or exceeds the box width, or at the cap. If that trial exceeds the width, reduce spacing one point at a time to the first fitting width. Height remains the height of the chosen size. Use the resulting temporary spacing for the draw.

requirements.heading: Nominal size and spacing
requirements.text: Use effective `Dx=trunc(72 × device_width / world_width)` and `Dy=trunc(72 × device_height / world_height)` from the **current** WORLD and device frame. Changing WORLD changes the realization scale and leaves the spacing row in place. Use the [per-byte ordinary outline advance equations](../techspecs/2.4-outline-advance-and-cache.md#ordinary-scalar-advance) with `Q`, face scale `H=140` and `P` from the table. For each glyph, apply the extra gap `trunc((P−100) × w / 100)` to its own unspaced device advance `w`, including the final byte. Use `Dx` along X and `Dy` along Y. Use raw font byte slots and no pair kerning. A nonpositive device or WORLD dimension supplies no draw.

requirements.heading: Direction and anchor
requirements.text: The [classic justification flags](#justification-and-special-effect-flags) resolve to the along-run alignment (left/start, right/end or centered) and the perpendicular reference line (top, middle, baseline or bottom). RIPtel 3.1 passes those two selectors separately to FastFont. Direction 0 passes rotation 0° for both the string and glyphs. Direction 1 passes 90° counterclockwise for both, so advance is upward and the baseline is on the right.

requirements.heading: Direction and anchor
requirements.text: **Portable placement:** use the current DEVICE graphics cursor for `T`. For `@`, convert its WORLD point once and add the current viewport origin to obtain the DEVICE anchor. Let `A` be that anchor and `L` the sum of the spacing-adjusted glyph steps. From `A`, move opposite the advance direction by 0 for start, `L` for end, or `trunc(L/2)` for center.
