requirements.heading: 4.1 JPEG Images
requirements.text: Photographic images - a capability of the 2.0/3.x generation with no 1.54 counterpart: a host delivers a compressed image file to the terminal and displays it scaled into an **image area**, a sub-region of the current viewport established by [RIP_IMAGE_STYLE](#rip_image_style). JPEG is the only compressed image format in shipping 3.x - the ALPHA 4 draft also added GIF _(v2.A4)_, but GIF was dropped over LZW licensing before shipping, and PNG was announced but never shipped (see the [white paper](../text/RIPScrip-3.x-technical-whitepaper.txt)) - and SyncTERM's `RIPSCRIP030001` mode has no raster support at all, making JPEG display a clean 3.x-only differentiator.
requirements.reason: Connected JPEG and transfer fixtures exercise rendering, completed-file registration and session cleanup.

requirements.heading: RIP_IMAGE_STYLE
requirements.text: This command replaces the current port’s image rectangle and flags for subsequently displayed JPEGs, including local playback and received-image display. The rectangle also supplies HCL bitmap playback geometry, with the distinct flag/presentation boundary below. Coordinates use current world/device conversion; reversed corners are ordered. RIPtel 3.1 stores the converted far coordinates plus one. The setter accepts flags **0..63**, replaces the previous flags and rejects a larger value without changing the style. Unlike the [IMGSTYLE macro setter](5.1-text-variables.md#imgstyle), the wire handler can change a protected current port. _Evidence: original driver 0xc39a and [native style checks](../research/issue-21-image-style.md#native-style-checkpoint)._

requirements.heading: RIP_IMAGE_STYLE
requirements.text: **An inactive viewport does not block this wire setter.** Valid `1i` immediately replaces the stored per-port image area/flags while inactive, including on a protected current port. Reactivation retains that new configuration, so `deactivate; 1i new-area/new-flags; activate; 1p existing-jpeg` displays using the **new** style. An intervening `1p` while inactive skips image lookup/decoding/painting. The IMGSTYLE macro setter has a separate inactive-target gate and does not provide the same exception. _Evidence: [original setter/activation/display sequence and native checks](../research/issue-21-image-style.md#integration-review-inactive-viewport-wire-setter)._
requirements.reason: Wire 1i replaces the current stored record while inactive, including protected screen/offscreen ports. Independent radix/width/canvas state matrices and port-service deactivation/reactivation around byte-split 1i/1p commands prove the exception. An intervening inactive 1p skips allocator, file and decoder services even when bindings are absent; reactivation retains the newly stored style, with independent full-screen index/palette captures. Native and JPEG-disabled fixtures cover capability/error recovery. The separate IMGSTYLE inactive/protection gates are tested rather than inferred from the wire setter.

requirements.heading: RIP_IMAGE_STYLE
requirements.text: **All-zero coordinates do not disable JPEG viewing in RIPtel 3.1.** The inherited ALPHA 4 claim that they disable viewing is not implemented by this driver: the command stores (0,0,1,1), and subsequent display reaches the decoder through a lower-level size fallback. In the full-viewport fixture this uses the physical display dimensions. Do not implement an all-zero “ignore and delete” branch as shipped behavior. A separate internal raw-zero rectangle sentinel suppresses explicit IMAGE/playback before lookup, but is not produced by all-zero IMAGE_STYLE; the client’s received-image export bypasses that guard. _Evidence: [full original presentation chain and zero-area checks](../research/issue-21-image-style.md#full-presentation-and-zero-area-checkpoint)._
requirements.reason: The received entry uses the current style, bypasses the explicit raw-zero guard and leaves the source file in cache.

requirements.heading: RIP_IMAGE_STYLE
requirements.text: **Bitmap playback boundary:** HCL [`$<file.BMP$`](5.3-local-playback.md#local-bitmap-playback---filebmp) consumes this stored rectangle directly with exclusive far edges and fixed COPY/current-palette/auto-dither requests. It ignores all six image-style flag bits, including ASPECT, NOCLEAR and wallpaper; the detailed presentation/zero-area/flag behavior below describes JPEG. See the bitmap contract for its distinct all-zero 1×1 target and clipping/dither completion.
requirements.reason: Live bitmap playback uses the original target in device coordinates, bounded port clipping and the existing indexed COPY/dither renderer. Independent connected vectors cover both encodings.

requirements.heading: Clearing, aspect margins and write mode
requirements.text: JPEG rows use **COPY (SRCCOPY)**, independently of the current vector Write Mode. Unless NOCLEAR is set, the initial fill uses a **black replacement fill**, not the current background color or XOR/OR/AND mixing. With ASPECT, the driver first fits the image, then clears only that fitted rectangle. It leaves the surrounding margins unchanged. Thus **XOR + ASPECT + NOCLEAR** leaves the margins exactly as they were and copies the JPEG into the fitted rectangle; no black margins are XOR’d or otherwise combined with their previous contents. Wallpaper is a separate subsequent COPY operation when bit 16 is set.
requirements.reason: The complete named rendering sequence is implemented in the separate engine: initial black COPY clear over only the fitted rectangle unless NOCLEAR, JPEG COPY independently of vector mode, retained aspect margins, then optional COPY wallpaper from raw stored image-area pixels. Literal independent fill regions, complete index/palette captures, all 64 flags under every vector mode and post-draw staging/error recovery prove these effects. Native and JPEG-disabled fixtures distinguish actual decoder coverage. Full device/port-coordinate and delivered-image/application integration remain separate acceptance work.

requirements.heading: 4.2 Mouse Fields & Pointer
requirements.text: [Mouse fields](../../glossary.md) - host-defined rectangular hot regions that transmit a [host command](../../glossary.md) when clicked - the commands that delete them, and control of the mouse pointer shape.

requirements.heading: 4.2 Mouse Fields & Pointer
requirements.text: Two global rules apply to all mouse regions (fields and buttons alike):

requirements.heading: 4.2 Mouse Fields & Pointer
requirements.text:
- Up to 128 mouse fields, 128 mouse buttons, or any combination may exist simultaneously, but combined their total number cannot exceed 128 - they share the mouse field [data table](7.1-data-tables.md#mouse-field-table). _(v1.54)_
- When the user clicks the mouse on the screen, all mouse regions (whether mouse fields or mouse buttons) are scanned from most recent to the least recent ("last in, first out"): if regions overlap, the newest one wins the click. _(v1.54, revised v2.A3)_
requirements.note: Simple fields with clr=0, shared 128-entry owner, newest-first hit testing and common owned host evaluator are connected. clr=1, identity/hover, button creation and remaining host facilities stay incomplete. The detailed common host processor rule in 5.2 supersedes the inherited template restriction.
requirements.reason: 1M and plain mouse-active 1U share the same 128 fields, newest-first owner and snapshot global PORT0 geometry; decorations consume no slots. Connected shared-capacity and native viewport/edge tests cover this statement.

requirements.heading: 4.2 Mouse Fields & Pointer
requirements.text: Mouse fields exist only on the screen (port #0) - they cannot be placed on offscreen [drawing ports](7.0-drawing-ports.md). The corpus confirms both rules operate as documented in the shipping 3.0 driver. _Evidence: 2.00a4; corpus._
requirements.note: Connected simple-field path. Feedback uses native both-plane rectangle capture/restore, existing cell damage and scroll mapping. Active viewport geometry is stored in absolute DEVICE coordinates; 1K/MKILL/SOFT share deletion. Gesture commitment is provisional under #113; button creation remains pending.

requirements.heading: 4.2 Mouse Fields & Pointer
requirements.text: **Portable hit/eligibility completion:** Stored resident hit bounds are positive global device rectangles with exclusive far edges: `L <= x < R`, `T <= y < B`. Press, movement feedback, release and hover use that same predicate. New fields are clipped to active PORT0's viewport and screen; an inactive effective viewport or empty intersection creates no field/painting and consumes no region slot. Later viewport changes do not reclip or resurrect definitions. The [full extent/eligibility policy and edge examples](4.3-buttons.md#face-extents-and-input-eligibility) distinguish these explicit completion choices from the old nonuniform native edge tests, and cover button face/effect bounds and degenerate geometry.

requirements.heading: Left-button Gesture Commitment
requirements.text: A field's **click host command** commits once, on a left-button release inside the same field that acquired the preceding press. A press alone gives temporary depression feedback; it does not expand/transmit that click command. Releasing outside cancels activation. Dragging outside removes temporary depression and dragging back inside restores it; a final release inside activates once. Pressing outside every field and releasing inside one does not activate it. Simple `1M` fields and mouse-active `1U` buttons share this rule; `clk=0` suppresses simple-field visual inversion, not the press/release requirement. Keyboard/hotkey activation and the existing persistent radio/checkbox selection rules are separate. _Evidence: original RIPtel 3.1 press/release/move dispatch and simple/ordinary-button action paths; [derivation](../research/issue-113-mouse-gesture-identity.md)._
requirements.reason: Checkbox press, drag-out, reentry, cancel and release are exercised on a palette without an exact complementary entry. The field sends its host action once on commitment.

requirements.heading: Left-button Gesture Commitment
requirements.text: Keyboard buttons use a [separate explicit profile](4.3-buttons.md#keyboard-activation): byte matching/default/wildcard priority and translated key-down commitment do not require a pointer hit. A winning keyboard activation cancels an outstanding pointer capture safely; unmatched input does not. It never synthesizes pointer coordinates or transfers the held gesture to a replacement field.
requirements.reason: Connected PR121 keyboard profile: per-instance CP437 byte binding, symmetric ASCII folding, explicit/default/wildcard priority with newest ties, zero unbound, repeat/key-up and noncharacter separation, consumed empty/error actions, HKEY control, stable snapshot/feedback/pointer-cancellation and callback/reset/delay FIELDID. Independent native tables and literal connected vectors prove this source unit; composite HEADER/query/restore/LED clauses remain separate.

requirements.heading: Left-button Gesture Commitment
requirements.text: Only the newest hit field acquires the **press**. Release does not perform a new winner scan. Hover queries are independent actions and can run during pointer movement, including while a click is held; the rule above delays the region's click command, not those separate hover actions. The existing coordinate, clipping, 128-region and rendering rules remain adopted.

Native and live CP437/UTF-8 vectors cover overlap/boundaries, self-deletion, same-ID replacement, actual editor prompts, once-only traversal and parse-failure recovery. After cancellation, require release and a fresh press before another activation. Remove temporary depression before applying deletion's specified painting; this adds no scene erase to `1K` and does not override enclosed deletion's fill/clear flags.

requirements.heading: Hover and Callback Context
requirements.text: Identified fields have independent hover membership. On movement, process **exits before entries**, newest first within each pass. Overlapping identified fields can each run the shared exit/entry handler; this is separate from the single winner chosen for a click press. A field without a valid ID does not run the shared mode-5/mode-6 hover query. The identified field being entered or exited supplies `$FIELDID$` during its handler. _Evidence: original two-pass hover consumer and temporary FIELDID writes; [derivation](../research/issue-113-mouse-gesture-identity.md)._

requirements.heading: Hover and Callback Context
requirements.text: **Handler-independent membership:** each stable field starts outside. Every delivered movement updates its geometric inside/outside membership, whether entry-only, exit-only, both handlers, or neither is configured. Membership is per instance, not public ID; duplicate-ID fields remain independent. Unidentified fields still do not invoke the shared queries. Enabling, replacing or removing a handler does not change membership or synthesize a transition. Thus a field entered while entry is absent stays inside when entry is later enabled; another movement at the same point sends no entry. Movement outside can still invoke a configured exit even if no entry callback ever ran. _Evidence: membership writes precede identity/handler-pointer checks in the original consumer; [derivation](../research/issue-132-hover-handler-lifetime.md)._

requirements.text: **Explicit traversal/commitment completion:** snapshot the movement point, existing field-instance tokens, hit rectangles and old memberships. Form exits and entries from that snapshot, newest first within each pass. Before each candidate's turn, verify the original instance still lives and the traversal's interaction boundary remains valid; skip removed tokens, defer newly created fields until a later movement. Commit that instance's new membership **before** considering its applicable current handler. An absent handler means no host callback, not a deferred callback. Then read the **current** shared exit/entry definition and, if present and the ID is valid, atomically own its source bytes, numeric FIELDID and host continuation. Each such transition commits at most one callback. Do not hold field/table locks over providers/prompts.

requirements.heading: Hover and Callback Context
requirements.text: The applicable handler is selected **per callback**, not copied once for the movement. An earlier exit can replace the handler used by a later exit or entry. Clearing it suppresses later uncommitted callbacks but does not suppress their membership updates. Once a callback commits, removing/replacing the handler, deleting its field or a full reset cannot alter its owned source/FIELDID or replay it. Resume a suspended callback once at its saved stage; use the then-current handler for later candidates. Completed membership/effects are not rolled back by host failure, and no automatic retry occurs. Serialize movement traversals while a callback is suspended; queued movements run afterward from their own point/snapshot. Definition/deletion/reset/focus/cancellation notifications may still apply during suspension. These safe ownership/serialization choices complete the original live-pointer/live-index paths.

A fully framed empty `!|1<ESC>5000` reports nonfatally and preserves entry; so does a 1024-byte source under the explicit bound, while 1023 accepted bytes are stored intact. A stored `$NAME$` whose later value is `$OFF$` invokes NAME only during a committed host callback, never during definition, and does not remove that handler. Pure membership updates, absent-handler transitions, definition/removal, deletion, backup save and reset invoke zero hover host providers. requirements.heading: RIPtel 3.1 Compatibility
requirements.text: The shipped driver uses the shared array from slot zero and checks Ctrl and Shift in its Tab character branch. Its focused Enter and Escape precede the ordinary hotkey matcher. It requests a focus rectangle four device pixels beyond the stored rectangle. The original backward step retains a decremented index only when it is **greater than zero**. Thus with A, B and C in slots 0–2, Shift+Tab from no focus selects A, then goes A → C → B → C. The portable step from B returns to A. The driver also clears focus at entry to `1M`, `1U`, `1k` and `1K`, before admission or deletion, and on other drawing commands such as `1B`. The portable lifetime table ties these changes to actual field mutations and input boundaries. [Primary source and profile comparison](../research/issue-197-tab-navigation.md).

requirements.heading: RIP_MOUSE
requirements.text: After the hotkey, the collector requires three valid digits in active Base Math or a leading period for the reserve. It supplies reserved value zero and starts the host text after that field. The hotkey and reserve each accept their own [one-period zero shorthand](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#period-as-a-zero-field). With Base Math 36 and XY width 2, `!|1M...1E1E....click` supplies a rectangle from `(0, 0)` to `(50, 50)`, zero for `clk`, `clr`, hotkey and reserve, and text `click`. With one fewer period, the reserve is still unfinished at `c`. Base Math 36 discards that command. Base Math 64 consumes `cli` as the reserved digits and collects `ck` as text. [Wire derivation and staged captures](../research/issue-258-mouse-field-suffix.md#staged-captures).

requirements.heading: Simple field reset after the host action
requirements.text: On a [captured inside release](#left-button-gesture-commitment), end the gesture and commit the simple field's host action. Expand and execute it with the field's usual `FIELDID` context. The action sees the current text window and drawing state, including any changes it makes itself. When the action returns, unwind its `FIELDID` context. If the action completed successfully and requested a clear, perform SOFT once on the interpreter's then-current state. Success is the outcome of the whole host program and can include a purely local action with no outbound bytes. A press, an outside release or cancellation before commitment does not request a reset. Focused Enter or an ordinary hotkey match on a simple field commits the same action. A mouse button created with `1U` follows its own [style flag 4 ordering](4.3-buttons.md#rip_button_style).

requirements.text: **Portable ownership rule.** At commitment, copy the normalized clear flag along with the host source and field identity into the action's continuation. If the action deletes its field, replaces the mouse table or installs another field with the same ID, the original action still owns the decision. An enabled request clears any replacement as part of SOFT on success. A replacement's own flag cannot enable a clear for an action committed with `clr=0`. Renderers can release the field record before executing or suspending the host program. Ordinary prompt cancellation that supplies a value or empty expansion follows the host program's eventual outcome. A hard abort ends the action immediately. requirements.heading: 3.x extensions to the `<text>` parameter
requirements.text:
- **`ID=n:` prefix** - assigns a numbered mouse-field identity, readable back through the `$FIELDID$` [text variable](5.1-text-variables.md) and used by the `.MSE` overlay scenes' entry/exit queries to drive hover status lines and cursor changes (the example above, from NEWSPAPR.RIP's navigation, is field ID 2). The prefix is not transmitted to the host. The mechanism - and RIPtel's canonical nine-field menu built on it - is documented in [5.0 Host Commands](5.0-host-commands.md#mouse-field-identities---idn). _Evidence: HLP (`$FIELDID$` - "current mouse field ID"); corpus (NEWSPAPR.RIP, MENU.MNU/MENU.MSE)._
- **Inline conditionals and macros** - `<<if $RETURN$!="">>$<<RETURN>>$<<else>>$NULL$<<endif>>` as a host command (BUTTONS.RIP), and [`$GOTOURL(WEBURL)$`](5.0-host-commands.md#launching-web-urls---gotourlname) launching a web URL from a variable (TELLISTS.MNU/.MSE - 1997-era web integration). The conditional/macro layer is [5.2 Templates & Conditionals](5.2-templates-and-conditionals.md). _Evidence: corpus (BUTTONS.RIP, TELLISTS.MNU, TELLISTS.MSE)._
requirements.reason: The input owner tracks the captured instance, ordered hover membership and scoped identity. Connected gesture, handler, backup and pointer fixtures exercise interaction, mutation and reset.

requirements.heading: 3.x extensions to the `<text>` parameter
requirements.text: Hover is configured separately with [RIP_QUERY](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_query) **mode 5 for entry and mode 6 for exit**. The corpus uses these handlers for `.MSE` status-line updates and `$MCURSOR(n)$` pointer changes. The [callback rules above](#hover-and-callback-context) distinguish independent hover membership from press ownership. _Evidence: HLP, corpus (MENU.MSE), original hover/query dispatch and [#51 derivation](../research/issue-51-deferred-query-order.md)._
requirements.note: Reviewed changed normative block in PR #111/#114/#115; runtime acceptance tracked separately.
requirements.reason: Connected wire modes 5/6 own unexpanded global entry/exit strings; real physical movement resumes exits before entries, newest first, under independent stable field tokens and callback FIELDID. Normal pointer/keyboard commitment stays separate, including held buttons and asynchronous redraw/prompt/query work. Native and live CP437/UTF-8 vectors cover overlap/boundaries, self-deletion, same-ID replacement, actual editor prompts, once-only traversal and parse-failure recovery. This unit records grammar/normal dispatch, not all resident-query storage or the B132 handler-definition/reset edge contract.

requirements.text: This command removes selected simple mouse fields and mouse-active buttons, with optional screen painting. Nonmouse decorations have no resident field to select. **Explicit portable completion:** the inherited terminology and old corner/margin predicates do not establish a complete contract for the adopted half-open geometry. The following classification, clipping/paint and failure rules complete it; [source findings and differences](../research/issue-120-selective-field-deletion.md) remain separate from policy.

requirements.heading: Selector Coordinates and Region Predicates
requirements.text: Interpret the numeric corners in the **current ENV's WORLD**, order each axis before WORLD→device conversion, then use the resulting rectangle as **absolute screen coordinates**. Add no PORT0/current-viewport/port origin. Do not clip the selector to a viewport or screen before classifying fields. The unrelated current/offscreen port and PORT0's activation do not gate logical deletion. Later viewport changes do not relocate stored global field snapshots. _Evidence: original wire ordering/conversion and metadata deletion consumers; [derivation](../research/issue-120-selective-field-deletion.md#primary-sources-and-bounded-findings)._

requirements.heading: Selector Coordinates and Region Predicates
requirements.text: Positive intersection means `max(FL,SL) < min(FR,SR)` and `max(FT,ST) < min(FB,SB)`. Equal rectangles are contained, not crossing. Thus bit 2 excludes fully contained fields; it means crossing the selector boundary, resolving the draft's “non-intersecting” containment wording. Region bits form a **union**, with each field selected once: 3=C+P (all overlapping), 5=C+O, 6=P+O (not-contained), 7=all. With no region bits, **nothing is deleted or painted**, even with paint/128 bits.
requirements.reason: PR123 absolute normalized WORLD selector, disjoint C/P/O selection, full byte-mask validation, delete-before-paint, COPY index0/pattern and once-only cleanup; all 256 masks plus failure/capture and connected physical-screen tests.

requirements.heading: Selector Coordinates and Region Predicates
requirements.text: Apply type exclusions after region classification: bit **8** excludes simple `1M` fields; bit **16** excludes mouse-active `1U` buttons. Both bits exclude all fields from deletion. A type exclusion never changes a rectangle's class or the meaning of a whole-selector paint request.

requirements.heading: Painting and Failure Ordering
requirements.text: Flag **128 replaces per-field painting** with one selector-interior paint. It applies even with zero matching fields, an empty field table or exclusions 8+16, provided a region bit and 32/64 are set. With region bit 4 it still paints **S**, not its outside complement. Painting can cover surviving fields without changing their logical definitions; its extent is not another deletion predicate.
requirements.reason: PR123 absolute normalized WORLD selector, disjoint C/P/O selection, full byte-mask validation, delete-before-paint, COPY index0/pattern and once-only cleanup; all 256 masks plus failure/capture and connected physical-screen tests.

requirements.heading: Painting and Failure Ordering
requirements.text: Painting addresses the **physical screen only**, clipped to its canvas, with no current-port/viewport clipping or PORT0-activation gate. Use opaque **COPY**, no border; ignore but preserve current W, draw color, line settings and graphics cursor. Bit 32's “black (color 0)” means current palette **index 0**, so remapping that entry to red makes the cleanup red; it is not the outer SOFT reset's literal RGB-black rule and does not use STYLE background. Bit 64 uses the existing Fill Style/Fill Color and pen-background semantics: mask one selects fill, zero selects background. Its [8×8 pattern phase](2.3-shapes-and-fills.md#fill-pattern-origin-and-scaling) stays anchored at physical screen `(0,0)` in device pixels, with no WORLD magnification or restart for each field. Ordinary solid/empty-mask meanings remain adopted.
requirements.reason: PR123 absolute normalized WORLD selector, disjoint C/P/O selection, full byte-mask validation, delete-before-paint, COPY index0/pattern and once-only cleanup; all 256 masks plus failure/capture and connected physical-screen tests.

requirements.heading: Painting and Failure Ordering
requirements.text: Validate flags/selector and snapshot eligible **instance tokens and hit rectangles**, plus the current paint color/pattern bindings, before mutation. Remove selected temporary depression and cancel capture only if its instance is selected, then delete the entire selection set while retaining survivor order, capture identity and existing hover/FIELDID lifetime rules. Paint **after deletion** from the snapshot list (newest first for individual rectangles), or S once with 128. A paint failure does not restore definitions or transfer/cancel a surviving capture; attempt remaining requested regions without logical rollback. This is deterministic failure completion, not a native transaction guarantee. No deletion or painting executes a field's click/hover host action. The [gesture lifetime rules](#left-button-gesture-commitment) also govern deletion during a running callback.

requirements.heading: Literal Selection and Paint Vectors
requirements.text: For each flags field, use the same coordinate prefix, e.g. `!|1k0K142S3C004H`. If palette index 0 is red, STYLE background and pen background are blue, and fill is green, 32 paints red despite an XOR W setting. With custom mask rows `80 00 00 00 00 00 00 00`, whole-selector fill makes `(16,24)` green and `(17,24)` blue by the absolute pattern phase. If painting fails after selecting A–D, those four definitions remain deleted; capture on surviving E stays E through compaction, whereas capture on deleted A is canceled and cannot pass to a newly created ID-1 field. These are explicit protocol/policy vectors, not original raster executions.

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: This command allows you to alter the current mouse cursor shape that is shown on the screen. This feature lets you change the cursor to another shape to give the user of the terminal an idea that something is going on. For example, changing the cursor to the shape of an hourglass or a watch could give the idea that they should wait for a moment because something is going on.

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: The four-digit reserve is optional. Supply valid digits in active Base Math, a single [leading period](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#period-as-a-zero-field), or omit it at the delimiter. A nonempty short reserve also completes at the delimiter. The collector supplies zero in each case, and the handler uses only the cursor number. A shortened cursor number can end at the delimiter with the reserve omitted. For example, `!|1c6`, `!|1c0601` and `!|1c06.comment` followed by CR all dispatch cursor number 6. In the third example the period completes the reserve and `comment` is surplus. `!|1c060.` is discarded because the period follows a digit in the unfinished reserve. [Original descriptor and vectors](../research/issue-258-mouse-field-suffix.md#staged-captures).
requirements.reason: The decoder accepts a shortened cursor or omitted reserve, validates a present suffix and ignores its value. ENV ownership and cursor range are checked before presentation.

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: The `<cursor_style>` parameter selects the **same logical number** as [`MCURSOR`](5.1-text-variables.md#mcursor). **Canonical RIPscrip 3.0 range: 0..7.** The inherited documentary table establishes 0..6; both original cursor-handle arrays and the original color/monochrome resources establish 7 as the unavailable/prohibited symbol. [Exact tables, resource fingerprints and source/policy boundary](../research/issue-125-cursor-number-mapping.md).

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: **Presentation completion:** retain the selected logical number separately from the native cursor handle. Exact original artwork, color, size, animation and hotspot pixels are not protocol requirements; native/accessibility equivalents are permitted. When the backend cannot supply a requested shape, show the default arrow while retaining that number, so a later refresh or environment activation still knows the requested style. A native watch and hourglass can share artwork without merging stored values 1 and 6. This fallback is an explicit portable policy consistent with the original missing-handle arrow path.

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: Value **7 is an ordinary visible shape selection**, not a hidden/no-change/default sentinel. It stores 7 and replaces the displayed shape just like other values; it does not hide the pointer, disable input, cancel/transfer capture, change hover membership, alter keyboard bindings or synthesize a movement/click. A not-allowed symbol conveys appearance only; input enable, HEADER lock and the adopted gesture rules remain separate. Native cursor constants need a translation table; their numeric values are not RIP numbers.

requirements.text: **Explicit accepted-range completion:** reject values outside 0..7 before changing cursor state or presentation, as a nonfatal command/variable error; retain earlier state. The original wire outer guard admits 8/9 to a shared setter that does not store them; that legacy refresh path is not an additional logical style or a portable range extension.

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: **State ownership (RIPtel 3.1):** the number is stored in the current environment, not in the graphics style. This wire command checks current environment protection; style protection is irrelevant. [`MCURSOR`](5.1-text-variables.md#mcursor) performs the same state change without that protection check. Style switching does not restore a mouse number; environment switching selects the stored number for the next refresh. _Evidence: [original handlers/setter and native cases](../research/issue-24-drawing-state-ownership.md#ownership-and-switching-observations)._

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR

requirements.heading: 4.3 Buttons
requirements.text: [Buttons](../../glossary.md) - styled interactive controls with plain, icon (BMP), or clipboard faces, optional [hot-icon](../../glossary.md) pressed states (`.BMH`), special effects (bevel, chisel, recess, sunken), labels, hotkeys, and radio/check-box grouping. A style is defined once ([RIP_BUTTON_STYLE](#rip_button_style)) and then instantiated by [RIP_BUTTON](#rip_button) commands; up to 36 styles live in the button style [data table](7.1-data-tables.md#button-style-table) and are switched with [RIP_SWITCH_BUTTON_STYLE](#rip_switch_button_style).

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: This RIPscrip command is probably one of the most complex in the entire protocol. It defines how subsequent [RIP_BUTTON](#rip_button) commands will be interpreted. The purpose of this command is to define what a Button is and how they operate. Buttons can have many different configurations, flags, and styles. With the diversity of modes that the Button can take on, complexity is a necessary evil.

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: There are 36 separate button style slots that can be defined simultaneously. This command allows you to alter the current button style slot. This button style slot is used by the RIP*BUTTON command to define buttons of particular types. Button style slots can be used to avoid retransmitting button styles over and over again. *(v2.A4)\_
requirements.reason: The connected button fixtures send 1B/1U and inspect style state, natural clipboard/icon sizing, clipping, press ownership, host action and auto-stamp ordering.

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: This command stores the style for subsequent buttons.
requirements.reason: The style decoder requires other_port after the corner color. It validates and ignores the port and the optional reserved field.

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: After the corner color, the collector requires `other_port` as one digit in active Base Math or one [leading period](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#period-as-a-zero-field). The definition ignores its value. The following five-digit reserve may be supplied in full, shortened by dropping leading zeros, replaced by a period or omitted at a delimiter. The collector supplies zero for the reserve in every case. CR immediately after the corner color leaves `other_port` absent and discards the command. [Original slot and boundary cases](../research/issue-257-button-wire-widths.md).

requirements.heading: Initial and Reset Style
requirements.text: RIPtel 3.1 starts with current button-style slot **0**, only slot **0** in use and every slot unprotected. All 36 records contain this fixed default. Selecting an undefined nonzero slot installs the same default, marks it in use, clears protection and selects it; it does not copy the previously selected style. The [state transitions below](#undefined-current-slots-and-first-use-selection) distinguish explicit definition from selection, including the inherited inconsistent metadata case.

requirements.heading: Initial and Reset Style
requirements.text: Specific unprotected-slot reset restores these fields; zero stays in use and a nonzero slot becomes undefined. Table reset restores unprotected records and clears their nonzero in-use flags, retaining protected records. **Shipped defect:** resetting the current entry (`$RESET(BUT,CUR)$`, or the current-entry default) instead copies the default bytes into selection/in-use metadata: the records remain unchanged, current becomes zero and the first 26 in-use bytes are overwritten. It does not overwrite protection bytes. A protected current entry rejects the reset unchanged. This corrupt current-reset path must not be mistaken for a different default style. _Evidence: original initialization/selection/reset and bounded native matrices; [derivation](../research/issue-27-button-style-contract.md)._
requirements.note: Reconciled against adopted PR #111/#114/#115 with independent native and connected expected results. Button rendering, hover and synchronous playback remain separate pending clauses.

requirements.heading: Undefined Current Slots and First-use Selection
requirements.text: A valid `1B` does not require the selected slot to be in use, does not select/default another slot and does not leave an edited record undefined. It checks the current **protection byte independently of in-use**: a protected current slot rejects the write even if marked undefined. Invalid field/type validation likewise does not define the slot. The [existing validation rules](#validation-and-flag-precedence) and protected auto-clip exception remain unchanged. If no definition was accepted before a later explicit selection, that selection still takes the undefined-slot default branch. If a definition was accepted, the slot is now in use, so selection preserves that new style.
requirements.note: Reconciled against adopted PR #111/#114/#115 with independent native and connected expected results. Button rendering, hover and synchronous playback remain separate pending clauses.
requirements.reason: Connected undefined-current 1B definition/selection/protection rules. The protected auto-clip exception is now invoked through real plain/clipboard button construction, with flags-only mutation and retained definition/protection metadata.

requirements.heading: Undefined Current Slots and First-use Selection
requirements.text: **Completion for inherited inconsistent metadata:** Normally an undefined slot cannot be protected. The [already documented current-reset overwrite](#initial-and-reset-style) can leave a protected record with a false in-use byte. In that case, apply the undefined-slot selection row above: replace its fields with fixed defaults, mark it in use and clear the surviving protection. This follows the original selector's first-use branch and is the explicit completion adopted here for that inconsistent state; it does not permit overwriting a **defined** protected style. Selection is not rejected merely because an undefined destination retains protection. If an overwritten in-use byte is **nonzero**, it counts as in use, so selection retains the fields and protection instead. Queries do not perform this selection or repair metadata.
requirements.note: Reconciled against adopted PR #111/#114/#115 with independent native and connected expected results. Button rendering, hover and synchronous playback remain separate pending clauses.

requirements.heading: Selecting a protected record hidden by the inherited overwrite
requirements.text: Start with defined unprotected slot 7 containing a nondefault style, protect it with `$PROT(BUT,7)$`, then select an unprotected slot 0. Apply the already specified `$RESET(BUT,CUR)$` metadata overwrite. Its published default bytes leave current 0 and in-use[7]=0, while record 7 and protection[7]=1 survive. At this point `$INUSE(BUT,7)$` returns `0`, numeric `$ISPROT(BUT,7)$` returns `-1`, and `$ISPROT(BUT,CUR)$` returns `0` because current is 0.
requirements.note: Reconciled against adopted PR #111/#114/#115 with independent native and connected expected results. Button rendering, hover and synchronous playback remain separate pending clauses.

requirements.heading: Selecting a protected record hidden by the inherited overwrite
requirements.text: Now `$CUR(BUT,7)$` installs **all fixed default fields**, sets in-use[7]=1, clears protection[7] and selects 7. Both ISPROT forms for that now-current slot return `0`, and a following `1U` uses the fixed default style. This is a bounded logical state example using the already published bytes; it requires no invalid memory write or reproduction of an obsolete-client failure. A protected slot whose in-use byte remains nonzero follows the defined selection row and retains its style/protection.

requirements.heading: Validation and Flag Precedence
requirements.text: The shipped style definition validates orientation **0..4**, group **0..35**, flags 2 **0..255**, the seven colors and current-style protection. A protected current style rejects an explicit definition. At least one of CLIPBOARD 1, ICON 128 or PLAIN 256 must be set; no type bit rejects the command without changing the record. More than one type bit is accepted. Other low-word flags, including combinations marked N in the compatibility tables, are retained: those tables describe applicability, not an additional definition-time rejection or normalization matrix. BEVEL absent is the exception: its stored size becomes zero. The wire `other_port` field is ignored.
requirements.reason: Connected 1B/2B and BUT query/backup/reset bindings use the session-owned 36-record table. Independent native vectors verify defaults, all 65536 low-word flags, all flags2 bytes, nonuniform definition-time conversion, palette-only color decoding, protection, reset metadata bytes and owned snapshots. CP437/UTF-8 live captures cover four device rasters, first use, aliases, protected saves, SOFT retention and nonfatal recovery. Button creation/rendering/input and undefined-current edges under B112 remain separate.

requirements.heading: Validation and Flag Precedence
requirements.text: Rendering chooses **ICON first, otherwise CLIPBOARD, otherwise PLAIN**. Creation checks for an existing clipboard whenever CLIPBOARD is set, even if ICON is also set and would win rendering; an undefined clipboard rejects creation. HOT applies to the icon path, and mouse interaction options require a mouse field. These retained combinations do not make a nonmouse decoration interactive. The separate rule against mixing radio and checkbox groups still applies.
requirements.reason: Live cases cover combined ICON/CLIPBOARD/PLAIN with and without an assigned clipboard, the expected normal/hot icon choice, nonmouse decorations, and plain or clipboard feedback with a retained HOT bit. Group fixtures cover both conflicting group kinds and conflicting live membership.

requirements.heading: Validation and Flag Precedence
requirements.text: For top/center/bottom labels, flags 2 LEFT 8 wins when RIGHT 16 is also set. NOFILL 32 wins over PATTERN 64: both set means no interior fill; PATTERN alone uses the current fill pattern, neither uses solid surface color. These decisions do not clear the stored flags. _Evidence: complete 65,536-value definition matrix, all flags 2 byte values and original creation/renderer captures; [derivation](../research/issue-27-button-style-contract.md)._
requirements.reason: Connected tests verify TOP/CENTER/BOTTOM LEFT precedence over RIGHT with and without chisel, and NOFILL precedence over PATTERN, including one-color masks after a color mode change. The native style test verifies that all flags 2 values remain stored.

requirements.heading: Button Types
requirements.text: There are three basic "types" of Buttons. There are Icon buttons, Clipboard buttons and Plain buttons. Each of these differ in the way that they create the button's image. A description of each type is as follows: _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Button Types
requirements.text: **ICON BUTTON (flag 128)** - An Icon Button means that the actual image of the button will be created by loading a bitmap icon image from the disk and load it at the given locatino. Any special effects (see below) can be applied to the Icon to further enhance the image. The filename for the Icon is supplied with the RIP*BUTTON command, as is the Icon's upper left X/Y coordinate. Icon Buttons are always stamped in COPY mode. *(v1.54)\_
requirements.reason: Connected literal ICON and paired HOT rendering: initial chosen image determines creation-WORLD geometry; later redraws keep captured face/viewport/font, COPY nearest current palette with no key, field-local quiet HOT fallback to INVERT, nonfatal normal failure and owned deletion/shutdown. Independent BMP fixtures cover four entry rasters in both encodings. RGB inversion maps back to nearest current-palette index as client rendering policy.

requirements.heading: Button Types
requirements.text: RIPtel 3.1 loads the normal `.BMP` directly. When HOT 4096 is enabled and the button is selected, it first tries the paired `.BMH` quietly; any nonzero loader error retries `.BMP`. Successful fallback clears HOT and sets INVERT in that created field, retaining the style record; failure of the normal/fallback load returns an error. All requests use the current palette with mode 2 and fixed SRCCOPY, including when the surrounding effect renderer changes its pen ROP2. See [bitmap palette handling](4.0-icons-and-bitmaps.md#rip_load_bitmap) and the bit-128 finding below. _Evidence: original caller and request captures; [derivation](../research/issue-27-button-style-contract.md)._
requirements.reason: Connected literal ICON and paired HOT rendering: initial chosen image determines creation-WORLD geometry; later redraws keep captured face/viewport/font, COPY nearest current palette with no key, field-local quiet HOT fallback to INVERT, nonfatal normal failure and owned deletion/shutdown. Independent BMP fixtures cover four entry rasters in both encodings. RGB inversion maps back to nearest current-palette index as client rendering policy.

requirements.heading: Button Types
requirements.text: **CLIPBOARD BUTTON (flag 1)** - Uses the current clipboard port's viewport as the base image. An undefined clipboard rejects button creation. Although the inherited draft assigned explicit-port semantics to `<other_port>`, RIPtel 3.1 ignores that wire argument and uses the clipboard pointer. Effects can be applied to the pasted image. _Evidence: original definition, constructor and clipboard renderer; [derivation](../research/issue-27-button-style-contract.md)._
requirements.reason: The connected button fixtures send 1B/1U and inspect style state, natural clipboard/icon sizing, clipping, press ownership, host action and auto-stamp ordering.

requirements.heading: Button Types
requirements.text: **PLAIN BUTTON (flag 256)** - A plain button is exactly that, plain. No special graphics are used to create the button. The entire button region is simply filled-in with a solid colored rectangle using the `<surface>` color. Any special effects can be further applied to enhance the button's appearance. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Size and Color Parameters
requirements.text: For **PLAIN faces only**, the `<hgt>` and `<wid>` parameters provide fixed dimensions only when **both stored dimensions are nonzero**; the button command's far corner is then ignored. If either is zero, both dimensions come from the command's corners: a single positive style dimension does not independently fix that axis. An empty nonmouse plain button with no complete fixed size and both command far coordinates zero is skipped. RIPtel 3.1 converts the style dimensions from the definition-time world into device units once; creation adds those stored dimensions directly to the converted anchor. A world change after definition does not reconvert them.
requirements.reason: PLAIN fixed/mixed sizes and normalized corners; whole native clipboard viewport ignores style/far values, reads inactive/protected source and pads missing pixels with index0 after overlap-safe COPY. Raw internal inclusive rectangles adapt the reference half-open extents.

requirements.heading: Size and Color Parameters
requirements.text: With BEVEL 512, `<bevsize>` is converted once using the definition-time **X** ratio, `floor(bevsize × device_width / world_width)`, stored as a WORD, then its low byte is copied into a created button. The same device size is used on both axes. Without BEVEL the stored size is zero. See [effect coordinate units](#effect-coordinate-units) for chisel, recess, sunken and label insets. _Evidence: original B/U handlers and native scale/mixed-zero matrices; [derivation](../research/issue-27-button-style-contract.md)._
requirements.reason: The connected button fixtures send 1B/1U and inspect style state, natural clipboard/icon sizing, clipping, press ownership, host action and auto-stamp ordering.

requirements.heading: Size and Color Parameters
requirements.text: There are a large number of flag values that can be combined to achieve a great many effects. There are two flag parameters for the RIP_BUTTON_STYLE command, `<flags>` and `<flags2>`. They are detailed in the two tables that follow in this Section. You may combine any of the flags in the first table together simply by adding the "Value" of each one together and representing that number as a MegaNum.

requirements.heading: Size and Color Parameters
requirements.text: The `<dfore>` and `<dback>` parameters are used with the text label. The `<dfore>` parameter is the foreground color for the text. It is always used to determine the color of the text label. The `<dback>` color is the color of the dropshadow (if any). This parameter is only used when you have specified the "Dropshadow" flag in the `<flags>` parameter (see below).

requirements.heading: Size and Color Parameters
requirements.text: NOTE: There are seven (7) color parameters in this command. These parameters are ALWAYS used in Color Map mode. Direct RGB Color Mode cannot be used for these parameters. With Color Map mode, you have up to 256 separate color combinations possible for each color, providing you with a great deal of flexibility. The color parameters always use the Base Math set by the global Base Math setting. _(v2.A0)_
requirements.reason: The connected button fixtures send 1B/1U and inspect style state, natural clipboard/icon sizing, clipping, press ownership, host action and auto-stamp ordering.

requirements.heading: Size and Color Parameters
requirements.text: The `<bright>`, `<dark>` and `<surface>` parameters are used with Plain Buttons and with the Special Effects styles (see `<flags>` below). These colors represent the highlighted color, the shadowed color, and the regular surface color that is used in Special Effects. Typical color combinations for these colors might be White, Dark-Gray and Light-Gray respectively for a "chiseled steel" appearance. Each of these values can contain a two-digit value representing any valid color code that may be used in the [RIP_COLOR](2.0-color-modes-and-palettes.md#rip_color) command.

requirements.heading: Size and Color Parameters
requirements.text: In addition to the special effects colors, are two additional colors that can be used, `<uline_color>` which is used for the color of the underline (in the text label), and `<corner_color>` which is used to display the colors of corners for things like the Bevel, Recess, etc.

requirements.heading: Size and Color Parameters
requirements.text: The `<grp_no>` parameter determines which Button Group subsequent RIP_BUTTON commands will be associated with. Button Groups are used to maintain groups of Buttons for things like Radio Buttons and/or Checkbox Buttons. See the section on the BUTTON COMMAND for more information on these modes, and what Button Groups can offer. This value can range anywhere from 0-Z (i.e., 0-35). A live group cannot mix checkbox and radio members; conflicting creation rejects under the [grouped selection contract](#grouped-selection-and-feedback).
requirements.reason: PR134 is connected to live sessions: stable-instance checkbox/radio state commits before optional redraw and clicked source, with opaque creation and selected-radio exclusivity. Each surviving owner retains post-angle ordinary-unexpanded A[N]; current group publications assemble selected owners in creation order with a 4096-byte prefix and ordinary-baseline/last-publisher precedence. Required radio selection depends on actual membership, independently of slot bytes. Native failure/suspension and independent CP437/UTF-8 TCP vectors cover OFF-source execution, duplicate IDs, stale writes, cross-slot publication, SOFT effective-byte preservation, no provider calls during composition, and recovery without disconnecting. Explicit mouse-family backup/restore and host-template-clearing operations remain separate pending units.

requirements.text: The Icon Button, Clipboard button and Plain flags have already been discussed. Following, will be more discussion of the various flags used in the preceding table: _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: **BUTTON IS INVERTABLE (flag 2)** - This means that the button will be inverted when clicked. This flag is only useful when combined with the "Button is a Mouse Button - flag 1024) flag. Even if the button has special effects, those will be inverted as well as they are considered part of the button - all except for the Recessed effect. The recessed effect is NEVER considered part of the actual button image, and will never be part of the mouse field, button's image or anything - it is just extra graphics. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: **RESET SCREEN AFTER BUTTON CLICK (flag 4)** - This flag is used when the button is considered a Mouse Button (flag 1024). What this means is that when the user clicks on the button, the screen will be reset exactly the same as a [RIP_RESET_WINDOWS](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_reset_windows) command will do. requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: **AUTO-STAMP IMAGE INTO CLIPBOARD SLOT (flag 64)** - Subject to the same-destination guard below, after rendering the face and effects but before the label, captures the button image through the current clipboard mechanism. It excludes the recess. RIPtel 3.1 uses the existing clipboard slot or chooses the first free nonzero port; the ignored `<other_port>` field does not select a destination. On capture success it changes both the created field's flags and the **actual current style record's flags** to `(field_flags & 0x7c37) | 1`: ICON, PLAIN, CHISEL, BEVEL, AUTOCLIP and SUNKEN are cleared and CLIPBOARD is set. This write occurs **even if the current style is protected**; protection still rejects an explicit style edit. Other style fields and protection are retained. The initial recess has already been removed from the field's persistent flags, so that field-based write also removes it from the style. On capture failure, drawing returns an error and the style flags remain unchanged; earlier painting or clipboard-port work is not rolled back. Later buttons use the captured face. _Evidence: original renderer and protected/unprotected success/failure fixtures; [derivation](../research/issue-27-button-style-contract.md)._ The [auto-stamp redraw contract](#auto-stamp-geometry-and-redraw) defines the baked footprint, source crop, provider stages and same-target continuation boundary.

requirements.heading: Measuring and positioning the label
requirements.text:
1. Expand the label under the existing [button expansion contract](5.2-templates-and-conditionals.md#graphical-consumer-expansion). Measure the expanded bytes with the selected outline's per-character X advances and spacing, including the last gap. The same per-byte positions govern painting and hotkey decoration. On a full redraw use the then-current expanded label with the instance's captured font, size, WORLD and original face geometry.
2. **Portable vertical metrics:** scale the face's 750-unit baseline height and 250-unit descent separately by `Q × Dy / (72 × 1000)`, truncating in DEVICE units. Use the baseline height for the placement height, adding the descent for an above-face or center label only when flags 1 bit 8192 is set and the label contains a descender according to `low_char` below. A below-face label keeps its top offset. Use the actual baseline height to place the baseline even when the descent participates in centering.
3. For placement, convert these dimensions, label width, original face bounds and face width and height separately from DEVICE into the captured WORLD, truncating toward zero. Use the original inner face `F` as the reference. All offsets in the following table are creation-WORLD units. Use truncation toward zero for each half difference.

requirements.heading: Hotkey decoration
requirements.text: On an eligible mouse button with a nonzero explicit hotkey, find the first case-insensitive match in the expanded label. Flags 2 bit 2 highlights that glyph in `uline_col`. Flags 1 bit 2048 draws an underline in `uline_col`. When both bits are set, apply both effects to the same glyph. When the match is absent, the entire label uses normal foreground and there is no hotkey mark.

requirements.heading: Hotkey decoration
requirements.text: The decorated glyph starts at the label X plus the sum of all **spacing-adjusted** prefix steps. Let `w` be that glyph's **unspaced** DEVICE advance. Its underline occupies one pixel row at baseline +3 and the half-open X interval from the glyph start to start + `w`. The suffix starts after the matched glyph's full step, including its gap. The font-zero underline uses this baseline offset with or without a descender on that glyph. Painting stays one run, with no CHR prefix measurement or reset of spacing after the hotkey.

requirements.heading: Effect Coordinate Units
requirements.text: For a captured world width W and canvas width D, label LEFT adds **10** world units without chisel or **20** with chisel; RIGHT subtracts label width plus **9** or **19** from the far extent boundary. LEFT wins both flags. The right-edge boundary convention accounts for its one-unit difference from the draft's nominal 10/20 description. For example, at X ratios D/W of 1, 1/2 and 1/4, a left inset of 10 becomes 10, 5 and 2 device pixels for integer-aligned positive fixtures. The chisel/recess/sunken one-pixel strokes remain one device pixel at all three ratios. Default bevel 3 is already a literal device value; an explicitly defined bevel is scaled by the formula above. These rules apply at every device canvas; there is no additional hard-coded 640×350 scaling stage. _Evidence: original helpers and label coordinate consumers, native 1/2/4 ratio matrices; [derivation](../research/issue-27-button-style-contract.md)._

requirements.heading: Flags Field 2
requirements.text: > **Shipped flags 2 bit 128:** the product history attests an icon-transparency flag added in RIPterm 2.20.01. In the recovered **RIPtel 3.1** driver, this bit is accepted and stored but has **no effect on normal, hot or fallback button-icon loading**. Every such call passes key **-1** (no transparency), current-palette mode **2**, stretch **1** and **SRCCOPY**, with the bit either clear or set. Thus this driver's button path selects no transparent color/index and no special normal/hot palette key. Do not infer the separate [LOAD_BITMAP keyed contract](4.0-icons-and-bitmaps.md#rip_load_bitmap) from this flag. This finding does not establish how RIPterm 2.20.01 implemented its advertised feature. _Evidence: complete original renderer trace and normal/hot/failure request captures; [derivation](../research/issue-27-button-style-contract.md)._

requirements.text: Following is a more complete description of the flags described in the `<flags2>` parameter: _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 2
requirements.text: **BUTTON IS IN A CHECK BOX GROUP (flags 2 bit 1)** - Members toggle independently and any number may be selected. A live group cannot mix checkbox and radio members. Initial selection does not process the opaque host source; both ON and OFF committed activations later process their own source once. See the [grouped selection](#grouped-selection-and-feedback) and [template ownership](5.2-templates-and-conditionals.md#associated-template-ownership-and-lifetime) rules.
requirements.reason: PR134 is connected to live sessions: stable-instance checkbox/radio state commits before optional redraw and clicked source, with opaque creation and selected-radio exclusivity. Each surviving owner retains post-angle ordinary-unexpanded A[N]; current group publications assemble selected owners in creation order with a 4096-byte prefix and ordinary-baseline/last-publisher precedence. Required radio selection depends on actual membership, independently of slot bytes. Native failure/suspension and independent CP437/UTF-8 TCP vectors cover OFF-source execution, duplicate IDs, stale writes, cross-slot publication, SOFT effective-byte preservation, no provider calls during composition, and recovery without disconnecting. Explicit mouse-family backup/restore and host-template-clearing operations remain separate pending units.

requirements.heading: Flags Field 2
requirements.text: **HIGHLIGHT HOTKEY CHARACTER (flag 2)** - When this flag is active, then the first occurence of the hotkey character in the label will be hilighted using the `<uline_col>` color. This gives the user a visual impression of what keystroke they need to type in order to activate the button without the mouse. _(v1.54)_
requirements.reason: Two matching glyphs on CHR and Dixon outline labels identify the first hotkey match. Highlight-only and underlined labels establish one underline row, lower for a descender. The font-zero fixture checks its distinct fixed baseline offset.

requirements.heading: Flags Field 2
requirements.text: **EXPLODE (ZOOM OUT WHEN CLICKED) (flag 4)** - This optional flag is designed to "zoom out" from the button when the user clicks on it. What is generally done is a dotted rectangle is drawn initially around the button and it is repeatedly redrawn over itself in XOR mode, constantly getting larger and larger until it hits the full size of the screen. This gives the visual impression that the button is zooming out to another screen. Each time another frame of the zooming rectangle is drawn, the previous rectangle on the inside of the new one is erased by XOR drawing the same rectangle over itself again. This option does not need to be supported in order to be considered a RIPscrip terminal, although it would be nice. In other words, this is not a "make or break" feature. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 2
requirements.text: **LEFT JUSTIFY LABEL (TOP/CTR/BTM) (flag 8)** - If this option is enabled, then any TOP, CENTER or BOTTOM label orientations will be left justified to the left edge of the button. The exact indentation of the label from the interior of the button's base image depends on whether the chisel effect is active. RIPtel 3.1 adds 10 creation-world units without chisel or 20 with chisel; see [effect coordinate units](#effect-coordinate-units). This option can be combined with the Adjust Vertical Centering flag only if the label orientation is CENTER. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 2
requirements.text: **RIGHT JUSTIFY LABEL (TOP/CTR/BTM) (flag 16)** - If this option is enabled, then any TOP, CENTER or BOTTOM label orientations will be right justified to the right edge of the button. The exact indentation of the label from the interior of the button's base image depends on whether the chisel effect is active. RIPtel 3.1 subtracts label width plus 9 creation-world units without chisel or 19 with chisel from the far boundary; see [effect coordinate units](#effect-coordinate-units). This option can be combined with the Adjust Vertical Centering flag only if the label orientation is CENTER. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 2
requirements.text: **DON'T FILL-IN BUTTON INTERIOR** - If this option is enabled and the button is a Plain Button, then the interior of the Button will not be filled in with the surface color. By default, any plain button will have its interior filled in with the surface color. Use this option if you don't want the button face to be drawn. _(v2.A0)_

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: The last numeric field is required. Consume one valid digit in active Base Math or one [leading period](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#period-as-a-zero-field), then supply reserved value zero. Begin the text payload immediately after that byte. For example, `!|1U..1E1E.0Z<>label` in Base Math 36 with XY width 2 supplies corners `(0, 0)` and `(50, 50)`, zero for hotkey, flags and reserve, and the text `<>label`. [Original slot and boundary cases](../research/issue-257-button-wire-widths.md).

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: Mouse-active buttons use the [shared left-button gesture contract](4.2-mouse-fields-and-pointer.md#left-button-gesture-commitment): press captures one field, release inside commits its host action, release outside cancels, and dragging out/back updates temporary depression. The explicit mutation policy prevents overlapping/replaced/restored definitions from inheriting another instance's press. This governs pointer click actions and momentary feedback; existing keyboard/hotkey and persistent checkbox/radio rules remain separate. The optional [identity prefix](5.0-host-commands.md#identity-grammar-and-fieldid-lifetime) is parsed at the start of the full `1U` text payload before label/host splitting.

Commit selection exactly once, rebuild existing group-owned slot bytes without providers, then perform optional redraws and the clicked host continuation. Source deletion, reset, replacement or a duplicate numeric ID cannot retarget the action or replay its selection on resume. Skip stale redraw targets; newly added fields do not acquire the old activation or run their sources. A later independently committed action may change current state; an older continuation must not restore its earlier selection afterward. Optional redraw cancellation follows the adopted NONE/transparent-empty lookup rules; a hard redraw abort also cannot undo the already committed action. No rendering path evaluates host text as a test.
requirements.reason: PR134 is connected to live sessions: stable-instance checkbox/radio state commits before optional redraw and clicked source, with opaque creation and selected-radio exclusivity. Each surviving owner retains post-angle ordinary-unexpanded A[N]; current group publications assemble selected owners in creation order with a 4096-byte prefix and ordinary-baseline/last-publisher precedence. Required radio selection depends on actual membership, independently of slot bytes. Native failure/suspension and independent CP437/UTF-8 TCP vectors cover OFF-source execution, duplicate IDs, stale writes, cross-slot publication, SOFT effective-byte preservation, no provider calls during composition, and recovery without disconnecting. Explicit mouse-family backup/restore and host-template-clearing operations remain separate pending units.

requirements.heading: Auto-Stamp Geometry and Redraw
requirements.text: **Documented same-destination guard:** If the selected capture target/current clipboard is also this definition's **effective drawing destination**, ignore auto-stamp **before** deleting/replacing that port, allocating a capture or applying capture-success style writes. For a mouse-active button the destination is PORT0; for a nonmouse decoration it is the captured current port. Compare those destinations, not an unrelated current port. Evaluate this guard at the capture boundary, after filename preparation and face/effect rendering but before destructive capture work, using the then-current clipboard target and the already captured destination identity. A permitted filename setter may have changed the clipboard selection. This is a skipped capture, not a pure-preflight rejection of the whole definition. The primary draft expressly requires the guard; the shared legacy capture helper alone does not implement that complete protocol rule.

requirements.text: **Explicit portable completion of the inherited validation sentence:** “cannot be parsed” does not authorize executing or eagerly validating the stored host source while defining the button. Creation performs pure checks of numeric/style/type/clipboard/field-count constraints, the raw positional payload/field lengths and geometry. It must not resolve its variables/templates, evaluate its conditionals, run active providers/delays/assignments/playback or transmit it to test whether it will succeed. requirements.heading: Face Extents and Input Eligibility
requirements.text: **Explicit portable geometry/input completion:** The source uses far-minus-near device drawing sizes but different pointer and hover edge tests. This reference adopts one positive **half-open** stored hit rectangle for all mouse fields and mouse-active buttons: `L <= x < R`, `T <= y < B`, with width `R-L`, height `B-T`. Stored R/B remain extent boundaries; do not decrement them for storage or add 1 to dimensions. Use the same predicate for press, drag feedback, release and hover. This deliberately excludes the old pointer helper's near-edge tolerance and inclusive hover far edge; exact native raster/input parity is not claimed. [Evidence and policy boundary](../research/issue-116-button-payload-hit-geometry.md#geometry-source-facts-and-explicit-input-policy).

requirements.heading: Face Extents and Input Eligibility
requirements.text: For **effective PLAIN** dynamic `1U`, order each WORLD corner pair first, then convert once and add the effective viewport origin under the existing rules. Reversed corners are accepted by reordering, not by interpreting negative dimensions. If both stored style dimensions are nonzero, the command's far coordinates remain ignored; if either is zero, use the command's corners for both axes. For PLAIN only, both far coordinates zero without a complete fixed size are omitted/empty geometry, not a full-viewport shorthand. Image faces use their independent natural sizing and must not be suppressed by that guard. Reject a nonpositive **device face** width/height, including a positive WORLD span that collapses under conversion, **before** effects can inflate it into a clickable line. This positive-area/empty guard is the portable completion; original degenerate recovery paths are not required.

requirements.heading: The shipped 3.x button aesthetic
requirements.text: The 3.x corpus shows how TeleGrafix itself built buttons: rather than 1.54-style chiseled plain buttons, scenes stamp **bitmap skins** with [RIP_LOAD_BITMAP](4.0-icons-and-bitmaps.md#rip_load_bitmap) (TELBUT.BMP, RADIONEW.BMP, CHECKBOX.BMP) and lay `1U` buttons or [`1M` mouse fields](4.2-mouse-fields-and-pointer.md#rip_mouse) over them; the corresponding `.BMH` files on disk are the pre-rendered **highlight-state** variants automatically shown while a hot-icon button is depressed (they are never named in any script - pairing is by filename convention; see [6.1](6.1-content-file-roles.md#bmh---button-highlight-variants)). `1B` + `1U` with empty `<><>` blocks also serve as pure chisel-frame decorations. The example above is a plain radio-group demo button whose host command is empty - its behavior comes from the button-style flags. _Evidence: corpus (ICONS/\*.BMH pairs; BUTTONS.RIP, TELDEMOS.MNU)._

requirements.heading: 4.4 Tone & Sound Generation
requirements.text: The Active [Text Variables](5.1-text-variables.md) below request synchronous tones. This chapter specifies the requests made by **RIPtel 3.1's original RIPscrip 3.0.7 driver**, including its differences from the inherited [1.54](../../1.54/ripscrip/4.3-tone-and-sound-generation.md) and [2.0](../../2.0/ripscrip/4.4-tone-and-sound-generation.md) recipes. Earlier-version reference and verbatim text remain separate historical records. Exact device waveform reproduction is outside this contract. [WAV playback](4.5-audio-files.md) is a separate capability.

requirements.heading: 4.4 Tone & Sound Generation

The inherited draft, help strings and SyncTERM are not executable oracles for these shipped sequences.

requirements.text: Frequencies are in **Hz** and durations in **milliseconds**. Successful actions return no characters. Invalid arguments set the variable error and issue no tone: they do **not** play a default effect. In ordinary text expansion the invalid expression remains literal. The callback ignores the audio service's success/failure return; an unsuccessful audio request does not itself make the text variable invalid.

requirements.heading: Sound Related Text Variables
requirements.text: Supplied numeric fields must fit **0..65535**; negative, nonnumeric, oversized or extra fields reject the action. BEEP/BLIP/T forward zero frequency or duration to the audio service without a macro error. ALARM/MUSIC accept count zero as no requests. Sweep increment and time must instead be **1..65535**, and their strict endpoint ordering is checked before any tone. Defaults apply only to omitted trailing arguments, not to invalid values. _Evidence: original callbacks and exhaustive simple-tone WORD/boundary/arity matrices; [derivation](../research/issue-28-tone-variable-contract.md)._

requirements.heading: Sound Related Text Variables
requirements.text: The pseudocode uses `tone(hz, ms)` for one synchronous request. It has no implicit trailing silence. The callbacks do not insert the inherited BEEP 75 ms or BLIP 10 ms gaps, nor a separate gap between repeated notes. Actual audio-service timing is not specified.

requirements.heading: Shipped Sweep Arithmetic Defect
requirements.text: Both callbacks use an **unsigned 16-bit frequency accumulator**, including their update and loop comparison:
requirements.reason: Uses WORD frequency updates and stops before repeating the first frequency of a cyclic sweep.

requirements.heading: Shipped Sweep Arithmetic Defect
requirements.reason: Uses WORD frequency updates and stops before repeating the first frequency of a cyclic sweep.

requirements.heading: Shipped Sweep Arithmetic Defect
requirements.text: A step can wrap rather than finish a sweep. With descending STOP=0, or ascending STOP=65535, the loop cannot pass its exit test. Other steps can also cycle if their modulo-65536 progression never reaches a value beyond the stop. This is a shipped implementation defect, not fallback-to-default behavior. Native verification bounds execution after 65536 requests; implementors should bound this defect rather than reproduce an endless audio loop. The usual default sweeps terminate without wrapping. _Evidence: original WORD instructions and bounded modular sequence captures; [derivation](../research/issue-28-tone-variable-contract.md)._
requirements.reason: Uses WORD frequency updates and stops before repeating the first frequency of a cyclic sweep.

requirements.heading: 4.5 Audio Files (WAV)
requirements.text: Digitized audio files: Microsoft **WAVE** (`.WAV`) PCM audio, played in the background while graphics and command processing continue - triggered from the command stream with [RIP_PLAY_AUDIO](#rip_play_audio) or at the host-command layer with the `$)FILE.WAV$` playback prefix ([5.3 Local File Playback](5.3-local-playback.md#local-audio-playback---filewav)), and distinct from the terminal's own speaker-tone generation ([4.4 Tone & Sound Generation](4.4-tone-and-sound-generation.md)), which needs no files at all.

requirements.heading: 4.5 Audio Files (WAV)
requirements.text: > **Editor's note - provenance:** WAV audio is not a 3.x innovation. RIP_PLAY_AUDIO entered the 2.0 specification at ALPHA 3 ("Added the RIP_PLAY_AUDIO command to playback a WAVE file" - 2.00a4 changelog) and **shipped** in RIPterm Professional 2.0 (January 1995): its manual introduces "digitized sound, in the form of .WAV files" (RIPTERM.DOC §4.3) with an Audio Setup screen for 19 sound boards (Sound Blaster, Pro Audio Spectrum, Gravis, etc.) and a `-A` command-line switch to disable digitized audio (RIPTERM.DOC §2.3), and the install carries HMI "Sound Operating System" drivers and a `RIPTERM.WAV` - both preserved (see the [RIPterm 2.30 audio assets](../../2.0/assets/audio/README.md)). TeleGrafix's December 1995 "RIP-2 Internet Multimedia" press release advertised the same "digital WAV sound". Like several other "3.x" features, it belongs to the RIPterm 2.30 product era that 3.x inherits (see the [revision history](1.0-introduction.md#revision-history)).

requirements.heading: Audio (Sound & Music) Formats
requirements.text: RIPscrip permits the support of digitized audio to be played in the background whild graphics and other operations are being performed. This includes playing sounds while graphical commands are being received from the host (without interruption).
requirements.reason: Waveform playback is independent of the RIP input clock and terminal graphics. Both encodings exercise prompt and reply order over the active connection; the native pull fixture checks PCM while more wire commands are processed.

requirements.heading: Audio (Sound & Music) Formats
requirements.text: The format of audio data used by RIPscrip is formally defined as straight audio data in the Microsoft WAVE file format. When dealing with host systems and downloading digitized audio data, or being told to play back audio data, RIPscrip will assume that you are working with WAVE files. For example, you might be told to playback a file named SOUND.WAV. If you are not internally supporting the actual WAVE format, but some other format, then you need to translate the name of the file to the correct name in your environment (if necessary) and perform the playback.
requirements.reason: The WAV service validates the RIFF/PCM header before invoking the shared decoder. Native fixtures check accepted samples, malformed inputs and unavailable decoder recovery.

requirements.heading: Audio (Sound & Music) Formats
requirements.text: When dealing with the [RIP_FILE_QUERY](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_file_query) command, you need to be careful if you're not dealing with true WAVE files. The RIP_FILE_QUERY command is used to "detect" if a particular file is present on the target system and if so, if it is the right date/time and file size as the file on the host. The file on the host will be in WAVE format so if you're translating the files as they're received, you need to translate the RIP_FILE_QUERY information returned to the host so that it thinks that the file you have on your local hard disk is actually a WAVE file (ie, translate the file size to a WAVE equivalent). If the sizes and, or the time/date don't match, the host could download a new file to you (via the [RIP_ENTER_BLOCK_MODE](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_enter_block_mode) command) thinking that your's is out of date.
requirements.reason: Requirements for clients converting WAV to a different on-disk format. SyncTERM reads received WAV resources directly.

requirements.heading: Audio (Sound & Music) Formats
requirements.text: If you receive a WAVE file via the RIP_ENTER_BLOCK_MODE command, or by some other meanss, and you're dealing with anther digitized audio file format, it is up to you to translate that WAVE file to your destination format. Consequently, if you are requested to send a WAVE file to the host system, and the host system is requesting a .WAV file, then you must translate your file to WAVE format before sending it.
requirements.reason: Requirements for clients converting WAV to a different on-disk format. SyncTERM reads received WAV resources directly.

requirements.heading: Audio (Sound & Music) Formats
requirements.text: A Microsoft WAVE file is actually a normal "Pulse Code Modulation" digitized audio file stored with a bit of header information to identify whether it is stereo, 16-bit, 8-bit, etc, and other pieces of critical information for the decoding of the data. See the "Microsoft Windows Programmer's Reference Guide" for more specific information on the internal format of WAVE files.
requirements.reason: The audio service decodes the PCM WAV stream and passes decoded samples to the mixer.
