requirements.heading: RIP_PLAY_AUDIO
requirements.text: The collector reads one flags digit followed by a three-digit reserve in active Base Math. Each field can use its own [leading period](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#period-as-a-zero-field) to supply zero. The reserve is required, and the collector supplies zero for it after validating its spelling. The filename starts immediately afterward. A period inside the reserve discards the unfinished command.

requirements.heading: RIP_PLAY_AUDIO
requirements.text: Flag bit value 1 requests repeated playback. With that bit clear, play once. Ignore the remaining bits. A successfully started file replaces the current sound on the single background channel. Repeated playback continues until a successful replacement or a stop action. A missing file leaves the current playback alone.
requirements.reason: Original field and playback rules verified through native PCM, parser and connected expansion vectors.

requirements.heading: RIP_PLAY_AUDIO
requirements.text: An empty text tail reports a local error and leaves playback alone. If the collected text is exactly `$OFF$` apart from ASCII case, stop the waveform immediately before expanding variables or scanning the filename. For any other tail, use the same [filename expansion as wire READ_SCENE](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#scene-name-and-lookup). Apply angle preprocessing and one ordinary expansion pass with data variables, user-variable fallback and backslash quoting. Then prepare the filename and append `.wav` if it has no extension. A name that becomes `$OFF$` only after expansion or unquoting goes through ordinary file lookup. Look up the prepared name in the [local resource namespace](6.2-asset-delivery-and-storage.md#lookup-order-file-override). [Original collector, expansion and playback flags](../research/issue-269-play-audio-repeat.md).

requirements.heading: Stopping, resets, and capability negotiation
requirements.text:
- **Stopping playback** - issue [RIP_PLAY_AUDIO](#rip_play_audio) with `$OFF$` as the filename, or the [`$RESET(SOUND)$`](5.1-text-variables.md#reset) text variable, which aborts any playing digitized sound immediately (the DLL string table names a dedicated `resetKeywordSOUND` handler). _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._
- **Reset interaction** - the shipped [`RIP_HEADER`](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#rip_header) uses type-7 segment flag 1 to stop waveform playback, with no audio table slot. Global header flag 2048 belongs to the superseded Alpha 4 layout and is rejected by this driver. A hard reset also stops waveform playback. See the [audio header action](7.1-data-tables.md#audio-header-action-new-in-3x). During a [`$D(time)$`](5.1-text-variables.md#d) delay, sound-related activity continues while everything else pauses. _Evidence: DLL ([header derivation](../research/issue-5-scene-headers.md)); 2.00a4 (delay behavior)._
- **Terminal-side switch** - the RIPtel installer creates the master toggle **`AUDIO=TRUE`** in the `[CONFIG]` section of `RIPscrip.ini`; the driver also exposes a `RIP_AudioSupport` client-API entry point. _Evidence: HLP._
- **Capability negotiation** - before relying on audio, query [`$IFS(WAV)$`](5.1-text-variables.md#ifs): the terminal answers `1` if it can play WAVE files, `0` if not. `$IFS(LIST, _AUDIO)$` lists every audio format the terminal supports. The `$IFS$` processor is present in the 3.0 DLL's variable table. _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._
- **Delivery and housekeeping** - hosts deliver `.WAV` files with [RIP_ENTER_BLOCK_MODE](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_enter_block_mode) (or a UU-encoded block), check freshness with [RIP_FILE_QUERY](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_file_query), and clean up with [`$FILEDEL$`](5.1-text-variables.md#filedel); audio files live alongside the icon files in the [connection directory](../../glossary.md)/default-directory family - see [6.2 Asset Delivery & Storage](6.2-asset-delivery-and-storage.md). _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._
requirements.reason: RESET(SOUND) and wire playback stop use the shared waveform stop operation.

requirements.heading: 5.0 Host Commands
requirements.text: The **Host Command Language (HCL)**, as the RIPscrip 3.0 White Paper names it - the action language that mouse regions, buttons, hotkeys and query expressions speak back to the host, divided into five areas: control characters, pop-up picklists, local playback directives, template directives, and text variables. A [host command](../../glossary.md) is, at its simplest, raw text transmitted to the host when a button or mouse field is clicked; every HCL directive is something the terminal interprets _before_ (or instead of) transmitting.

requirements.heading: Where Host Commands Run
requirements.text:
- **Buttons** (`1U`) - the command block of the Text Parameter segment, executed when the button is clicked. Template groups are associated with buttons; the [shipped common processor](5.2-templates-and-conditionals.md#shipped-processing-order) also accepts template-enabled blocks without a button association.
- **Mouse fields** (`1M`) - the host command executed when the field is clicked.
- **Queries** (`1` + ESC) - the query text itself is a host-command string, executed or deferred per the mode digit (below); full entry at [RIP_QUERY](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_query).
- **Keystroke macros / hotkeys** - hotkey-triggered buttons execute their command block exactly as if clicked.

requirements.text: Thus `^m` and `^M` both produce CR, `^?` sends the two literal bytes 5e 3f rather than DEL, and **`^@` sends 5e 40 rather than NUL**. The inherited “following character minus @” formula applies only to the accepted letters/punctuation above. Invalid/unrecognized pairs and trailing prefixes do not reject the response. A decoded literal prefix is skipped rather than decoded again: `^^M` sends literal `^M`. Non-ASCII character classification depends on the CRT locale and is not specified by this ASCII contract.

requirements.heading: Rejected Dollar Arguments in Ordinary Responses
requirements.text: When an ordinary pass reaches a dollar reference, the delimiter scan first looks for its closing dollar. Its close is the next dollar whose immediately preceding byte is something other than a backslash. If the parser explicitly rejects the argument syntax and reports the complete span, keep the original bytes including both dollars and resume after its closing dollar. The rejected span calls no provider and performs no replacement. It is skipped as a unit within that pass. With no eligible close, retain the opening dollar as text and advance past that byte. [Dollar argument grammar](5.1-text-variables.md#argument-bytes-and-local-backslashes) · [Original scanner trace](../research/issue-315-host-argument-rejection.md).

requirements.heading: Rejected Dollar Arguments in Ordinary Responses
requirements.text: If the syntax succeeds and an eligible built-in returns an ordinary argument error, retain and skip its entire parsed span in the same way. The parser-rejected case never calls the built-in. The callback-rejected case calls it and can produce its local argument diagnostic. This error yields no substitution or same-name user-variable fallback. A successful empty result consumes the expression. Explicit provider aborts and structural errors in earlier stages retain their own rules. [Expansion order](5.2-templates-and-conditionals.md#shipped-processing-order).

requirements.heading: Identity Grammar and FIELDID Lifetime
requirements.text: The definition-time prefix grammar is ASCII **`[iI][dD]=[0-9]{1,5}:`**, with the decimal numeric value restricted to **0..32767 inclusive**, independent of Base Math. It must begin at byte zero of the command's text payload. Leading zeroes are allowed and count toward the five-digit maximum; signs, whitespace, hexadecimal/base-36 digits, missing digits or a missing colon do not match. For simple `1M`, this is the start of its host text. For `1U`, it is the start of the **full text payload before button label/host-command splitting**, not a later embedded host segment. _Evidence: shared original RIPtel 3.1 prefix parser and both constructor calls; [derivation](../research/issue-113-mouse-gesture-identity.md#exact-id-prefix-grammar)._
requirements.reason: Mouse definitions consume at most one valid decimal ID prefix. The input and query owners retain action bytes and captured identity across callbacks, deletion and synchronous local playback.

requirements.heading: Identity Grammar and FIELDID Lifetime
requirements.text: Recognize and remove **one** valid prefix before normal label/host processing. A nonmatching or out-of-range prefix assigns no identity (`-1`) and leaves the **entire text unchanged** for its normal processing; looking like an invalid ID prefix alone does not reject the enclosing definition. A valid prefix can leave an empty remainder, subject to the enclosing command's other rules. The number is not a macro expression. It is metadata, not the obsolete `1M` slot number or a unique gesture handle; duplicate IDs are allowed and do not merge/replace field instances. ID 0 is valid and differs from no identity.

requirements.text: Unidentified fields skip the shared entry/exit queries; their ordinary click action can still evaluate FIELDID to `-1`. Outside callback context, unavailable FIELDID follows normal macro error handling and does not prompt as an unknown user variable. It does not default to zero/−1, retain the last click's ID or become available merely because the pointer remains over a field. _Evidence: original FIELDID getter, temporary click/hover context writes and [derivation](../research/issue-113-mouse-gesture-identity.md#fieldid-and-hover-scope-evidence)._

requirements.heading: Identity Grammar and FIELDID Lifetime
requirements.text: **Explicit portable lifetime completion:** Snapshot the numeric identity for each synchronous handler. Nested field callbacks push their own context and restore the caller's identity on return; nested ordinary expansion/playback inherits the current one. Deleting/resetting/restoring the handler's field during that handler cancels future gesture/hover work under the [mutation rules](4.2-mouse-fields-and-pointer.md#left-button-gesture-commitment), but its current identity remains valid until return. After the outermost handler returns, no identity remains. Mouse backups carry definitions, not an active callback stack or held gesture. This is a deliberate lifetime policy for mutation/nesting; the original live-index implementation does not establish those safety guarantees.
requirements.reason: A mouse callback on field 8 deletes both fields while field 7 is suspended in paced playback. The native test checks the inner, resumed and unscoped replies. Connected nested files check field 7 after 1K, a delay and both returns.

requirements.heading: Identity Grammar and FIELDID Lifetime
requirements.text: For example, entry for ID 7 reads `7`; a nested field callback for ID 8 reads `8`; after it returns the outer handler reads `7` again. If the outer handler executes `1K`, it still reads `7` until it returns, after which FIELDID is unavailable. A later unrelated query does not inherit `7`. The exact identity grammar and normal temporary scope are source-derived; the snapshot/nesting/deletion behavior in this example is the explicit portable completion.

requirements.heading: Setting & Reading User Variables from Host Commands
requirements.text: The six directive characters are `*`, `+`, `=`, `#`, `-` and `&`. Prefix `=` selects session memory; `+` selects persistent storage and wins when both occur. **`%` is invalid**, rather than a memory alias: a read of the original help bytes and parser dispatch corrects the earlier transcription/synonym hypothesis. See the authoritative [directive and storage contract](5.1-text-variables.md#directive-characters-in-3x), including repeated flags and mixed-prefix examples.
requirements.reason: The decoder accumulates directive bits idempotently and rejects percent in any prefix. Live fixtures compare the full reply, then verify that invalid prefixes leave live and saved values unchanged.

requirements.heading: Setting & Reading User Variables from Host Commands
requirements.text: Transparency is conditional. `-` with a default assigns without prompting; without a default it can prompt. `&` retrieves an existing value without prompting, but prompts if both value and default are missing. The [complete prompt/effect matrix](5.1-text-variables.md#prompt-and-effect-matrix) specifies replacement bytes and storage for all sixteen cases. Cancellation inserts `NONE` for ordinary prompting and no bytes for transparent prompting; successful empty output uses the explicitly chosen `NULL` policy. Neither sentinel is implicitly stored.
requirements.reason: The native sixteen-row matrix checks replacement and storage effects. The connected fixtures verify no-store writes, the two storage lifetimes, precedence, copying across stores, cancellation, and a saved empty value.

requirements.heading: Setting & Reading User Variables from Host Commands
requirements.text: Limits per RIPTEL.HLP: variable names up to **20 characters** (letters, digits, underscore; must start with a letter; auto-uppercased), questions and defaults up to **100 characters**, values up to **255 characters**. SyncTERM's reconstruction differs on the name limit: its `rip_user_var` struct allows only 12 characters (`ripper.c:7774-7789`). These limits and the existing argument/evaluation rules are unchanged by the directive correction. The [source derivation](../research/issue-87-user-variable-directives.md) records the original artifact/offsets and separates documentary rules from explicit edge policies.
requirements.reason: Native parser tests cover name grammar and the 20-letter/digit/underscore boundary. Connected CP437 and UTF-8 tests verify the 100-character question/default limit and the 255-character value limit through persistent storage.

requirements.heading: The Set-Syntax: `$-=NAME=value$`
requirements.text: _Evidence: corpus (122 distinct occurrences; NEWSPAPR.RIP, MENU.DEF, TELLISTS.MSE)._

requirements.heading: The Set-Syntax: `$-=NAME=value$`
requirements.text: The single most common HCL construct in the RIPtel corpus - 122 distinct forms - is the silent assignment:

requirements.heading: The Set-Syntax: `$-=NAME=value$`
requirements.text:
```text
!|1^[0000$-=MAIN_STORY=story01.txt$|!     Filename containing main story
!|1^[0000$-=MAIN_AUTHOR=Jeff Reeder$|!    Author of main story
!|1^[0000$-=RETURN=>TELDEMOS.RET$
```

requirements.heading: The Set-Syntax: `$-=NAME=value$`
requirements.text: This is not new syntax but a _composition_ of the directive characters above: `-` (set without prompting) + `=` (memory table) + `=value` (default supplying the value). Nothing is prompted, nothing is transmitted - the variable is simply defined. MENU.DEF confirms the decomposition by writing the same two directives in the opposite order: `$=-MSG1=Visit your favorite Telnet sites$`. Whole `.DEF` files are nothing but these lines, turning scene scripts into configurable applications.

requirements.heading: The Dereference: `$&NAME$`
requirements.text: _Evidence: corpus (SHOWFONT.FN, NEWSPAPR.RIP, MENU.ENT); 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: The Dereference: `$&NAME$`
requirements.text: The `&` directive was defined in 2.0 as _transparent retrieval to the host_, subject to the missing-value/default cases above. The 3.x corpus shows its far more powerful role: **inline interpolation into command arguments**. A `$&NAME$` expands to the variable's value wherever it appears - including inside the argument block of drawing commands:
requirements.reason: Host expansion retrieves a user variable through the normal missing-value and prompt policy.

requirements.heading: The Dereference: `$&NAME$`
requirements.text:
```text
!|@I064$&FONT_NAME$:                    (text argument of RIP_TEXT_XY)
!|y0000010X000000001S1a000000Marin
!|@4L2L$&MAIN_TITLE$                    (headline drawn from a variable)
!|1R00000000$&MAIN_STORY$               (RIP_READ_SCENE filename from a variable)
```

requirements.heading: The Dereference: `$&NAME$`
requirements.text: Even the outline-font _name_ argument of `y` (RIP_EXTENDED_FONT_STYLE) can be `$&FONT_NAME$`. Together with the set-syntax this is the parameter-passing mechanism of the whole RIPtel demo: a scene sets variables, then calls a generic `.FN` "function" scene that dereferences them.

requirements.text: [RIP_DEFINE](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_define) defines a variable directly from the wire. It can silently set new or existing names when allowed by the record's confirmation policy. The policy and value may be saved together to the persistent store.

requirements.heading: Things to Take Special Care With Host Commands
requirements.text: Special care must be taken when executing host commands or query commands that contain local file playback or active text variables. Either of these operations could instruct the terminal to destroy all mouse fields by performing a [RIP_RESET_WINDOWS](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_reset_windows) command (`$RESET$`), a [RIP_KILL_MOUSE_FIELDS](4.2-mouse-fields-and-pointer.md#rip_kill_mouse_fields) command (`$MKILL$`), a restore mouse fields text variable (`$RMF$`) or other such things.

requirements.heading: Things to Take Special Care With Host Commands
requirements.text: If a situation like this happens, care should be taken to preserve the currently processed host buffer. If it is a mouse field's host command that is being processed, you wouldn't want your application destroying the very buffer that you're processing before you're done processing it. In the case of RIPterm, a sub-string search is done on the host buffer before any processing, for the following strings:
requirements.reason: Mouse definitions consume at most one valid decimal ID prefix. The input and query owners retain action bytes and captured identity across callbacks, deletion and synchronous local playback.

requirements.heading: Things to Take Special Care With Host Commands

```text
$RMF$    ... Restore Mouse Fields
$>       ... Beginning segment of a Local RIP playback command
$APP     ... Instruction to execute an external application
$RESET$  ... Performs a RIP_RESET_WINDOWS command
$MKILL$  ... Destroys the contents of the internal mouse table
```
requirements.reason: Mouse definitions consume at most one valid decimal ID prefix. The input and query owners retain action bytes and captured identity across callbacks, deletion and synchronous local playback.
requirements.scope: Survival of an executing RIP host action across changes to its source. External application launching is outside the goal.

requirements.heading: Things to Take Special Care With Host Commands
requirements.text: If any one of the above strings is found, the terminal physically backs the host buffer up into another location - one that won't be destroyed by the execution of the above commands - and processes the copy instead. In this way, the application can destroy the mouse table to its heart's content but the processing of the buffer will not be affected.

Shared host expansion covers controls, variables, prompts and delays. Pick lists remain tracked separately. A four-digit reserve or one period precedes the expression. requirements.heading: RIP_SET_REFRESH
requirements.text: This command sets a host command sequence in the terminal that can be sent to the host to refresh the current display screen. This refresh option would be chosen by the user to redisplay the screen in case line noise or some kind of corruption caused the screen to become distorted or corrupted. It can only be altered (or cleared) by another RIP_SET_REFRESH command or via a reset. To completely clear a refresh state, call this command with a `$OFF$` text variable as its host command or use the text variable `$NOREFRESH$`.

requirements.text: If you are implementing a client terminal and do not intend on supporting 100% of all pre-defined text variables, you SHOULD at least recognize them and do nothing - so that an unsupported sound variable, for example, is ignored instead of popping up a dialog asking the user to enter data for `$MUSIC$`. _(v1.54)_ Many of the text variables like `$PCB$` are very important to GUI design and should be implemented; if you omit any, do not omit the active text variables - they are critical to implementing a full GUI system using RIPscrip 2.0. _(v2.A1)_

requirements.heading: Text Variables
requirements.text: A special feature of RIPscrip allows it to understand what a Text Variable is. A text variable is a piece of text that both RIPaint and RIPterm know something about. For example, the Text Variable `$DATE$` is known to represent the current Date on your PC. The host may ask your system what the values of one or more of these variables are, and if your terminal knows these particular Text Variables, it will tell the host.

requirements.heading: Variable Resolution in 3.x
requirements.text: The shipped RIPtel 3.1 driver registers 179 built-in callbacks. It handles special directives and then looks up permitted built-ins case-insensitively; a missing name can enter the user-variable engine when the caller permits it. A known built-in rejected for invalid arguments does not fall back to a user variable of the same name. The user-variable path can prompt or retrieve stored data according to its directives; SyncTERM’s unconditional empty-string fallback for unknown names is not the shipped driver’s universal rule. [`$P$`](#p) illustrates the distinction: it has no paste built-in and follows the user-variable path.
requirements.reason: Immediate queries now route decoded unknown user references through the optional borrowed resumable processor after known-built-in recognition. They preserve whole-expression preflight, owned source text, final-token pending prompts and bounded source-pump continuation across delays/responses. Invalid/unsupported known built-ins never prompt or use same-named stored values. P is explicitly removed from the predefined registry and follows the user path. All-canvas native query/source fixtures check ownership, literal replacement bytes, state/replies, required/transparent cancellation, empty values, failures, abort and recovery. Actual dialog/editor presentation, full host two-pass/angle/template/control processing, deferred queries and application routing remain separately pending. This mixed requirement retains its existing status for the separate full-consumer obligations.

requirements.heading: Variable Resolution in 3.x
requirements.text: `TEXTDATA` has no ordinary built-in registration. Exact r/@ sentinels read a separate [retained text buffer](3.0-text-output-and-fonts.md#retained-textdata-lifetime); other positions use normal unknown/user-name rules where enabled.
requirements.reason: PR133 real-font metric contract is connected: all four modes, exact CHR rational and device-derived bitmap geometry, shared atomic outline X/Hcache, signed-WORD then current-axis WORLD conversion, cold/warm failure and inactive viewport. Retained TEXTDATA starts empty, exact r/@ bypass expansion, T/user names remain independent, and full SOFT cancels old graphical ownership and empties data. Independent original-font vectors, codepage/raw UTF-8 byte profiles, live post-prompt setters and late-reset responses are covered. HEADER and aggregate-save operations remain separately pending.

requirements.heading: Variable Resolution in 3.x

Eligibility follows callback registration, not the descriptive Value/Active labels: CUR/COORDSIZE/OVERFLOW/HOSTDIR setters are callable there, whereas WORLD is active-only and blocked even as a query. Metric permits user providers in its angle stage but no ordinary user fallback. Host execution retains its separate permissions and two ordinary passes.

requirements.heading: Variable Resolution in 3.x
requirements.text: Empty parentheses supply zero arguments. Empty comma fields are omitted: `$RAND(9,,2)$` is the two-argument form `$RAND(9,2)$`, not a third-argument minimum with an omitted width. The parser permits at most 40 nonempty arguments, each at most 20 bytes, in its fixed argument slots. Apply these rules before counting required/optional arguments in the recovered entries below. The [argument byte/backslash contract](#argument-bytes-and-local-backslashes) specifies payload acceptance and decoded length.

requirements.heading: Argument bytes and local backslashes
requirements.text: Double quotes do not introduce a quoted argument: both `""` and `"AB"` are rejected. Single quotes are ordinary retained bytes. There is no nested dollar-reference evaluation inside a parsed argument, and parentheses are not balanced recursively. The first unquoted closing parenthesis ends the argument list; later text belongs to the separate post-argument question/default/directive syntax.
requirements.reason: The reference parser bounds and unquotes arguments. Host processing performs the two ordinary passes and graphics processing performs one.

requirements.heading: Argument bytes and local backslashes
requirements.text: A local backslash is stored temporarily. The next non-backslash byte must pass the payload predicate; if it does, that byte **overwrites the backslash** without increasing stored length. This permits `\)` as a literal closing parenthesis and `\$` as a literal dollar, while `\A` simply stores `A`. It does not admit forbidden punctuation: `\,`, `\"` and `\/` reject. A second consecutive backslash rejects, so there is **no direct argument spelling for a literal backslash**. A pending backslash before a closing parenthesis quotes that parenthesis instead of ending the list; another unquoted closing parenthesis is needed.

requirements.heading: Argument bytes and local backslashes

Twenty repetitions of `\A` use 40 source bytes but store 20 `A` bytes and fit; 21 stored bytes reject. A quote prefix occupies the next slot until overwritten, so the quoted byte can complete slot 20. Empty comma fields still occupy no argument slot.

requirements.heading: Text Variable Creation and Query
requirements.text: As previously mentioned, Text Variables were described as either pre-defined variables, or as User Variables. Pre-defined variables are variables that RIPscrip products know things about "out of the box". They will always know what the variables mean, from the day you install the software. User Variables are variables that the user of RIPscrip products defines, and teaches the software new things it doesn't already know.

requirements.heading: Pre-Defined Text Variables
requirements.text: A pre-defined text variable is either a data text variable, or an active text variable. A data text variable is a text variable that inserts a piece of text wherever the text variable is used. For example, the sequence `$DATE$` might get replaced with 09/19/94. This is a simple example of a data text variable. An active text variable on the other hand does something (usually). They normally don't get replaced with other text information. For example, the text variable `$SAVE$` saves the contents of the screen to a disk file that can later be restored with `$RESTORE$`. In these situations, active text variables are removed from whatever text message they are present in (they are still activated though).

requirements.heading: What Are User Variables?
requirements.text: A User Variable is a Text Variable that RIPscrip doesn't know exists. They are custom-defined text variables that contain information that the terminal user will fill in. Transparent retrieval with `&` can return an existing value without user intervention. Other combinations follow the [prompt and effect matrix](#prompt-and-effect-matrix); existence alone does not suppress every prompt.
requirements.reason: Host queries dispatch built-ins or user variables, parse prompt directives and retain answers in the chosen store. Connected fixtures exercise required, optional, formatted and persistent values.

You can tell the terminal to store these values permanently, or they may be active only during the current session, or they may be defined as temporary where they are not stored for more than a brief moment.

requirements.heading: What Are User Variables?
requirements.text: > **NOTE:** This ability is configurable so that information exchange can be either interactive, or automatic. Automatic transfer of information does NOT prompt the user with the information unless the variable has not yet been defined. If it has not been defined, a pop-up question will appear asking the user a particular question, thus defining the text variable.

requirements.heading: What Are User Variables?
requirements.text: If the exchange is interactive, the data is displayed in a pop-up editor box, asking you if the information is correct. If it is, press ENTER and the retrieved information is sent to the host for you. If it is not correct, or it has not been created yet, just type it in and press ENTER and it will be saved automatically, and sent to the host all at once.

requirements.heading: How Can User Variables Be Important?
requirements.text: Lets take an example. You are the system operator of a large RIPscrip host. As you have read, RIPscrip can take advantage of database-like ability on the terminal end. If you can alter your host to ask questions with RIPscrip Text Variables built in, you can have the terminal calling your host automatically fill in questionnaires. Imagine if a user could sign-up on your host without having to type more than a single keystroke (i.e., "YES, this information is correct"). With User Text Variables, you can do this very thing.

requirements.heading: Creating User Variables
requirements.text: There are two ways of defining User Text Variables in RIPscrip. You can use either the [Define Text Variable command](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_define), or you can use Text Variable Queries, as described in the next section.

requirements.heading: Defining Text Variables
requirements.text: The RIPscrip command Define Text Variable is by definition, an interactive command with the user. The RIPscrip command will attempt to define a User Variable. This variable is some piece of information that the system operator deems important. You may specify a question, a default response, and how many characters long the response may be.
requirements.reason: Historical framing of the interactive operation. The shipped wire and record rules are specified in the following RIP_DEFINE contract.

requirements.heading: Defining Text Variables
requirements.text: Once the terminal has received a define command, the terminal pops up an appropriate question box on the user's screen, asking him the desired question that should be saved to a particular Text Variable. If you did not specify a question, a default question is used (i.e., "Enter <name of text variable>").
requirements.reason: Historical framing of the interactive operation. The shipped wire and record rules are specified in the following RIP_DEFINE contract.

requirements.heading: Defining Text Variables
requirements.text: Once the user has entered his response, it is recorded and saved. How long it is stored depends on what the host told the terminal. The host can tell the terminal "save this on your hard disk forever". The host may also tell the terminal "don't save this to disk, but remember this value until you exit RIPterm". You also have the option of saying "don't remember this value at all, just pop up a question, and send the value to me NOW" - i.e., don't save it at all, just enter it and send it to the host).
requirements.reason: Historical framing of the interactive operation. The shipped wire and record rules are specified in the following RIP_DEFINE contract.

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE in 3.x
requirements.text: The [RIP_DEFINE wire command](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_define) (`!|1D`) takes a name, an optional width and a nonempty definition body. It can prompt or save a value silently, including for a new name. The effective record's confirmation policy can require the editor. Its full entry defines default selection, accepted empty values, cancellation and the scope of the numeric flags.
requirements.reason: The effective live or saved record supplies the confirmation flag. The editor updates value and policy on acceptance, and preserves both on cancellation or interruption. Connected tests verify flag 4, byte width, rejected blank input and exact subsequent replies.

requirements.heading: Querying Text Variables
requirements.text: Now that you know how to define information on the terminal, you need to know the last method of asking the terminal about text variables. This feature is called "Data Query". Data Query is a generic query command that can ask the terminal one or more questions, and tell it how to transmit the information back to the host. This command is for use in non-button situations where you do not want to wait until the user clicks on a button to get your data back.

requirements.heading: Querying Text Variables
requirements.text: [Data Query](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_query) is a special RIPscrip command that can be used to ask the contents of one or more Text Variables.

requirements.heading: Examples of Text Variable Query
requirements.text: Lets take a simple example. You wanted to ask the terminal program some address information. You could do this with the following query (remember, the query also tells the terminal HOW to send the data back to the host):

requirements.heading: Examples of Text Variable Query
requirements.text:
```text
$FULL_NAME$^m$COMPANY$^m$ST_ADDR$^m$CITY$, $STATE$ $ZIP^m
```

requirements.heading: Examples of Text Variable Query
requirements.text: This would query the terminal the contents of 6 text variables, and format them in a manner similar to any normal address on an envelope. The results of this query might send the following back to the host :

requirements.heading: Examples of Text Variable Query
requirements.text:
```text
Joe Sixpack
ACME Corporation
13631 Palindrome Parkway
Surf City, CA 92649
```

requirements.heading: Positioned Variable Prompts
requirements.text: A position prefix has a comma and colon even when one or both axes are omitted. Each supplied axis is an unsigned ASCII decimal value from 0 through 65535. Leading zeros are decimal. Parse the complete prefix using checked arithmetic. An axis outside this numeric range is a malformed variable expression. The axes do not use Base Math or the wire XY field width. In the portable profile, a written `65535` is a coordinate and an empty axis field requests centering. Leaving out the whole prefix lets the client choose the dialog position. [Original parser and portable range](../research/issue-311-prompt-dialog-placement.md).
requirements.reason: Prompt placement uses checked decimal axes and projects through the active WORLD to the full drawing area. Fixtures check independent centering, zero WORLD extent, edge fitting, acceptance and malformed-expression recovery.

requirements.heading: Positioned Variable Prompts
requirements.text: Apply placement only when the expression opens a prompt. Use the RIP drawing client area as the placement rectangle, with DEVICE coordinates relative to its top-left. Use that area for every PORT, viewport and TW selection. Measure the dialog's outer extent before fitting it to the drawing area. A supplied coordinate specifies the requested **top-left** of the dialog on that axis. Resolve X and Y independently using the active WORLD and DEVICE extents. Its subsequent prose also uses `=` and explicitly ignores additional directive occurrences. The original parser sets the memory flag for prefix `=`; `%` is not a directive or an alias. Apply the enclosing malformed-expression handling, without treating `%` as part of a user-variable name. requirements.text: For example, with no stored NAME, `$=&NAME$` prompts. Accepting `Ada` saves session NAME=`Ada` and inserts `Ada`; accepting empty saves an existing empty NAME and inserts `NULL`; cancelling changes no store and inserts no bytes. requirements.heading: User Defined Variables and Data Security
requirements.text: When working with user-defined text variables, a topic arises which may or may not be addressed by the RIPscrip software developer: security! What if you had credit card information stored in a permanent text variable named `$CredCardNo$` and the host system asked your terminal for that information? Obviously the user should be informed about this request. Situations might arise where security is not a concern - like in a closed environment like an internal office system using RIPscrip. With these situations in mind, the designer of a RIPscrip terminal might wish to include some kind of "data security" feature into the software package.
requirements.reason: Historical/evidence/navigation, table heading or optional security discussion; shipping 3.x executable behavior is tracked in the corresponding individual requirements. Legacy SyncTERM divergences are not the v3 contract.

requirements.heading: User Defined Variables and Data Security
requirements.text: Data security can be in many forms. You could implement complete "tight" security which would overide all transparent forms of text variable operations - in effect, always making the user approve the request. A lighter security might be desirable - one where any action working on permanent database text variables requires the user's approval, but memory variables don't have to be approved. This kind of a situation would let allow a host system to have control over memory variables (which it presumably created anyway), but let access to permanent variables be under strict control. The exact form of data security that you offer your software's users is unimportant - but knowing that security is a concern is. You do not have to implement data security on your system - it is not an actual part of RIPscrip (per se), but it could be useful to your customers if security is an issue.

requirements.reason: The reference parser bounds and unquotes arguments. Host processing performs the two ordinary passes and graphics processing performs one.

requirements.heading: Limits on Length of Variable Names, Etc.
requirements.text: The maximum size of a text variable parameter is 12 characters. These are only available to text variables that are part of the RIPscrip specification.
requirements.reason: Inherited 12-character description. The v3 built-in argument grammar specifies 20 decoded bytes per parameter and up to 40 parameters.

requirements.heading: Limits on Length of Variable Names, Etc.
requirements.text: The maximum size of a question or default response is 100 characters. Anything longer than this length is truncated.
requirements.reason: Raw CP437 and decoded character limits preserve 100 question/default characters. Native tests check four-byte UTF-8 characters and live fixtures check the 100th displayed character and the exact default reply.

requirements.heading: Limits on Length of Variable Names, Etc.
requirements.text: The maximum length of a text variable text field is 255 characters. Anything longer than this length is truncated.
requirements.reason: Values retain 255 characters after codepage conversion or UTF-8 input. Live fixtures check exact replies and saved value reload after reconnect. Native fixtures cover wide record lengths and older files.

requirements.heading: Limits on Length of Variable Names, Etc.
requirements.text: The RIPtel help confirms the shipping limits: variable names are **20** characters (letters, digits, underscore; must start with a letter; auto-uppercased), question and default text are **100** characters each, and variable content (the value) is **255** characters. _(HLP)_
requirements.reason: Native parser tests cover name grammar and the 20-letter/digit/underscore boundary. Connected CP437 and UTF-8 tests verify the 100-character question/default limit and the 255-character value limit through persistent storage.

requirements.heading: Limits on Length of Variable Names, Etc.
requirements.text: > **Divergence:** SyncTERM caps variable names at **12** characters (`name[13]` storage; validation additionally forbids a leading digit _or underscore_). Scripts targeting both should stay within 12 characters. _(SyncTERM (ripper.c:103-109, 7774-7789))_
requirements.reason: Historical/evidence/navigation, table heading or optional security discussion; shipping 3.x executable behavior is tracked in the corresponding individual requirements. Legacy SyncTERM divergences are not the v3 contract.

requirements.heading: Examples of User-Defined Text Variables
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A1._

requirements.heading: Examples of User-Defined Text Variables
requirements.text: Below are some examples of user defined text variables as might be used in a real world situation:

requirements.heading: Examples of User-Defined Text Variables
requirements.text:
```text
$*+20,50:NAME(ToName),30@What's your name?=John Doe$
```

requirements.heading: Examples of User-Defined Text Variables
requirements.text: _(example as of v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: Examples of User-Defined Text Variables
requirements.text: This is about as complex as they get. Going from left to right, lets look at what all the codes mean. First, the "\*" means that a response to this request is required (they cannot hit ESC or CANCEL to get out of it). The "+" means to save the response to the internal database permanently. The sequence "20,50:" means to place the dialog box's upper left corner at location (20,50) on the screen. The "NAME" is the name of the data variable. The format option "(Name)" means that this should be a formatted name field where the first letter of any word should be capitolized and the remaining characters should be set to lower case. The value ",30" after the variable name/format indicates that this field is up to 30 characters in length. "@What's your name?" indicates that the question "What's your name?" should be displayed when the user is prompted for the information. Finally, the "=John Doe" indicates that if the field doesn't exist, it should be filled in with "John Doe" before any editing is allowed. This gives the user the ability to choose a default name if they wish.

requirements.heading: Examples of User-Defined Text Variables
requirements.text:
```text
$*#20,10:PASSWORD,10@Please enter your password$
```

requirements.heading: Examples of User-Defined Text Variables
requirements.text: This example is a required data variable that echos #'s in place of the keystrokes you entered. The field is placed at (20,10) on the screen with a variable name of PASSWORD. The field is 10 characters wide and the prompt is "Please enter your password".

requirements.heading: Examples of User-Defined Text Variables
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP - both examples above appear verbatim in the RIPtel help file._

requirements.heading: Persistence
requirements.text: Variables defined with the `+` directive or [RIP_DEFINE](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_define) flag `001` are saved to a client-side persistent store and survive across sessions. For `1D` the persistent record includes the confirmation requirement alongside the value, so a restored record can still force an editor. Implementation storage may use any suitable representation for the name, value and applicable policy. A session-only `1D` update changes the live record and leaves the backing record available for later sessions.
requirements.reason: A persistent definition refreshes the live entry and saves value and confirmation together. A session-only definition shadows the saved entry. Connected reconnects and the native versioned file fixtures verify policy retention and old-file compatibility.

requirements.heading: Persistence
requirements.text: _Evidence: [RIP_DEFINE store trace](../research/issue-175-rip-define.md#editor-and-store), [RIPtel help variable-database strings](../../3.0/research/riptel-resource-containers.md) and SyncTERM (ripper.c:7899-7961, 19008)._
requirements.reason: Section label, table layout, recommendation or original evidence for the RIP_DEFINE contract.

requirements.heading: Silent Set & Dereference
requirements.text: The [directive/storage rules](#directive-characters-in-3x) and [prompt/effect matrix](#prompt-and-effect-matrix) are authoritative for these forms, including missing values and cancellation.
requirements.reason: Host queries dispatch built-ins or user variables, parse prompt directives and retain answers in the chosen store. Connected fixtures exercise required, optional, formatted and persistent values.

requirements.heading: Silent Set & Dereference
requirements.text: The user-variable system is 3.x's client-side data store in action: the host defines named variables, the terminal prompts the user (or not), and later `$NAME$` references expand to the stored value - including as arguments _inside RIPscrip commands_ (the demo corpus passes `$&FONT_NAME$` as a font name and `$&MAIN_STORY$` as a filename).

requirements.heading: Silent Set & Dereference
requirements.text:
- **`$-=NAME=value$`** assigns a value without prompting. This is the workhorse of the demo corpus - 122 distinct set-forms observed, wiring menu state: `$-=RETURN=>NEWSPAPR.RIP$`, `$-=WEBURL=http://…$`, `$-=TITLE=Telnet Site Listings$`.
- **`$&NAME$`** retrieves an existing stored value without prompting, usable inline in command arguments (a missing value without a default follows the prompt matrix): `$&FONT_NAME$` as the font-name field of an extended-font-style command, `$&MAIN_STORY$` as a read-scene filename, even computed names via macro expansion (`$&MSG<<FIELDID>>$`).
requirements.reason: Host queries dispatch built-ins or user variables, parse prompt directives and retain answers in the chosen store. Connected fixtures exercise required, optional, formatted and persistent values.

requirements.heading: Silent Set & Dereference
requirements.text: _Evidence: HLP (`-` and `&` directives); corpus (TELLISTS.MSE, SHOWFONT.FN, NEWSPAPR.RIP)._

requirements.heading: Template-Slot Dereference (`$?N$`)
requirements.text: `$?N$` - where `N` is one of the 36 slot characters `0`-`9`/`A`-`Z` - expands to the stored [template](5.2-templates-and-conditionals.md) text for that slot. _(SyncTERM (ripper.c:11918-11923))_
requirements.reason: Immediate host responses support all 36 case-folded $?N$ slot references in either of exactly two ordinary passes, with required-empty selection/abort and regular-empty insertion. PR95 bounds each stored raw definition, response entry and every dollar/template replacement to 4096 working bytes. Monotonically bounded unread suffixes prevent discarded callbacks/syntax from executing or returning after later shortening; retained callbacks and causing assignment effects remain. Controls/backslashes decode only in pass two, including literal trailing outer backslash. Independent all-canvas native tests cover every published boundary/side-effect vector, both-pass growth, decoded-prefix capacity, generic results, accepted assignments, incomplete retained references, raw UTF-8 cuts, per-block rather than session bounds, owned definitions, allocation/recovery and all slot spellings. Earlier angle preprocessing, button/group aggregation/highlighting, playback, deferred modes and application routing remain pending; runtime parsing remains below void command/session boundaries.

requirements.heading: Template-Slot Dereference (`$?N$`)
requirements.text: This ordinary embedding feature is enabled for host responses, but disabled for graphical filename/label/T/@/metric consumers, where `$?N$` stays literal. Their enabled angle spelling `<<?N>>` is a separate preprocessing operation; see the [graphical permission table](5.2-templates-and-conditionals.md#eligible-providers-and-rejected-codes).
requirements.reason: Host ordinary expansion can insert a slot. Graphical text enables angle insertion and leaves ordinary slot references literal.

requirements.heading: Host Deletion and Data Queries in 3.x
requirements.text: The host may delete a variable; RIPtel asks the user to confirm ("The host wants to delete the variable %s. Proceed?"). A _data query_ is simply a host-sent template of variable references - e.g. `$FULL_NAME$^m$ST_ADDR$^m$CITY$, $STATE$ $ZIP$^m` - which the terminal returns filled in; protected variables trigger a "Data Security Activated" notice (see [User Defined Variables and Data Security](#user-defined-variables-and-data-security) above). _(HLP)_

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text: Each text variable's description details the exact syntax of that variable. The syntax is described in concise detail so that you can easily spot at the glance of an eye exactly what parameters are allowed, and if omitted, what the default values are for those parameters. You can also determine what text variables have optional parameters, and what parameters are required.

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text: There are two basic text variables - those that take parameters, and those that don't. Those that don't use any parameters are the simplest of all to describe syntactically. If a text variable does not require any parameters, then its syntax description would be nearly identical to the following:

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text:
```text
Syntax:  $TEXTVAR$
```

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text: This simply states that in order use this text variable in an expression, you insert the text `$TEXTVAR$` in your host command.

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text: For text variables that require parameters though, more detailed descriptions are necessary. Here is an example listing of a text variable requiring one parameter and having an optional second parameter:

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text:
```text
Syntax:  $TEXTVAR(req:PARAM1, opt:PARAM2)$
```

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text: You should notice the text "req:" and "opt:". The "req:PARAM1" text indicates that the parameter named "PARAM1" is required. The second piece of text is "opt:PARAM2", which means that the parameter named "PARAM2" is optional.

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text: But what values can PARAM1 or PARAM2 be? It's not mentioned at all what values they can obtain. This is where the parameter value notation comes in. Suppose that PARAM1 can be set to "TRUE" or "FALSE", and that PARAM2 can be set to "BLUE" and "RED". To describe these values our new syntax description would be:

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text:
```text
Syntax:  $TEXTVAR(req:PARAM1, opt:PARAM2)$
                      ──────      ──────
                      TRUE        BLUE
                      FALSE       RED
```

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text: From the above description, it is quite simple to determine what parameters are required, which ones are optional, and which ones can be set to what values. Now, let's add a new color to PARAM2, called "GREEN", and let's say that it can only be used as PARAM2 when PARAM1 is equal to "TRUE". We denote this like the following:

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text:
```text
Syntax:  $TEXTVAR(req:PARAM1, opt:PARAM2)$
                      ──────      ──────
                      TRUE        BLUE
                      FALSE       RED
                                  GREEN:PARAM1=TRUE
```

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text: Notice the "GREEN:PARAM1=TRUE". This means that PARAM2 can be set to "GREEN" only if PARAM1 is equal to TRUE. What if we added another value to PARAM1 that could also be green, called "MAYBE". Then our example would look like this:

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text:
```text
Syntax:  $TEXTVAR(req:PARAM1, opt:PARAM2)$
                      ──────      ──────
                      TRUE        BLUE
                      FALSE       RED
                      MAYBE       GREEN:PARAM1=TRUE,MAYBE
```

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text: Now the description of GREEN has "PARAM1=TRUE,MAYBE". This means that PARAM2 can be set to "GREEN" only if PARAM1 is equal to TRUE or MAYBE. Pretty simple. This same situation could be written more shortly (in this case) with the "not equal" expression <> as in the following:

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text:
```text
Syntax:  $TEXTVAR(req:PARAM1, opt:PARAM2)$
                      ──────      ──────
                      TRUE        BLUE
                      FALSE       RED
                      MAYBE       GREEN:PARAM1<>FALSE
```

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text: This means that PARAM2 can be set to GREEN only if PARAM1 is not equal to FALSE. If PARAM2 could only be set to GREEN if PARAM1 was equal to TRUE, we could list this (using a previously described notation):

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text:
```text
Syntax:  $TEXTVAR(req:PARAM1, opt:PARAM2)$
                      ──────      ──────
                      TRUE        BLUE
                      FALSE       RED
                      MAYBE       GREEN:PARAM1<>FALSE,MAYBE
```

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text: Optional parameters do not need to be specified. If they are not, then some "suitable" default value will be used for that parameter. Let's take a variation of our previous example:

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text:
```text
Syntax:  $TEXTVAR(req:PARAM1, opt:PARAM2)$
                      ──────      ──────
                      TRUE        BLUE
                      FALSE       RED
                      MAYBE       GREEN
                                  ──────
                              def=BLUE
```

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text: This says that if PARAM2 is omitted, that BLUE will be the default. What if BLUE is only the default when PARAM1 is set to TRUE, and RED is default all the other times? Then you would have the following syntax description:

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text:
```text
Syntax:  $TEXTVAR(req:PARAM1, opt:PARAM2)$
                      ──────      ──────
                      TRUE        BLUE
                      FALSE       RED
                      MAYBE       GREEN
                                  ──────
                              def=BLUE:PARAM1=TRUE
                                  RED:PARAM1<>TRUE
```

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text: Lastly, a number of text variables have a variable number of parameters. This means that one of the parameters can be repeated more than once, but it must be specified at least once. This is represented in the actual text variable "short description" with an ellipse "..." shown in the parameter list like the following:

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text:
```text
$TEXTVAR(param1,param2,...)$ - Perform some kind of operation
```

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text: In the syntax description, it is also shown as an ellipse "...". The parameter immediately preceding the ellipse is the one that is repeated and all subsequent instances of that parameter use the same syntax as the first one repeated. Here is an example if we allowed PARAM2 to be repeated multiple times:

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text:
```text
Syntax:  $TEXTVAR(req:PARAM1, req:PARAM2, ...)$
                      ──────      ──────
                      TRUE        BLUE
                      FALSE       RED
                      MAYBE       GREEN
                                  ──────
                              def:BLUE
```

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text: Notice how PARAM2 is set to "req:". This means that PARAM2 must be specified at least once, but can be repeated. It is also possible that the repeated parameter itself may be optional (eg, "opt:"). If this is the case then there can be zero or more occurrences of that parameter.

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text: If no specific default value is allowed for an omitted parameter (ie, it has special significance if it is omitted), then the default value would be listed as "\<none\>".

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4 - the syntax-description notation is inherited into 3.x unchanged._

requirements.text: These text variables are for version number, vendor determination, and software features of a RIPscrip package. These are used heavily for "detecting" what kind of RIPscrip software a host is connected with. _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: $IFS$
requirements.text: This is a unique and powerful text variable. This is the mechanism by which the host can find out what capabilities are supported in the remote terminal. For example, if the host needs to know if the terminal supports JPEG files, the host could send a query: _(v2.A2)_
requirements.reason: RIP3 queries report capabilities configured for the active session, including the available image decoder and transfer worker.

requirements.heading: $IFS$
requirements.text:
```text
!|1Σ0000$IFS(JPEG)$
```
requirements.reason: A level-one ESC query can evaluate IFS on the actual connection and return its result to the peer.

requirements.heading: $IFS$
requirements.text: Note that the character "Σ" is actually an escape character (ASCII value 27). _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: $IFS$
requirements.text: The terminal would respond with `1` if it has JPEG display ability, or "0" if it doesn't. _(v2.A4)_
requirements.reason: The JPEG feature bit uses the active decoder's availability. The connected media fixture checks image presentation against the advertised bit.

requirements.heading: $IFS$
requirements.text: Because the number of features supported by a software package can get quite extensive, they are categorized for the purposes of this command. This allows the host to be able to query particular sub-sets of information (eg, what file transfer protocols are supported, etc). These categories are simple keyword names just like the keyword names used to identify particular features, but with one slight difference. Categories begin with an underscore character (_) to differentiate them from actual feature keywords. These categories are used in conjunction with a special `$IFS$` directive called LIST. This will list out all keywords for a specific category, or if no category is specified, it will list out all categories. The basic categories and their corresponding sub-items are as follows: _(v2.A4)\_

requirements.heading: Bookmark credential lifetime and approval
requirements.text: RIPtel 3.1's connection setup deletes the previous live records for `USERNAME` and `PASSWORD` and defines each nonempty bookmark field separately. It uses the ordinary live-variable APIs with confirmation requested. Both names are absent from the driver's built-in registrations. The installed records participate in ordinary live lookup and the usual definition and deletion authorization. An absent record leaves ordinary same-name lookup in scope. This evidence establishes the storage and confirmation request. [Client and driver derivation](../research/issue-277-bookmark-variable-policy.md).
requirements.reason: Historical observations, chapter overview or table structure for the portable credential policy.

requirements.heading: Bookmark credential lifetime and approval
requirements.text: **Portable credential profile.** These two names are reserved case-insensitively. Keep their bookmark values in client-owned, connection-scoped state. Clear the previous association when the connection ends or a new connection attempt starts. On successful connection with a user-selected bookmark, associate only its nonempty fields with that connection. An empty field stays unavailable. A manual connection without a bookmark leaves both unavailable. Reconnecting through another bookmark uses only its own current values and starts with fresh authorization.
requirements.reason: Conditional local submission rules. This implementation uses the explicitly permitted always-unavailable host profile.

requirements.heading: $RAND$
requirements.text: One to three nonempty decimal-digit arguments are required after empty fields have been omitted. For ordinary range-valid inputs, maximum is 1..32767, length is 0..5 (default 0), and minimum is 0..maximum-1 (default 0). Bare `$RAND$` and `$RAND()$` reject; the former help-only syntax did not describe an executable zero-argument query.

requirements.heading: $RAND$
requirements.text: The handler obtains a random integer `r` in 0..32767 and computes:
requirements.reason: Pinned grammar and value behavior verified by native vectors and the connected query path.

requirements.heading: $RAND$
requirements.text:
```text
minimum + ((maximum - minimum + 1) * r) / 32767
```
requirements.reason: Pinned grammar and value behavior verified by native vectors and the connected query path.

requirements.heading: $RAND$
requirements.text: For normal inputs division truncates toward zero. The decimal result is left-padded with zeroes to at least `length` characters and is never truncated to that width. **Shipped endpoint defect:** `r=32767` returns maximum+1. For `$RAND(9,3,2)$`, normal results are `002` through `009`, with `010` possible at that endpoint. Hosts must not assume the declared maximum is an absolute upper bound in this client.
requirements.reason: Pinned grammar and value behavior verified by native vectors and the connected query path.

requirements.heading: $RAND$
requirements.text: For exact driver compatibility, decimal conversion wraps modulo 2^32. The converted maximum must be 1..32767; length is checked with signed `<=5`, and minimum with signed `<maximum`, so oversized positive tokens can wrap into accepted values. Checked examples: maximum `4294967297` becomes 1; length `4294967295` becomes -1 and causes no padding; minimum `4294967295` becomes -1 and returns `-1` when r=0. Arithmetic follows the original 32-bit operations. These quirks do not add a signed-token syntax: a literal minus is not accepted by this handler’s digit validator.
requirements.reason: Pinned grammar and value behavior verified by native vectors and the connected query path.

requirements.heading: $RAND$
requirements.text: The original CRT generator updates `state = state*214013 + 2531011` modulo 2^32 and returns `(state >> 16) & 32767`. This identifies the shipped generator; no portable initial seed or cross-session sequence is promised by the variable grammar.
requirements.reason: Pinned grammar and value behavior verified by native vectors and the connected query path.

requirements.heading: $DATETIME$
requirements.text: Returns the current **local** date and time as exactly **17 ASCII characters**, `MM/DD/YY HH:MM:SS`. All six fields contain exactly two decimal digits with leading zeroes: month 01–12, day 01–31, year 00–99, hour 00–23, minute 00–59 and second 00–59. Separators are literal `/`, one ASCII space between date and time, and `:`. There is no weekday, month name or four-digit year, and **no trailing newline or carriage return**. The driver's C-string NUL terminates storage; it is not part of the expanded value. No arguments are accepted.
requirements.reason: Native examples verify the 17 ASCII bytes and two-digit rollover. Connected tests verify live local time, elapsed time within a query and recovery from a rejected argument.

requirements.heading: $DATETIME$
requirements.text: **Example:** `$DATETIME$` **Returns:** `12/05/93 14:38:50` for Sunday December 5, 1993 at 14:38:50 local time. December 19 at the same time returns `12/19/93 14:38:50`.
requirements.reason: Native examples verify the 17 ASCII bytes and two-digit rollover. Connected tests verify live local time, elapsed time within a query and recovery from a rejected argument.

requirements.heading: $DATETIME$
requirements.text: > **Correction to the inherited description:** RIPtel 3.1's original driver formats `%c` using its built-in numeric date/time templates. It does not return Unix/asctime-style text; none of `Sun Dec  5 …`, `Sun Dec 05 …` or `Sun Dec 5 …` matches its output. The inherited `Sat Dec 19 14:38:50 1993` example also had the wrong weekday (that date was Sunday). Merely correcting Sat to Sun would still give the wrong output format. This correction establishes this driver's behavior; it does not assert that earlier clients used the same format.

requirements.heading: $FIELDID$
requirements.text: Returns the current field callback's numeric identity as a decimal integer: the entering/exiting ID in a shared hover handler, or the captured ID during a committed click action (`-1` for an unidentified click field). It is available to synchronous nested expansion/playback, not between handlers or in later queued work; outside field context it fails as a recognized unavailable variable. Merely hovering or clicking earlier does not leave a persistent value.
requirements.reason: The connected input and ENV services supply callback identity, cursor style and coordinates. Fixtures distinguish input scope and protected ENV behavior.

requirements.heading: $FIELDID$
requirements.text: The [identity grammar and lifetime table](5.0-host-commands.md#identity-grammar-and-fieldid-lifetime) specify case-insensitive ID prefixes, decimal range 0..32767, invalid-prefix retention, duplicate identities and the explicit portable snapshot/nesting/deletion policy. The [shared pointer contract](4.2-mouse-fields-and-pointer.md#left-button-gesture-commitment) supplies press/release ownership. The demos use FIELDID for computed names such as `$&MSG<<FIELDID>>$`. _Evidence: RIPtel help/corpus, original getter and temporary context writes, plus explicitly labeled lifetime completion; [derivation](../research/issue-113-mouse-gesture-identity.md)._

requirements.heading: $M$
requirements.text: This Text Variable returns a 3-character code representing the status of each mouse button. This variable works with two button and three button mice. The format of the code is LMR where L=Left, M=Middle (if any), and R=Right. If any button is clicked, the code for that button is "1". If the button is not depressed, it is "0". "100" would mean the left mouse button is depressed, but none of the others are.
requirements.reason: Connected input events update independent left, middle and right state. M returns the three digits in that order.

requirements.heading: $MCURSOR$
requirements.text: This command changes the current mouse cursor style to one of the pre-defined mouse cursor styles as defined in the [RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR](4.2-mouse-fields-and-pointer.md#rip_set_mouse_cursor) command. The cursor_no parameter is identical to the cursor style numbers permitted for the RIPscrip command to alter the cursor. If you omit the CURSOR_NO parameter, the default "pointer" cursor is activated.

requirements.heading: $MCURSOR$
requirements.text: **RIPtel 3.1 ownership/protection:** this changes the current environment's mouse number and refreshes its presentation; it changes no graphics-style record. The variable accepts 0..7 (or no argument for zero) and bypasses environment protection. The corresponding wire command checks environment protection; protecting a graphics style does not block either path. _Evidence: [original setter and native matrix](../research/issue-24-drawing-state-ownership.md#ownership-and-switching-observations)._
requirements.reason: The connected input and ENV services supply callback identity, cursor style and coordinates. Fixtures distinguish input scope and protected ENV behavior.

requirements.heading: $MCURSOR$
requirements.text: The [canonical 0..7 mapping and fallback](4.2-mouse-fields-and-pointer.md#rip_set_mouse_cursor) apply unchanged: 4 is pointing finger, 6 hourglass, and **7 is the visible slashed-circle not-allowed symbol**, stored distinctly even if a native backend substitutes arrow. It is not a hidden/no-change sentinel and does not disable input or cancel capture. Both forms reject values outside 0..7 under the explicit portable range rule; argumentless MCURSOR selects 0 rather than querying the current number.

requirements.heading: $MSTAT$
requirements.text: _Query availability of mouse input_

requirements.heading: $MSTAT$
requirements.text: **Format:** `$MSTAT$` or `$MSTAT()$`. An argument rejects the variable.

requirements.heading: $MSTAT$
requirements.text: **RIPtel 3.1.** The callback evaluates Win32 `GetSystemMetrics(SM_MOUSEPRESENT)` on each query and returns ASCII `YES` for a nonzero result or `NO` for zero. The operating system metric can include virtual mouse devices. [Microsoft GetSystemMetrics documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winuser/nf-winuser-getsystemmetrics)

requirements.heading: $MSTAT$
requirements.text: **Portable policy.** If the client has no enabled mouse-equivalent input path, return `NO`. Otherwise use the frontend's current direct presence signal when available. A usable physical or virtual mouse, or a compositor seat with pointer capability, returns `YES`. Explicit absence returns `NO`. With enabled mouse input and no presence signal, return `YES` from frontend capability alone. A touch, tablet or remote input path counts when it supplies mouse-equivalent movement and button actions.

requirements.heading: $MSTAT$
requirements.text: | Frontend state | `$MSTAT$` |

requirements.heading: $MSTAT$
requirements.text: | Enabled mouse input with a usable virtual pointer or seat pointer capability | `YES` |

requirements.heading: $MSTAT$
requirements.text: | Enabled mouse input with a presence signal that explicitly reports absence | `NO` |

requirements.heading: $MSTAT$
requirements.text: | Enabled event-only mouse input, before or after the first event | `YES` |

requirements.heading: $MSTAT$
requirements.text: | Headless or keyboard-only session with mouse input unavailable or disabled | `NO` |

requirements.heading: $MSTAT$
requirements.text: The result is independent of pointer visibility, position, transient focus, button state and mouse fields. The local playback [`?` substitution](5.3-local-playback.md#shared-filename-contract) reads a separate tracked press bit. [Original callback and portable choice](../research/issue-211-mstat-presence.md)

requirements.heading: $XY$
requirements.text: All position forms use the [shared capture and initial-point rule](#mouse-coordinate-capture). Outside a text-window query, omission means WORLD. WORLD converts the captured device coordinates using the current world/device dimensions, with integer truncation; DEVICE returns the captured device coordinates directly. Both return zero-padded **decimal** `XXXX:YYYY` using signed 16-bit values and a minimum width of four, independently of Base Math. With captured position (297,321), DEVICE returns `0297:0321`; with world/device ratios of 2, WORLD returns `0594:0642`.

requirements.heading: $XY$
requirements.text: Inside a text-window query, omission instead returns cell coordinates for the query’s text window as decimal `XX:YY`, minimum width two. The original cell helpers clamp positions to the window’s bounds. Explicit WORLD or DEVICE overrides this cell-coordinate default. For (297,321) in an 80×25 window with 8×16 cells at origin, bare XY returns `37:20`. The format widths are minimum padding, not universal 99/9999 limits. Other domains or extra arguments reject.
requirements.reason: The reusable XY formatter clamps default text-window queries to the cell grid. Explicit domains bypass this conversion.

requirements.heading: $TEXTXY$
requirements.text: _Return a drawing port’s current graphics-text cursor_
requirements.reason: TEXTXY label/provenance; executable grammar, conversion, narrowing and omission/explicit selection are reviewed individually.

requirements.heading: $TEXTXY$
requirements.text: **Format:** `$TEXTXY([port[,domain]])$`
requirements.reason: TEXTXY accepts optional decimal port/CUR then WORLD/DEVICE, with case-insensitive keywords. WORLD reads stored cursor coordinates; DEVICE applies the current frame conversion again with integer truncation. Both components narrow explicitly to signed16 and emit unpadded X:Y. Explicit undefined/inactive ports return -1; bare omission reads the current cursor despite deactivation. Independent negative/wrap/domain/grammar/capacity/error cases and the exact 800x600/1280x960 MOVE/TEXT example verify results without deriving expectations from the emulator.

requirements.heading: $TEXTXY$
requirements.text: Port is CUR or decimal 0..35, default current; domain is WORLD or DEVICE, default WORLD. A domain requires the port argument first: use `$TEXTXY(CUR,DEVICE)$`. Other selectors/domains or more than two arguments reject.
requirements.reason: TEXTXY accepts optional decimal port/CUR then WORLD/DEVICE, with case-insensitive keywords. WORLD reads stored cursor coordinates; DEVICE applies the current frame conversion again with integer truncation. Both components narrow explicitly to signed16 and emit unpadded X:Y. Explicit undefined/inactive ports return -1; bare omission reads the current cursor despite deactivation. Independent negative/wrap/domain/grammar/capacity/error cases and the exact 800x600/1280x960 MOVE/TEXT example verify results without deriving expectations from the emulator.

requirements.heading: $TEXTXY$
requirements.text: WORLD returns the raw stored per-port cursor; DEVICE converts it using the current global world/device dimensions with integer truncation. These domain names do not guarantee the stored units: RIPtel 3.1’s MOVE and outline text paths store converted device positions, while classic TEXT_XY stores a different mixed-unit result. See the [original cursor-update rules](3.0-text-output-and-fonts.md#rip_text_xy). DEVICE can therefore apply another conversion to a pair already converted by its producer. The result is **unpadded signed decimal** `X:Y`, narrowed to signed 16-bit values. Stored (297,321) returns `297:321`; under world/device ratios of 2, DEVICE returns `148:160`.

requirements.heading: $TEXTXY$
requirements.text: With an explicit port argument, an undefined port or deactivated viewport returns the sentinel `-1`. **Omission differs from explicit CUR:** bare `$TEXTXY$` bypasses that definition/viewport check and reads the current cursor even with a deactivated viewport. It is a current cursor query, not an immutable log of the last rendered string.

requirements.heading: $TEXTXY$
requirements.text: TEXTXY reads the current cursor after command updates. Nonempty TEXT advances X by its integer string width and retains Y, irrespective of justification/orientation. A later MOVE replaces the query result without text output. Empty TEXT leaves it unchanged silently; empty TEXT_XY leaves it unchanged with an error. Fractional classic CHR raster advances do not produce fractional TEXTXY values: the original metric sums raw glyph widths, scales the entire string and truncates toward zero; two 6.25-pixel advances give integer width 12, while separate one-character TEXT calls each advance 6.
requirements.reason: TEXTXY reads the active port cursor after MOVE or text.

requirements.heading: $TEXTXY$
requirements.text: **Measured example:** world 1280×960, device 800×600, viewport origin(5,7), classic font 1 with controlled A/B advances 6.25 each. MOVE(10,20) stores(11,19); TEXT("AB") stores(23,19). WORLD/default returns **`23:19`**, DEVICE returns **`14:11`** (another conversion of the stored pair, without removing the origin). Later MOVE(30,40) makes default TEXTXY **`23:32`**. A literal `m(10,20);T("AB")` result therefore depends on active font metrics and conversion/origin state. Under unit mapping/origin 0 it is X=10+integer string width, Y=20. These values come from original cursor/metric instructions and callback checks with controlled glyph drawing; [exact fixture, bytes and derivation](../research/issue-6-macro-evaluation.md#integration-review-exact-textxy-cursor-and-fractional-metrics).

requirements.text: The WINNO parameter specifies a text window data table entry to move the cursor in. Valid settings for WINNO are 0-35 for a specific text window data table entry, or "CUR" to indicate the current text window. If the specified window is not the current text window then the cursor in that window's definition is moved but no visible things occur on the screen. If the specified window is "CUR" or the window number happens to be the current text window, then the cursor that is (potentially) on the screen is moved to the new location.

requirements.heading: $TWGOTO$
requirements.text: The X/Y coordinates are zero-based text-cell coordinates; the inherited “1 based” sentence was wrong. Specifying both coordinates allows you to place the cursor anywhere in the chosen window. You may omit the Y parameter entirely to move the cursor horizontally only. Either the X or Y parameter (or both) may be specified as "CUR" to indicate the row or column is not to change. In other words, if you wanted to move the cursor to row index 2 (the third line) in text window 5, but leave its column unchanged, you would use `$TWGOTO(5,CUR,2)$`.

A window-relative `(0,0)` always means its upper-left cell; ANSI origin mode and scrolling margins do not offset or restrict this operation. It does not scroll, change margins/origin mode or alter the saved cursor. TW definition protection and graphics PORT/viewport state do not prohibit the movement.
