requirements.heading: Creation, Redraw and Prompt Continuations
requirements.text:
1. Run the adopted pure `1U` preflight before providers or painting. Freeze the field's style/font attributes, creation WORLD, geometric inputs and effective destination identity/generation before filename expansion. Completed setters can change live tables/environment for later providers/commands, but cannot retroactively reflow this pending field. This does not freeze user values, image contents or future lookup results.
2. Expand the common filename slot once, then prepare/resolve it and choose/load an image under the existing normal/hot/fallback rules. Finish natural image geometry from that initially chosen image. Non-ICON types still prepare a nonempty first slot without turning it into an icon face. A filename-stage hard failure precedes new face/effect painting.
3. Render face/effects, and perform requested auto-stamp capture and its existing clipboard/current-style mutation. Expand and render the label afterward; a requested capture must succeed first. Thus a label prompt can occur with the face already painted, the clipboard changed and auto-stamp flags already written. It is not part of pure preflight.
4. Store the original filename/label **sources**, not just a globally cached expansion. Repeat a nonempty filename's common preparation and a nonempty label's expansion whenever their renderer stages actually run on creation or redraw, using then-current variables, while retaining the instance's captured geometry/font/style/destination. An auto-stamped field follows its now-CLIPBOARD type; re-expanding an old filename does not force an icon load or a fresh auto-capture. A redraw taking an earlier restore/skip path need not evaluate later stages it never reaches.

PR129 F/H/C geometry, exact COPY crop/padding, same-destination guard and provider-free feedback undo have independent native and connected vectors. Suspended admission rechecks scene/destination/capacity; committed activation owns its source and runs once after feedback. Failures are consumed below void parser/session processing.

requirements.heading: Creation, Redraw and Prompt Continuations
requirements.text: A permitted user prompt suspends that specific continuation without holding renderer/table locks. Keep owned source/working bytes, scan offset, captured drawing state and stable instance/destination generations. Resume once at the suspended lookup after success or the [documented cancellation](5.1-text-variables.md#empty-input-cancellation-and-no-output): ordinary cancellation supplies `NONE`, transparent cancellation supplies no text, neither writes storage; successful empty and `*` rules remain adopted. These are normal lookup outcomes, **not** an automatic cancellation of creation or a held gesture. A separate hard abort stops rendering. Never restart prior stages/providers or repeat auto-stamp merely because a prompt completed.
requirements.reason: Native staged button tests check port generations across a suspended filename or label and a captured clipboard generation after resumption. Connected modal, cancellation and hard-failure cases exercise actual fields.

requirements.heading: Creation, Redraw and Prompt Continuations
requirements.text: Serialize subsequent interpreter/input dispatch behind the suspended continuation; retain physical release/cancel information against the original capture token and process it in order before a later activation. Reset/deletion/destination replacement invalidates suspended drawing immediately. The [auto-stamp same-destination guard](4.3-buttons.md#auto-stamp-geometry-and-redraw) prevents replacing the destination during capture; a legacy helper's PORT0 fallback does not authorize rebinding a label continuation. On resume, abandon a stale instance/destination without painting, restoring old feedback onto a replacement or admitting a pending field into a new scene. A held redraw that survives resumes the same gesture; its later inside/outside release decides commitment under the existing pointer rules. An already committed keyboard/release action retains its snapshot and once-only host continuation even if optional feedback fails or its field disappears. Prompt completion never synthesizes a click/repeat, transfers capture or forwards a consumed key.

requirements.heading: Creation, Redraw and Prompt Continuations
requirements.text: A pending new field becomes input-eligible only after successful creation rendering. Later provider/font/file/capture failures admit no new field, but do **not** undo completed user-variable effects, painted pixels, palette/file effects, clipboard capture or style writes. For existing fields, redraw failure does not delete their definition or roll back already committed selection/action state; remove temporary feedback safely only from the surviving original instance. Preserve live setter effects when restoring private drawing context. T/@ hard expansion failure draws none of that argument; metric hard expansion failure sends no metric reply. Already completed providers/retained TEXTDATA assignments are not rolled back by a later font/metric failure; the metric entry's cached-font/result rules still apply. None of this executes the third host slot as a rendering test. Rendering itself creates no FIELDID activation scope; existing outer callback scopes remain in force. Recheck field capacity and destination/scene generation before admitting a suspended creation; failure cannot evict an earlier field to make room.
requirements.reason: PR134 is connected to live sessions: stable-instance checkbox/radio state commits before optional redraw and clicked source, with opaque creation and selected-radio exclusivity. Each surviving owner retains post-angle ordinary-unexpanded A[N]; current group publications assemble selected owners in creation order with a 4096-byte prefix and ordinary-baseline/last-publisher precedence. Required radio selection depends on actual membership, independently of slot bytes. Native failure/suspension and independent CP437/UTF-8 TCP vectors cover OFF-source execution, duplicate IDs, stale writes, cross-slot publication, SOFT effective-byte preservation, no provider calls during composition, and recovery without disconnecting. requirements.heading: Definitions, Composition and Side Effects
requirements.text: Angle preprocessing occurs **when the host-command string containing a definition is processed**, before the definition block is stored. requirements.heading: Radio Buttons and Check-Box Templates
requirements.text: Let's take a couple simple examples step-by-step to see how templates are maintained internally.

requirements.heading: Radio Buttons and Check-Box Templates
requirements.text: **EXAMPLE 1 - RADIO BUTTON TEMPLATES**

requirements.heading: Radio Buttons and Check-Box Templates
requirements.text: Let's say you have four buttons in Button Group #3, and that button group is defined as a Radio Button group. Here are the host command definitions for each of those buttons in this example:

requirements.heading: Radio Buttons and Check-Box Templates
requirements.text:
```text
Button #1:   [3:]ABCD
Button #2:   [3:]EFGH
Button #3:   [3:]IJKL
Button #4:   [3:]MNOP
```

requirements.heading: Radio Buttons and Check-Box Templates
requirements.text: Now, if none of the buttons are clicked, then template group #3 is blank. If button #1 is clicked, the template for group #3 would be defined as "ABCD". Now, if button #4 is clicked, what would the template definition for group #3 be? That's right, "MNOP". Notice how only one of the given templates is active at any given moment.

requirements.heading: Radio Buttons and Check-Box Templates
requirements.text: **EXAMPLE 2 - CHECK BOX TEMPLATES**

requirements.heading: Radio Buttons and Check-Box Templates
requirements.text: Now let's explore the slightly more complex world of check box templates. As stated previously, check box templates can be strung along together to make a larger template - template construction of sorts. Let's say you have a Button Group #2 defined as a check box group with 7 buttons defined in it. Each of the buttons are initially drawn as "unselected", or unclicked (inactive). Here are the button host command definitions for each of the 7 buttons:

requirements.heading: Radio Buttons and Check-Box Templates

```text
Button #1:   [2:]Apples^m
Button #2:   [2:]Oranges^m
Button #3:   [2:]Cherries^m
Button #4:   [2:]Grapes^m
Button #5:   [2:]Pears^m
Button #6:   [2:]Banannas^m
Button #7:   [2:]Lemons^m
```

requirements.heading: Radio Buttons and Check-Box Templates
requirements.text: Now, if all 7 buttons are not clicked, then template group #2 would be blank. Let's click on some buttons and see what the template will become as we change which buttons are clicked and which aren't:

requirements.heading: Radio Buttons and Check-Box Templates
requirements.text:
```text
Button #3 clicked (ON) .... Template:  Cherries^m
Button #5 clicked (ON) .... Template:  Cherries^mPears^m
Button #3 clicked (OFF) ... Template:  Pears^m
Button #5 clicked (OFF) ... Template:  <blank>
Button #2 clicked (ON) .... Template:  Oranges^m
Button #1 clicked (ON) .... Template:  Apples^mOranges^m

A pure rebuild changes **only slots still published by that group**, so it cannot overwrite a later ordinary assignment or another group's claim. While G lives, an empty aggregate publishes empty. When its last member disappears, release its publications to B[N] (or undefined/empty if no baseline); do not resurrect an older superseded group publisher. requirements.heading: Embedded Templates - `$?N$`
requirements.text: There are two ways of using templates: Template Embedding and Template Chaining. Template embedding is a way of "inserting" a template inside another host command - you can insert the contents of an active template inside of a button's Direct Host Command. The direct host command is "expanded" around the inserted template and the contents of the specified template are made part of the direct host command.

requirements.text: Template Chaining is the second form of using templates. Rather than inserting the contents of a template into a host command, like in embedding, template chaining feeds data into a template and then takes the result and transmits that to the BBS. In other words, Template Embedding inserts a template into a Host Command. In Template Chaining, a Host Command is inserted into a template (the exact opposite).

requirements.heading: Template Chaining - `[ABC]`
requirements.text: What's the difference? In the case of the `[5:]`, a template for group #5 is defined. In the `[5]` example, the template chaining instruction is invoked on Template #5. The phrase "This is template chaining" will be fed into template number 5. If template number 5 has a generic insertion code `$?$` in it, then it will be replaced with the phrase "This is template chaining". The final result after the replacement will be a direct host command that will be transmitted to the BBS. Since template #5 doesn't have an insertion code, the phrase "This is template chaining" will be lost in the chaining process and the final host command would be "This is template definition".

requirements.text: This last phrase is then sent to the BBS verbatim. requirements.heading: Comparison Semantics
requirements.text: The left operand is a variable reference (with or without surrounding dollar delimiters) or a `?N` template reference. The right operand is literal text, optionally double-quoted. Quoted text preserves its spaces; unquoted text ends at its first unescaped whitespace or closing group parenthesis, and decoded trailing whitespace is trimmed. The [operand byte grammar](#conditional-operand-byte-grammar) defines the separate lexical stages, escapes and bounded limits. Dollar codes inside the literal or returned operand values are not recursively evaluated by the comparison. A quoted literal on the left, such as `<<IF "2"<"10">>`, is rejected; use a variable with value `2` to ask that comparison.
requirements.reason: The private conditional source parser validates complete >>-terminated structure without allocation/providers, then owns decoded typed operands in one prepared allocation. It implements ASCII ALPHA/WS, one-digit templates, bare/dollar left scanning, independent local escapes, exact $&L$ provider synthesis/whole-reference validation, right quote/terminator/trim order, ASCII-space-suffixed connectors and 255-byte pre-trim bounds. The provider bridge passes template indexes directly, preserves ordinary reference case/bytes, rejects malformed providers without invoking unintended prefixes, bounds results and feeds the existing non-short-circuit typed reducer. Independent native published examples, exhaustive 256-byte initial/quoted-payload classes, long escaped byte limits, whitespace/quote boundaries, no-rescan values, provider failure/empty/oversized cases, ordering/lifetime, 128-level nesting, owned source, allocator failure and subsequent recovery pass. Full IF/ELSEIF/ELSE/ENDIF preprocessing, real host/user/template provider bindings, UI and application routing remain pending; helper statuses are private below the required void processing boundary. The owned continuation also pauses at each validated provider request, consumes borrowed answers before returning, retains completed leaves without replay, and resumes/reduces without allocation. Native budget/wait, independent-ownership, failed/oversized/empty values, pending destruction and resource-recovery cases pass; synchronous program evaluation uses this same continuation. This does not claim the pending outer branch or application integration.

requirements.heading: Comparison Semantics
requirements.text: Operators are `=`, `!=`, `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=`. If **both** values consist of decimal digits, with an optional leading minus and at least one digit, compare signed integers after the driver’s wrapping 32-bit decimal conversion. Otherwise use case-insensitive byte-string comparison. A leading plus, empty string or embedded/trailing whitespace does not satisfy that numeric predicate. Equality also uses numeric comparison when both values qualify; quotes on the right do not force lexical comparison.
requirements.reason: The connected host and graphical tests distinguish CP437 wire collation from raw UTF-8 byte collation with the same two characters. Native comparisons cover numeric wrap, ASCII fold and lexical boundaries.

requirements.heading: Comparison Semantics
requirements.text: The reducer repeatedly scans adjacent Boolean/operator/Boolean triples from left to right, then NOT/Boolean pairs, then parenthesized single Boolean values, until one result remains. NOT therefore does not have conventional precedence over an eligible binary reduction. requirements.heading: Comparison Semantics
requirements.text: IF/ELSEIF/ELSE/ENDIF structure is validated, including nested inactive IF syntax; missing ENDIF rejects preprocessing. requirements.heading: Conditional Operand Byte Grammar
requirements.text: Use byte strings, with NUL as end of input. **Portable classification choice:** `WS` is exactly ASCII HT, LF, VT, FF, CR and space (`0x09..0x0d`, `0x20`); `ALPHA` is ASCII `A..Z`, `a..z`. This fixes locale-dependent classification without promising a Unicode identifier or rejecting all control/high bytes as the separate dollar-argument lexer does.

requirements.heading: Right Literal Scanning
requirements.text:
1. NUL ends scanning; an open quote is an error. The enclosing expression still requires a real terminator or connector.
2. In unquoted mode, unescaped `WS` or `)` ends the literal without consuming that separator.
3. Backslash quotes the following non-NUL byte: consume the backslash and append the next byte. **Special pair:** when the next two bytes are `>>`, consume and append both together. Neither closes the condition. Reject a dangling backslash before reading/appending beyond the input.
4. Otherwise unescaped `>>` ends scanning **even inside double quotes**. With a quote still open, this is a missing-quote error; it does not silently end a valid quoted literal.
5. Otherwise a double quote closes a quoted literal and is consumed. In unquoted mode, a quote after the first byte is ordinary payload; it does not enter quoted mode.
6. Append any other non-NUL byte unchanged and continue.

requirements.heading: 5.3 Local File Playback
requirements.text: Local playback directives instruct the terminal to process a file _already on the user's disk_ instead of pulling content over the modem - the client/server heart of the [Host Command Language](5.0-host-commands.md), which the White Paper singles out as the way "to simulate menus on an online service locally, thus making it so that you don't have to transmit hardly anything over the modem." They are prefix [text variables](5.1-text-variables.md), usable from within any host command or query.

requirements.heading: 5.3 Local File Playback
requirements.text: _Evidence: WP; 2.00a4; HLP._

requirements.heading: 5.3 Local File Playback
requirements.text: All four playback forms share one shape: `$`, a one-character prefix, the filename, `$`. RIPtel searches for the named file in the current host's [connection directory](../../glossary.md) first, then in `ICONS\`, then along the user-configured Search Path (which allowed CD-ROM-resident resources for games) - the [file override](../../glossary.md) lookup order detailed in [6.2 Asset Delivery & Storage](6.2-asset-delivery-and-storage.md#lookup-order-file-override). _Evidence: HLP._
requirements.reason: The playback scanner bounds and transforms the filename before media dispatch. Connected fixtures exercise quoting, state substitutions, nested scenes, image style and the writable-host/shared lookup policy. Background waveform semantics are covered by the native service.
requirements.scope: Lookup in the per-BBS cache followed by the shared read-only directory. Additional configurable search paths are outside the storage policy.

requirements.heading: Dollar Quoting, Bound and Recovery
requirements.text: A filename terminator is a dollar **not immediately preceded by backslash**. At a dollar, a preceding stored backslash is overwritten by that dollar and parsing continues: `\$` contributes **one literal dollar**. This is an immediate-previous-byte rule, not odd/even slash-pair quoting. Two backslashes before a dollar leave one backslash plus the quoted dollar. Other non-NUL filename bytes, including commas, parentheses, quotes and control notation, are copied as name data rather than recursively parsed as HCL arguments/lists/controls. Other backslashes remain literal; there is no general filename quote decoder. Wire framing and outer HCL quoting remain separate stages.
requirements.reason: Bounded ordinary token and shared name preparation with independent native request vectors. The connected JPEG fixture observes filename resolution and capture scope. Scene and BMP presentation remain separate.

requirements.heading: Dollar Quoting, Bound and Recovery
requirements.text: The limit is **20 decoded working-name bytes before state substitution/default extension**, excluding prefix, delimiters and NUL. Twenty are accepted; a 21st ordinary byte rejects the reference without truncated playback. A quoted dollar can finish byte 20 despite occupying two source bytes. Twenty stars can expand to **100 decimal bytes**, then 104 with a default extension; the 20-byte check is not reapplied. Use safe owned storage, without requiring the native buffer layout.

requirements.text: Let N20 be twenty ASCII A bytes, N21 twenty-one. The enclosing HCL response continues after playback, including any suffix. See the [shared file boundaries and reply examples](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#file-boundaries-and-nested-scenes).

requirements.heading: Local Audio Playback - `$)FILE.WAV$`
requirements.text:
- Audio plays **in the background, asynchronously** - graphics keep drawing and host data keeps arriving while sound plays.
- There is a **single playback channel**: starting a new file terminates whatever is currently playing.
- The wire `1w` filename `$OFF$` silences the current sound. The escaped WAV macro name follows [ordinary filename lookup](#extensions-lookup-and-wav-stop), so use `$RESET(SOUND)$` to stop from HCL.

requirements.heading: Local Bitmap Playback - `$<FILE.BMP$`
requirements.text: `$<FILENAME.BMP$` displays a supported local BMP on the **current screen or offscreen drawing port**, using that port's stored [image-style rectangle](4.1-jpeg-images.md#rip_image_style), or its current viewport if the rectangle is at the default marker. It requests **COPY, current palette, auto-dithering and no transparent-color key**. It has no wire-loader duplication, palette-adoption, put-mode or wallpaper options. The [shared filename contract](#shared-filename-contract) still supplies aliases, substitutions, bounds, lookup and token consumption.
requirements.reason: Live bitmap playback uses the original target in device coordinates, bounded port clipping and the existing indexed COPY/dither renderer. Independent connected vectors cover both encodings.

requirements.heading: Bitmap Target and Clipping
requirements.text: Image-style setters normalize WORLD corners, convert them to DEVICE coordinates and store the far coordinates **plus one**, as already specified for `1i`/IMGSTYLE. Bitmap playback consumes that stored DEVICE rectangle **directly**, with half-open right/bottom edges: `I=[L,R)×[T,B)` has width `R-L` and height `B-T`. Do not decrement its far edges, add another pixel, perform WORLD conversion again or add the current port/viewport origin. Screen rectangles address the shared screen; bitmap rectangles address their own local surface.
requirements.reason: Live bitmap playback uses the original target in device coordinates, bounded port clipping and the existing indexed COPY/dither renderer. Independent connected vectors cover both encodings.

requirements.heading: Bitmap Target and Clipping
requirements.text: If the stored rectangle is the **all-minus-one default marker**, take the current viewport rectangle at playback time, including its current origin/far edges. Stretch the entire bitmap to that target width/height. A later viewport edit changes this fallback target; it does not change an explicitly stored image rectangle. WORLD changes after the style was set do not rescale its stored DEVICE coordinates.
requirements.reason: Live bitmap playback uses the original target in device coordinates, bounded port clipping and the existing indexed COPY/dither renderer. Independent connected vectors cover both encodings.

requirements.heading: Bitmap Target and Clipping
requirements.text: For example, at WORLD=DEVICE, style corners `(2,2)..(5,5)` store `[2,6)×[2,6)` and produce a **4×4** bitmap target. The all-zero style command stores **`[0,1)×[0,1)`** and produces a **1×1** target, subject to clipping; it does not disable bitmap playback or invoke the JPEG wrapper's separate far-edge adjustments/size fallback. The internal **raw-zero** record is a suppression sentinel, distinct from the all-zero command; do not use it as the default viewport marker. The original wrapper also suppresses a raw stored zero right or bottom edge before lookup; ordinary valid style setters store far positions at least one.
requirements.reason: Live bitmap playback uses the original target in device coordinates, bounded port clipping and the existing indexed COPY/dither renderer. Independent connected vectors cover both encodings.

requirements.heading: Bitmap Target and Clipping
requirements.text: An inactive current viewport skips image lookup, decoding and painting. Protection of an existing active port does not block content drawing; the style setter's own protection rules remain separate. No fallback selection or creation of another port occurs.
requirements.reason: Live bitmap playback uses the original target in device coordinates, bounded port clipping and the existing indexed COPY/dither renderer. Independent connected vectors cover both encodings.

requirements.heading: Bitmap Target and Clipping
requirements.text: **Explicit portable clipping completion:** form the full target first, then paint only its intersection with the current viewport, current port bounds and physical backing surface. Preserve the full source-to-target map; clipping does not refit the image to the remaining visible rectangle or restart its sampling/dither phase. A nonpositive target extent or empty intersection writes no pixels. No pixel outside that intersection changes on successful presentation. This defines both screen and offscreen ports without exposing inherited backend clip history.
requirements.reason: Live bitmap playback uses the original target in device coordinates, bounded port clipping and the existing indexed COPY/dither renderer. Independent connected vectors cover both encodings.

requirements.heading: Which Image-Style Flags Apply
requirements.text: **The bitmap macro uses the image rectangle, but none of the six stored image-style flag bits.** The full original bitmap wrapper does not read those flags; its successful path calls the ordinary BMP renderer with fixed arguments and returns without JPEG preparation or the wallpaper helper. requirements.heading: Palette and Dither Boundary
requirements.text: The **destination's current graphics palette**, selected when the macro executes, remains owned by the interpreter. An indexed file's color table supplies **source RGB colors**, not destination palette indices: file index 0 is not automatically destination index 0, black or transparent. True-color input supplies its decoded RGB directly. Neither input kind changes palette entries, current palette selection or the colors of existing pixels outside the target.

requirements.heading: Palette and Dither Boundary
requirements.text: **Explicit portable color completion:** on a destination requiring indexed/reduced-color output, approximate the scaled source colors with the currently available destination colors and enable automatic dithering where approximation needs it. Colors exactly representable in that destination remain exact; dithering must not damage a uniform exact palette color. A true-color destination may use the decoded colors directly at its supported precision, without importing a file palette or forcing a needless indexed conversion. This preserves the documented current-palette/auto-dither intent, without requiring a particular Windows palette realization, quantizer, stretch filter, threshold matrix or error-diffusion algorithm.

requirements.heading: Palette and Dither Boundary
requirements.text: Choose sampling/quantization/dither behavior consistently for a given renderer and image request. **Explicit phase completion:** use coordinates relative to the **full unclipped target origin `(L,T)`**, and preserve any dither history as if the complete target were rendered before masking writes to the clip. With identical source, target, palette and renderer settings, a clipped draw must equal cropping that full result. A clipped left/top edge does not become a new dither origin or restart an error-diffusion row. Implementations need not allocate an actual full-size intermediate image. This image-local dither rule is separate from the screen/bitmap-origin [vector fill-mask phase](2.3-shapes-and-fills.md#fill-pattern-origin-and-scaling).

requirements.heading: 5.4 Pop-Up Lists
requirements.text: Pop-up pick lists offer choices while building an eligible [HCL response](5.0-host-commands.md). Selecting an entry splices its **original response bytes** into the working response; canceling an optional list inserts empty. A list is recognized only when that consumer enables pick lists. Permission to use ordinary text variables in another filename/label/metric consumer does not independently enable modal lists there. Pixel-exact dialog styling, font rasterization and OS widgets are outside this profile.
requirements.reason: The ordinary query waits for the modal result, inserts the raw selected span, and resumes its existing two-pass scheduler. Tests cover withheld output, nested refresh, later-pass directives and final raw selections.

requirements.heading: Syntax and Source Spans
requirements.text: All scanners work on bytes. Backslash quotes the next byte for delimiter recognition; double/single quotes have no delimiter-protection role. Thus `A\,B` is one response, `A\@B` contains a literal response @, and `A\)\)` does not terminate the list. Escape at least one colon to keep `::` inside data instead of making it the prompt separator. These list-level quoting pairs are distinct from [wire framing](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md) and the later HCL backslash pass; each layer receives the bytes left by its caller.
requirements.reason: Native vectors exercise the modal grammar, display text and raw spans. The connected adapter provides keyboard, hotkey and mouse selection with required and optional cancellation behavior.

requirements.heading: Syntax and Source Spans
requirements.text: No unescaped nested list is parsed as a balanced child. An unescaped `((` inside a response is ordinary list data to this close finder; the first eligible `))` still closes the outer list. Do not add nesting depth 64 or a fresh recursive interpreter call from the legacy SyncTERM implementation.
requirements.reason: Native vectors exercise the modal grammar, display text and raw spans. The connected adapter provides keyboard, hotkey and mouse selection with required and optional cancellation behavior.

requirements.heading: Prompt, Entries and Display
requirements.text: The original stock prompt for **absent** `Question::` is **`Please enter requested value`**. An explicitly blank prompt, `((::A,B))`, is **empty**, not the default. This corrects the inherited `Choose one of the following:` wording for this identified client. For an explicit prompt, retain its first **60 raw bytes**, then remove backslash quoting pairs; do not evaluate dollar/template/control codes in display text.
requirements.reason: Native vectors exercise the modal grammar, display text and raw spans. The connected adapter provides keyboard, hotkey and mouse selection with required and optional cancellation behavior.

requirements.heading: Prompt, Entries and Display
requirements.text: Entries retain their order. A leading comma or consecutive commas creates an empty entry with an empty response/label. A trailing comma creates **no additional final empty entry**. An empty response with a description, as in `@Nothing`, is selectable and returns empty. Spaces are data. A second unescaped @ in a description makes the closed list malformed; quote a description @ when it is literal.
requirements.reason: Native vectors exercise the modal grammar, display text and raw spans. The connected adapter provides keyboard, hotkey and mouse selection with required and optional cancellation behavior.

requirements.heading: Prompt, Entries and Display
requirements.text: Display text is separate from response text: normalize `_` to `~`, remove backslash quoting pairs, and interpret the first marked character as a hotkey. Remaining markers affect highlighting only; an unmatched marker highlights the remainder under the inherited markup rule. These operations execute no HCL providers. Markers are not escapable as literal hotkey punctuation merely by preceding them with a backslash: display normalization still gives them markup meaning. Put markup in a description when it must not be transmitted. For `Sysop@_S_ysop`, selecting returns `Sysop`; without @, selecting `_S_ysop` returns those original underscore bytes.
requirements.reason: Native vectors exercise the modal grammar, display text and raw spans. The connected adapter provides keyboard, hotkey and mouse selection with required and optional cancellation behavior.

requirements.heading: Prompt, Entries and Display
requirements.text: **Explicit safe display bound:** use at most the first **60 raw bytes of each chosen display-label source** before normalization/dequoting. The original allocator caps its allocation calculation at 60 while its subsequent copy is not a bounded long-label contract. This profile truncates safely without executing or requiring that path. The full original response span remains independently available for selection; a long response without @ can have a short displayed label and a longer returned value. A dangling backslash left at a display truncation boundary contributes no quoted next byte and is omitted from display; do not read beyond the retained span.
requirements.reason: Native vectors exercise the modal grammar, display text and raw spans. The connected adapter provides keyboard, hotkey and mouse selection with required and optional cancellation behavior.

requirements.heading: Prompt, Entries and Display
requirements.text: `*` is special **only immediately after the opener**, before position/question parsing. It prevents optional cancel/ESC; it does not select an entry automatically. In `((Q::*A,B))`, the first response is literally `*A`: choosing B still returns B, choosing the first returns `*A`, and a dialog is required. To express a first response beginning with `*` without accidentally requiring selection, use an explicit prompt separator or quote that response byte. Whitespace before `*` makes it data, not the required marker.

requirements.heading: Ordinary Passes and Transmission
requirements.text: The ordinary HCL response runs **two ordinary passes**, after its existing angle preprocessing/block preparation. requirements.heading: Position Prefix and Placement
requirements.text: The immediate prefix after optional `*` is recognized only as ASCII decimal digit runs and punctuation: **`digits,digits:`**, **`digits,:`**, **`,digits:`** or **`,:`**. Leading zeros are decimal. There is no Base Math/UltraNum decoding, sign, whitespace, fraction or exponent form. If no complete recognized prefix exists, leave those bytes in the question/choices and center both axes; a stray numeric-looking prefix is not silently discarded. Parse the question separator after any accepted position prefix.
requirements.reason: The positioned modal takes the active WORLD/DEVICE frame, centers omitted or zero-WORLD axes, and clamps the measured rectangle independently. Native parsing and live raster captures verify decimal prefixes and placement.

requirements.heading: Position Prefix and Placement
requirements.text: **Explicit bounded portable placement:** accept each supplied decimal value in **0..65535** using checked/wide arithmetic. An out-of-range digit run makes the whole position prefix unrecognized; do not wrap, consume a prefix of the number or partially apply one axis. For each present axis use its corresponding active WORLD and physical DEVICE extent, truncating the nonnegative ratio `value * DEVICE_extent / WORLD_extent` toward zero. An omitted axis, or one with zero WORLD extent, centers independently. Do not add the current PORT/viewport/TW origin or clip the modal list to its viewport.
requirements.reason: The positioned modal takes the active WORLD/DEVICE frame, centers omitted or zero-WORLD axes, and clamps the measured rectangle independently. Native parsing and live raster captures verify decimal prefixes and placement.

requirements.heading: Position Prefix and Placement
requirements.text: Place the modal rectangle on the available client surface: a supplied axis is an offset from that surface's origin, an omitted axis centers the measured dialog on it. Clamp/fix the final rectangle to that surface after measurement; for surface extent C and dialog extent D, fit an offset into `[0,max(C-D,0)]`. Centering uses `max(floor((C-D)/2),0)`. Oversized dialogs pin at the origin and must keep choices accessible by scrolling or an equivalent mechanism. Exact chrome, size measurements, hotkey glyphs and OS/window-manager screen positioning remain implementation-defined.
requirements.reason: The positioned modal takes the active WORLD/DEVICE frame, centers omitted or zero-WORLD axes, and clamps the measured rectangle independently. Native parsing and live raster captures verify decimal prefixes and placement.

requirements.heading: Position Prefix and Placement
requirements.text: The original numeric helpers narrow to signed words (and a signed byte in the Y-only path), use the X-conversion argument for both supplied axes and include host-specific far-edge adjustments. Those static facts and their exact limits are [recorded separately](../research/issue-159-pick-list-contract.md#static-parsing-and-pass-ledger). The canonical rule above is the explicit consistent world-position intent; it does not require those asymmetric narrowing/scaling paths or claim native pixel equality.

requirements.heading: 5.5 File Transfer & Queries
requirements.text: **None of the level-3/level-9 commands on this page appears anywhere in the RIPtel demo corpus**: the demos are local scene files whose resources (bitmaps, JPEGs, fonts) already sit on disk, so nothing ever needs transferring or rate-limiting. All are nonetheless attested for 3.x - each is named in the RIPSCRIP.HLP inventory (one under a new name, noted below), and SyncTERM implements the block-mode transfer with a full protocol table. The query commands, by contrast, are the most heavily used commands in the corpus. _Evidence: HLP; corpus; SyncTERM._

requirements.heading: 5.5 File Transfer & Queries
requirements.text: Capability negotiation in brief: query [`$IFS(keyword)$`](5.1-text-variables.md#ifs) (Is Feature Supported) for a `1`/`0` answer on any feature - protocols (`$IFS(ZMODEM)$`), image formats (`$IFS(JPEG)$`), audio (`$IFS(WAV)$`), emulations, languages - or use its `LIST` directive to enumerate whole categories; query [`$TERMINFO(keyword)$`](5.1-text-variables.md#terminfo) for the terminal's name, vendor and version. These supersede the vendor codes of the [auto-sense response](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#ansi-sequences-auto-sensing). Full variable inventory in the [Text Variable Reference](9.1-text-variable-reference.md). _(v2.A4)_ _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._

requirements.heading: 5.5 File Transfer & Queries

The capability is nonetheless implemented - as a text variable rather than a command: `RIPSCRIP.HLP` carries the handler symbol `tvarProcFILEDEL`, whose `tvarProc` prefix marks a text-variable processor, and the literal `FILEDEL` is present in the shipping RIPterm 2.0, 2.20.01 and 2.30 executables. Use [`$FILEDEL(file,…)$`](5.1-text-variables.md#filedel) (no wildcards, no paths) - the variable form is the 3.x mechanism. requirements.heading: RIP_QUERY
requirements.text: The collector requires mode, window number and reserve in that order. Each field can use one [leading period](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#period-as-a-zero-field) for zero. A full reserve takes two valid digits in active Base Math and supplies zero to the handler. Query text begins immediately after the reserve. With literal ESC in place of `<ESC>`, `!|1<ESC>001Zhello` and `!|1<ESC>...hello` both collect `(0, 0, 0)` and `hello`. Mode 0 passes the text to immediate host-command execution. The window number only affects numbered resident queries. [Original descriptor and staged cases](../research/issue-263-resource-query-text-boundaries.md).
requirements.reason: The collector consumes the mode, window and reserve, accepting the period form for each. The query handler uses the supplied window only for numbered residents; the immediate query accepts a valid nonzero reserve.

requirements.text: This command is unique in RIPscrip in the fact that the command character that is used is NOT a printable character. The escape character (ASCII 27) introduces this command as a measure of security: since the query command can query the terminal for critical (potentially private) information, you would not want a user to be able to query another user's terminal for something like his address information. Since most hosts do not allow the user to enter an escape character, this character is ideal for this purpose - using escape allows only the host (under most circumstances) to be in control of any queries.

requirements.text: The `<mode>` parameter selects immediate execution or a stored query. **RIPtel 3.1 accepts and stores modes 1–4 but does not execute them on mouse clicks.** Its original left-down/up event paths only dispatch mouse fields; the client forwards those events directly to the driver. An overlapping numbered viewport query, numbered text-window query and both floating queries therefore execute **none** of those four expressions. This shipping omission replaces the inherited click-order claim for RIPtel 3.1; it is not evidence about earlier clients. _Evidence: original handler/event/client paths and [72,972 native query checks](../research/issue-51-deferred-query-order.md#event-path-and-native-checkpoint)._

requirements.heading: Stored Click Modes and Historical Intent
requirements.text: **No same-click mutation policy exists for modes 1–4 in RIPtel 3.1.** The event path does not scan those queries, execute an earlier one, snapshot their eligibility, or re-evaluate later regions. Disabling, deleting or moving a later region, or changing the current selection through an earlier mode 1–4 expression, cannot occur during that click because the earlier expression is never invoked. Implementors reproducing this client must preserve that omission; a client that implements the older documented click feature needs a separately specified mutation policy. Immediate-mode and mouse-field actions retain their actual [host-expression behavior](5.2-templates-and-conditionals.md); this finding does not suppress those execution paths.

requirements.heading: Definition text
requirements.text: The first colon is mandatory and must have at least one byte after it. The first comma before that colon introduces the width. A name is 1–19 ASCII bytes, starting with a letter and followed by letters, digits or underscores. Lookups are case-insensitive. These fields are parsed as supplied, without trimming or host-command evaluation.
requirements.reason: The connected parser decodes current-radix fields and the literal name, width, question and default. Native checks cover reserved digits, grammar failures, a wrapped decimal width and a 60-byte fallback.

requirements.heading: Definition text
requirements.text: If present, the width starts with a decimal digit immediately after the comma. Read the decimal digit prefix and retain its low 16 bits. Interpret that word as signed and use it if it is in 1–60. Omitted or out-of-range widths use 60. For example, `V,5tail:abcdef` and `V,65541:abcdef` both select width 5, while `V, 5:abcdef` is invalid.
requirements.reason: The connected parser decodes current-radix fields and the literal name, width, question and default. Native checks cover reserved digits, grammar failures, a wrapped decimal width and a 60-byte fallback.

requirements.heading: Definition text
requirements.text: When the definition begins with `?`, the bytes up to the next `?` are the question and the bytes after it are the default. If there is no second `?`, the remainder is the question and the supplied default is empty. Otherwise, when the definition starts with any other byte, the entire definition is the literal default. For example, `COLOR:?Pick a color` supplies a question only, `COLOR:??Blue` supplies an empty question and a default, and `COLOR:?` is valid with both fields empty. `COLOR:` is invalid. An invalid definition has no store effect.
requirements.reason: The connected parser decodes current-radix fields and the literal name, width, question and default. Native checks cover reserved digits, grammar failures, a wrapped decimal width and a 60-byte fallback.

requirements.heading: Value and editor selection
requirements.text:
1. Clip the supplied default to width minus one bytes. If that result is empty, use up to the first 60 bytes of the effective existing value, or an empty value for a new name. Look for a live record first, then the persistent record. A nonempty clipped default takes precedence over an existing value.
2. Start with the effective record's confirmation requirement, or allow silent updates for a new name. Open the editor if flag `004` is clear or the record requires confirmation. Otherwise write the selected value as it stands, including a possible empty value or a fallback longer than width minus one bytes.
3. Prefill the editor with the selected value. The original editor uses the generic caption `Please Enter Information for "<name>"` for an empty question and appends `?` to a nonempty question. Accept at most width minus one bytes. With flag `002`, require a nonempty accepted value. A space is a byte for this purpose. An accepted empty value with the flag clear is a real write.
4. The editor can offer the original **Prevent unauthorized access to this information** checkbox or an equivalent confirmation control. Initialize it from the effective record. On a successful edit, a checked control makes future `1D` updates prompt, and an unchecked control permits future silent updates. If the client omits the control, keep the incoming policy. A silent write also keeps that policy. Save the resulting policy alongside the value in the selected store. A live-only update can shadow a saved record for the session.
5. If the user cancels or the edit ends without acceptance, leave the live and persistent records, including their confirmation policies, as they were. This is the portable cancellation rule. The original handler's fallback write of an empty string after an unsuccessful edit is recorded in the derivation.

requirements.text: `1R` plays the selected local file synchronously. The caller waits while that file is the input source and resumes when playback returns. The shared file engine is also used by [HCL scene playback](5.3-local-playback.md#local-scene-playback---filerip). [RIPtel 3.1 derivation](../research/issue-170-local-scene-boundaries.md)

requirements.heading: Scene Name and Lookup
requirements.text: The full-width numeric prefix has two digits for the first ignored field and six for the final reserve, in active Base Math. Each field can use one [leading period](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#period-as-a-zero-field) for zero. The collector passes the first value through and supplies zero for the reserve. The scene handler ignores both. The filename begins immediately after the reserve. For example, `!|1R00000000Child.RIP`, `!|1R..Child.RIP` and `!|1R00.Child.RIP` all collect `Child.RIP`. A single period supplies only one field. `!|1R0000.Child.RIP` is discarded because the period is inside the six-digit field. [Original descriptor and staged cases](../research/issue-263-resource-query-text-boundaries.md).
requirements.reason: The connected command consumes the two- and six-digit fields in active Base Math. Both may be spelled with a period. The handler ignores their values and runs the scene according to the synchronous playback rules.

requirements.heading: Scene Name and Lookup
requirements.text: Supply a nonempty RIP text parameter for the wire filename. After framing, apply angle preprocessing and one ordinary expansion pass with the same feature mask as graphical text. This permits data variables, user-variable fallback and ordinary backslash quoting. The filename pass skips inserted text for the rest of that pass. The ordinary host-response pass pair, control notation, pick lists and playback filename substitutions do not apply. For example, if `SCENE` holds `child.fn`, `!|1R00000000$&SCENE$` looks up `child.fn`. A literal `child.fn` takes the same lookup path.

requirements.heading: Scene Name and Lookup
requirements.text:
1. Apply the [ASCII filename-tail predicate](#name-preparation-and-lookup) to the expanded name. An unacceptable final byte or an empty result leaves nothing to open. Otherwise retain the longest acceptable suffix. Append `.RIP` if that suffix contains no period. For example, `prefix*child` selects `child.RIP`, while `child*` is unusable. The star here has its literal byte value and does not substitute the field ID.
2. Resolve the resulting scene resource name using the configured host directory, shared `ICONS` and ordered icon search path. The supported resource names are case-insensitive. Retain an explicit extension such as `.FN` or `.TXT`. Scene lookup has no FILE_QUERY alias step or reply record. The 20 decoded byte bound and the `*?[]` replacements belong to the HCL prefix's [shared filename contract](5.3-local-playback.md#shared-filename-contract).
3. On a hit, open and play that file. A lookup miss or a failure to open the file returns to the caller without entering a child scene or generating a status reply. The client can report a local diagnostic. The resolver disables retrieval, including when invoked by wire `1R`. Globally disabled RIP graphics processing suppresses the wire command before filename evaluation.
requirements.reason: Resource lookup is limited to the active BBS RIP cache and read-only Global RIP Directory by user policy.
requirements.scope: Preserve the RIP filename and lookup behavior under the supported resource namespace. Use the per-BBS RIP cache and the shared read-only RIP directory; the cache owns all host-writable paths.

requirements.heading: File Boundaries and Nested Scenes
requirements.text: Start each file at a fresh RIP line boundary and with no partial ANSI escape from its caller. The local text reader folds CRLF to LF. A bare CR, LF or form feed still terminates an ordinary RIP command, subject to the normal [backslash continuation rules](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#chaining-continuation-and-line-endings). The byte loop skips NUL. The RIPtel 3.1 text reader also treats DOS Ctrl+Z as end of file. Any bytes routed as ordinary text use the terminal/column path, which supplies CR before LF. RIP consumes its own terminator before that text path.

requirements.heading: File Boundaries and Nested Scenes
requirements.text: EOF does not add a CR or dispatch an unfinished command. Discard any incomplete RIP command or ANSI escape from the file. Execute the remainder of the caller in its own input context. Keep completed child effects on drawing state, pixels and text. For example, a color or font left changed by the child still affects the parent's next draw.

requirements.heading: File Boundaries and Nested Scenes
requirements.text: An authored nested `1R` **must be the final command on its line, followed by CR**. A following CRLF is also suitable. The shipped ordinary parser dispatches a valid `1R` on pipe as well as on a line ending. After normal return it uses the same delimiter to select the command-opcode state for pipe or line-end state for CR. This describes the compatibility parser's ordinary case. A pipe followed by another opcode remains outside the inherited authoring rule.

requirements.heading: File Boundaries and Nested Scenes
requirements.text: The shipped nesting counter records active playback depth for cancellation and supplies no numeric recursion limit. A portable implementation may bound active scenes. If it cannot admit another scene, treat the refused invocation as a local no-action return before consuming child data. Keep the active callers and their completed effects. A refused HCL playback token still completes with an empty replacement. Authors must use finite scene chains.

requirements.heading: Scene Framing and Article Flow
requirements.text: For both wire `1R` and HCL `$>…$`, the file starts at a fresh RIP line boundary. If RIP processing is enabled at entry, feed the normalized file bytes to the ordinary [RIP framing parser](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#chaining-continuation-and-line-endings). Apply the same framing to every scene filename, including `.TXT` and `.COL`. An active article, its geometry and the bytes in the filename do not select a literal-text mode. A recognized RIP command runs with its normal effects and its command bytes stay out of the article.
requirements.reason: The connected scene reader runs RIP framing before routing ordinary text into the active article. Both 1R and the HCL playback prefix are tested with a .TXT file, an embedded color command, and independently derived DEFAULT EX glyph masks.

requirements.heading: Scene Framing and Article Flow
requirements.text: Only bytes classified as ordinary text reach the terminal text path. An eligible [active nonzero article](3.1-column-text-system.md#column-content---raw-text-lines-and-1e) receives those bytes before ordinary terminal interpretation. File playback alone leaves the article active. If RIP processing is disabled at entry and playback is otherwise permitted, the file's normalized bytes bypass RIP framing and go directly to that same text path. The separate enable gate on wire `1R` still applies.
requirements.reason: The connected scene reader runs RIP framing before routing ordinary text into the active article. Both 1R and the HCL playback prefix are tested with a .TXT file, an embedded color command, and independently derived DEFAULT EX glyph masks. Both playback entry points in SyncTERM run inside the active RIPv3 engine.

requirements.heading: Local Input and Replies
requirements.text: Scene bytes are processed locally as input. They are never forwarded verbatim as output. Commands reached during playback can still generate normal host replies. This holds for both `1R` and `$>FILE.RIP$`. For example, an immediate [RIP_QUERY](#rip_query), a valid [FILE_QUERY](#rip_file_query), or an enabled ANSI device status report uses its usual output path. An active connection is required for transmission. Client [output conversion](9.2-versions.md#engine-replies-and-terminators) is separate from file input normalization.

requirements.heading: Local Input and Replies
requirements.text: On normal return, HCL playback completes with an empty replacement. The parent response finishes its remaining expansion and sends any nonempty result as usual. A child reply produced during playback therefore precedes the parent's response. It is an independent reply and does not replace or become part of the parent's working text.

requirements.heading: Independent Playback Examples
requirements.text: The file changes draw color to 2 and sends the five bytes `CHILD`. It does not draw (2,0), since the last command has no delimiter. The caller draws (3,0) in color 2. Replacing the two child terminators with CR, LF, CRLF or form feed gives the same RIP results. Appending CR to the file instead also draws (2,0) in color 2. The shipped parser's normal pipe case `!|1R00000000CHILD|X0300\r` also dispatches the parent point after playback. The line-final CR form is the authored nested form.

For independent reply cases, use a child containing `!|1F000000PRESENT.RIP\r`, with a locally readable resource at that name, or the ANSI status request `ESC [ 5 n` (bytes `1b 5b 35 6e`). The former sends ASCII `1`. The latter sends `1b 5b 30 6e`. Neither result depends on which playback form opened the file.

requirements.heading: Name Preparation and Lookup
requirements.text: Keep two distinct names: **N**, the prepared name placed in a mode 04 reply, and **Q**, the resource name used for lookup. Neither is the resolved filesystem path or a spelling read back from the directory.
requirements.reason: Connected file queries use exact name and alias preparation, local resource ordering and the canonical engine reply bytes. Independent native faults verify separation of open, length, metadata and time failures.

requirements.heading: Name Preparation and Lookup
requirements.text:
1. Copy the supplied filename. This handler performs **no HCL evaluation or playback filename substitutions**: `*`, `?`, `[` and `]` do not stand for field identity, mouse buttons or modifiers here. Dollar text is not evaluated as a variable or local-playback directive.
2. The original ASCII filename-tail preparation rejects an empty string or an unacceptable final byte. Its acceptable byte set is **0x20..0x7f**, excluding `" * + , / ; < = > ? [ ] |`. If the final byte is acceptable, keep the longest trailing run of acceptable bytes. If every byte is acceptable, keep the whole string. This is a byte predicate, not whitespace trimming; spaces, periods, dollar signs, colon and backslash pass it. Uppercase ASCII a..z in that retained run to form N. A name with no usable tail produces no reply.
3. Split N into DOS drive/directory/name/extension components and reconstruct **only name+extension** as Q. Discard drive and directory for this lookup; do not add those prefixes to the resource search path. N retains its prepared spelling for the reply.
4. Apply the original ordered legacy-marker rewrites to Q: try `.ICN→.BMP`, then `.HIC→.BMH`, then `.MSK→.BMM`, stopping at the first matching rule. A rule finds its first occurrence of the old marker, replaces that marker **and the remainder of Q** with the new marker, and marks this query as an alias. Ordinary names ending in an alias extension therefore have the expected extension translation. N is not rewritten. No default extension is appended when none is supplied.
requirements.reason: Connected file queries use exact name and alias preparation, local resource ordering and the canonical engine reply bytes. Independent native faults verify separation of open, length, metadata and time failures.

requirements.heading: Name Preparation and Lookup
requirements.text: For example, `MiXeD.RiP` prepares N=Q=`MIXED.RIP`. `PiXeL.iCn` prepares N=`PIXEL.ICN` and Q=`PIXEL.BMP`. The string-rewrite helper is not a last-extension parser: `A.ICN.EXTRA` looks up `A.BMP` but reports N=`A.ICN.EXTRA`. Tail preparation also is not placeholder expansion: `Ab*tail.icn` keeps N=`TAIL.ICN` and looks up `TAIL.BMP`, whereas a final `*` produces no usable tail. Backslashes are not HCL escapes in this handler. These preparation rules describe the bounded string operation; available resources remain governed by the existing [lookup namespace](6.2-asset-delivery-and-storage.md#lookup-order-file-override), not arbitrary path access.

requirements.heading: Exact Engine Reply Bytes
requirements.text: A lookup hit followed by **open failure sends no reply in any mode**, including existence-only modes. That is different from a miss. Modes 02..04 require the subsequent file-metadata call even though file length was obtained earlier; if that call fails, the leading `1` remains but size/date/time use the zero placeholders above. On metadata success, the handler formats the selected length as signed decimal; a failed underlying length request can therefore yield `-1` unless successful alias conversion replaced it. Do not reinterpret an open failure or signed length error as an ordinary lookup miss.

requirements.heading: Exact Engine Reply Bytes
requirements.text: The engine hands the reply string directly to the client send boundary; it does not run it through HCL substitutions. The recovered RIPtel client can append **LF (0x0a) after CR** according to its output setting, so an engine `...\r` may appear on that client's connection as `...\r\n`. Mode 00 has neither ending. The command's canonical reply above is the engine byte sequence; this client-level conversion does not add a second CR or make CRLF an intrinsic FILE_QUERY format. See the existing [engine/client terminator distinction](9.2-versions.md#engine-replies-and-terminators).

requirements.heading: Legacy Bitmap Alias Sizes
requirements.text: This is the legacy planar icon-equivalent length: six header bytes and four plane rows of ceil(W/8) bytes each. The same formula is used for **ICN, HIC and MSK aliases**, regardless of the BMP's actual bit depth or file length. It does not use DWORD-padded BMP row bytes or add an extra hot-icon/mask record. Direct BMP lookup never performs this conversion merely because the content begins BM. The date/time still comes from the opened translated resource; only the reported size is converted.

requirements.heading: Legacy Bitmap Alias Sizes
requirements.text: **Explicit portable completion:** use ordinary L for unsupported header layouts, zero/negative dimensions or dimensions outside **1..32767**, rather than adopting signed-low-word wrap or negative translated lengths from an invalid/out-of-domain header. For modes 03/04, a timestamp that cannot be represented/converted is treated as metadata unavailable and uses that mode's metadata-failure record. requirements.heading: RIP_DELAY
requirements.text: RIPtel 3.1 dispatches `3D` with one four-digit field in the active radix, MegaNum or UltraNum. Ordinary final-field shortening and the leading-period zero form apply. The command dispatches at its delimiter. Sixty ticks equal one second. In Base Math 36, `001O` is 60 ticks and `002D` is 85 ticks. Zero requests no pause. [Numeric collection and dispatch](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#numeric-collection-and-dispatch).

requirements.heading: RIP_DELAY
requirements.text: During the delay, retain later incoming RIPscrip and raw-text bytes, including the remainder of the same receive buffer. Postpone processing those bytes until the delay expires, then resume with the buffered bytes in stream order before processing newer input. Clients can use their ordinary receive buffer and scheduling mechanism for this portable rule.

requirements.heading: RIP_DELAY

requirements.text: The inherited [2.00a4 form](../../2.0/ripscrip/5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_baud_emulation) specifies four digits. RIPtel 3.1 decodes the first two numeric digits and its handler uses only that value. For instance, the inherited four-digit `01UN` example delivers 1 to this client. Use two digits for RIPtel 3.1 or use the decimal [BAUDEMUL setter](5.1-text-variables.md#baudemul) for larger rates. Zero selects full speed.
requirements.reason: The two-digit final playback-rate field also accepts a short final number and period zero. Connected tests verify setting the file playback rate and clearing it with a period.

requirements.heading: Live Playback Rate and ENV State
requirements.text: There is one live rate per interpreter. `3e` and `$BAUDEMUL(rate)$` replace it. `$BAUDEMUL$` reads it. The value governs local file playback through the shared file engine. It does not change connection receive speed or set a delay on received network bytes.
requirements.reason: The two-digit final playback-rate field also accepts a short final number and period zero. Connected tests verify setting the file playback rate and clearing it with a period.

requirements.heading: Live Playback Rate and ENV State
requirements.text: The live value starts at 0 and survives ordinary [RIP_RESET_WINDOWS](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_reset_windows), including a reset reached during a scene. ENV records have no rate fields. Selecting a different slot with `2E` does not assign a rate, and defaulting ENV records during SOFT leaves the live value in effect. [ENV backup](7.2-data-backup-areas.md#environment-table-save-area) saves the live rate alongside the table and current index. Restoring such a backup explicitly restores that rate.

requirements.heading: Live Playback Rate and ENV State
requirements.text: Playback uses the live value while reading the file. In RIPtel 3.1, a nonzero value supplies a byte group size and a nominal delay between groups, approximating ten bit times per byte. A live change to another nonzero rate is picked up during the byte loop. At 2,400, a group has seven bytes with a scheduled delay of 29 ms. At 9,600, a group has fifteen bytes with a scheduled delay of 15 ms. File decoding, rendering and clock resolution affect elapsed time. Zero disables the pacing waits. [Original timing and state derivation](../research/issue-172-local-playback-baud.md)

requirements.heading: Independent Rate Examples
requirements.text: Set the live rate with `$BAUDEMUL(2400)$` and start local playback with a defined nonzero ENV selected. Replay these three lines. The markers `\x1b` and `\r` represent ESC and CR bytes.

requirements.heading: Independent Rate Examples
requirements.text:
```text
!|1\x1b0000BEFORE=$BAUDEMUL$\r
!|*\r
!|1\x1b0000AFTER=$BAUDEMUL$\r
```

requirements.heading: Independent Rate Examples
requirements.text: The connected host receives `BEFORE=2400` and `AFTER=2400` as two replies. ENV 0 is selected by the reset. Reader bytes on both sides of the reset remain paced at the same rate. The reset does not start a new pacing group. Timing measurements can isolate the scheduled waits from time spent executing the reset.

requirements.heading: Independent Rate Examples
requirements.text: For a separate fixture, start with defined ENV 0 and ENV 5 and select 0. Set 2,400 and save `$SENV$`. Select 5 with `!|2E500`. The getter still returns `2400`. Set 9,600 with `$BAUDEMUL(9600)$`, then select 0 with `!|2E00`. The getter returns `9600`, and the next file uses that rate regardless of the selected slot. The draft form `$BAUDEMUL(5,2400)$` is rejected and leaves 9,600 in effect. Now apply `$RENV$`. The backup explicitly restores `2400` alongside ENV 0 and the saved table.
requirements.reason: Local playback pacing remains interpreter-owned across the wire environment switch. Native playback timing and connected environment, backup and media fixtures verify the relevant state.

requirements.heading: Transfer Protocols
requirements.text: Modes above 1, codes above 10 and types above 6 are rejected by the DLL. Every accepted combination in the table permits each type 0–6 at the DLL boundary. The upload column applies to both an empty and a nonempty tail in the DLL. Authors must still supply filenames for uploads under the portable language rules. [XFER](5.1-text-variables.md#xfer) applies its own argument rules first. Its `RECEIVE,YMODEM,NONE` form can reach this handler with an empty tail, which the common DLL check then rejects.

requirements.heading: Transfer Protocols
requirements.text: After preparing the filename tail, the DLL posts message `0x4C9` for receive or `0x4CA` for upload, with the numeric protocol as the request code. It packs the file type into the low 16 bits and the first two reserved digits into the high 16 bits of the message's file metadata. The last two reserved digits have no effect in the handler. These posts and their metadata are local implementation details. The connected receive handler reads the stored protocol from the DLL; the upload handler checks the message's request code. Receive codes 7 and 8 both use the same ZMODEM receiver arguments and take names from the file transfer, even when the command supplied a filename. The source does not establish different recovery behavior for those two codes or a successful wire-initiated upload. [DLL and client dispatch trace](../research/issue-205-block-mode.md).
requirements.reason: Original Windows message IDs and packed callback metadata are implementation evidence. Portable block-mode requests use the supported transfer service.

requirements.heading: File Types
requirements.text: The original JPEG dispatch for types 3 and 5 checks the file's JFIF header. A filename suffix alone does not qualify and the file-type branch provides no GIF presentation. After the applicable archive, image or playback tests, the shared fallback recognizes legacy `.ICN`, `.HIC` and `.MSK` names and invokes the [icon converter](4.0-icons-and-bitmaps.md#legacy-icon-suffixes-and-conversion). For an ordinary completed transfer with reserved zeroes, the client leaves the file in the [host resource directory](6.2-asset-delivery-and-storage.md#where-files-land) after presentation. The original handler interprets bit value 1 of the first reserved word as a temporary-file request. This can register a completed non-archive file for [session cleanup](6.2-asset-delivery-and-storage.md#temporary-resource-lifetime). It is separate from [JPEG image-style flags](4.1-jpeg-images.md#rip_image_style).
requirements.reason: The completed-file path classifies JFIF by header, routes scenes and legacy icons, and registers the received filename for later cleanup when the first reserved word has bit value 1. Image-style DELETE remains separate.

requirements.heading: Completion and Refusal
requirements.text: For a portable receiver, hand bytes over to the chosen transfer protocol after accepting the request. Only publish a file as a local resource or act on its type after that file completes successfully. Process a previously committed file independently of a later file's failure. The RIP command supplies no disk-retention rule for partial data kept privately for transfer recovery. Do not display or play back a refused or incomplete file. A permitted upload requires a nonempty filename and the client's normal authorization. A refused request starts no payload transfer. Return control to the terminal and use any cancellation signaling defined by the selected transfer profile.
requirements.reason: RIPv3 removes an opened, unfinished destination on receive failure before the host regains control. Connected X/Y/ZMODEM cases cover remote cancellation, local abort, disconnect mid-batch, lookup after failure and processing of earlier completed files.

requirements.heading: Completion and Refusal
requirements.text: In RIPtel 3.1, the ZMODEM receiver collects filenames and the client examines the list **after the receiver returns**. Scene and image bytes do not enter the RIP parser as they arrive. A native failure can close and attempt to remove a partial file, and the wrapper can still visit earlier completed files. The native list is not itself a success status for the entire batch. The [source trace](../research/issue-205-block-mode.md#completion-failure-and-cancellation) records the static limits of the failure and cancellation evidence.

requirements.heading: Completion and Refusal
requirements.text: The [Alpha 4 refusal rule](../../2.0/ripscrip/5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_enter_block_mode) describes ten CAN bytes at 100 ms intervals for a denied upload. The original request dispatcher does not establish that timed response. The native receiver has a separate abort sequence. Its existence does not make it a RIP reply or an upload-refusal timing rule.
requirements.reason: Reference framing, historical dispatch detail or fixture setup.

requirements.heading: Request Vectors
requirements.text: Reading top to bottom, the DLL rejects the first, posts receive codes 5, 6, 7 and 8, rejects code 9, and posts receive code 10 with type 6. Only codes 7 and 8 reach the original connected receive engine. Replacing mode 0 with mode 1 requests upload. The DLL posts the same codes as send even for an empty tail on 5; 9 still rejects, and only code 7 reaches the client send wrapper. The mode 1 matrix describes the internal request boundary. A portable sender still must provide a filename. For each otherwise accepted request, file types 0–6 leave transport dispatch unchanged and type 7 fails validation.

requirements.text: Pass the filename as literal text after command framing. Dollar references and playback placeholders receive no expansion. Use a bare resource name, including the extension when needed. The portable profile accepts up to 255 filename bytes. An empty or unusable name or a longer tail leaves the command without a retrieval action. Resolve a valid name in host directory, shared ICONS and configured icon-search order. The command requests lookup/retrieval only. It adds no extension, opens no image or scene, and emits no RIP reply of its own. [Resource namespace](6.2-asset-delivery-and-storage.md#lookup-order-file-override).

requirements.heading: Resource Retrieval (9D)
requirements.text: For an embedding that provides pending retrieval, retain the unconsumed stream bytes. On success, make the resource available before resuming. On refusal, failure or cancellation after accepting the request, resume with the lookup unresolved. Continue with the first unconsumed byte in stream order. The portable operation completes the lookup once and resumes without replaying `9D`. Any transfer traffic belongs to the embedding's own exchange. This command defines no transfer request, status byte, filename reply or ZMODEM negotiation. [Original suspension boundary](../research/issue-291-wire-resource-retrieval.md#callback-results-and-resumption).

requirements.heading: Client Registration (9R)
requirements.text: Send all three fields in active Base Math. Each field takes its stated number of valid digits or a single leading period for zero. Full-width digits in the final reserved field contribute zero. The next byte starts the text tail, which can be empty. A delimiter before the numeric prefix is complete discards the command. The driver dispatches a complete prefix with three values even if the text tail is empty.
requirements.reason: Standalone registration framing and delimiter recovery are exercised without a proprietary registration service.

requirements.heading: Client Registration (9R)
requirements.text: In Base Math 36, `!|9R00030200000000sample` and `!|9R000302.sample` both collect `(3, 2, 0)` and `sample`. `!|9R...` collects `(0, 0, 0)` with an empty tail. Finish each stream with CR to dispatch. A period after a digit inside a field discards the command. Text uses ordinary RIP escapes and continuation. The registration wrapper passes that text literally after framing, with dollar expressions and angle markup still present. [RIP text framing](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#escaping-in-text-parameters).
requirements.reason: Standalone registration framing and delimiter recovery are exercised without a proprietary registration service.

requirements.heading: Client Registration (9R)
requirements.text: The standalone RIPtel 3.1 client registers a proprietary purchase and registration callback. Its state-dependent handling includes modes 0 through 3. Some branches can send data on the connection. A portable client without that service consumes a complete command through its unquoted pipe, CR, LF or form-feed delimiter. It leaves client and scene state alone and sends no reply. Continue normal framing at the delimiter. In `!|9R...sample|c04` followed by CR, the pipe chains to `c04`. Bytes after a line ending follow the usual rules for raw text and RIP introducers.
requirements.reason: Standalone registration framing and delimiter recovery are exercised without a proprietary registration service.

requirements.heading: RIP_BEGIN_UUENCODE_BLOCK
requirements.text: The original 3.0.7 dispatch record uses a two-digit file type and a four-digit reserve in active Base Math. The delimiter can finalize a short type when the reserve is omitted. The reserve can also be supplied in full, shortened, or given as a [leading period](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#period-as-a-zero-field). All these spellings supply reserve zero. A leading period can also supply type zero. `!|9U1`, `!|9U01`, `!|9U0101` and `!|9U01.ignored` followed by CR all collect type 1 and reserve 0. `!|9U` lacks the type. `!|9U010.` and `!|9U0.0000` contain a period inside an unfinished field. These three forms are discarded. [Original descriptor and staged cases](../research/issue-270-coordinate-and-fixed-field-edges.md).
requirements.reason: The public session accepts valid types with optional reserve, diagnoses malformed and unsupported values, and resumes ordinary text without starting a decoder.

requirements.heading: RIP_BEGIN_UUENCODE_BLOCK
requirements.text: The shipped operation is named **RIP_BeginEncodedStream**. The complete shipped handler only flushes pending host work, accepts types **0 or 1** without further action, and reports an invalid-type error for larger values. It does **not** start a UU decoder, consume a following encoded file, write a file, display a JPEG or delete one. Its presence in the HLP name inventory is not evidence that the draft feature works.
requirements.reason: The public session accepts valid types with optional reserve, diagnoses malformed and unsupported values, and resumes ordinary text without starting a decoder.

requirements.heading: RIP_BEGIN_UUENCODE_BLOCK
requirements.text: The [ALPHA 4 entry](../../2.0/ripscrip/5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_begin_uuencode_block) described eight reserved characters and a subsequent UU-encoded file with the block-mode file-type meanings. That is the historical intended mechanism, not the recovered RIPtel 3.1 behavior. In particular it supplies no alternative implementation of image-style DELETE. _Evidence: original dispatch slot 128 at RVA 0x81c20 and complete handler 0x252c0–0x252f1; [native type matrix and cleanup derivation](../research/issue-21-image-style.md#received-file-cleanup-and-encoded-stream-checkpoint)._

requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: International Support in RIPscrip
requirements.text: The RIPscrip language itself is not tied to any particular language. However, there is a need to establish a means of determining and specifying what RIPscrip / text window fonts with special characters should be used, and what language should be used in the terminal software. It is up to the individual application to use whatever files it needs to support a particular language. RIPscrip provides a standardized way of specifying the language support to use: a character code for each of the languages supported. _(v2.A2)_

requirements.heading: International Support in RIPscrip
requirements.text: Currently, English is the only supported language in RIPscrip. For the purposes of multi-lingual extensibility, the convention was established in the 2.x draft: _(v2.A4)_

requirements.text: | Code | Description of Language |
