requirements.heading: International Support in RIPscrip
requirements.text: The means of setting the language is for the user to specify in the terminal, preferably in the dialing directory. This allows the user to select a different language for different systems. There is no ability for the host to specify to the terminal what language to use. _(v2.A2)_

requirements.heading: International Support in RIPscrip
requirements.text: The means of finding out what languages the terminal supports is handled via the [`$IFS()$`](5.1-text-variables.md#ifs) text variable. For example, if the host were to query the terminal with a `$IFS(ENG)$`, the terminal would respond affirmatively. _(v2.A2)_

requirements.heading: 6.0 Writing 3.x .RIP Files
requirements.text: _Reconstructed edition - every claim carries an evidence tag; see [Contents](README.md) for the legend._

requirements.heading: 6.0 Writing 3.x .RIP Files
requirements.text: Authoring-level conventions for 3.x script files: encoding and line endings, line length and continuation, comments and grouping, the script-container family, and the prologue/epilogue conventions of TeleGrafix's own 116 shipped RIPtel demo scripts.

requirements.heading: 6.0 Writing 3.x .RIP Files
requirements.text: _The 2.0 authoring conventions this page extends are in [6.0 of the v2.0 reference](../../2.0/ripscrip/6.0-writing-rip-files.md); the 3.0 engine inherits the 2.0 parser conventions documented in the [stream conventions techspec](../../2.0/techspecs/1.0-stream-conventions-delta.md)._

requirements.heading: What a .RIP file is
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; corpus._

requirements.heading: What a .RIP file is
requirements.text: A `.RIP` file is not a distinct binary format: it is a captured RIPscrip command stream - exactly the bytes a host would transmit - stored as a text file. Everything in [1.1 Protocol & Command Hierarchy](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md) applies verbatim to file content. A file can be transmitted by a host, replayed locally via the `$>file$` playback prefix ([5.3 Local File Playback](5.3-local-playback.md)), played back by [RIP_READ_SCENE](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_read_scene), or delivered and auto-played through [block mode](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_enter_block_mode).

requirements.heading: The script-container family
requirements.text: _Evidence: corpus (116-file census - [script census](../../3.0/research/riptel-script-census.md))._

requirements.heading: The script-container family
requirements.text: All script extensions in the RIPtel corpus - `.RIP`, `.FN`, `.DEF`, `.MNU`, `.MSE`, `.RET`, `.ENT`, `.EXT`, `.COL` - are plain-ASCII RIPscrip command streams distinguished only by **role**, not by format. The corpus-attested roles:

requirements.text: | Extension | Role |

requirements.text: | `.RIP` | A scene - the general-purpose script container |

requirements.text: | `.FN` | A "function" scene invoked as a subroutine via [RIP_READ_SCENE](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_read_scene) or the `$>file$` playback prefix - the WIPE00-24 transition library, effects, and reusable setup blocks |

requirements.text: | `.DEF` | A variable-definition script (TELCMDS.DEF, MENU.DEF …) that seeds [text variables](../../glossary.md) for a scene group |

requirements.heading: The script-container family
requirements.text: `.TXT` story files flowed into column regions are the one non-RIPscrip participant: inside an open column region they are word-wrapped as raw content, never parsed as commands ([3.1](3.1-column-text-system.md)). Playback search paths for all of these are covered in [5.3](5.3-local-playback.md) and [6.2 Asset Delivery & Storage](6.2-asset-delivery-and-storage.md).

requirements.heading: Encoding and line endings
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; corpus; SyncTERM (ripper.c:18557-18580)._

requirements.heading: Encoding and line endings
requirements.text:
- **Line endings are CRLF** throughout the RIPtel corpus (the 1.54 spec said bare CR). They parse identically because CR dispatches the pending command while LF is unconditionally swallowed mid-command - see [1.1](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md). Line endings are significant to the parser, so script files should be stored and transferred byte-exact - never re-wrapped or "normalized". Script files also contain **literal control bytes** - SOH (`0x01`) introducers and ESC (`0x1B`) command characters - so they are not safely editable in tools that strip or transcode control characters.
- Text content (graphics text, button labels, embedded raw text) is [CP437](../../glossary.md) - the code page of the BBS world, and the character set the 3.x client's MicroANSI terminal fonts render in full (all 256 glyphs; see [6.1](6.1-content-file-roles.md)). There is no in-band encoding declaration. _Evidence: 2.00a4; corpus (FONTS/RIPscrip.maf glyph complement)._
requirements.reason: Authoring history describes LF as swallowed mid-command. The pinned wire framing chapter explicitly dispatches at bare LF, CR or FF.

requirements.heading: Line length and continuation
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4 rules 4-5, 13; corpus._

requirements.heading: Line length and continuation
requirements.text: Any command or line may be split with a backslash (`\`) immediately before the line break; continuation lines carry **no introducer** - they are bare argument bytes. Authoring practice:
requirements.reason: The RIP stream scanner joins continued commands, including numeric and text fields, and consumes comments up to the next delimiter.

requirements.heading: Line length and continuation
requirements.text:
- The split may land anywhere - mid-parameter, mid-number. The RIPtel corpus uses continuation for long vertex lists (POLYPOLY.RIP's RIP*FILL_POLYGON runs); the RIPterm 2.30 shipped corpus shows it as heavy production traffic (one palette-fade file is 1,024 physical lines of which 960 are continuations). \_Evidence: corpus (POLYPOLY.RIP); 2.00a4.*
- The 2.0-era 80-column discipline for command lines remains sound authoring advice - wrap for tool compatibility, but don't rely on readers enforcing any limit; terminals accept arbitrarily long lines. _(Inherited RIPterm 2.30-corpus observation - see the [v2.0 page](../../2.0/ripscrip/6.0-writing-rip-files.md).)_
- Watch trailing backslashes: an **odd** count means continuation, an **even** count means escaped literal backslashes. If you need a literal `\` at end-of-line, write `\\`; a continuation after a literal backslash needs `\\\`. _Evidence: 2.00a4 rule 13; SyncTERM (ripper.c:18563-18576)._
- Multi-command lines are the norm - `|` chains commands on one line (`!|c0F|=00000001|S010F`), and the standard 3.x prologue is itself a four-command chain (below). Commands that must be last on their line (RIP*READ_SCENE, RIP_ENTER_BLOCK_MODE) cannot be chained past. \_Evidence: 2.00a4 rule 4; corpus.*
requirements.reason: The RIP stream scanner joins continued commands, including numeric and text fields, and consumes comments up to the next delimiter.

requirements.heading: Escaping, comments and grouping
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4 rules 11, 14; corpus._

requirements.heading: Escaping, comments and grouping
requirements.text: Inside text parameters, `\!` → literal `!`, `\|` → literal `|`, `\\` → literal `\`; [host command](../../glossary.md) and text-variable metacharacters (`$`, `[`, `]`, `(`, `)`) are quoted with a backslash where they could be misread (`\$Name\$`) - see [1.1](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md). At the file level:

requirements.heading: Escaping, comments and grouping
requirements.text:
- **Comments** - `!|!comment text` embeds a comment anywhere ([RIP_COMMENT](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#rip_comment), _(v2.A2)_); everything from the `!` opcode to the next `|` or end of line is ignored, and the comment string is exempt from text-variable substitution. The RIPtel corpus contains **1,683 comment commands** (305 with prose): `!|command|! comment` chains are ubiquitous, and TeleGrafix's authors left positional field-layout cribs above complex commands (`!|! xxyyxxyycaffffccrrrrrrrr`). _Evidence: 2.00a4; corpus._
- **Trailing text after fixed-length arguments is tolerated** and used as inline commentary - the shipping driver stops reading once a command's fixed fields are consumed: `!|fZKQO                 Set world coordinats to 1280x960` _(sic)_. Robust for the shipping driver, but not guaranteed by the language - prefer explicit `|!` comments. _Evidence: corpus (ONLINE.RIP)._
- **Grouping** - `!|(` … `!|)` bundles commands into logical groups for paint programs ([RIP_GROUP_BEGIN](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#rip_group_begin)/[RIP_GROUP_END](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#rip_group_end), _(v2.A2)_); terminals ignore them, and the 2.00a4 advice to strip groups from files placed online is consistent with their total absence from the shipping demo corpus. _Evidence: 2.00a4 - not in the RIPSCRIP.HLP inventory, not observed in the RIPtel demo corpus._
- **UU-encoded data blocks** - a file (or stream) may embed raw binary content behind a [RIP_BEGIN_UUENCODE_BLOCK](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_begin_uuencode_block) command _(v2.A1)_; the 3.0 driver renamed the mechanism `RIP_BeginEncodedStream`. _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP - not observed in the RIPtel demo corpus._
requirements.reason: The RIP stream scanner joins continued commands, including numeric and text fields, and consumes comments up to the next delimiter.

requirements.heading: Mixing ANSI, raw text and column content
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4 rule 6; corpus._

requirements.heading: Mixing ANSI, raw text and column content
requirements.text: Lines that do not begin with an introducer pass through to the current [text window](../../glossary.md) ([1.4 Terminal & ANSI View](1.4-terminal-ansi-view.md)), so script files freely intermix RIPscrip with ANSI sequences and plain text. The flowed-text machinery extends the 2.0 modal wrinkle: after a text-region or column-region definition ([3.0](3.0-text-output-and-fonts.md), [3.1](3.1-column-text-system.md)), raw lines are consumed as region/column content until a command line ends the block - the `.COL` scenes and their `.TXT` story files are built entirely on this.

requirements.heading: The SOH scene-start opener
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4 rule 12; corpus._

requirements.heading: The SOH scene-start opener
requirements.text: Ctrl-A (SOH, byte `0x01`) or Ctrl-B (STX, `0x02`) may replace the `!` introducer and - unlike `!` - are accepted anywhere in the stream, not just at line start ([1.1](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md)). TeleGrafix's 2.2-era convention was to open a standalone scene file with `\x01|*` (SOH + [RIP_RESET_WINDOWS](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_reset_windows)); the 3.x corpus systematizes the SOH opener: **111 of 116 files begin their _first_ command line with SOH + `|`**, then use `!|` for every subsequent line - SOH apparently flags start-of-scene to the 3.0 stream parser, while `!|` remains the 1.54-compatible introducer. (Three files invert the pattern, nearly all-SOH; SOH mid-scene is legal and does appear, e.g. in DRAGON.RIP below.) Files that are deliberately non-destructive (wipes, fades, fragments) omit the `*` reset.

requirements.heading: Scene prologue and epilogue conventions
requirements.text: _Evidence: corpus (90+ files); HLP._

requirements.heading: Scene prologue and epilogue conventions
requirements.text: TeleGrafix never specified how a script file should begin or end, but their shipped 3.x scenes are consistent:

requirements.heading: Scene prologue and epilogue conventions
requirements.text: - **The standard prologue** opens 90+ of the 116 files: `!|J10|n2000|M08|fZKQO` - pinning the scene's numeric conventions _before_ any coordinate-bearing command arrives (order matters). Decoded:

requirements.text: | Piece | Command | Meaning |

requirements.heading: Scene prologue and epilogue conventions
requirements.text: | `!\|` | - | line introducer + command delimiter |

The shipped opcode is level-0 `J`; the ALPHA 4 draft's `b` assignment collided with RIP_EXTENDED_TEXT_WINDOW - see the [1.2 note](1.2-math-and-coordinates.md#rip_set_base_math) |

requirements.text: | `\|fZKQO` | [RIP_SET_WORLD_FRAME](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_set_world_frame) | world frame ← 1280×960 (`ZK`=1280, `QO`=960) |

requirements.heading: Scene prologue and epilogue conventions
requirements.text:
- **Reset first** - standalone scenes open with the SOH reset opener (`\x01|*` or `!|*`), then the prologue; [RIP_KILL_MOUSE_FIELDS](4.2-mouse-fields-and-pointer.md#rip_kill_mouse_fields) (`!|1K`) clears stale fields so they cannot fire during the redraw (8 corpus files; TELKILL.FN wraps it as a reusable subroutine scene). _Evidence: corpus._
- **Query-command setup** - the demos do much of their scene setup through [RIP_QUERY](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_query) terminal-control variables alongside the prologue: `$COFF$` (cursor off), `$DTW$` (deactivate text window), `$SBAROFF$` (hide status bar), `$RESET(OVERFLOW)$` (clear column-overflow state). _Evidence: corpus._
- **Scene header segments** - [`RIP_HEADER`](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#rip_header) uses a base-64 block of eight digits in full-width form (revision, global flags, segment count), followed by concatenated typed segments. The ordinary fields support [numeric shorthand](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#numeric-shorthand-and-segment-selectors). Send each segment selector as a literal digit. The reference gives exact fields, reset/protection behavior, shipped defects and parser-checked examples. A pipe ends the whole header. The RIPtel demos use explicit prologue commands instead; the checked header examples are constructed from original-driver evidence. _Evidence: DLL; [derivation](../research/issue-5-scene-headers.md)._
- **State re-assertion** - authored streams re-assert unchanged state constantly (background color, write mode, fonts); state is inherited from whatever ran before, so well-behaved scenes re-establish everything they depend on. _Evidence: 2.00a4; corpus._
- **Epilogue** - [RIP_NO_MORE](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#rip_no_more) (`!|#`) marks scene end, activating mouse regions and queued clicks; nearly every RIPtel demo scene ends with one (287 uses in 95 of 116 files). The spec's advice to transmit three or more consecutively for noise immunity stands - the shipped RIPterm 2.30 scenes ended `!|#|#|#` - and terminals should also time out and assume NO*MORE if the stream goes quiet. \_Evidence: 2.00a4; corpus.*

requirements.heading: Authoring-robustness notes from the corpus
requirements.text: The shipping driver's parser is markedly tolerant, and shipped TeleGrafix files lean on that tolerance - a caution for authors targeting other terminals:

requirements.heading: Authoring-robustness notes from the corpus
requirements.text:
- **Harmless corpus typos.** A missing `!` introducer (`|1<ESC>0000$COMPAT$`, CURVES.RIP) and bare `!|` lines pass through the shipping driver without visible failure. A stray `!|----` separator selects the filled skewed oval opcode, then fails [numeric collection](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#numeric-collection-and-dispatch) on the next dash. It draws nothing.
- **Truncated reserved fields are routinely omitted** (`!|2s002` for a documented 6-character argument block; `!|1c06` with no reserved digits). The documented practice remains to send reserved fields as zeros for forward compatibility.
requirements.reason: Corpus or historical commentary for the adjacent reviewed wire rule.

requirements.heading: Naming and delivery
requirements.text: Files referenced from commands and playback variables use bare DOS-style names - no path or sub-directory information (commands that take filenames reject paths). Extensions may be omitted where a command documents a default (`.RIP` for playback variables, `.BMP` for icon commands). Where files live on the terminal and how a host delivers them is covered in [6.2 Asset Delivery & Storage](6.2-asset-delivery-and-storage.md).

requirements.heading: File roles
requirements.text: Commands reference host-deliverable files by bare name, without a path or sub-directory. Omit the suffix to select the command's default, such as `.BMP` for icon loads or `.RIP` for playback variables. RIP_LOAD_ICON and RIP_LOAD_BITMAP apply the [legacy suffix aliases](#legacy-icn-icons-ripscrip-154) to explicit `.ICN`, `.HIC` and `.MSK` suffixes and use other explicit suffixes as supplied. _Evidence: 2.00a4 defaults and original driver lookup._

requirements.heading: Legacy `.ICN` icons (RIPscrip 1.54)
requirements.text: The [1.54 ICN/HIC/MSK raster](../../1.54/techspecs/3.0-icon-format.md) has sixteen indexed colors and no embedded RGB palette. RIPtel 3.1's original **RIP_ConvertIconToBmp** export converts it to an uncompressed 4-bit Windows BMP with a **fixed default EGA color table**. It samples neither the active drawing palette nor the desktop/OS palette. Slot 1 becomes RGB **0000AA** even if a script previously changed drawing slot 1 to red; all sixteen RGB values and the packed output layout are in the [bitmap delta](../techspecs/3.0-bitmap-mask-delta.md#legacy-icon-conversion-palette). Pixel indexes survive conversion. Later bitmap rendering/palette mapping is a separate operation.
requirements.reason: Completed downloads use the fixed EGA palette and preserve every source index. Connected tests compare the packed file and draw from it.

requirements.heading: Legacy `.ICN` icons (RIPscrip 1.54)
requirements.text: **Conversion and loading are distinct.** Ordinary RIP_LOAD_BITMAP and RIP_LOAD_ICON normalize `.ICN`→`.BMP`, `.HIC`→`.BMH` and `.MSK`→`.BMM` case-insensitively before a single lookup of the resulting image name. They do not fall back to decoding a raw legacy file when the normalized bitmap is missing. The recovered RIPtel client invokes the conversion export on received ICN/HIC/MSK files after file transfer; that export always replaces the source extension with **BMP**, even for HIC/MSK. This differs from the image loaders' BMH/BMM substitutions. There is one converter and one fixed palette policy; the [2.x startup scan/prompt](../../2.0/techspecs/3.0-icon-formats.md#conversion-from-154-icons) is not established as inherited by this recovered client's converter call graph. Do not implement a distinct startup or on-load palette selection by analogy with that older UI.

requirements.heading: Legacy `.ICN` icons (RIPscrip 1.54)
requirements.text: **Filesystem effects of this driver:** conversion opens the source, opens/creates the uppercased destination filename for writing **without truncating an existing file**, and writes the new BMP body. A longer existing destination can retain stale bytes beyond the new body's embedded BMP file size. On the successful write path it closes both descriptors, attempts destination timestamp setting, then **attempts to delete the source**. Neither timestamp nor source-deletion failure changes its success status. A source that cannot be deleted remains. Detected header/palette/row read/write failures instead retain the source and attempt to delete the partial destination; failure of that deletion can leave partial output. These operations are not atomic replacement.
requirements.reason: Connected icon conversion preserves the destination tail and removes the source after successful publication. Atomic publication and failure cleanup follow the client cache policy.
requirements.scope: Successful legacy-icon conversion within the per-BBS cache. Native failure-time filesystem side effects are historical.

requirements.heading: Legacy `.ICN` icons (RIPscrip 1.54)
requirements.text: > **Timestamp defect:** the converter calls fstat on its source descriptor **after closing it**. Original fstat fails with EBADF and leaves its stat structure untouched; the converter ignores that failure and passes uninitialized access/modification fields to utime. Consequently, the 2.x documentation's promised source date/time preservation **cannot be relied on for RIPtel 3.1**. The attempted values are stack residue and have no reproducible timestamp contract. Deliberately preserving valid source timestamps in a new implementation corrects this defect; it is not an observed guarantee of this driver.
requirements.reason: Source provenance, historical timestamp defect, or presentation markup. The operative converter clauses have separate implementation evidence.

requirements.heading: Legacy `.ICN` icons (RIPscrip 1.54)
requirements.text: The recovered MSI includes some legacy LORD ICNs beside paired BMPs, so the earlier assertion that no ICNs ship was too broad. That package observation does not establish an automatic startup conversion policy.
requirements.reason: Source provenance, historical timestamp defect, or presentation markup. The operative converter clauses have separate implementation evidence.

requirements.heading: Windows BMP / DIB
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A1._

requirements.heading: Windows BMP / DIB
requirements.text: The 2.00a4 decision to adopt the Windows **Device-Independent Bitmap** stands in 3.x. The older 1.54 icon format was completely inadequate for resolution- and color-independent environments: it carried no color palette and no notion of pixel format. The DIB format accommodates monochrome (1-bit), 16-color (4-bit), 256-color (8-bit), and 24-bit uncompressed images, and stores palette information in the file so that color approximation or dithering can make the image appear correct in any color environment. Explicitly _not_ supported: RLE-compressed BMPs ("Can't show compressed bitmaps") and OS/2-style BMPs. Display options include stretching to any size, dithering, transparency, color-palette manipulation, and wallpapering.

requirements.heading: Windows BMP / DIB
requirements.text: BMPs are pervasive in the corpus (102 of the 234 files in RIPtel's `ICONS/`): backgrounds, button skins (via [RIP_LOAD_BITMAP](4.0-icons-and-bitmaps.md#rip_load_bitmap)), and UI décor. Content creators normally never touch the bytes - icons are produced in a paint program, or captured on the terminal itself via [RIP_GET_IMAGE](4.0-icons-and-bitmaps.md#rip_get_image) + [RIP_WRITE_ICON](4.0-icons-and-bitmaps.md#rip_write_icon) (or per-port via [RIP_PORT_WRITE](7.0-drawing-ports.md#rip_port_write)). Implementers decoding or generating icon files should work from the [icon formats techspec](../../2.0/techspecs/3.0-icon-formats.md), whose basic header/color-table/pixel-block layout is retained; the [RIPtel 3.1 delta](../techspecs/3.0-bitmap-mask-delta.md) adds the executable BMM/depth/compositing contract.

requirements.heading: Windows BMP / DIB
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; WP (§3.7.1); HLP ("Can't show compressed bitmaps"); corpus._

requirements.heading: `.BMH` - button-highlight variants
requirements.text: A `.BMH` file is a **plain Windows BMP** whose extension marks it as the _highlighted/pressed_ state of a same-named `.BMP` UI skin. RIPtel ships five pairs (BUTTON, CHECKBOX, RADIO, RADIOBUT, RADIONEW): each pair has identical dimensions, bit depth, and palette, differing only in pixel data (the `.BMH` shifted toward white/highlight tones). The client swaps the `.BMH` image in on hover/click for BMP-skinned buttons, checkboxes, and radio buttons; pairing is by filename convention - `.BMH` files are never named in any script ([4.3 Buttons](4.3-buttons.md)).

requirements.heading: `.BMH` - button-highlight variants
requirements.text: _Evidence: corpus (ICONS/\*.BMH byte comparison - see [binary triage §3](../../3.0/research/riptel-binary-formats.md))._

requirements.heading: JPEG (and GrayPEG)
requirements.text: JPEG remains the only compressed image format in shipping 3.x (GIF was dropped over LZW licensing; PNG was announced but never shipped - see the [white paper](../text/RIPScrip-3.x-technical-whitepaper.txt)). All JPEGs are 24-bit; the white paper notes support for the **GrayPEG** grayscale variants. JPEG decoding is built into the driver (`jpegShow`, `LoadJPEGBuffer`, JPEG scaling-table error strings), images can be placed anywhere at any size, and progressive ("display while downloading") rendering was advertised but noted as not working in RIPtel 3.1. Seven JPEGs ship in the demo corpus, driven by [RIP_IMAGE](4.1-jpeg-images.md#rip_image) and the `$(file.JPG$` [playback prefix](5.3-local-playback.md). Byte-level decoder notes are in the [JPEG techspec](../../2.0/techspecs/3.1-jpeg-images.md).
requirements.reason: The JPEG reader decodes grayscale, baseline and progressive images and the connected image command displays the decoded image.

requirements.heading: JPEG (and GrayPEG)
requirements.text: _Evidence: WP (§3.7.2, GrayPEG); HLP (jpeg_ strings; readme progressive-display note); corpus (N2*PHOTO.RIP, SPECLEFX.RIP).*

requirements.heading: `.WAV` audio
requirements.text: A digitized audio file, played in the background by [RIP_PLAY_AUDIO](4.5-audio-files.md#rip_play_audio) or the `$)FILE.WAV$` playback prefix ([5.3](5.3-local-playback.md)), and stoppable with `$OFF$`. The 3.0 driver plainly supports audio (audio configuration, `AUDIO=TRUE` in RIPscrip.ini, the DLL export `RIP_AudioSupport`), but the demo corpus ships no audio files and never issues the command. Terminals that store audio in a translated local format must still answer [file queries](6.2-asset-delivery-and-storage.md) as if the WAVE original were on disk. Format details: [audio techspec](../../2.0/techspecs/3.4-audio.md).

requirements.heading: `.WAV` audio
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP - not observed in the RIPtel demo corpus._

requirements.heading: Fonts are not content files
requirements.text: Fonts are **global client resources, never host-delivered per connection** - they resolve only from the client's font store (`FONTS\`), outside the [connection directory](../../glossary.md) model of [6.2](6.2-asset-delivery-and-storage.md). The 3.x client ships three font systems plus a catalog file; creators select them by name/number through the font commands ([3.0 Text Output & Fonts](3.0-text-output-and-fonts.md)):

requirements.heading: Fonts are not content files
requirements.text:
- **`.RFF` outline fonts (Atech FastFont)** - the scalable outline-font system is a licensed third-party engine, Atech Software's "FastFont"; `.RFF` is evidently "RIPscrip FastFont", renamed from Atech's `.FF1`. Eight shipped faces (BRUSH, COBB, DEFAULT, DIXON, EUREKA, MARIN, OAKLAND, SYMBOL), 224 glyphs each (0x20-0xFF) on a 1000-units-per-em square, with **ten style variants per file** - base, `Th`in, `Cn` condensed, `Wd` wide, `Ex` expanded, plus hollow versions of all five - exactly the family-suffix names the corpus passes in extended-font-style commands ("Marin", "Cobb Th", …). RIPterm 2.30 (October 1997) shipped five of the families as byte-identical `.RFF` files - both generations are preserved in the [RIPterm 2.30 font assets](../../2.0/assets/fonts/README.md). _Evidence: corpus (FONTS/\*.RFF - [binary triage §1](../../3.0/research/riptel-binary-formats.md)); WP (§3.4.1)._
- **`atf.cfg`** - the FastFont engine's binary **catalog/cache**: a pre-scanned registry mapping style names to files so the rasterizer needn't open every font at startup. Machine-generated and safe to rebuild. _Evidence: corpus (FONTS/atf.cfg)._
- **`.maf` MicroANSI bitmap fonts** - `FONTS/RIPscrip.maf` holds the fixed-cell fonts used for ANSI/text-window emulation: six resolution records, each with five font-size subrecords of raw glyph bitmaps for the full 256-character (CP437) set - the per-resolution renderings behind the terminal text modes and the `$TWFONT$` "MicroANSI" font numbers ([1.4 Terminal & ANSI View](1.4-terminal-ansi-view.md)). _Evidence: corpus (FONTS/RIPscrip.maf); HLP (MicroANSI font-loading error strings; MESSAGES.HLP text-mode list)._
- **`.CHR` Borland BGI stroked fonts** - the classic 1.54 vector "system font" set survives untouched: ten standard Borland BGI stroked-font files (BOLD, EURO, GOTH, LCOM, LITT, SANS, SCRI, SIMP, TRIP, TSCR). The format is Borland's, publicly documented, and unchanged; nothing RIPscrip-specific was added. _Evidence: 2.00a4 (system-font lineage); corpus (FONTS/\*.CHR); HLP ("BGI font" error strings)._

requirements.heading: Fonts are not content files
requirements.text: **Classic CHR rendering clarification:** BOLD.CHR contains six opcode-01 “do scan” records; the inherited “never emitted” claim is corrected in the [BGI format reference](../../1.54/techspecs/3.1-bgi-stroked-fonts.md#scan-records-and-riptel-rendering). RIPtel's original classic renderer consumes them without painting, pen movement, closure or fill, and `scan_flag` does not enable a different behavior. Quote/colon/equals therefore have explicit outline contours with unpainted interiors. See the [original-driver derivation and geometry oracle](../research/issue-17-chr-scan-records.md). The same format correction records TSCR's nonzero unused-header bytes; original font assets remain byte-exact.

requirements.heading: Fonts are not content files
requirements.text: > _Editor's note:_ the FastFont format has full byte-level documentation under the earliest-version rule - the header, style-record, glyph-section, kerning, and `ATF.CFG` layouts live in the [v2.0 FastFont techspec](../../2.0/techspecs/3.2-fastfont-fonts.md), with the RIPtel-specific delta (the BRUSH/EUREKA/OAKLAND families and the regenerated `atf.cfg`) in the [v3.0 techspec](../techspecs/3.2-fastfont-additions.md). MicroANSI likewise: [v2.0 base](../../2.0/techspecs/3.3-microansi-fonts.md), [v3.0 `.maf` delta](../techspecs/3.3-microansi-maf-delta.md); the 1.54 stroked/bitmap lineage is in the [v1.54 techspecs](../../1.54/techspecs/3.1-bgi-stroked-fonts.md). Those pages supersede the research triage for format details.

requirements.heading: Fonts are not content files
requirements.text: > _Editor's note:_ the RIPtel install also contains client-internal binary files - resource containers and the variable database behind the [persistent variable store](../../glossary.md). These are implementation artifacts of one client, **not host-deliverable content and not specification surface**; they are decoded as research context in [`riptel-resource-containers.md`](../../3.0/research/riptel-resource-containers.md).

requirements.heading: The delivery workflow
requirements.text: A well-behaved host delivers assets in two steps:
requirements.reason: Source provenance, historical summary or structural introduction; concrete storage requirements are tracked in the adjacent normative blocks.

requirements.heading: The delivery workflow
requirements.text:
1. **Staleness check** - [RIP_FILE_QUERY](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_file_query) asks whether a file already exists on the terminal's disk, and (modes 02-04) its size, date and time. The host compares the response against its own copy to decide whether a download is needed at all - the host side of the 3.x resource-caching story. Terminals that store audio in a translated local format must answer as if the WAVE original were on disk ([4.5](4.5-audio-files.md)). _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP (`RIP_FileQuery`); SyncTERM (ripper.c:16104) - not observed in the RIPtel demo corpus, whose scenes are local and have no host to answer._
2. **Download** - [RIP_ENTER_BLOCK_MODE](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_enter_block_mode) requests a supported transfer and specifies how to use a received file. RIPtel 3.1 starts a ZMODEM receiver for codes 7 and 8 and handles the returned files after reception. Its [encoded stream command](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_begin_uuencode_block) is a stub. The 2.00 Alpha 4 draft describes a separate UUencoded delivery mechanism.

requirements.heading: The delivery workflow
requirements.text: The recovered 3.0 [FILE_QUERY contract](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_file_query) distinguishes lookup misses from later open/metadata failures and reports a legacy planar icon-equivalent size for eligible ICN/HIC/MSK aliases. A direct BMP query instead reports actual file length. Compare the host resource in the requested representation; do not assume the translated cache file has that same byte length. Mode 04 uses a colon between prepared filename and size, with the exact engine/client endings defined there.
requirements.reason: Connected file queries use exact name and alias preparation, local resource ordering and the canonical engine reply bytes. Independent native faults verify separation of open, length, metadata and time failures.

requirements.heading: The delivery workflow
requirements.text: Once delivered, the host uses the assets by name - stamping icons, displaying images, playing audio, replaying scenes - with no further transmission cost, from the command stream (chapter 4) or from [host commands](../../glossary.md) via the playback prefixes ([5.3](5.3-local-playback.md)).
requirements.reason: Transfer completion classifies files by request type and extension, then dispatches eligible scenes and media. Connected transfer tests observe receipt order, storage and automatic display.

requirements.heading: The delivery workflow
requirements.text: Mode 1 requests upload. The [capability and refusal rules](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#completion-and-refusal) distinguish the draft’s cancellation sequence from the recovered client dispatch.
requirements.reason: Draft and original-client refusal history. The applicable request and completion behavior belongs to chapter 5.5.

requirements.heading: The delivery workflow
requirements.text: Housekeeping uses [`$FILEDEL(file,...)$`](5.1-text-variables.md#filedel). The host is required to name only files it created/downloaded, but the original RIPtel 3.1 driver does not track or enforce that provenance. It resolves each filename using **host directory → shared ICONS → ordered icon search path**, deleting only the first existing match. With no configured host directory, resolution begins at shared ICONS and still includes the search path. Deletion failure does not try a lower-tier duplicate, does not stop later filenames and produces no per-file result.
requirements.scope: Use the per-BBS RIP cache and the shared read-only RIP directory; the cache owns all host-writable paths. RIP directory selection is scoped to the cache.

requirements.heading: The delivery workflow
requirements.text: > **Correction to the earlier hypothesis:** FILEDEL is not host-directory-only, and the user search path is not read-only for this operation. The original callback calls ordinary resource lookup and then unlink without a creator/session check. Shared/search-path files may predate the current connection and are still eligible. Asset delivery's target-directory policy does not establish deletion scope.
requirements.reason: RIPtel's installer paths, bookmark options and search-path settings are client configuration. Writable asset operations use the per-BBS cache.

requirements.heading: The delivery workflow
requirements.text: Hosts should send bare filenames. requirements.heading: Where files land
requirements.text: The 3.x client carries the 2.0 storage model forward intact and renames its surface. Every host-deliverable media type still flows through **one directory family** - there is no separate audio, image, or scene directory:
requirements.reason: Source provenance, historical summary or structural introduction; concrete storage requirements are tracked in the adjacent normative blocks.

requirements.heading: Where files land
requirements.text:
- The **default icon directory** (`ICONS\`) houses the whole host-deliverable media family: `.BMP`/`.BMH` icons (and legacy `.ICN`), `.JPG` images, `.WAV` sounds, and the script containers. RIPtel's installer creates `ICONS`, `FONTS`, and `Files` under the install root.
- Each **bookmark** (RIPtel's name for a dialing-directory entry) can name a per-host sub-directory - the **host directory**, the 3.x name for the connection directory (RIPterm 2.30's "System Dir", the 1.54 manual's DIR field) - configured in the bookmark editor's Advanced options. When one is specified, any icon, RIPscrip, sound, or image files sent by the host are automatically placed there. New bookmarks import their defaults from RIPtel's setup configuration, and auto-creation carries over from the DOS clients: "Many online services create their own host directories for you, without your knowledge."
- **New constraint in 3.x** - the host directory can only exist under the directory where the client is installed: "For security reasons, the host directory cannot exist in any arbitrary location on your hard drive." Directories the _host_ can populate are jailed under the install root; directories only the _user_ configures (the search path, below) may live anywhere. Implementations should preserve this property - host-influenced writes stay inside a client-owned sandbox.
- **New third lookup tier in 3.x** - the setup-level, user-configurable **icon search path**: extra directories consulted only after the two classic tiers fail, aimed at CD-ROM-distributed resource sets. Multiple directories are separated by semicolons (`C:\Windows;D:\;Icons\MyIcons`). Host deliveries do not write new files there, but [FILEDEL](5.1-text-variables.md#filedel) uses the same lookup path for deletion.
- **Fonts are the exception** - stroked, outline and terminal fonts are global client resources resolved only from the font store (`FONTS\`), never per connection ([6.1](6.1-content-file-roles.md)).
- **User file transfers stay outside the model** - ordinary Zmodem downloads land in a `Files` directory (with separate user-configurable download and upload directories), a different namespace from host-deliverable resources, exactly as in the 2.0 block-mode rule.
requirements.reason: RIPtel's installer paths, bookmark options and search-path settings are client configuration. Writable asset operations use the per-BBS cache.

requirements.heading: Temporary Resource Lifetime
requirements.text: [RIP_WRITE_ICON flag bit value 1](4.0-icons-and-bitmaps.md#rip_write_icon), [RIP_PORT_WRITE flag bit value 1](7.0-drawing-ports.md#export-flags-and-filename) and the [completed-transfer temporary flag](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_enter_block_mode) request later cleanup through the same original instance-owned registry. RIPtel 3.1 registers an export's resolved name before attempting the write, and appends a transfer's resolved name after reception. Registration and export are independent operations. The native purge attempts removal of the registered names and then retires the list.

requirements.heading: Temporary Resource Lifetime
requirements.text: The recovered client invokes purge during normal disconnect cleanup and on interpreter/application teardown. A drawing or scene reset, resource lookup, clipboard reassignment, or display of a registered image does not run that purge. Directory selection affects new writes. Earlier registrations keep the resource locations resolved when they were recorded.
requirements.reason: The interpreter owns registrations for successful temporary exports and completed downloads in the resolved writable directory. They survive reset, scene playback and same-location replacement. Disconnect and destruction consume the list through confined FILEDEL storage lookup. The portable rule retains the previous registry on failed export.

requirements.heading: Temporary Resource Lifetime
requirements.text: **Portable ownership.** Register a successful temporary export or transfer under the receiving interpreter session and the resource's resolved logical directory and name in its writable resource store. Preserve the registration across RIP resets, local scene playback and resource-directory changes within that scope. Another owner's resource is identified separately even if it uses the same basename. A later same-session replacement at an already registered resource location keeps that registration until cleanup. Export attempts that fail leave the portable registry unchanged. This avoids assigning ownership of an unrelated existing resource on a failed write.

requirements.heading: Lookup order ("file override")
requirements.text: When a command or playback variable references a file by name, the terminal searches the **host directory first**, then the default `ICONS\` directory, then the icon search path entries in order; first hit wins, and an error is reported only after all tiers fail. RIPTEL.HLP states the order outright: the client "will look for these kinds of files in that directory first. If the file cannot be found, then it checks the ICONS\ directory. If the file still cannot be found, then [it] checks any additional search directories that you have defined." The macro layer documents the same resolution order for the local-playback prefixes (`$>FILE.RIP$`, `$)FILE.WAV$`, `$<FILE.BMP$`, `$(FILE.JPG$` - [5.3](5.3-local-playback.md)).
requirements.reason: Host directory changes select within the per-BBS cache. Resource and file-query fixtures verify writable host overrides and the shared read-only fallback. The native administrative API and arbitrary search paths are outside scope.

requirements.heading: Lookup order ("file override")
requirements.text: The point of the scheme is unchanged from 2.0: same-named assets from different hosts do not collide - each host's `MENU.BMP` resolves to that host's own copy, while genuinely shared assets can live once in `ICONS\`. The RIPterm manuals call this behavior "file override". Commands never carry path information - filenames are bare DOS-style names, and the terminal decides where they resolve. (Modern implementations should also treat lookups as case-insensitive, as the DOS originals inherently were - see the [connection directory model techspec](../techspecs/4.0-connection-directory-model-delta.md).)

requirements.heading: RIP_SWITCH_DIRECTORY
requirements.text: `\x1b` represents a single ESC byte, not four printable characters. Explanatory spaces are omitted on the wire. The reserve consumes four valid digits in active Base Math or one [leading period](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#period-as-a-zero-field). The collector supplies zero and begins the directory name immediately afterward. For example, `!|2\x1b.LOCAL` collects the name `LOCAL`. A period inside the reserve discards the command. [Original descriptor and staged cases](../research/issue-263-resource-query-text-boundaries.md).

requirements.heading: RIP_SWITCH_DIRECTORY
requirements.text:
1. Reject a literal empty argument, then trim leading/trailing whitespace and uppercase it.
2. If the normalized literal is exactly `$OFF$`, clear the selected host-directory name and return without creating a directory.
3. Otherwise expand text variables, then require at most 12 bytes. Reject exact `.` and `..`, and reject any of these characters: `\ : * ? + / " , ; > < = [ ] |`. Interior spaces are not independently rejected.
4. Store the resulting host-directory name and attempt to create `installation-root\name`. Creation failure is ignored; it does not roll back the selection.

requirements.heading: RIP_SWITCH_DIRECTORY
requirements.text: Normalization precedes expansion. Thus a variable that expands to `$OFF$` selects a directory literally named `$OFF$`; it does not invoke the clear sentinel. A nonempty literal that becomes empty after trimming or expansion is accepted: it clears the stored name and attempts creation of the root path. Expanded text is not uppercased a second time by this handler.

requirements.heading: Drawing Ports - What Are They?
requirements.text: A drawing port is an area where graphics can be drawn. This is much like having a tablet of paper, where each page can be drawn to individually. However, just like a tablet of paper, only the piece of paper that is on the top of the tablet can be drawn to (the current piece of paper). The same concept applies to drawing ports. At any one moment in time, there is a "current drawing port". This current port is the one that will display graphical drawing operations when they are received.
requirements.reason: The connected port table provides screen and bitmap backings, clipping, port-local state and fitted rectangle copies. PCB and port backup fixtures check live coordinates, pixel sources, clipping, overlap and restored state.

requirements.heading: Screen Drawing Ports
requirements.text: A screen drawing port is the most commonly used form of drawing ports. A screen drawing port is a port that is somewhere on top of the screen. What this means is when a graphical drawing operation occurs, it is displayed in that port and subsequently to the screen immediately. Screen drawing ports are methods of dividing up the user's screen into separate regions, of which each can be thought of as completely separate drawing areas. You can switch between them pretty much at will to draw your graphics.

requirements.heading: Screen Drawing Ports
requirements.text: As you can see, you have quite a bit of flexibility in placing your ports around on the screen. In this example, we have five ports defined on the screen. You might notice that port number 0 doesn't seem to have a rectangle associated with it. Actually, it does - it is the screen's boundary. Port number 0 is defined as the actual screen and cannot be redefined (you can alter its viewport though - see below for more details about viewports). Port 0 is always the full size of the screen. You can create your own screen ports, but port 0 is one that you cannot redefine the boundary of. This gives you the ability to always switch to port 0 to address the entire screen, but have the luxury of other ports when you only want to work with a portion of the screen.

requirements.heading: Offscreen Drawing Ports (Clipboard Ports)
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._
requirements.reason: Historical evidence, descriptive introduction or diagram scaffolding; the normative port behavior is tracked separately.

requirements.heading: Offscreen Drawing Ports (Clipboard Ports)
requirements.text: An offscreen bitmap port, otherwise known as a "clipboard port", is very much like a screen port, but it isn't actually a part of the screen. It is more like another screen that you cannot see, but one that you can still draw to. You might be asking yourself why something like this is part of RIPscrip? The answer is quite simple - they are extremely powerful! An offscreen port can be used for placing a piece of graphics data temporarily while you are showing a dialog box on the screen, only to restore the original graphics when the user clicks the "OK" button on the dialog box. The graphical data that was overwritten by the dialog box isn't deleted - it's been saved temporarily on a screen that you cannot see, but is restored to the screen when necessary. Another use of this might be if you had a very complicated scene to display, but you didn't want the user to see each little graphics operation until the entire scene was complete; switch to an offscreen bitmap port, draw your scene, then switch back to the screen and copy the offscreen port's graphics to your screen. Voila, the user sees the scene appear on his screen complete - not piecemeal!
requirements.reason: Historical evidence, descriptive introduction or diagram scaffolding; the normative port behavior is tracked separately.

requirements.heading: Offscreen Drawing Ports (Clipboard Ports)
requirements.text: There are numerous reasons why you would use offscreen ports; things like storing a bitmap that you just loaded from the hard disk onto an offscreen port so that when you paste it to the screen a large number of times, there isn't a large amount of disk activity on the user's machine. Another good example is in the situation of an online game where the screen is some kind of map, and one or more offscreen ports are used to hold small "icons", or bitmaps of game pieces. Simply copy the images from the offscreen port(s) to appropriate locations on the map and you've accomplished a rather complicated situation without adversely affecting the user's system with intense hard drive activity due to constantly loading bitmaps off the disk - the side effect, the game moves much more swiftly and with a lot less "jerkiness" due to the hard disk accesses.
requirements.reason: Historical evidence, descriptive introduction or diagram scaffolding; the normative port behavior is tracked separately.

requirements.heading: Offscreen Drawing Ports (Clipboard Ports)
requirements.text: Just like with screen drawing ports, you can select an offscreen bitmap port as the one which will receive graphical drawing operations. Selecting an offscreen port as the current port lets you draw simple graphics objects, photos and other such things to it. But remember, the graphics you draw to an offscreen port are of little value unless at some point you actually copy it to the screen so that the user can see it.

requirements.heading: Offscreen Drawing Ports (Clipboard Ports)
requirements.text: Some things cannot be done to offscreen ports. For example, you cannot place a mouse field or a clickable button on an offscreen port. The reason for this is that the mouse only has any meaning to the screen - the environment that the user interacts with. How can the user click on a button that he can't see? He can't. You also cannot place [text windows](1.4-terminal-ansi-view.md) or assign resident query expressions to offscreen ports. The 3.0.7 driver enforces the rule with its own error string ("No mouse/button fields on offscreen drawing ports"). _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._

You can work with it to your heart's content, but the user can't see the contents of it until you copy the data to the screen. As long as you keep this one fundamental concept in mind, there should be no confusion about ports.

requirements.heading: The Port Table
requirements.text:
- **Port 0 is always the screen.** It is the full size of the display, exists at all times, and cannot be created, deleted, or redefined - confirmed verbatim by the 3.0.7 driver's error strings "Can't delete graphics port #0" and "Can't create drawing port #0". You can always switch to port 0 to address the entire screen (its viewport may still be altered).
- **Ports 1-35** are user-definable - the driver rejects out-of-range numbers with "The given port number is invalid (1-35 only)". Each may be a screen sub-region or an offscreen bitmap.

requirements.heading: Ports and Coordinates
requirements.text: A port is a specific drawing area. No matter whether the port is a screen port or an offscreen bitmap port, it is still a drawing area, and as such, it has a legal number of horizontal and vertical pixels that can be drawn to. Every graphical drawing operation uses graphical coordinates with which they draw their image to the current port. For example, a circle needs to know the center point, and the radius of the circle in order to draw itself.
requirements.reason: The connected port table provides screen and bitmap backings, clipping, port-local state and fitted rectangle copies. PCB and port backup fixtures check live coordinates, pixel sources, clipping, overlap and restored state.

requirements.heading: Ports and Coordinates
requirements.text: Each port has what can be thought of as its own set of coordinates. Just like the screen where (0,0) is the upper-left corner of the screen, when a port is active (ie, current), (0,0) is the coordinate of the upper-left corner of the drawing port. If a port had a width of W and a height of H, then the lower-right coordinate would be (W-1,H-1). This holds true for all drawing ports, even offscreen bitmap ports. These are **pixel positions**. The shipped [RIP_DEFINE_PORT](#rip_define_port) and [RIP_PORT_COPY](#rip_port_copy) handlers instead use lower-right **extent boundaries** for their rectangles: width is right minus left, without adding one. A 640-pixel surface has last pixel X=639 and right boundary X=640. Do not turn a last-pixel illustration into a wire rectangle by treating both conventions as identical. _Evidence: [original driver extent/copy derivation](../research/issue-10-port-geometry.md)._

requirements.text: As you can see, each port can be thought of as its own little drawing universe, with its own set of coordinates. This makes drawing things like graphs, or showing game map windows easy - without having to make extensive calculations in the host software to figure out where things need to be placed. This is considered "port relative" coordinates.

requirements.heading: Ports and Coordinates
requirements.text: Screen ports are defined as some location on the actual screen from the upper-left corner to the lower-right corner (in the current [world coordinate](../../glossary.md) system). From this information, the width and height of the port can be easily calculated, and the physical pixel dimensions are derived and remembered.

requirements.heading: Ports and Coordinates
requirements.text: Offscreen ports are a bit different though. Since they're not part of the user's actual screen, they don't have this upper-left location on the screen. In this manner, an offscreen port is always thought of as having an upper-left corner of (0,0) and its lower-right corner as (W-1,H-1).

requirements.heading: Ports and Viewports
requirements.text: The coordinate illustrations below describe the intended port-relative model. For exact RIPtel 3.1 behavior after an explicit viewport command, the [original producer](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_viewport) stores directly converted context coordinates without adding the screen-port origin or intersecting with port bounds. [POINT uses that stored origin; PIXEL omits it](2.1-lines.md#rip_point). Newly created ports begin with their default port-sized viewport. MVP and HEADER 2048/4096 store the full screen canvas for eligible ports. requirements.heading: Ports and Viewports
requirements.text: Each drawing port has an associated viewport, or clipping rectangle. A viewport is a rectangle inside the port that defines the drawing limits inside that port. It's similar in concept to a coloring book with invisible lines. You can draw all you want, but you can't go outside the lines. If any operation would extend beyond the edge of this clipping rectangle, it will be truncated. For example, if you have a drawing port that is 100x100 pixels in size, and you define the viewport to be from (25,25) to (74,74), you would have a 50x50 drawing area right in the center of the drawing port. If you then draw a circle in the exact center of the drawing port with a radius of 60 pixels, you would have pieces of the circle that extend beyond the top, left, bottom and right borders of the viewport. What you would see would be four arcs in each corner of the viewport as in the following example:

requirements.heading: Ports and Viewports
requirements.text: You can alter the location and size of the viewport inside any given drawing port. By default, the viewport is set to the full size of the drawing port when the port is created. If you attempt to make the viewport go outside the actual port, it will be adjusted to fit so that it is completely within the port. If an attempt is made to define a viewport that is completely outside the boundary of its port, then the definition is ignored as an error condition. If the lower-right corner is outside the boundary of the port, then the lower-right corner of the newly defined viewport is set to the lower-right corner of the port itself.

requirements.heading: Ports and Viewports
requirements.text: Just like drawing ports, a viewport also "adjusts" drawing coordinates. When you alter the location of a viewport inside of a drawing port, the origin (0,0) for drawing operations relates to the upper-left corner of the viewport itself, not the actual underlying drawing port. All drawing operations pertain to a port's viewport, not the port itself. The port is considered the maximum limits for the viewport inside - just like the screen, you can only draw to areas inside the screen; the same applies to viewports and ports.

requirements.heading: Copying Data From One Port to Another
requirements.text: When you copy graphical data from one port to another (or to another location on the same port for that matter), you are duplicating the graphical contents of the source port onto the destination port. Whether the result is an exact replica of the original image or not is another matter. Whenever you copy a rectangle of data from one port to another, you need to specify a rectangle in the source port, and another one in the destination port. These two rectangles do not need to be the same pixel size. If they are different either in the width or height dimensions, then scaling of the source image will occur! requirements.text: Let's take another example but this time we will show scaling because this situation may not be intuitive. Let's assume that our source rectangle is twice as large as our destination rectangle both in the width and height dimensions. This means that our image will be reduced by 1/2. But what happens if the source image needs to be "truncated" to fit in the viewport? For this initially unequal-size copy, only the data that remains after truncation is scaled into the destination rectangle. If the destination rectangle also had to be truncated, then the scaling is still performed. In this fit branch no vertical or horizontal "blank" zone is created during scaling. requirements.heading: Copying Data From One Port to Another
requirements.text: The fit explanation above applies to initially unequal extents. Initially equal-size copies, including the zero-endpoint verbatim shorthand, use the [coupled clipping rule](#rip_port_copy) and stay unscaled. _Evidence: original DLL; [derivation](../research/issue-10-port-geometry.md)._
requirements.reason: Reconciled with adopted PR #71 / issue-10 port geometry. 2C projects WORLD boundaries once in wide arithmetic, resolves all-zero source/destination and destination zero-ending forms after projection, and gives full-destination precedence. Half-open extents choose equal/unscaled versus unequal/fit before clipping; equal copies trim counterpart far boundaries together, unequal copies clip independently. Wholly external operands and undefined/inactive ports do not copy. Protection permits source/destination content operations; protection, current selection and metadata are retained. Independent literal geometry/RGB captures on all canvases cover both source kinds, both axes, source/destination clipping, explicit/synthesized equal extents, fit/full-view precedence, overlap and all five indexed modes. A 25920-copy width/origin matrix covers screen/offscreen destinations; both bases/widths 2..5 cover projected-zero forms. Canonical literals, reserved lengths 0..5, huge unequal/equal projected boundaries, parser recovery, and fit/unscaled snapshot failure are checked. Full-color device/ROP semantics and active application integration remain separate implementation work; complete PORT_COPY compliance is not claimed.

requirements.heading: Copying Data From One Port to Another
requirements.text: **Ownership clarification (RIPtel 3.1):** each port exclusively owns its graphics-text cursor and image rectangle/flags. STYLE switches do not copy or restore these fields, and PORT switches do not select another style. See the [alternating-switch example](7.1-data-tables.md#graphical-style-table) and [PORT backup cursor exception](7.2-data-backup-areas.md#drawing-port-table-save-area). _Evidence: [original selectors and backup derivation](../research/issue-24-drawing-state-ownership.md)._
requirements.reason: Graphics cursor and image fields live exclusively in each PORT; STYLE owns font/drawing attributes, ENV owns color-mode/mouse fields. The external text binding now carries only encoding and an immutable font override. Alternating protected screen/offscreen ports and STYLE/ENV selections preserve independent cursor/image state; changing viewport origin does not move a stored absolute cursor. Owned PORT restore retains live cursors while restoring saved image/selection fields, matching the documented exception.

requirements.heading: Observed Usage in the 3.x Era
requirements.text: The port system is the workhorse of TeleGrafix's own 3.x demo material. The RIPtel demo corpus contains **9,104 uses of `2C` (RIP_PORT_COPY)** - by far the most frequent command after RIP_LINE - almost all of them in the WIPE00-WIPE24 "wipe" transition library: each wipe composes the next scene in an offscreen port, then reveals it with a sequence of narrow port-to-screen copies to animate slides, splits, and dissolves. The supporting pattern (define port 1 full-screen, copy the screen into it, switch, draw, copy back) appears throughout the `.FN` function scenes, with TeleGrafix's own comments narrating it: "Create a port for the status line backup area, and copy the area where the status line will go into that drawing port."

requirements.heading: Reserved port command fields
requirements.text: For `2P`, `2p` and `2C`, the reserved sender value is zero. Its full-width spelling is `0000`, `00` and `00000`, respectively. The receiver validates transmitted digits in current Base Math and supplies integer zero to the handler. A [leading period](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#period-as-a-zero-field) completes the entire reserved field in one byte.

requirements.heading: Reserved port command fields
requirements.text: A command delimiter can finish a short reserved field or complete an omitted reserved field with zero. It can also finish the shortened preceding numeric field when the reserved field is omitted. Keep at least one digit in a shortened ordinary number. A space or other invalid byte during numeric collection discards the command. Once the reserved field is complete, the ordinary [fixed-field surplus rule](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#numeric-collection-and-dispatch) applies until the delimiter. [Original descriptors and supplied captures](../research/issue-244-port-reserved-fields.md).

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE_PORT
requirements.text: The `<port-num>` parameter determines which entry in the master Port Table you wish to define. When working with ports, you need to be concerned about the port number you're working with - that's the location of the port, and that's how you access it when you need to switch ports - by port number. You are allowed up to 36 separate graphical ports (0-35 in decimal). Port #0 cannot be re-defined because it is always defined as the Screen Port. You can however, alter the viewport for Port #0 to make a sub-area on the screen to draw in (and clip). The viewport for Port #0 may also be deactivated as can the viewport on any other graphical Port. _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE_PORT
requirements.text: Port geometry uses **extent boundaries** in the current world coordinate system, without an extra inclusive pixel. For a screen port, convert both corners to device coordinates, then use `width = device_x1 - device_x0` and `height = device_y1 - device_y0`. For an offscreen port, the effective near corner is **(0,0)**: send x0=y0=0, and interpret x1/y1 as the far extent boundaries from that origin. The protocol's flag-1 rule treats supplied nonzero x0/y0 as zero; they do not reduce the requested offscreen dimensions. With equal world/device dimensions, an offscreen request (2,1)–(6,4) therefore means a **6×4** port at (0,0); its canonical form is (0,0)–(6,4). A sender needing a 4×3 port sends (0,0)–(4,3). _Evidence: ALPHA 4 §3.4.3.1, coordinate paragraph and flag-1 definition; [origin/extent derivation](../research/issue-72-define-port-contract.md#offscreen-origin-and-extents)._

requirements.text: On successful definition, initialize the viewport to cover the whole port, then apply the requested initial state. Flag 4 makes that viewport inactive; flag 8 protects the new definition; flag 2 selects the new port. These are independent postconditions, so setting protection does not prevent the same command from establishing its requested viewport state. For example, decimal flags 15 create an offscreen port that is current, has an inactive viewport and is protected. You may later change an unprotected port's viewport with [RIP_VIEWPORT](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_viewport).

requirements.text: The example above is the corpus's standard form (TELPORT.FN, FONTS.RIP, DRAGON.RIP): it requests the full **world extent** 1280×960 (`ZKQO`) with flags `0003` (offscreen + switch). There is no 641×481 extra edge and it is not a physical 1280×960 bitmap. Offscreen allocations are not clamped to the display: endpoints 2560,1920 under the same conversion create a 1280×960 bitmap, subject to the ordinary pixel budget. _Evidence: corpus for the wire example; [original allocation instructions and native observations](../research/issue-10-port-geometry.md#native-allocation-and-copy-checkpoint) for physical dimensions._

requirements.heading: Resource-failure guarantees
requirements.text: The documented protected-target rejection above is distinct from a failure to allocate a new port. The source describes unprotected replacement as deletion followed by creation, but supplies **no atomic-replacement or rollback guarantee**. An allocation failure therefore does not guarantee that the old target definition or its pixels survive. The resulting target definition, current selection and clipboard assignment after a resource failure are implementation-defined; applications cannot assume a particular recovery state.

requirements.text: **Unprotect wins within each operand:** values 1+2 (3) leave the destination unprotected; values 4+8 (12, MegaNum `0C`) leave the source unprotected. These combinations are accepted. If source and destination are the same port, destination actions happen last, so they can override source actions. A same-port command still applies all its flags. Port 0’s protection cannot be changed by any of these actions.

requirements.heading: RIP_SWITCH_PORT
requirements.text: **Failure is not transactional.** Source flags run before selection and remain applied if creation fails. Destination flags refer to the actual fallback port 0 in that case; they do not target the still-undefined requested entry or return to the old source. Port 0 ignores them. In particular, destination-unprotect cannot rescue a protected-but-undefined target: the constructor has already failed before that action runs. An out-of-range target (36 or above), or disabled graphics processing, returns before any protection writes.
requirements.reason: Between wire disable and enable, 2s and 2Y leave the source protection bit, current selection and undefined target unchanged. The same bytes after enable select and protect the target and protect the source even with the original viewport inactive.
requirements.scope: Apply the specified range and protection ordering during RIP processing. The host-accessible disable/enable condition is RIP autosense selectors 1 and 2. The private RIPtel client graphics option is outside the SyncTERM protocol contract.

requirements.text: The shipped `2s` descriptor has two fields in current Base Math. The port uses one digit and the flags use two at full width. A delimiter can finalize a one-digit flags field, and a leading period supplies flags zero. Once the flags are complete, the parser ignores surplus bytes until the delimiter. Only flag bits 1, 2, 4 and 8 select protection actions. [Original descriptor and dispatch captures](../research/issue-244-port-reserved-fields.md#reserved-collection-and-switch).
requirements.reason: Native and connected cases verify active radix, flags and reserved field boundaries, nonfatal malformed input, and port selection and copy state.

requirements.heading: RIP_SWITCH_PORT
requirements.text: With a separately fed CR, bodies `2s10`, `2s1. tail` and `2s1000` each dispatch port 1 and flags 0. The space in `2s10 comment` interrupts the flags field and discards the command. In base 64, `2s1a0` delivers port 1 and flags 2,304, and `2sa00` delivers port 36 and flags 0. Both lowercase forms fail numeric collection in base 36. The switch handler applies its port range check after dispatch.

requirements.heading: RIP_DELETE_PORT
requirements.text: This command physically deletes one or more graphical ports. The exact port depends on the `<port_num>` parameter. If the port number specified is between 1-35, then the given port is deleted (providing of course that it is unprotected). If you attempt to delete a protected port, then this command will fail. If you attempt to delete port #0 (the screen port), then you will be activating a special case of this command - all unprotected ports from 1-35 are automatically deleted. This is a good garbage collection command mode when you want to start with a new slate of ports without the overhead of sending many delete port commands.
requirements.reason: The application fixture covers protection rejection, collection of unprotected screen and bitmap ports, preserving protected resources and clearing a deleted clipboard pointer.

requirements.heading: RIP_DELETE_PORT
requirements.text: The `<dest_port>` parameter defines the port number that will be switched to after the delete operation is finished. Typically, this will be set to port #0 (switch to screen port), but it need not be. If the destination port is undefined, then it will automatically switch to port #0. If you instruct this command to delete all ports, then the destination port may or may not be set to the screen port - it all depends on whether or not the destination port both exists, and is protected - remember, a protected port cannot be deleted with this command without first being unprotected. So, if you delete all ports and switch to another port that isn't port #0, and that port is protected, then that protected port is selected as the new active port. If however, that port doesn't exist (ie, it did exist at the beginning of this command, but wasn't protected), then the screen port #0 will be selected.
requirements.reason: The live session selects a surviving protected inactive destination and falls back to 0 for an undefined or just-deleted destination.

requirements.text: This command copies graphics data from one port to another (or possibly even the same port). The area copied is a rectangular area based on the (sx0,sy0)..(sx1,sy1) parameters in the `<source_port>` and the (dx0,dy0)..(dx1,dy1) parameters in the `<dest_port>`. They may be set to the same port number which signifies that a bit-blit operation is to occur from one location of the current port to another. Both the source and destination ports are specified as port numbers from 0-35. If either port doesn't exist (or is deactivated) then this command will do nothing.

requirements.text: The following portable rules apply to both the unscaled and fit branches. Clip and select a logical source sample for each covered destination pixel, then apply the requested operation once. In a fit, a sampled pixel keeps its representation. A constant source retains its logical color, including its index or RGB representation, across the fit. If a filter synthesizes a direct RGB sample, use that as the source color. Any drawing-index lookup needed by the filter uses the palette published at the start of `2C`. The existing fit rules leave the sampling filter open. [Source and portable completion](../research/issue-233-port-copy-color-domain.md).

requirements.text: After obtaining S*/D*, preserve their correspondence while clipping raster access to the physical destination and rejecting source samples outside physical source storage. requirements.heading: Physical Storage and Sample Coverage
requirements.text: A physical source boundary can map to a fractional destination boundary. **Do not round it into Rs/Rd, derive the pair from raster coverage/counts, or substitute a backend's smaller physical blit pair.** A sampler may touch a different edge subset, and skipped samples or zero coverage need not form a useful integer pair. Even when a backend can return a coupled integer physical blit rectangle, the protocol publishes the full final logical pair. P is geometry; it does not assert that all represented pixels were initialized/written or preserve a damage/coverage layer. requirements.heading: Independent Rectangle and State Vectors
requirements.text: For lifecycle cases, save PORT with P5=A and P6 absent; later change P5 to B and establish P6=C. A successful full restore reinstates A and absence respectively, and reuse of that BASE repeats the same result. A protected live port absent from the snapshot retains its own pair. A viewport-only reset preserves A, a full SOFT clears P0 and any deleted unprotected slot but keeps a protected surviving P5, and HARD leaves every default/new pair absent. Redefining slot 5 never resurrects A; successful new creation is absent until a listed transfer succeeds. Failed replacement that retains the old definition retains A; deletion followed by allocation failure loses A, and a newly allocated target whose transfer fails is defined but has no pair. Capture's already documented pointer/current effects still apply; pair handling introduces no additional table or selection changes.

requirements.heading: RIP_PORT_WRITE
requirements.text: **Screen source:** use a half-open device rectangle. The original handler uses the decoded coordinates directly as device offsets relative to the stored viewport origin, without the ordinary world-to-device conversion. When all four coordinates are zero, copy the full stored viewport. When both ending coordinates are zero, retain the given start and use the viewport's right/bottom boundaries. Otherwise require x1>x0 and y1>y0 before clipping, then clamp the ending axes **independently** to the viewport's right and bottom. A valid ending axis is retained; neither axis expands merely because the other is outside. The old “lower-left corner” wording was incorrect: it is the **lower-right boundary** being trimmed. No extra inclusive pixel is added.

requirements.heading: RIP_PORT_WRITE
requirements.text: **Offscreen source:** the writer serializes the **entire backing bitmap**, ignoring the crop rectangle computed by the handler. Both requested partial rectangles above therefore export the whole 8×4 bitmap when that is its actual allocation. A 10×6 backing bitmap with an 8×4 viewport exports 10×6. This is a shipped omission, not a rule that all ports crop identically. An explicitly nonzero rectangle failing the handler's x1>x0/y1>y0 check still rejects before reaching the writer.
requirements.reason: The live decoder collects flags and the required ignored reserved field separately. Bit value 1 records a successful export for disconnect cleanup. A failed export preserves the prior file and registration. Flags leave screen crop and offscreen backing geometry intact.

requirements.heading: RIP_PORT_WRITE
requirements.text: **Inactive/protected/undefined source:** the command tests definition, but never tests the stored viewport-deactivated bit or rejects a protected defined source. A defined deactivated source still exports its stored screen rectangle or whole offscreen bitmap and replaces the output file. An undefined source reports `Drawing port is not in use` and returns before opening/replacing the file. An explicit empty rectangle likewise diagnoses and leaves the old file unchanged. Export does not change current-port selection, stored geometry, protection or cursor state. The native probe checks labeled output pixels, dimensions and a pre-existing file sentinel with RAM-only file services; no real file is replaced during verification.

requirements.heading: Data Tables - A Fundamental Concept
requirements.text: RIPscrip 2.0 was different from its previous versions architecturally on a number of levels, and one of the key fundamental differences - the data table - carries into 3.x unchanged. _(v2.A1)_
requirements.reason: Provenance, chapter navigation or explanatory example. The table operations have separate requirements.

requirements.heading: Data Tables - A Fundamental Concept
requirements.text: A data table is a table of information used in RIPscrip. Data tables may be the color palette table (where each table entry is a complete color palette definition), graphical style tables, button style tables, [drawing port](7.0-drawing-ports.md) tables, text window definition tables, mouse field tables, or environment data tables. Some data tables have an entry that is "currently active". This might be the currently active text window in the text window data table, or the currently active color palette in the palette data table. Every data table has one or more entries in it, in which each entry is a specific piece of data. Data table entries can be "in use" and/or protected (see below). _(v2.A3)_
requirements.reason: Table dispatch distinguishes the six numbered live families, mouse fields and whole-table saves. Query, protection, copy, error and reset vectors exercise the applicable selectors and special handling of entry zero.

requirements.heading: Data Tables - A Fundamental Concept
requirements.text: Data can be moved from one table entry to another (in effect, making a copy of one table entry to another); this doesn't apply to all data tables (eg, mouse field data table). Also, most tables' entries can be protected so that the contents of a particular entry cannot be modified or deleted until either an unprotect entry function is executed, or a hard reset is performed (a hard reset completely resets the entire RIPscrip environment to ground zero). Again the mouse field data table cannot have individual entries protected. _(v2.A4)_
requirements.reason: Table dispatch distinguishes the six numbered live families, mouse fields and whole-table saves. Query, protection, copy, error and reset vectors exercise the applicable selectors and special handling of entry zero.

requirements.heading: Data Tables - A Fundamental Concept

Entry contents survive until overwritten, cleared by a reset, or removed by a hard reset. _Evidence: HLP._

requirements.heading: Entry 0 - the Common Modifiable Entry
requirements.text: Entry 0 of each table is special: it is the always-present working entry that **cannot be deleted or protected**. The driver enforces this per table - "Cannot protect current text window slot when it is #0", "Can't protect environment data table entry #0", "Can't protect graphics style data table entry zero", "Can't protect color palette zero", and for ports, "Can't delete graphics port #0". Entry 0 is thus the common, freely modifiable entry every scene can rely on; protection is reserved for entries 1-35.

requirements.heading: Types of Data Tables
requirements.text: There are six different data tables for general data storage: the drawing port table, color palette table, graphical style table, text window table, the button style table and the RIPscrip environment data table. There are backup areas for these data tables so you can make complete backup copies for re-use later after some operation is performed (eg, executing a dialog box, running a door, etc). There are actually more data backup areas than there are data tables - see [7.2 Data Backup Areas](7.2-data-backup-areas.md). _(v2.A4)_
