requirements.heading: Drawing Port Table
requirements.text: One of the most fundamental aspects of the language is the concept of a [drawing port](7.0-drawing-ports.md). Any drawing of graphics occurs inside a drawing port. There may be up to 36 ports [defined](7.0-drawing-ports.md#rip_define_port) simultaneously. Port number 0 is always defined as the screen. Its dimensions are that of the screen. The remaining 35 ports may be sub-sections of the screen or may be offscreen memory drawing ports (ie, clipboard ports). At any one moment in time, only one port may be the current port - the port that will receive graphical drawing operations. If the current port is an offscreen clipboard port, then any drawing operations will not appear on the screen. The only way that those graphics can be viewed by the user is if the contents of the port are copied to a screen port. _(v2.A3)_
requirements.reason: Port definitions resolve world geometry to device bounds. Selection routes drawing to a screen or offscreen surface and preserves fixed and floating query state according to their different lifetimes.

requirements.heading: Drawing Port Table
requirements.text: All ports, when defined, are defined using the current [world coordinate](../../glossary.md) system. From those coordinates, the port's actual physical pixel dimensions are determined and those dimensions are remembered by the port. Any graphical operation that bypasses the viewport system pays close attention to coordinates and the boundaries of the drawing port. If any coordinate would go outside of the port, it is adjusted to fit inside. _(v2.A4)_
requirements.reason: Port definitions resolve world geometry to device bounds. Selection routes drawing to a screen or offscreen surface and preserves fixed and floating query state according to their different lifetimes.

requirements.heading: Drawing Port Table
requirements.text: Each port entry remembers its own drawing state - the full list is in [7.0](7.0-drawing-ports.md#the-port-table). The entire drawing port data table also keeps track of the "current viewport" query expression (otherwise known as a floating viewport query). _(v2.A4)_
requirements.reason: Port definitions resolve world geometry to device bounds. Selection routes drawing to a screen or offscreen surface and preserves fixed and floating query state according to their different lifetimes.

requirements.heading: Color Palette Table
requirements.text: In RIPscrip there is a graphical color palette. The color palette is a group of 256 separate color RGB values, also known as a color lookup table. This color palette is used to map a particular color number to some combination of red, green and blue color components. For example, color 0 is usually black (no red, green or blue), and color 255 is typically white (full intensity red, green and blue). This color palette is normally written directly into the video hardware of your computer to activate the colors. So when you try to draw in color 255, you see a white line appear on the screen. _(v2.A3)_
requirements.reason: Palette records have independent values and defined/protected flags. The connected reset retains selection and restores eligible entries.

requirements.heading: Color Palette Table
requirements.text: Up to 36 separate color palettes may be held at once. Only one entry in the color palette table may be current at any one moment in time. An entry in the color palette table is a complete 256 color palette. When you switch from one color palette entry to another, the colors on the screen will typically change instantly. This gives you the ability to quickly and easily switch from one color scheme to another without sending a large amount of information to the terminal every time you wish to switch color schemes. _(v2.A3)_
requirements.reason: Palette records have independent values and defined/protected flags. The connected reset retains selection and restores eligible entries.

requirements.heading: Color Palette Table
requirements.text: The language allows for two forms of color modes, color palette mapping mode (the default) and direct RGB color encoding - see [2.0 Color Modes & Palettes](2.0-color-modes-and-palettes.md). Under 24-bit configurations, a real hardware color palette is not possible; the palette is used as an RGB lookup table for subsequent drawing, and switching palettes will not change colors already on the screen. _(v2.A3)_
requirements.reason: The indexed backend republishes palette entries for indexed pixels. Direct RGB pixels retain their color across palette edits and uploads, as demonstrated in the connected reset fixture.

requirements.heading: Palette reset lifecycle
requirements.text: A slot's RGB values, defined/in-use state, protection and current selection are distinct. Selecting an unused palette defaults its RGB values and marks it defined. Resetting it restores RGB defaults and clears the nonzero slot's definition flag. It does not automatically change its current index or make another palette current. Slot zero remains defined and unprotectable.
requirements.reason: Palette reset now separates RGB defaults, in-use status, protection and current selection. Specific/current reset rejects protection; TBL skips protected slots and preserves selection, including undefined-but-current. All reset selectors and needed live/backup bindings validate before mutation. Base, numbered slots, stack and aggregate backup clearing preserve protected numbered saves. Live PAL COPY prevalidates all destinations, permits protected sources and copies protection except to zero. A selected-slot RGB view permits drawing, bitmap/image consumers and coherent capture without implicitly defining the slot; numeric and CUR protection reports remain distinct. Native independent cases cover all 36 slots, soft/hard table services, malformed/mixed/protected/self-copy rejection, named/aggregate save clearing, missing services, empty output capacity, nonfatal recovery and all-canvas wire drawing/status/capture. Whole-scene resets/headers, other live-entry copy/reset families and application routing remain pending.

requirements.heading: Palette reset lifecycle
requirements.text: Live-entry [`COPY`](5.1-text-variables.md#live-entry-copy-validation-and-protection) rejects an undefined source or any protected destination before modifying any destination. PAL/STYLE/TW/ENV copies carry source protection into writable nonzero destinations; BUT copies instead clear destination protection. Copies to zero always leave zero unprotected. Whole-table backup restoration has its own saved-state/protection rules.
requirements.reason: All five allowed live-entry COPY families are connected to session-owned tables, including TW numeric/CUR source/destinations. Validate defined source and every target, reject self/range/protection/mixed backup targets before mutation; retain current selection and permit duplicate writable targets. TW carries definition/protection except zero unprotected and independently owns resident queries without execution; floating TW and PORT queries stay in their existing scopes. Native window copies use existing definition capsules and raster views, preserving connection ANSI syntax and copying no cells/pixels/history. Resource failures after permission validation do not promise rollback: query OOM leaves a copied record with an empty query; a native helper failure is diagnosed privately and later destinations continue. Native tests cover independent queries, source/protection/current/zero/repeated targets, invalid late targets and injected helper/query failures. CP437/UTF8 TCP vectors at640x480,800x600,1024x768 and720x400 exercise literal COPY(TW,3,5), COPY(TW,CUR,5,7,9), current/zero/repeated targets, native fonts/geometry/attributes/cursors/tabs/margins/wrap/activation, unchanged planes at COPY, literal RGB output and retained partial ANSI parsing. This accepts COPY grammar/adapters and represented record/query transfer behavior; it does not declare unfinished charset/ESC7/8, full PORT payload/PCB, startup font policy, live TW reset or HEADER complete. Earlier independent evidence for the other COPY families is retained.

Flag 128 additionally has an invalid current-sentinel guard; see the [corrected header contract](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#button-graphics-style-palette-and-environment-flags). Do not use those flags as a substitute for PAL reset.
requirements.reason: HEADER uploads use the selected palette contents and the current-sentinel guard. Indexed pixels and a direct-color pixel are checked through a live connection.

requirements.heading: Graphical Style Table
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A1. Evidence: DLL; [ownership/default derivation](../research/issue-24-drawing-state-ownership.md). The following corrects the inherited 2.00a4 ownership lists for RIPtel 3.1._
requirements.reason: Provenance, chapter navigation or explanatory example. The table operations have separate requirements.

requirements.heading: Graphical Style Table
requirements.text: There are 36 graphical style entries. Initially, entry 0 is current. Each entry owns drawing/background/fill colors, fill pattern and user rows, line pattern/thickness/user mask/odd rule, write mode, border setting, classic font/size/direction/justification, and the [extended font fields](3.0-text-output-and-fonts.md#rip_extended_font_style).
requirements.reason: The fixed record has solid fill and line selectors, zero stored fill rows and user line mask, and a transparent gap policy. Copy and backup own those values. Wire draws after first use, replacement, reset and restore check the effective patterns.

requirements.heading: Graphical Style Table
requirements.text: **Drawing X/Y and image style belong exclusively to ports. Color mode and mouse pointer number belong exclusively to environments.** These are not additional copies in the style record. Changing style does not capture, restore or alter them; changing port does not select a different style. Environment selection does not select a different style or port either.
requirements.reason: Graphics cursor and image fields live exclusively in each PORT; STYLE owns font/drawing attributes, ENV owns color-mode/mouse fields. The external text binding now carries only encoding and an immutable font override. Alternating protected screen/offscreen ports and STYLE/ENV selections preserve independent cursor/image state; changing viewport origin does not move a stored absolute cursor. Owned PORT restore retains live cursors while restoring saved image/selection fields, matching the documented exception.

requirements.heading: Graphical Style Table
requirements.text: For example, give port 1 cursor (10,20)/image A under style 1, then port 2 cursor (30,40)/image B under style 2. Switching only to style 1 leaves port 2 active with (30,40)/B. From port 2/style 2, switching only to port 1 exposes (10,20)/A while retaining style 2. There is no last-switch-wins conflict between duplicate cursor/image records. [Backups](7.2-data-backup-areas.md#graphical-style-table-save-area) follow the same ownership, with specific restore defects noted there.
requirements.reason: STYLE selection leaves port cursor, image style and environment independent.

requirements.heading: Button Style Table
requirements.text: Button style data table entries contain a complete button style definition as defined by a [RIP_BUTTON_STYLE](4.3-buttons.md#rip_button_style) command. Having multiple button style slots defined at the same time allows you to have many commonly used button styles defined at once, so that you can simply reference an already defined button style rather than having to transmit a rather lengthy button style command each and every time you wish to define a button.
requirements.reason: Button slots own independent style definitions. First-use and reset metadata follow the completed button-table rules; retained styles feed connected button rendering.

requirements.heading: Button Style Table
requirements.text: RIPtel 3.1 initially selects slot 0 and defines only that slot; all 36 records hold the same fixed PLAIN+BEVEL default. Selecting an undefined slot installs that default, rather than copying the previous style. The [complete default fields and reset behavior](4.3-buttons.md#initial-and-reset-style) include the shipped current-reset metadata corruption; [auto-clip](4.3-buttons.md#rip_button_style) can also mutate the current style's flags even when protected. _Evidence: original initialization, selection, reset and rendering; [derivation](../research/issue-27-button-style-contract.md)._
requirements.reason: Button slots own independent style definitions. First-use and reset metadata follow the completed button-table rules; retained styles feed connected button rendering.

requirements.heading: Button Style Table
requirements.text: Explicit `1B` definition marks the current button-style slot in use even after a specific/table reset left it undefined. Those resets retain the current index; outer SOFT separately selects 0. A later first-use selection replaces an undefined record with fixed defaults and clears protection, while selecting a defined record preserves both. See the [complete state/query tables and sequences](4.3-buttons.md#undefined-current-slots-and-first-use-selection), including the explicitly completed inconsistent metadata case and numeric-versus-CUR ISPROT distinction. _Evidence: original definition/selection/query consumers and [derivation](../research/issue-112-undefined-button-style.md)._
requirements.reason: A valid 1B defines the currently selected button style after reset.

requirements.heading: Text Window Table
requirements.text: A [text window](1.4-terminal-ansi-view.md) is simply a region on the screen where raw, non-RIPscrip text is routed once it is received from the host. Initially, the text window is full screen, using the MicroANSI font #2 (80x25) - different from 1.54, whose initial setting was font #0 (80x43); 80x25 is more aesthetically pleasing to most people so it was made the default. A text window typically supports ANSI and VT-102 screen control codes. Each of the 36 text window table entries stores:
requirements.work_group: Connection mode and default MicroANSI font
requirements.scope: RIP connection startup text-window geometry and font. VT-102 and terminal emulator choices are outside this requirement.
requirements.reason: SyncTERM starts with the entry’s terminal mode and supplies MicroANSI 0 for newly defaulted RIP windows. The choice of the initial text window versus the connection mode remains deferred by the user.

requirements.heading: Text Window Table
requirements.text:
- The upper-left and lower-right corner definitions for the text window (coordinates are in text coordinates, not graphical screen coordinates).
- The MicroANSI screen font number for the given window.
- The current ANSI color attributes
- The current cursor X/Y location
- The status of the cursor (is it on or off)
- The current vertical scrolling margins (ANSI formatting)
- Whether the window is activated or deactivated.
requirements.reason: Selection and redefinition apply window geometry, cursors, activation, font and colors. Deactivated windows suppress ordinary terminal text. Definitions and backups exclude previously painted pixels.

requirements.heading: Text Window Table
requirements.text: A text window can also be deactivated. If the current text window slot is deactivated then any raw text that is received from the host will be discarded (ie, not shown on screen at all). _(v2.A4)_
requirements.reason: Selection and redefinition apply window geometry, cursors, activation, font and colors. Deactivated windows suppress ordinary terminal text. Definitions and backups exclude previously painted pixels.

requirements.heading: Text Window Table
requirements.text: Having multiple defined text windows allows you to quickly switch from one text window configuration to another without losing any previously used information (color, location, cursor, etc). Note that the text contained inside the current text window is not stored as part of the text window definition - only the window's raw definition is preserved. See [1.4 Terminal & ANSI View](1.4-terminal-ansi-view.md) for the extended (resolution-independent) text window added in the 3.x era.
requirements.reason: Selection and redefinition apply window geometry, cursors, activation, font and colors. Deactivated windows suppress ordinary terminal text. Definitions and backups exclude previously painted pixels.

requirements.heading: Text Window Table
requirements.text: The [live TW reset contract](5.1-text-variables.md#live-text-window-reset-contract) distinguishes fresh slot-zero state from nonzero deletion, protected survival and existing-zero selection. Numeric/CUR/TBL reset retains independent backups and the floating TW query; ALL additionally deletes TW backups. Fixed queries belong to applied entry definitions; connection parsing and the entry screen raster remain separate.
requirements.reason: Live RESET(TW) is bound through actual connections. Complete syntax/binding validation precedes mutations; CUR resolves left to right, per-target failures diagnose privately and continue, including ALL backup deletion. Forced zero replacement uses the existing fresh default-window constructor without painting; applied nonzero deletion selects existing zero only when current. Protected/undefined targets, fixed versus floating queries and independent backups follow the completed profile. Native injected resource failures/five configured font geometries plus coherent CP437/UTF8 connection state/pixel/parser checks cover the stated operation. Separate charset, larger ESC7/8 and startup-font-policy source units remain pending; this acceptance does not claim the entire fresh-state profile or other RESET families complete.

requirements.heading: Environment Table
requirements.text: The environment data table is a central table for the maintenance of critical values that define the characteristics of the RIPscrip environment. This data table holds up to 36 separate environments. For RIPtel 3.1, world dimensions, Base Math, coordinate width, RGB precision and mouse pointer number belong to the environment. The [local playback rate](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#live-playback-rate-and-env-state) is one live value outside the table, so activating a slot leaves it in effect. **Current STYLE, BUT, PORT, TW and PAL selections are separate state:** the driver's environment selector does not save or restore those selections, their records, or mouse fields. The draft's proposed whole-context-swap example is not the shipped behavior. _Evidence: DLL; [activation derivation](../research/issue-24-drawing-state-ownership.md#ownership-and-switching-observations)._

requirements.heading: Environment Table
requirements.text: Wire color-mode and mouse-pointer commands check the current **environment's** protection, independently of the current style's protection. A protected style does not block those changes, and neither change modifies the style. [`COLORMODE`](5.1-text-variables.md#colormode) can edit an already defined noncurrent environment without changing active mode; the new value becomes active when that environment is selected. Both that variable and [`MCURSOR`](5.1-text-variables.md#mcursor) bypass environment protection. COMPAT also bypasses protection and uses its own current and numbered eligibility rules. [COMPAT](5.1-text-variables.md#compat).
requirements.reason: Native selector checks and connected vectors cover protected and undefined targets, live versus stored format, and retained playback rate.

requirements.heading: Environment Table
requirements.text: **Environment activation order and defect:** the selector reads the target's Base Math, RGB precision and coordinate width, invokes their active setters, activates target world dimensions, requests a mouse refresh if the number differs, and finally changes the current environment index. Because those first three setters run before the index changes, they also overwrite the **departing environment's** Base Math, RGB precision and coordinate width, even if it is protected. They do not overwrite its saved world dimensions or mouse number. Target protection does not prohibit selection.
requirements.reason: CUR(ENV,n) and fixed-two-current-base-digit wire2E share protocol activation through the actual session-owned table. Unused targets take basic defaults; target mode fields overwrite the departing record before selection, bypassing protection but retaining its WORLD/pointer/baud. Existing native refresh reads the new current pointer. Other table selections/ANSI state/pixels/raster stay live. Numeric/CUR ENV entry COPY validates source and every destination before any mutation, carries source protection except to zero, defines targets, retains selection and permits repeated destinations. Native literal state/copy/split/failure tests and connected CP437/UTF8 expectations cover all presets/custom, protected/default/bypass cases, real plotted coordinates/pointer metadata, nonzero backups and zero-WORLD/error recovery. Header and other unfinished families remain separate; no ordinary text or RIP154 path changes.

requirements.heading: Environment Table
requirements.text: For example, start with environment 0 = base 36, two-character coordinates, palette mode, world 640×480, cursor 2; environment 5 = base 64, four-character coordinates, RGB 8, world 1280×960, cursor 6. Switching 0 → 5 activates 5's values and leaves every other table's current selection unchanged. Switching back to 0 activates **base 64 / width 4 / RGB 8**, because 0's three fields were overwritten, but restores **640×480 / cursor 2**, whose stored values survived. Mouse presentation uses the newly current environment at its next refresh. Implementations targeting this client must distinguish this sequencing defect from independent, correctly preserved records.
requirements.reason: CUR(ENV,n) and fixed-two-current-base-digit wire2E share protocol activation through the actual session-owned table. Unused targets take basic defaults; target mode fields overwrite the departing record before selection, bypassing protection but retaining its WORLD/pointer/baud. Existing native refresh reads the new current pointer. Other table selections/ANSI state/pixels/raster stay live. Numeric/CUR ENV entry COPY validates source and every destination before any mutation, carries source protection except to zero, defines targets, retains selection and permits repeated destinations. Native literal state/copy/split/failure tests and connected CP437/UTF8 expectations cover all presets/custom, protected/default/bypass cases, real plotted coordinates/pointer metadata, nonzero backups and zero-WORLD/error recovery. Header and other unfinished families remain separate; no ordinary text or RIP154 path changes.

requirements.heading: Environment Table
requirements.text: A [live ENV reset](5.1-text-variables.md#live-style-and-env-reset-contract) retains the current index. The portable profile activates defaults if the selected entry is reset, even when the reset clears that entry’s definition.
requirements.reason: Live ENV reset retains selection and activates defaults immediately even when it clears definition.

requirements.heading: Environment Table
requirements.text: Each ENV also stores a [legacy character-set override](5.1-text-variables.md#dcs), initialized to inherited. The [SDCS fallback](5.1-text-variables.md#sdcs) is one instance value shared across the ENV table.

requirements.heading: Environment Table
requirements.text: The environment table is central to the 3.x backup/dialog system: HLP confirms the 36 slots, the unprotectable slot #0, the `$SENV$`/`$RENV$` backup variables, and environment header segments carrying coordinate-size and RGB-bit settings (below). _Evidence: HLP._
requirements.reason: Environment selection, protection, backup and scene reset use the session family bindings. HEADER and HARD share the live reset path.

requirements.heading: Mouse Field Table
requirements.text: The mouse field data table is unlike the other data tables. It can hold up to 128 separate mouse field definitions and does not have a "current mouse field" entry number. Each mouse field that is defined gets added to the mouse field data table at the very end until 128 fields are defined, or the table is deleted and things start over. Mouse fields only pertain to drawing port #0, so they can only be on the screen, not on an offscreen drawing port. See [RIP_MOUSE](4.2-mouse-fields-and-pointer.md#rip_mouse), [RIP_BUTTON_STYLE](4.3-buttons.md#rip_button_style) and [RIP_BUTTON](4.3-buttons.md#rip_button) for more details on this special data table.
requirements.reason: The append-ordered mouse field table holds 128 entries and uses screen geometry. Field dispatch binds numeric identity for action expansion.

requirements.heading: Mouse Field Table
requirements.text: The [portable INUSE live aggregates](5.1-text-variables.md#live-mouse-aggregates) query this shared pool. ANY tests for a resident simple field or mouse-active button, and ALL tests for 128 combined members.
requirements.reason: Live MOUSE counts the existing shared mouse field and button pool even when scene gates are set. CP437 and UTF-8 tests cover empty to full occupancy, nonmouse decorations, deleting a member, saved state, and invalid numbered selectors.

requirements.heading: Mouse Field Table

requirements.heading: Scene Header Segments and Table State
requirements.text: [`RIP_HEADER`](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#rip_header) supplies typed operations for button/style/port/text-window/palette/environment tables, mouse fields, audio and the screen. The reference now gives the byte grammar, current versus supplied-slot operations, reset/backup/protection effects, validation defects and checked examples. Table segments run in wire order after global header operations; they do not declare new table dimensions. Audio is a single stop action. A malformed character-set descriptor is also present but has no consistently usable standalone wire framing. The demos’ explicit prologue commands remain valid alternatives.
requirements.reason: Segment decoding and session dispatch apply typed operations in order after the global flags. Invalid descriptors recover at RIP framing boundaries.

requirements.heading: Protected Data Table Entries
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._
requirements.reason: Provenance, chapter navigation or explanatory example. The table operations have separate requirements.

requirements.heading: Protected Data Table Entries
requirements.text: Data table entries by themselves have quite a bit of usefulness in short-term situations where a lot of different configurations need to be switched between fairly often. Their usefulness becomes even more powerful with the concept of protected data table entries. A protected entry is one that cannot be cleared by a normal reset operation or a clear table entry operation until the entry is unprotected, or until a "hard reset" operation is performed. In addition, they cannot be modified while they are protected (see below). _(v2.A1)_
requirements.reason: Table dispatch distinguishes the six numbered live families, mouse fields and whole-table saves. Query, protection, copy, error and reset vectors exercise the applicable selectors and special handling of entry zero.

requirements.heading: Protected Data Table Entries
requirements.text: A "hard reset" is a complete reset of the RIPscrip environment. Typically, a hard reset should only be performed immediately after connection to a RIPscrip compatible host system to clear the slate so to speak. Other uses for a hard reset are when the RIPscrip environment is hopelessly corrupted due to line noise, or when a complete re-synchronization of the environment is about to commence. _(v2.A1)_
requirements.reason: Environment selection, protection, backup and scene reset use the session family bindings. HEADER and HARD share the live reset path.

requirements.heading: Protected Data Table Entries
requirements.text: Protected entries become quite powerful when you look at a larger host system. For example, let's say that throughout your system you use five different graphical style configurations all over the place, all of which require quite a bit of transmitted RIPscrip code. If you define each of these styles as separate entries and then protect them, you don't need to re-transmit those blocks of data again unless a hard reset operation is performed! This can mean quite a bit of saved data transmission, and consequently faster transmission times. The same concept applies to text windows, ports, button styles, graphics style, palette and environment tables. When taken from a system-wide perspective, where many sections of the system may be made by other manufacturers (eg, doors, BBS modules, etc), you may not be able to count on whether a section of the system uses one style or another, or does one kind of reset or another. Having protected entries gives you the ability to protect your data configurations so that these sub-sections do not destroy your data. When you return from the sub-section, simply re-activate your table configuration(s) and away you go. _(v2.A1)_
requirements.reason: Provenance, chapter navigation or explanatory example. The table operations have separate requirements.

requirements.heading: Protected Data Table Entries
requirements.text: We just described that a protected data table entry cannot be deleted. We also mentioned that they cannot be modified. Let's clarify what we mean by not modifiable. A data table entry that is protected cannot be modified by any of the normal RIPscrip commands or [text variables](5.1-text-variables.md) that alter their basic configuration (eg, you cannot alter the foreground drawing color in a protected graphical style data table entry, etc). It should be noted however, that normal drawing operations like rectangles, circles, etc, can still be performed to a port that is protected. In this case, the port is protected from having its "configuration" modified (eg, the viewport cannot be modified nor can the actual port's orientation). The same applies to text windows (eg, you can output text to a text window, perform ANSI/VT-102 operations to it, erase it, etc, but you cannot redefine it or delete it). One tiny exception rests with text windows that support VT-102. VT-102 has an ANSI escape sequence that allows you to alter the wrap/chop setting of text windows. Since ANSI operations are allowed on protected text windows, this is permissible even though it seemingly violates the nature of modifying a text window's protected status. _(v2.A4)_
requirements.reason: Table protection gates configuration edits. Drawing, supported window output, outer resets and selective HEADER operations follow their own protected-entry rules.
requirements.scope: RIP table protection on drawing, window output and configuration. Terminal escape semantics are owned by SyncTERM.

requirements.heading: Protected Data Table Entries
requirements.text: Terminal emulation modes are also unaffected by a text window's protection status. If a text window is enabled, VT-102 mode can be turned on or off because this is a "global" setting, not a text window specific setting. Also, RIPscrip processing can be disabled via a special ANSI escape sequence ([1.1](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md)). This does not affect protection of text windows or drawing ports either. _(v2.A4)_
requirements.reason: Global terminal emulation policy belongs to SyncTERM. RIP enablement is covered by the stream controls in chapter 1.1.

requirements.heading: Protected Data Table Entries
requirements.text: With these things in mind, performing operations like "copying a port's data to another port" where one or both are protected is allowable because you are not altering the basic configuration of the ports in question, you are simply altering their data contents. This applies to "clipboard" related commands too which might dynamically pick and choose ports to define. Since a clipboard related command will auto-define a new port if one doesn't already exist, it will pick a currently undefined drawing port and define it (if it's not defined, then it cannot be protected). _(v2.A4)_
requirements.reason: Copying image content and assigning a clipboard use the port-specific rules. The clipboard vectors cover selection of free slots among defined and protected entries, exhaustion and assigned-port replacement.

requirements.heading: Protected Data Table Entries
requirements.text: The 3.0.7 driver's PROTECT machinery is confirmed by its error strings, including the entry-0 exclusions listed above, and by the `$PROTECT$`/`$ISPROT$`/`$UNPROT$`-family text-variable processors present in its string table. _Evidence: HLP._
requirements.reason: Table dispatch distinguishes the six numbered live families, mouse fields and whole-table saves. Query, protection, copy, error and reset vectors exercise the applicable selectors and special handling of entry zero.

requirements.heading: Table switch wire fields and protection
requirements.text: [RIP_SWITCH_PALETTE](2.0-color-modes-and-palettes.md#rip_switch_palette), [RIP_SWITCH_ENVIRONMENT](#rip_switch_environment), [RIP_SWITCH_TEXT_WINDOW](1.4-terminal-ansi-view.md#rip_switch_text_window) and [RIP_SWITCH_STYLE](#rip_switch_style) each collect one target digit followed by two flags digits in active Base Math. The target and flags are both required. A leading period supplies zero for either field. The delimiter also finalizes a nonempty [shortened flags field](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#parameters). After both fields complete, surplus bytes are ignored until the delimiter.
requirements.reason: The live decoder collects one slot digit and up to two final flag digits in active Base Math. Period supplies zero for either required field and complete fields admit surplus. The switch applies source protect and unprotect, selects the entry, then applies destination protect and unprotect. Protect-zero is diagnosed without interrupting the sequence.

requirements.heading: RIP_SWITCH_STYLE
requirements.text: **Domain and suppression:** valid STYLE numbers are 0–35 (`0`–`Z` in either base). A decoded destination at least 36 is ignored before either protection pair or selection, without a range diagnostic from this command. Thus UltraNum `!|2Ya01` (destination 36) leaves the current STYLE and all protection bits unchanged; it does not protect the old current slot. When global graphics processing is disabled, the command similarly performs no STYLE selection/protection changes. This is a global processing gate, distinct from an inactive viewport.
requirements.reason: Between wire disable and enable, 2s and 2Y leave the source protection bit, current selection and undefined target unchanged. The same bytes after enable select and protect the target and protect the source even with the original viewport inactive.

requirements.heading: RIP_SWITCH_STYLE
requirements.text: This command selects one of 36 graphical styles (0–35, encoded 0–Z). It activates the [style-owned attributes and defaults](#graphical-style-table); it does not switch ports or environments and does not restore a graphics cursor, image style, color mode or mouse pointer.

requirements.heading: RIP_SWITCH_STYLE
requirements.text: **First-use correction:** RIPtel 3.1 initializes an unused destination from the fixed default record, not by copying the current style as the 2.00a4 draft claims. [`CUR(STYLE,n)`](5.1-text-variables.md#cur) uses the same selector and the same defaults. Use explicit [`COPY`](5.1-text-variables.md#copy) to duplicate a defined current style into another slot. Subsequent selections of a defined style preserve its stored attributes; selecting a protected style is allowed. _Evidence: original wire handler/selector and all 35 unused-slot cases in the [derivation](../research/issue-24-drawing-state-ownership.md)._
requirements.reason: STYLE and BUT live-entry COPY are connected to session-owned tables. Full destination preflight rejects undefined source, range, self and raw protected targets before mutation, including late and protected-undefined targets; duplicate writable destinations are valid. STYLE carries source protection except at zero; BUT marks destinations defined/unprotected. Selection is retained and copies into current are immediately consumed. Native independent tests compare every represented value, ownership and error state. CP437/UTF8 TCP vectors at640x480,800x600,1024x768 and720x400 assert actual copied drawing/fill colors, button dimensions/face/hotkey action, other selectors/cursor/rendition/pixels and nonfatal recovery. STYLE defaults are checked for all35 first-use entries. This accepts the COPY adapter/record behavior, not a full STYLE attribute or RIP3 compliance inventory.

requirements.heading: Data Backup Areas
requirements.text: A data backup area is a backup area that composes one base save area and ten data save regions for specific data table types. The data save regions are broken collectively up as a set of individually addressable data save slots (like an array in most programming languages), and a data save stack. Each data backup area can contain up to eleven separate, complete data tables of one particular type - one in the base save area, and up to ten other data tables in the data save slots or the data save stack, or in some combination of the two (save slots or stack).
requirements.reason: The shared backup service implements the base area, ten shared slot/stack positions, protection, consume/retain rules and independent family ownership. COPY and aggregate tests cover full capacity, transfers between locations and restore semantics.

requirements.heading: Data Backup Areas
requirements.text: The 3.0.7 driver confirms all three mechanisms directly: the `$SAVE0$`-`$SAVE9$` / `$RESTORE0$`-`$RESTORE9$` slot variables and the slot-less `$SAVE$`/`$RESTORE$` pair in RIPTEL.HLP's variable tables, stack PUSH/POP via the RIPSCRIP.HLP error strings **"No slots available for PUSH"** and **"No stack to pop"**, and per-object save/restore of button styles, graphics styles, text windows, palettes, mouse fields, environments, ports, and screens. _Evidence: HLP._
requirements.reason: Layout, provenance, motivation or illustration of the separately tracked backup lifecycle/capacity operations.

requirements.heading: Data Backup Areas
requirements.text: Each data backup area can store only one particular type of [data table](7.1-data-tables.md). For example, the color palette data backup area can only store color palette data tables (remember a color palette data table consists of 36 separate color palette definitions).
requirements.reason: The shared backup service implements the base area, ten shared slot/stack positions, protection, consume/retain rules and independent family ownership. COPY and aggregate tests cover full capacity, transfers between locations and restore semantics.

requirements.heading: Data Backup Areas
requirements.text: A data save slot is a backup area that is large enough to store an entire specific data table, or other object (graphics screen, mouse fields, etc). Each data backup area's save slots can hold one entire data table of the type designated for the data backup area. Each data save slot has a specific slot number associated with it (0-9). When the data in a data save slot is restored back to the actual RIPscrip drawing environment, that slot is deleted (cleared), providing that it isn't protected (see below).
requirements.reason: The shared backup service implements the base area, ten shared slot/stack positions, protection, consume/retain rules and independent family ownership. COPY and aggregate tests cover full capacity, transfers between locations and restore semantics.

requirements.heading: Data Backup Areas
requirements.text: A base save area is very similar to a data save slot, except that a base save area does not have a specific "slot number" associated with it. Unlike data save slots, when you restore a data table object from a base save area, the base save area is not cleared (ie, deleted) so it can be restored multiple times without losing the saved data (the base save area cannot be protected like data save slots can be - see below for more details).
requirements.reason: The shared backup service implements the base area, ten shared slot/stack positions, protection, consume/retain rules and independent family ownership. COPY and aggregate tests cover full capacity, transfers between locations and restore semantics.

requirements.heading: Data Backup Areas
requirements.text: Finally, we have stack save areas. Stack save areas are like a stack of plates - you put plates on top of the stack, and when you want one, you take one off the top of the stack. The plate at the bottom of the stack was the first plate placed on it, and to get to it, you need to take off each of the plates above it. When you place a data table onto a save stack, it is like placing a plate on top of our stack of plates. This is extremely useful (in fact, critical) to creating dialog boxes that overlap menus, and when you close the dialog box, you restore the menu's environment. The act of placing a data table onto a data save stack is called "pushing" a table onto the stack. The act of removing a table from the top of the stack is called "popping" a table from the stack. In order to remember where the "top" of the stack is (ie, how many layers are on the stack), a thing called a "stack pointer" is maintained internally which is simply a count of the number of items on the stack. Each time you add a new data table onto the stack, the pointer is increased by one (we have one more item on the stack).
requirements.reason: The shared backup service implements the base area, ten shared slot/stack positions, protection, consume/retain rules and independent family ownership. COPY and aggregate tests cover full capacity, transfers between locations and restore semantics.

requirements.text: Notice how there are ten different data save slots, and ten different data save stack "locations". What this means is that individually, either one of these may hold ten complete data tables. But combined, they cannot both contain more than 10 complete data tables. requirements.text: Our stack system is now full. We have four items on our stack and six in our data save slots. If we tried to push another data table onto our stack, the operation would be ignored (an error because our slot/stack system is full - the 3.0 driver's "No slots available for PUSH"). If we tried to store a data table to data save slot #2 (which is currently open), it would also be ignored because the slot/stack system is full. If however, we tried to save a data table onto data save slot #3 (which is occupied), the operation would be performed providing that data save slot #3 is not protected (see below).

requirements.heading: Data Backup Areas
requirements.text: A stack restore (also known as a "pop") is a method of restoring a data object from the data save stack into a data table. When you perform a stack pop, the data table at the top of the stack (the entry just below the stack pointer) is removed from the stack and placed in the appropriate data table (which one is based on the type of data that is stored in the data backup area). Once the restore operation is complete, the entry in that location of the stack is deleted (cleared), and the stack pointer is decremented by one, thus making room for one more entry in the data save slot/stack system to hold a new data table. (Popping an empty stack is an error - the 3.0 driver's "No stack to pop".)

requirements.heading: Data Backup Areas
requirements.text: All totalled, a data backup area can store eleven separate data tables, and each data table in a data backup area is of the same type of information (eg, text window, color palette, etc). If a data table has 36 separate data table entries in it, then a data backup area for that data table would hold 396 separate data table entries in it! This makes for a lot of backup storage. You cannot individually access sub-elements of a data table inside of a data backup area - you can only save/restore "entire" data tables at any one moment.

requirements.heading: Data Backup Areas
requirements.text: Push and pop operations are vital to the concept of multiple overlapping windows and dialog boxes in RIPscrip. When you close a window, you need to restore the background graphics, mouse regions, text windows and any other data tables that were in use at the time the dialog/window was created. What if that restored background is itself a window that is on top of some background menu? That window would also have tables pushed (the background environment). When that window closes, it will pop the information and restore the background environment's configuration.

requirements.heading: The Fourteen Copy Paths
requirements.text:

requirements.heading: Protection and Restoration
requirements.text: The way that a stack operates has been clearly outlined in the previous section. When you store a data table onto the stack, it grows by one table. When you pop a data table off of the stack, you reduce the contents of the stack by one data table (ie, that data table is deleted from the stack).
requirements.reason: The shared backup service implements the base area, ten shared slot/stack positions, protection, consume/retain rules and independent family ownership. COPY and aggregate tests cover full capacity, transfers between locations and restore semantics.

requirements.heading: Protection and Restoration
requirements.text: The base save area has already been described as a temporary storage location. A data table in the base save area remains in the base save area until it is either explicitly deleted, or until a hard reset of the RIPscrip environment is performed. In this manner, the base save area can be used as a source of data table copy operations many times and still read the same data table.
requirements.reason: The shared backup service implements the base area, ten shared slot/stack positions, protection, consume/retain rules and independent family ownership. COPY and aggregate tests cover full capacity, transfers between locations and restore semantics.

requirements.heading: Protection and Restoration
requirements.text: When you restore a data table from a data save slot back into the actual data table on the other hand, that data save slot is deleted (cleared) unless it is protected from deletion. In other words, just like individual data table entries, you can individually protect data save slots from deletion or overwriting. Only a data save slot that is actually "in use" can be protected - it is pointless to protect a data save slot that isn't holding a data table because what would you do with it? You couldn't store anything in it and you couldn't read anything from it, so this situation is not allowed.
requirements.reason: The shared backup service implements the base area, ten shared slot/stack positions, protection, consume/retain rules and independent family ownership. COPY and aggregate tests cover full capacity, transfers between locations and restore semantics.

requirements.text: It should be noted that when a data table is stored in the data backup area, any of the entries in that data table "retain" their protection status! requirements.heading: Protection and Restoration
requirements.text: You cannot protect an entire data table. This means that if you have entries in a data table that are protected and you perform a restore operation from a backup area, this will override any individual entries in the data table with those stored in the actual data table in the backup area. This is the only way that a data table entry's protection status can be bypassed.

requirements.heading: Graphical Style Table Save Area
requirements.text: **RIPtel 3.1 scope and restore defect:** STYLE saves only the current style index and all 36 style records; it contains no port cursor/image state or environment color-mode/mouse state. Its restore reads the saved index into the current style's foreground word, then immediately overwrites that word when restoring the table. The pre-restore current style index therefore survives and is reactivated. For example, saving while style 5 is current and restoring while style 7 is current restores all records but leaves style **7** current. _Evidence: DLL; [original save/restore and native case](../research/issue-24-drawing-state-ownership.md#backups)._

requirements.text: **RIPtel 3.1 cursor exception:** PORT owns and saves the image rectangle/flags, separately from STYLE; restore reinstates those image fields without touching style/environment records. requirements.heading: Grouped Mouse Snapshots and Template Publication
requirements.text: Take one consistent logical snapshot at the actual SMF capture point before serializing/backing it; later live changes cannot change that saved state. Capture only state already committed/reached at that point. An initially selected field whose opaque source has never activated still has no A entries. A host definition block not yet reached by a suspended continuation is not saved as an association. Each retained A[N] keeps its existing individual 4096-byte cap; the snapshot does **not** replace separate bodies with the capped group aggregate. A 3000-byte body followed by a 2000-byte body therefore remains 3000/2000 in the snapshot even when their effective concatenation is only 4096 bytes. Copy/save does not evaluate those bytes or alter live selection/publications.
requirements.reason: PR137 logical capture/current-publication contract accepted through native failure/deep-ownership oracles and connected literal vectors. Grouped SMF/RMF and whole-MOUSE COPY are live; no provider/paint/cache resurrection. Aggregate orchestration is assessed separately.

requirements.heading: Grouped Mouse Snapshots and Template Publication
requirements.text: On applying a mouse restore, restore the saved definitions, order, selected state, A maps and handlers with fresh stable tokens. Start all fields outside hover and with no captured press or [Tab focus](4.2-mouse-fields-and-pointer.md#focus-lifetime). This is definition restoration, not button creation/activation: no filename/label/host expansion, required-radio notification, repaint, hot-image loading or auto-stamp is performed. Existing pixels can disagree with restored logical selection until a separate actual redraw. Subsequent feedback/redraw uses the restored persistent state and captured configuration under its normal rendering rules, without reusing a saved held-gesture cache. Restoring the SCREEN family later in RESTOREALL can separately restore pixels; MOUSE itself does not.
requirements.reason: Mouse restore cancels capture and recreates field identities, order and saved handlers. The aggregate restore uses the same mouse binding and continues after independent family failures.

requirements.text: Ordinary [`SAVE`](5.1-text-variables.md#save)/[`RESTORE`](5.1-text-variables.md#restore), including numbered aliases, address only the **screen backup family**. Its capture/restore set is:

Restore copies the unscaled physical overlap without resizing/replacing port identity, overwrites current PAL RGB even if protected/undefined, and leaves all selectors/flags/styles/TW/mouse/status metadata live. BASE is reusable, slots/protection/stack/COPY use owned manager snapshots; numeric RESTORE requests deletion even after failure while POP is success-dependent. Valid failed actions return no value or variable error and report only the private lower-level diagnostic; syntax preflight remains distinct. RESET(SCREEN) clears physical index 0; explicit backup selectors retain protected saves. Native and TCP vectors cover 5-to-17 palette binding, empty/undefined palette flags, no extra state, split bytes, failed capture/presentation, malformed aliases, both planes, circular native scroll/cursor retention, and nonfatal continuation. requirements.heading: Screen Save Area
requirements.text: A portable SCREEN snapshot uses the underlying RIP canvas if a terminal status indicator is composited over it. The screen operation ignores the selected port's viewport and protection when choosing its **capture/restore target**: that target is port zero's screen DC. It does not restore port zero's viewport, the saved current port's viewport, all viewports, or an independent viewport setting. If port 1 was current at save and port 35 is current at restore, 35 remains current. Deleting, redefining or protecting port 1 between those operations does not change that result. Restore does not resize the canvas. The original calls are specified here; native fixtures use an unclipped indexed GDI model and do not establish exact Windows clipping/raster behavior.
requirements.reason: Connected status setting, display composition and underlying canvas behavior under PR #202.

requirements.heading: Palette binding example
requirements.text: Suppose palette **5** is current at SAVE, its index 15 is red, and the screen contains pixels of index 15. Before RESTORE select palette **17**, make its index 15 green, and protect entry 17. RESTORE writes 5's saved RGB values into **17**, leaves 17 current/protected, and presents the saved pixels using that restored mapping. It neither selects palette 5 nor restores the whole palette table. Its direct RGB overwrite does not change the target's defined/protected flags. In the original private stream the palette occurs twice—an outer RGB block and the bitmap codec's included palette—and both copies target the same live palette entry, causing two uploads. Private in-memory storage need not duplicate an identical palette to reproduce the resulting state.

requirements.heading: Aliases, protection and lifetime
requirements.text: Numbered aliases accept **no arguments**; all SAVE0..9 and RESTORE0..9 are registered in RIPtel 3.1. Parameter keywords are case-insensitive. Snapshot protection is separate from protection of a live palette or port. **Numeric restore requests deletion even if restoration fails**, so an unprotected snapshot can be consumed after a failed read; POP instead requires successful restoration before removing the stack entry. These action callbacks do not propagate the manager's success/failure as a value or variable error; invalid arguments do set the variable-error flag. Lower-level error reporting remains separate.

requirements.heading: Aliases, protection and lifetime
requirements.text: RIPtel 3.1 uses generated files in the configured engine directory, named **`%03hu%05hu.$$$`** from instance number and an incrementing counter, not RIPTERM.SAV or RIPTERM0.SAV..RIPTERM9.SAV. It closes but retains a reusable snapshot's file, unlinks on overwrite/consumption/deletion, and clears backups during normal manager teardown. These are client-owned backing files, not filenames named by the host command. A memory-backed implementation can preserve the same state/lifetime semantics without creating either the inherited RIPTERM*.SAV names or the driver's private generated files.

requirements.heading: SAVEALL / RESTOREALL composition
requirements.text: These wrappers operate on eight independent backup families in the following **actual order**, for BASE, numbered and PUSH/POP forms:
requirements.reason: SGS/RGS and SENV/RENV are connected to their existing typed snapshot families. SAVEALL/RESTOREALL dispatch TW, PORT, MOUSE, SCREEN, PAL, BUT, STYLE, ENV in exact order, continue after every failure without rollback and keep valid actions empty/nonfatal. Numbered restores retain all snapshots until a separate ordered delete phase, including failed unprotected snapshots; BASE stays reusable and POP consumes each successful family independently. Native event/ownership/failure tests and both TCP encodings cover executable behavior and independent expected colors, metadata and input. This accepts this syntax/lifetime/composition clause, not every subrequirement of each payload family; full PORT_COPY/PCB and remaining STYLE inventory stay separately pending.

requirements.heading: SAVEALL / RESTOREALL composition
requirements.text: The **PORT** component supplies the saved current port and viewport definitions of saved defined ports, unlike screen-only SAVE. Saved definitions replace even protected live targets; a deleted saved port is redefined. Initial PORT cleanup skips protected live ports, however, and an undefined saved slot does not overwrite them, so a protected live port absent from the snapshot can survive. The [PORT cursor exception](#drawing-port-table-save-area) and [STYLE current-index defect](#graphical-style-table-save-area) still apply to RESTOREALL. Status-bar state is not added by any of these families: its owner is separate engine/host state. Thus “all” means this exact eight-family composition, not every client/UI setting.

requirements.heading: 9.0 Command Reference
requirements.text: TeleGrafix never published a 3.x language reference, so this inventory is an editorial reconstruction assembled from the 2.00 ALPHA 4 specification, the RIPSCRIP.HLP command-name inventory (~90 `RIP_*` names recovered from the RIPtel 3.1 help files and DLL string tables), the 116-script RIPtel demo corpus, and SyncTERM's open-source RIP 3.0 implementation - the **Added/Status** column carries both lineage and evidence status per the legend below.

requirements.heading: 9.0 Command Reference
requirements.text:
- blank - carried from 1.54 or earlier into the 2.0 engine that 3.x inherits.
- `v1.54`, `v2.A0`-`v2.A4` - spec revision that introduced the command (2.00 ALPHA draft revisions; 3.x inherits the 2.0 engine).
- `3.0 (corpus)` - 3.x-era command recovered from the RIPtel demo-script census; documented in no published specification.
- `3.0 (HLP; corpus)` - 3.x-era command attested by the RIPSCRIP.HLP name inventory and the corpus, absent from the 2.00a4 draft.
- `DLL` - grammar and behavior traced in RIPtel 3.1’s RIPscrip 3.0.7 driver, with derivation/probe links in the full entry.
- `outside DLL contract` - a SyncTERM descriptor with no entry in the original driver’s complete dispatch table; explicitly excluded from this driver’s executable contract below.
- `deprecated v2.A2` - deprecated in that revision; still implemented by every shipping driver, so authors should avoid it and implementers still have to handle it. The linked page explains why.
- `obsolete v2.A1` - declared obsolete in that revision but still parsed by clients.
- (\*), (†), (‡), (¶) - footnotes for special cases, listed [at the end of the page](#footnotes).

requirements.heading: Unidentified & reserved opcodes
requirements.text: These four descriptors are **outside RIPtel 3.1’s executable RIPscrip 3.0.7 command contract**. The complete original dispatch table contains none of them, and the original byte parser emits no command callback for their test records. This is positive dispatch evidence, not a conclusion from corpus silence. Do not require or infer their fields from SyncTERM’s descriptor shapes. _Evidence: DLL; [complete dispatch audit and parser probes](../research/issue-5-scene-headers.md)._

requirements.heading: Footnotes
requirements.text:
- (\*) The 2.00a4 draft assigns letter `b` to **both** RIP_SET_BASE_MATH and RIP_EXTENDED_TEXT_WINDOW - an unresolved collision in the draft. The shipping 3.0 driver moved base math to **`J`** (90 of 116 corpus files open with `!|J10|n2000|M08|fZKQO`, and ONLINE.RIP annotates `J10` inline as "Set base math to MegaNums"), leaving `b` to the extended text window, exactly as SyncTERM's descriptor table also has it. _Evidence: corpus; SyncTERM._
- (†) The command name is an editorial hypothesis reconstructed from census evidence (demo comments, on-screen titles, or layout analysis); TeleGrafix's own name is unrecovered. The six skewed-oval names, by contrast, come verbatim from TeleGrafix's NEWCMDS.RIP comments and are not so marked; RIP_POLY_POLYGON's name, initially inferred from its demo title, is now confirmed by the [original driver's error literal](../research/issue-13-polygon-counts.md).
- (‡) The RIPSCRIP.HLP inventory lists the 3.0 name `RIP_BeginEncodedStream`. The shipped handler accepts types 0 and 1 as no-ops and reports an error for larger values.
- (¶) [RIP_EXTENDED_FONT_STYLE](3.0-text-output-and-fonts.md#the-shipped-3x-wire-layout) uses eleven UltraNum fields before the typeface name. The full-width form uses 26 digits. A leading period can supply any one field as zero. The shipped field sequence supersedes the draft’s 13-character layout. The [DLL derivation](../research/issue-3-extended-font-style.md) resolves the crib’s field roles: `OO` is shadow distance, `BB` is baseline displacement, the second `CC` is spacing percentage, and `WW` is ignored. `s` and `f` are stored compatibility bytes unused by the renderer. The 26-character form predates 3.x; semantic claims here are verified for driver 3.0.7.

requirements.heading: Announced but never specified
requirements.text: **RIP_FILE_DELETE** appears in the 2.00a4 v2.A3 revision history ("to remove unneeded JPEG or WAVE files off the user's hard disk") but received no command entry, opcode or argument list, and no such command name appears in the RIPSCRIP.HLP inventory. The capability is implemented as a text variable instead: `RIPSCRIP.HLP` carries the handler symbol `tvarProcFILEDEL` (the `tvarProc` prefix marking a text-variable processor), and `FILEDEL` is present in the shipping RIPterm 2.0/2.20.01/2.30 executables. Hosts use [`$FILEDEL(file,…)$`](9.1-text-variable-reference.md); see [5.5](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md). _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._

requirements.heading: 9.1 Text Variable Reference
requirements.text: _Reconstructed edition - every claim carries an evidence tag; see [Contents](README.md) for the legend._

requirements.heading: 9.1 Text Variable Reference
requirements.text: Every pre-defined [text variable](../../glossary.md) known for RIPscrip 3.x, with its parameter form, type, effect, and evidence status, linked to its full entry. **Value** variables return text to the host; **Active** variables perform an action on the terminal (some also return data when used to query). Parameters shown in parentheses are optional unless the full entry says otherwise; parameterized forms offer the selectors specified by each full entry and are preferred for new content. Fixed-name availability is defined per variable: RIPtel 3.1 retains all zero-argument `$SAVE0$`…`$SAVE9$` and `$RESTORE0$`…`$RESTORE9$` aliases of `SAVE(n)` / `RESTORE(n)`, including `RESTORE0`. The 3.x inventory combines the original driver’s 179 registrations with the RIPtel help files (roughly 60 data-returning and 60 command-performing variables), the demo corpus (269 distinct `$…$` forms in shipping scripts), and SyncTERM's 103-entry built-in table.
requirements.reason: Table heading, example setup or source attribution. The entries that follow carry the observable requirements.

requirements.heading: 9.1 Text Variable Reference
requirements.text: The Type column describes a callback's possible effect, **not consumer permission**. Use the [complete graphical eligibility sets](5.2-templates-and-conditionals.md#eligible-providers-and-rejected-codes) for filename/label/T/@/metric: mixed CUR/HOSTDIR/COORDSIZE/OVERFLOW callbacks are callable, while WORLD is active-only there even for its query form. Disabled/rejected ordinary codes remain literal without user fallback.
requirements.reason: Graphical consumers apply eligibility during expression processing, before invoking a built-in.

requirements.heading: 9.1 Text Variable Reference
requirements.text: _User-defined variables - any `$IDENTIFIER$` with the `*`/`+`/`%`/`#`/`-`/`&` directives, positioning, questions, defaults and format options - are covered in [5.1 Text Variables](5.1-text-variables.md#text-variable-creation-and-query); variables removed or renamed since 1.54 are listed in [5.1's rename note](5.1-text-variables.md)._

requirements.heading: 9.1 Text Variable Reference
requirements.text: The **Evidence** column uses the legend tags in compact form: `2.00a4` (documented in the published ALPHA 4 specification, which 3.x inherits), `WP` (3.0 white paper), `HLP` (RIPtel help / DLL string tables), `DLL` (original RIPtel 3.1 driver instructions and controlled native probes), `corpus` (RIPtel demo scripts), `ST` (SyncTERM implementation), _(hyp)_ (editorial inference). File names, `ripper.c` line numbers and divergence notes live on the full entries. A variable tagged only `2.00a4` is listed as inherited - documented for the engine 3.x inherits, with no independent 3.x-era attestation.

requirements.heading: Save/Restore & Backup Areas
requirements.text: All save/restore families share the same source/destination forms: `BASE` (default), slot `0`-`9`, and `PUSH`/`POP` stack operations - see [7.2 Data Backup Areas](7.2-data-backup-areas.md). The slot/stack machinery is confirmed for 3.x by the DLL's backup-system error strings ("No slots available for PUSH" / "No stack to pop").

requirements.heading: Save/Restore & Backup Areas
requirements.text: Screen-only SAVE/RESTORE and the eight-family aggregate operations have distinct capture sets. The summaries below follow the accepted [screen/aggregate contract](7.2-data-backup-areas.md#screen-save-area) and [#26 derivation](../research/issue-26-screen-backups.md): aggregate order is **TW → PORT → MOUSE → SCREEN → PAL → BUT → STYLE → ENV**, with independent family failures/consumption and no rollback. The screen step itself adds no viewport/style/table snapshot; status-bar visibility is not included by any family. MOUSE includes the explicitly completed [persistent selection/owner-map/handler and publication rules](7.2-data-backup-areas.md#grouped-mouse-snapshots-and-template-publication), with no button-pixel or held-gesture restoration.
requirements.reason: The table host binds save, restore, copy, protection and queries to the appropriate live family and backup area. Aggregate, PORT and STYLE fixtures verify restoration through their consumers.

requirements.heading: Save/Restore & Backup Areas
requirements.text: **Historical implementation note:** the previous index's SyncTERM `RESTORE0` omission annotation describes the inspected legacy implementation, not a RIPscrip 3.0 restriction or RIPtel 3.1's alias registry. All twenty numbered screen aliases remain available under the full [SAVE aliases](5.1-text-variables.md#savex) / [RESTORE aliases](5.1-text-variables.md#restorex) entries. [Editorial reconciliation and evidence scope](../research/issue-138-backup-index-summaries.md).

requirements.heading: Identification phrase
requirements.text: The inherited format is **`RIPSCRIPxxyyvs`**, totaling 14 ASCII bytes: `xx` is the two-digit language major version, `yy` the two-digit minor version, `v` a vendor code and `s` that vendor’s subversion digit. Vendor 0 is generic/unspecified, 1 RIPterm/TeleGrafix, 2 Qmodem Pro. These last two digits are not a two-digit language revision. [1.54 identity history](../../1.54/ripscrip/9.2-versions.md) and the [2.0 record](../../2.0/ripscrip/9.2-versions.md) preserve the earlier evidence.

requirements.heading: Engine replies and terminators
requirements.text: Default/0 phrase bytes are **`52 49 50 53 43 52 49 50 30 33 30 30 30 31`**. Selector 3 appends **`0d`**. No NUL is sent: the C-string storage terminator is not a wire byte. RIPVER accepts no arguments and adds no CR/LF; a surrounding host command can supply its own control characters. The original client may translate a supplied CR to CRLF according to its output setting, as recorded in the [reply-path trace](../research/issue-5-scene-headers.md#entry-point-effect-probes-and-client-reply-trace); default/0 have no CR to translate.
requirements.reason: The live ANSI path implements selectors 0 through 3, the first-parameter and 16-bit rules, and enabled/disabled reply boundaries. Connected tests compare exact bytes and exercise split input and same-buffer resumption.

requirements.heading: Engine replies and terminators
requirements.text: The autosense callback uses the first ANSI parameter only, ignores later parameters and sends no reply for other selector values; private-prefix `?0!` is a different ANSI dispatch. The ordinary ANSI decimal accumulator wraps to 16 bits. Enable/disable changes the emulation flag without resetting buffered parser state; [checked stream examples](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#esc-priority-and-resumption) distinguish this from a scene reset.
requirements.reason: The live ANSI path implements selectors 0 through 3, the first-parameter and 16-bit rules, and enabled/disabled reply boundaries. Connected tests compare exact bytes and exercise split input and same-buffer resumption.

It need not claim TeleGrafix vendor code 1 or copy a product name. This is an explicit interoperability policy using the inherited generic-vendor allocation, not a newly discovered historical response or a distinct RIPscrip language version.

requirements.heading: RIPscrip 3.0 - Language Reference (reconstructed record)
requirements.text: **RIPscrip 3.0** - the third-generation Remote Imaging Protocol scripting language (TeleGrafix Communications, Inc., 1996-1997), as shipped in **RIPtel Visual Telnet 3.1** (RIPscrip driver 3.0.7), the only client that ever shipped it. Chapter numbers align with the [2.0 reference](../../2.0/ripscrip/README.md) the generation evolved from, with the 3.x-era changes flattened into their proper sections and sections unique to this generation marked; the official [3.0 Technical White Paper](../text/RIPScrip-3.x-technical-whitepaper.txt) (December 1996, by Jeff Reeder - prose only, the sole TeleGrafix document for the generation) is preserved separately as a faithful conversion.

requirements.heading: Fill Defects (delta)
requirements.text:
- **Pie/chord source correction:** original I/i helpers invoke GDI Pie, _ invokes GDI Chord, and skewed filled variants submit Polygon contours. The [native derivation](../research/issue-14-arc-sweeps.md) contradicts this repository's earlier adoption of RIPlib `§BUG.6` as an observed arc-plus-radii flood construction. That attribution is withdrawn; it must not be generalized to earlier clients or new skewed commands merely from engine lineage.
- **Actual curve quirks:** original angle reduction, O/V separation, full-turn degeneracy and skewed pie center closure are now traced directly. The [angle reference](../ripscrip/2.2-curves.md#angle-ordering-and-sweeps) and [consumer contract](2.1-arc-consumer-contract.md) state those findings with API boundaries, separately from Windows rasterization.
- **RIP_FILL is an accepted no-op in RIPtel 3.1.** Physical slot 27 has zero arguments and a single RET at handler RVA `0x1b2fd`. The original image has neither ExtFloodFill nor FloodFill in its imports. This supersedes the attribution from RIPlib `§DEAD.7` for the fingerprinted PC Micro driver. [Source and framing derivation](../research/issue-279-rip-fill-framing.md).
- **Earlier-client scope:** 2.x behavior requires evidence from a 2.x binary. Shared resource magic and ancestry do not establish identical angle or fill defects.

requirements.text: **Protocol operation:** I/i radial contours have no fill area. N1 draws that outline using solid COPY and current thickness/Draw Color; N0 suppresses it. The historical unconditional LineTo call is not an N0 requirement. A nonempty I/i/_ region uses current W for fill and, with N1, a solid COPY outline afterward. This also governs a full Pie's internal radius. See the [composition contract](2.3-drawing-composition.md).

requirements.heading: Axis-aligned endpoint rays
requirements.text: For a geometric adapter, Arc/Pie/Chord use the intersections of the center-to-endpoint rays with the ellipse and advance counterclockwise. This is a **radial-bearing** construction; converting to ellipse parameter angles may be necessary for a renderer whose arc API uses parametric angles. Microsoft's [Arc](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/wingdi/nf-wingdi-arc), [Pie](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/wingdi/nf-wingdi-pie) and [Chord](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/wingdi/nf-wingdi-chord) contracts define that boundary. Their complete-ellipse cases do not override the driver's earlier identical-integer-endpoint branches. Consequently 0..360 and 450..810 do not reach a full-ellipse GDI call in A/V/I/i/_.

requirements.heading: Affine Ellipse Contours
requirements.text: These contours serve the [five affine ellipse commands](../ripscrip/2.2-curves.md#affine-ellipse-commands). Coordinates name the center C, conjugate radius endpoints A/B and, where supplied, ray endpoints S/E. Apply the X and Y WORLD-to-device ratios independently to every coordinate pair before deriving any vector. Truncate the projected coordinates to integers. These primitives use projected port-space positions directly and clip to the selected viewport. The viewport origin supplies no translation to these contours.

requirements.heading: Ring and Direction
requirements.text: If both projected A and B equal C, return the open one-point run `[C]`. Otherwise order the radius endpoints by integer polar angle. Given `(dx,dy) = endpoint - C`, use 90 for vertical up and 270 for vertical down or the zero vector. For nonzero dx compute `a = atan(-dy/dx) × 180/π` in degrees. Truncate a toward zero, then add 180 when dx is negative, or 360 when dx is positive and a is negative. If B has the smaller angle, swap A and B. A tie preserves input order.

requirements.heading: Ring and Direction
requirements.text: Compute `U = A - C` and `V = B - C` after ordering. Form the 72 points in increasing `t = 0,5,…,355` using the separate [Q14 cosine and sine arrays](data/skewed-ellipse-q14.json). For each axis component:

requirements.heading: Ring and Direction
requirements.text:
```text
P[t/5] = C + floor((U * cosQ14[t] + V * sinQ14[t]) / 16384)
```

requirements.heading: Ring and Direction
requirements.text: Sum the two products before taking the signed shift. A whole ellipse returns this 72-point path with closed topology, including the edge from P[71] to P[0]. No duplicate endpoint is required. With collinear radii or a single zero radius, use the same samples and later ray selection. The integer contour controls the resulting stroke and any enclosed area.

requirements.heading: Ring and Direction
requirements.text: Within the ordinary signed-device range the above formula is the shipped sample arithmetic. The DLL uses 32-bit products and sums, followed by an arithmetic shift and sign extension of the low 16 bits of each shifted offset and each center coordinate. Those width rules describe the original numeric path for callers reproducing large coordinates. The one-point early return copies the projected C directly.

requirements.heading: Partial Contours
requirements.text: For a projected ray endpoint equal to C, use the ordered A for the start ray or ordered B for the end ray. This substitution occurs after ordering. An interior point and an exterior point on the same forward ray both give its direction. For each ray, visit segments `P[i] → P[(i+1) mod 72]` in order starting at i=0.

requirements.heading: Partial Contours
requirements.text: Solve the intersection of the segment's line and the ray's line. Skip parallel lines, including collinear lines and zero-length segments. Truncate the intersection X and Y toward zero **before** checking inclusion. Keep the first integer point within the segment's inclusive X/Y bounds and on the ray's forward side in both axes. To implement that test, an increasing or zero ray component requires the corresponding hit coordinate to be at or above C's coordinate, and a decreasing component requires it to be at or below C's. There is no circular distance comparison or requirement that S/E themselves lie on the ring.

requirements.heading: Partial Contours
requirements.text: Let the selected hits be Hs and He, with segment indices i and j. Apply the original fallback rules in order:

requirements.heading: Partial Contours
requirements.text:
1. If the start ray misses, set Hs=P[0] and i=0.
2. If the end ray misses, set He=P[71] and set **i=71**, retaining Hs. Keep j absent.
3. If Hs equals He, return the full 72-point closed ring. This is also the result for different rays that quantize to identical hits.
4. Otherwise start the run at Hs. If j is present and i differs from j, append ring vertices from P[(i+1) mod 72] forward through P[j], with wrapping. If the two indices agree, append those vertices on a full wrap only when He precedes Hs in that segment's direction. Compare X on nonvertical segments and Y on vertical segments. If j is absent, append no ring vertices.
5. Append He. The arc returns this open run. Pie appends C and the first point and returns closed. Chord appends the first point and returns closed.

requirements.heading: Partial Contours
requirements.text: Keep repeated points in the run. A one-point result has no polygon or line segment. A two-point result remains a segment, and a closed contour with no enclosed samples has an empty interior. The [portable presentation rules](2.3-drawing-composition.md#affine-ellipse-composition) handle the selected stroke or fill.

requirements.text:
```text
q[j] = wrap32(P[j] << 8), j=0..3
for level = 3,2,1:

        product = wrap32(difference * i)
        q[j] = wrap32(q[j] + trunc0(product / N))
output = signed16(floor(q[0] / 256))
```

Bounds are accumulated from generated outputs, rather than the ideal curve's extrema.

requirements.text: The poly consumer rejects zero N if any cubic is present. requirements.text: For C cubic records and L point records, the common poly consumer checks `C*N + L + 1 <= 4095`. If exceeded, it sets **N=floor((4094-L)/C)** for every cubic, rejecting if this becomes zero. The original 80,000-byte workspace allocation does not define this usable limit.

requirements.heading: Drawing color operands on mixed surfaces
requirements.text: Apply the drawing operation to each covered pixel after the normal geometry and clipping. Use the selected contribution's Draw, Fill or Back Color as S. A drawing color decoded in palette mode supplies a RIP drawing index. A direct color supplies the RGB value produced by normal color decoding. Changing the active ENV's color mode affects subsequent decoding. It leaves existing destination pixels in their stored color domain. [Drawing palette and color decoding](../ripscrip/2.0-color-modes-and-palettes.md#palette-mapping-and-direct-rgb-mode) · [Coverage, source selection and equations](../../2.0/techspecs/2.3-drawing-composition.md#operations-and-operands).
